REVIEW OF ACHIEVEMENTS AND PERFORMANCE FOR THE YEAR
King's College
The School provides a very high standard of education and this is validated in review of the academic
results, the measurements of added value and through external inspection. The School offers a broad
curriculum and educates children with a wide range of ability. It demonstrates particular excellence in
Design Technology, Science, Music, Art, Mathematics, Modern Languages and English and is a
strong force on the sporting front, especially in Rugby, Cricket, Hockey giris' Football and Netball.
King's College has an outstanding choir and orchestra and its drama programme is full, varied and of
a high standard.
The School aims to support children in reaching their potential in all areas of their activity at the
School. This may be in academic subjects but could just as easily be reflected in success in art,
drama, sport, music, dance, CCF, Duke of Edinburgh or community links. The School produces well-
rounded individuals who are able to make a positive contribution to society.
Academic Performance
The School once again enjoyed strong exam results at A level. At A level, 82% of exams entered
attracted an A* to C grade. Thomas Prayer gained five A* grades - a new King's record. In
Economics 33% of pupils gained A* grades, and 83% A* to B grades. The Chemistry department
continued their history of success with 52% of pupils gaining A* or A grades whilst the Mathematics
department achieved superb results, with 50% of candidates achieving A* or A. All candidates taking
Further Maths and Latin achieved A* or A.
At GCSE, particularly strong departments included Music (67% A*/A), Art, (56%), Design Technology
(58%), Geography (63%) and Latin (67%).
Sport
The senior giris' football team won the ISFA National championships. The U18 and U16 7-a-side
teams won their respective national ISFA championships.
Neil Brand was the first King's cricketer to score 1,000 runs in a season. Our XI cricket team once
again went for a whole season without losing a regular school fixture. The U14 cricketers were
unbeaten and were the county champions. The girls 2nd VI tennis team were unbeaten this season.
Our U18 and U15 giris' tennis pairs both won their respective plate events at the ISTA tournament at
Eton.
The number of pupils representing their county, region or country at sport continued to rise.
Drama, Art and Music
The main school production was the popular musical Guys and Dolls, performed to wide acclaim. The
junior play was a "play in a day" performance, in which the cast devised and performed a play about
the First World War in 24 hours.
In academic drama, the A level group devised and staged a powerful and challenging play, White
Noise, and gained exceptional marks from the examiner. The AS level group gave an excellent
performances of Whale Music, by Anthony Minghella and The Memory of Water, by Shelagh
Stephenson which, again, earned them top marks. The GCSE Drama pupils performed scenes from
Much Ado About Nothing for their exam piece.
The choir continued to lead the weekly Eucharist service. Once again we staged a large number and
variety of concerts, from formal classical music in the Chapel to informal Octagon concerts and two
well-attended rock and pop concerts in the theatre. The jazz band once again flew the King's flag at a
number of venues, including prep schools and summer events around Taunton.
9
KING'S SCHOOLS TAUNTON LIMITED
DIRECTORS' REPORT (incorporating the STRATEGIC REPORT)
YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2014
The School once again hosted several visiting artists and was a display venue for the annual
Somerset Arts Weeks programme.
Community Activity
The King's weekly outreach programme continued to flourish, with pupils working in local hospitals,
care homes, charity shops and primary schools. A group of pupils helped to coach athletics in local
primary schools and King's was the venue for several local primary school cross-country events.
The Classics Department continued with its very successful and popular programme of Latin teaching
for gifted and talented pupils from Bishop Fox, a local maintained secondary school. Other facilities
used by local schools and clubs include the Chapel, the swimming pool, the hockey pitches, the
Convent Gym, rugby, cricket and football pitches, the Music School and the sports hall. The School
boarding houses and cricket pitches were used for six weeks over the summer for a national cricket
festival, involving boys and girls of all ages.
King's College continues to offer the Somerset Scholarship for pupils from the maintained sector in
Somerset who wish to join the sixth and the third forms. This scholarship has now been running for
seven years and has allowed a good number of pupils to enjoy the benefits of a King's education who
would otherwise not have been able to do SO.
CCF and Outward Bound Activities
The CCF continues to flourish at King's. The Marines section won the prestigious Sir Steuart Pringle
Trophy, the fourth win in five years. The CCF continues to arrange and attend camps for all three
sections throughout the year and attendance at these is excellent. Two teams completed the Ten
Tors Challenge (35 and 55 mile distances) and participation in the Duke of Edinburgh Bronze and
Gold Awards remains strong.
Over the summer a group of 12 pupils climbed Mount Kilimanjaro, accompanied by three members of
staff. Also over the summer, a group of eight sixth form boys cycled from London to Monaco to raise
funds for a forces support charity, SSAFA.
Developments
A new tennis and netball facility was built, providing six tennis and five netball courts. This facility
finally brings all of our giris sport to the centre of the school. New cricket nets were built as part of the
same project.
Thanks to a generous donation from an ex-pupil we were able to build a new 300-seater
amphitheatre, which was opened in May by Professor Alan Outram, Head of Archaeology at Exeter
University.
Over the summer a great deal of refurbishment work was carried out in two boys' boarding houses.
King's Hall School
King's Hall School provides a very high standard of education and this is validated by review of the
academic results and other achievements and through external inspection. In May 2014 the school
underwent a Full Integrated Inspection conducted by ISI and were delighted with the universally
positive outcomes. The School offers a broad curriculum and educates children with a wide range of
ability. It has an exceptional 'Forest School' on site utilised by Year 5 and below which makes full use
of the School's stunning rural position and proves very popular with children and staff alike.
'Woodland Adventures' and a variety of Courses run during the school holidays as part of the wrap-
around care provision. As well as achieving high academic attainment the School is a strong force on
the sporting front, especially in rugby, cricket, hockey, netball, tennis and athletics. The School has
impressive musical performers; its drama programme is full, varied and of a high standard.
The School aims to support children in reaching their potential in all areas of their activity at the
School. This may be in academic subjects but could just as easily be reflected in success in art,
drama, sport, music or design technology: Year 8 leavers gained nearly 200 awards to senior schools
in these six disciplines over the last six years. The School produces well-rounded individuals who are
10

YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2014
able to make a positive contribution to society. An effective democratically elected Pupil Council
operates successfully from Year 3 upwards There are constant charitable events taking place, with
the main focus this year being towards Educaid.
Academic Performance
Year 8 leavers gained sixteen academic scholarships to senior schools including the top scholars to
two schools. There was a 100% pass rate for all pupils who sat the Common Entrance examinations:
two subjects with over 90% A to C grades and a further five subjects achieving 80% or more A to
C
grades. Year 6 children gained five academic scholarships to continue to King's College after Year 8.
Sport
King's Hall School continues to compete at a very high level, especially in rugby, hockey, cricket,
athletics, tennis and netball. The 1st XV in particular and Colts rugby teams had very strong seasons
and the 1st VII competed regionally, winning the Sherborne Sevens Tournament and being Runners-
Up in the Bryanston Tournament, as well as at the Rosslyn Park National Sevens. The Under 9 boys
team won a tournament at Blundell's. The boys' and girls' hockey teams won the vast majority of their
matches with the U12 giris Hockey team taking part in the finals of the IAPS National Hockey
Tournament and winning Bronze Medals. The girls' Under 13 Hockey team were County Champions
and the 1st XI boys only lost once. The 1st XI cricket team was unbeaten, for the sixth season in a
row, with six boys selected to play for Somerset at their age group. During the year the School was
either county champions or runners up at U13, U12 and U11 levels.
Our giris' U13 tennis team performed exceptionally well in the AEGON league with both boys and girls
playing for their County and one boy is the U14 County Tennis Champion. Our girls and boys
compete in the County Cross Country championships with two girls representing the South West. Our
athletics team came third in the South West Schools Cup and children again competed at the South
West Regional Athletics Championships from which some qualified for the National Athletics Finals. A
large number of children competed in the Exmoor Challenge whilst our riding team won several Show
Jumping Classes during the year as well as in one-day events.
Sixteen children gained sports scholarships to their senior schools including both a boys' and a giris'
top sports scholarship and two won awards in Year 6 to continue on to King's College.
Art, DT, Music and Drama
An impressive and diverse Art and DT exhibition at the end of the year displayed the various creative
talents in the School. We had many children benefit from the visits of established artists to the School
whilst the Specialist Art group visited sculpture gardens, galleries and museums to extend their
knowledge and understanding. Mosaic workshops and the creation of a willow herd of deer were
highlights. The music department put on a high quality concert each term at school as well as being
an integral part of a spectacular concert at Exeter Cathedral and a smaller but no less high quality
event at Orchard Portman. Frequent informal concerts allow budding talent to develop their
performance skills in an unthreatening arena. The ever-popular House Music Competition saw very
strong individual performances and the House songs were inspired by traditional spirituals. There
was huge successes in the Taunton Music Festival with twelve first places.
Drama productions were plentiful with the Michaelmas Term seeing Year 6 give a spectacular
performance of 'Flipside' and two nativity productions from Pre-Prep. In November Year 8 produced a
sumptuous presentation of 'The Lion, The Witch and The Wardrobe' with extremely high quality
performances, sound, lighting, set, make-up and costumes. Pre-Prep's lavish summer show 'Humpty
Dumpty - was he pushed or did he fall?' drew the year to a close. Years 3 and 4 each performed
smaller scale plays in the Summer Term. The Speech and Drama activity continues to thrive with
many children taking part in the Taunton Drama Festival and a high proportion receive distinctions
and win their classes.
Two art, three music, two Design Technology and four drama scholarships were gained by Year 8
children to senior schools and three Year 6 music scholarships were won.

Significant projects
A listed outbuilding has been completely refurbished to provide outstanding accommodation to allow
the school to expand and now take children from the age of 2 (previously 3). A further seven
classrooms have been completely refurbished (making 11 in the last twelve months). Bathrooms in
the boarding house have also been refurbished. We continue to improve external areas as wel as
invest in the look and feel of the whole school site. The Development Plans for the 2020 Vision have
had one aspect completed and plans for the next two stages are well in hand.
FINANCIAL REVIEW AND RESULTS FOR THE YEAR
The net incoming resources for the year amounted to E253,071. Gross income for the year was up by
some 2% on last year. The trading company continues to hire out the Schools' facilities during
holidays and school hours, as well as undertaking commercial activity on behalf of the Schools and
externally. The Company contributed f147,000 to the Schools' operating results. Group tota funds
increased by f303,531 for the year.
The parents of pupils often make significant sacrifices to pay the fees. In doing so they help to relieve
UK taxpayers of the financial burden of educating a significant number of UK based children. The
saving made by the Schools is estimated to have a value in the last year of E3.8 million.
The Company is unable to recover the VAT on purchases it makes. During the past year, King's
Schools Taunton Limited has paid an estimated f644,055 in VAT on goods and services.
RESERVES POLICY
It has been the Council's policy to utilise funds to ensure that high quality up-to-date facilities are
provided for the benefit of pupils. The aim is to budget so as to provide sufficient working capital to
meet the present needs and future development requirements of the Schools without the requirement
to have recourse to sales of tangible fixed assets, except where those are no longer required for the
primary purpose of the Schools.
At the present stage in the development cycle the free reserves are being utilised in order to finance
on-going improvements and the provision of additiona facilities in accordance with the Schools'
strategic plan. The Schools continue to invest in their infrastructure, both with new capital projects and
to deliver significant repairs and improvements to existing facilities.
Impairment reviews have been undertaken in line with accounting practice requirements and, in the
Directors' view, properties are not impaired below their recorded cost in the accounts. Investments
(other than endowment assets) are held to create income and capital growth pending utilisation.
The Council continues to keep the Schools' banking facilities under review to ensure they remain
appropriate to support the Schools' working capital requirements. The restricted reserve is invested
both in cash and a balanced range of quoted investments. The unrestricted reserves are primarily
invested in tangible fixed assets which are al used for the Schools' direct charitable activities.
Investment Policy and Objectives
The Company's memorandum and articles of association permit funds to be invested in such manner
as the Directors see fit, providing that such powers of investment are only exercised for the purpose
of attaining the objects and in a manner that is legally charitable. The Council's policy is to preserve
and enhance the capital value of investments and maximise income consistent with maintaining a
balanced investment return from income and capital, with moderate risk.
Investment Performance against Objectives
The Company's investment portfolio was managed by Brooks Macdonald Asset Management Limited
during the period. The portfolio continued to meet the stated income requirements. Over the
accounting period the portfolio generated a net tota return of 8.14%, compared with a total return of
10.26% recorded by the FTSE WMA Total Return Stock Market Balanced Index.

1. ACCOUNTING POLICIES
The principal accounting policies, al of which have been applied consistently throughout the year and in
the preceding year are:
a) Basis of accounting
The accounts of the Group have been prepared in accordance with the Statement of Recommended
Practice 'Accounting and Reporting by Charities' and with applicable accounting standards. They are
drawn up on the historical cost accounting basis except that investments held as fixed assets are
carried at market value. The accounts have been prepared on a going concern basis.
b)
Going Concern
The accounts have been prepared on a going concern basis. The King's Schools Taunton Limited
Board reviews the financial information for the Company and the Group, and considers whether the
Group and Company are a going concern for a period of at least 12 months from the date of
approval of the accounts. After making enquiries, the Directors have a reasonable expectation that
the Group has adequate resources to continue in operational existence for the foreseeable future.
Accordingly, they continue to adopt the going concern basis in preparing the Annual Report and
Accounts.
c)
Group accounts
The financial statements consolidate the financial statements of the Company, and all its subsidiary
companies, charitable trusts and funds with all inter-company balances being eliminated.
d) Fees and similar income
Fees receivable are accounted for in the period in which the service is provided Fees receivable are
stated after deducting allowances, scholarships and other remissions granted by the School, but
include contributions received from restricted funds for Scholarships, Bursaries and other grants
Fees in Advance are those fees received in advance of the following year's education and are shown
as a short term liability until taken to income in accordance with this policy.
Advance Fees are those fees received in advance of education to be provided in future years under
an Advance Fees Contract which are held as interest bearing liabilities until either taken to income in
the term when used, or else refunded.
e) Donations and Appeals
Donations, subject to specific wishes of the donors, are credited to relevant restricted funds or to
endowed funds where the amount is required to be held as permanent capital. Donations received
for the general purposes of the schools are credited to other unrestricted funds, to distinguish them
from direct school income.
On occasions the Schools may set up appeals to raise finance at times when particular building
projects are being undertaken. Monies received are treated in accordance with the terms of the
appeal documentation and are recognised as Designated Funds and shown under 'Unrestricted
Funds' in the Statement of Financial Activities (SOFA), rather than as Restricted Funds. Appeal
documentation explains that monies can be used for general purposes.
21

1. ACCOUNTING POLICIES (continued)
f) Expenditure
Expenditure is allocated to expense headings either on a direct cost basis or apportioned according
to time spent. The irrecoverable element of VAT is included with the item of expense to which it
relates.
The cost of refurbishing and converting existing buildings is written off in the year in which it is
incurred except where the useful life has been extended. Bad debts are provided for in accordance
with the Woodard Corporation's bad debt policy.
g)
Governance costs
Governance costs include the costs attributable to King's Schools Taunton Limited's compliance with
constitutional and statutory requirements, including audit, strategic management and Council
meetings and reimbursed expenses. Such costs include both direct and allocated support costs.
h) Finance and other costs
Other costs include amounts accrued in accordance with the terms of Advance Fee Contracts.
i)
Pension costs
The Company participates in The Teachers' Pensions Scheme, which is an unfunded Government
scheme, and The Pensions Trust scheme, both of which provide benefits based on final pensionable
pay. The funds of the schemes are separate from the Company, although the Company share of the
schemes cannot be identified as the schemes are multi-employer schemes, and SO the pension
costs are accounted for on the basis of contributions payable. The Company also contributes to
other defined contribution pension schemes for non-teaching staff.
The Company offers membership of The Pensions Trust Growth Plan to employees other than the
full-time academic staff. The Pensions Trust Growth Plan is a multi employer pension scheme
where the scheme assets are pooled for investment purposes and cannot be atributed to individual
employers. Benefits are paid from the total scheme assets. It is in most respects a money purchase
arrangement, but has some guarantees. As a result it is not possible or appropriate to identify the
assets and liabilities of the scheme which are attributable to the Company, though, due to the
guarantees inherent in the scheme, the Company remains potentially liable for a debt on withdrawal
from the scheme. In accordance with Financial Reporting Standard 17 (FRS) therefore, the scheme
is accounted for in a fashion which is similar to a defined contribution scheme. More detail is given
in notes 26 and 27.
j)
Tangible fixed assets and depreciation
Tangible fixed assets are stated at cost less depreciation. Individual capital items, or projects, with a
value greater than f10,000 are capitalised Assets in the course of construction are stated at cost
less any provision for impairment They are transferred to completed assets when substantially all of
the activities necessary to get the asset ready for use are complete. Where appropriate cost
includes our own labour costs in relation to construction, and directly attributable overheads.

1. ACCOUNTING POLICIES (continued)
j)
Tangible fixed assets and depreciation (continued)
Where tangible fixed assets have been acquired with the aid of specific grants they are included in
the balance sheet at cost and depreciated over their expected useful economic life. The related
grants are credited to a restricted fixed asset fund (in the statement of financial activities and carried
forward in the balance sheet). The depreciation on such assets is charged in the statement of
financial activities over the expected useful economic life of the related asset on a basis consistent
with the depreciation policy. Depreciation is provided at rates calculated to write off the cost, less
estimated residual value of each asset over its expected useful life, as follows:
- Freehold land is not depreciated

The Company has reviewed its tangible assets, which comprise land, buildings and initial fixtures
and fittings. Where the directors consider that the expected useful life is in excess of 50 years and
the carrying value in the financial statements is not more than the estimated recoverable amount, no
depreciation is charged out and, in accordance with FRS11, the Directors have and will continue to
carry out annual reviews of impairment.
k) Stocks
Stocks comprise raw materials, consumable stores and goods held for resale: they are valued at the
lower of cost and net realisable value.
D) Investments
Investments are carried at market value in accordance with the Charities (Accounts and Reports)
Regulations 2008 and The Statement of Recommended Practice 'Accounting and Reporting by
Charities'.
Realised gains are the difference between sales proceeds and opening market value where the
investment was held at the beginning of the year, or sales proceeds less cost of purchase where the
investment was acquired in the year.
Unrealised gains are the change in value of investments after taking into account any movements in
investment holdings such as purchases and disposals of investments.
Realised and unrealised gains are accounted for within the SOFAs on pages 17 and 18.
m) Leasing commitments
Assets held under finance leases and hire purchase contracts are capitalised in the balance sheet
and are depreciated over their useful lives or the period of the lease whichever is the shorter. The
interest element of the obligations is charged to the SOFA over the period of the lease. Rentals paid
under operating leases are charged to expenditure as incurred.

1. ACCOUNTING POLICIES (continued)
n) Fund Accounts
Endowment funds are subject to specific conditions by donors that the capital must be maintained by
the Company.
Restricted funds are subject to specific conditions by donors as to how they may be used. The
purposes and uses of the restricted funds are set out in the notes to the financial statements.
Designated funds comprise funds which have been set aside at the discretion of the directors for
specific purposes. The purposes and uses of the designated funds are set out in the notes to the
financial statements.
o) Trading Activity
Income from shop sales, holiday and sports hall lettings are recognised in the SOFA activities when
the goods are sold or services provided.
p) Taxation
King's Schools Taunton Limited is a registered charity and as such is exempt from income tax and
corporation tax under the provisions of Section 478 of the Corporation Tax Act 2010. There is no
similar exemption for VAT, which is included in expenditure or in the cost of assets as appropriate.
The Company has a subsidiary company that is subject to taxes including corporation tax and VAT in
the same way as any commercia organisation. The tax charged to the profit and loss account is
based on the subsidiary company's profit for the year and takes into account tax arising because of
timing differences between the treatment of certain items for tax and accounting purposes. The
subsidiary company pays over the majority of its profits to King's Schools Taunton Limited under Gift
Aid and tax liabilities are kept to a minimum.
q)
Cash flow statement
The cash flows of King's Schools Taunton Limited are included in the consolidated cash flow
statement of The Woodard Corporation. King's Schools Taunton Limited is exempt under the terms
of FRS 1 (Revised) from publishing a cash flow statement.

26 PENSION SCHEMES
Teachers' Pension Scheme
The School participates in the Teachers' Pension Scheme (England and Wales) ("the TPS"), for its teaching staff. The
pension charge for the year includes contributions payable to the TPS of E 664,430 (2013: E 620,600). At the year-end
E
62,319 (2013 - 59,424) was accrued in respect of contributions to this scheme.
The TPS is an unfunded multi-employer defined benefits pension scheme governed by the Teachers' Pensions Regulations
2010 and, from 1 April 2014, the Teachers' Pension Scheme Regulations 2014. Members contribute on a "pay as you go"
basis with contributions from members and the employer being credited to the Exchequer. Retirement and other pension
benefits are paid by public funds provided by Parliament
The employer contribution rate is set following scheme valuations undertaken by the Government Actuary Department. The
latest valuation report in respect of the TPS was prepared at 31 March 2012 and was published in June 2014. This report
confirmed that the employer contribution rate for the TPS will increase from 14.1% to 16.4% although, recognising that
teaching establishments work on an academic and not financial year, the Government has deferred the implementation of this
increase to 1 September 2015.
The Department of Education is also proposing that scheme administration costs will be devolved to scheme employers in the
form of an administration charge. The Department provisionally estimates that the administration charge will be 0.08% of the
employers' salary costs which would increase the employer payment rate from 16.4% to 16.48%.
The next revision to the employer contribution rate is not expected to take effect until 1 April 2019. This will follow on from the
next actuarial valuation which is due at 31 March 2016. This valuation will also determine the opening balance of the cost cap
fund and provide an analysis of the cost cap as required by the Public Service Pensions Act 2013.
Pensions Trust's Growth Plan
The Company participates in The Pensions Trust's Growth Plan (the Plan). The Plan is funded and is not contracted-out of
the State scheme. The Plan is a multi-employer pension plan. Contributions paid into the Plan up to and including September
2001 were converted to defined amounts of pension payable from Normal Retirement Date. From October 2001 contributions
were invested in personal funds which have a capital guarantee and which are converted to pension on retirement, either
within the Plan or by the purchase of an annuity.
The rules of the Plan allow for the declaration of bonuses and/or investment credits if this is within the financial capacity of the
Plan assessed on a prudent basis. Bonuses/investment credits are not guaranteed and are declared at the discretion of the
Plan's Trustee.
The
Trustee commissions an actuarial valuation of the Plan every three years. The purpose of the actuarial valuation is to
determine the funding position of the Plan by comparing the assets with the past service liabilities as at the valuation date.
Asset values are calculated by reference to market levels. Accrued past service liabilities are valued by discounting expected
future benefit payments using a discount rate calculated by reference to the expected future investment returns.
The rules of the Plan give the Trustee the power to require employers to pay additional contributions in order to ensure that
the statutory funding objective under the Pensions Act 2004 is met. The statutory funding objective is that a pension scheme
should have sufficient assets to meet its past service liabilities, known as Technical Provisions.
If the actuarial valuation reveals a deficit, the Trustee will agree a recovery plan to eliminate the deficit over a specified period
of time either by way of additional contributions from employers, investment returns or a combination of these.
The rules of the Plan state that the proportion of obligatory contributions to be borne by the member and the member's
employer shall be determined by agreement between them. Such agreement shall require the employer to pay part of such
contributions and may provide that the employer shall pay the whole of them.
The Company paid contributions at the rate of either 3% or 10% during the accounting period. Members paid contributions at
the rate of either 3% or 5% during the accounting period. As at the balance sheet date there were 32 active members of the
Plan employed by King's Schools Taunton Ltd. The Company has closed the Plan to new entrants.
It is not possible in the normal course of events to identify on a reasonable and consistent basis the share of underlying
assets and liabilities belonging to individual participating employers. The Plan is a multi-employer scheme, where the assets
are co-mingled for investment purposes, and benefits are paid out of the Plan's total assets. Accordingly, due to the nature of
the Plan, the accounting charge for the period under FRS17 represents the employer contribution payable.
34
KING'S SCHOOLS TAUNTON LIMITED
NOTES TO THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2014
The valuation results at 30 September 2011 were completed in 2012 and have been formalised. The valuation of the Plan
was performed by a professionally qualified Actuary using the Projected Unit Method. The market value of the Plan's assets
at the valuation date was E 780 million and the Plan's Technical Provisions (i.e. past service liabilities) were E 928 million.
The valuation therefore revealed a shortfall of assets compared with the value of liabilities of E 148 million, equivalent to a
funding level of 84%.
The financial assumptions underlying the valuation as at 30 September 2011 were as follows:

In determining the investment return assumptions the Trustee considered advice from the Scheme Actuary relating to the
probability of achieving particular levels of investment return. The Trustee has incorporated an element of prudence into the
pre and post retirement investment return assumptions; such that there is a 60% expectation that the return will be in excess
of that assumed and a 40% chance that the return will be lower than that assumed over the next 10 years.
The Scheme Actuary has prepared a funding position update as at 30 September 2013. The market value of the Plan's assets
at that date was E 772 million and the Plan's Technical Provisions (i.e. past service liabilities) was E 927 million. The update,
therefore, revealed a shortfall of assets compared with the value of liabilities of E 155 million, equivalent to a funding level of
83%.
If an actuarial valuation reveals a shortfall of assets compared to liabilities, the Trustee must prepare a recovery plan setting
out the steps to be taken to make up the shortfall.
The Pensions Regulator has the power under Part 3 of the Pensions Act 2004 to issue scheme funding directions where it
believes that the actuarial valuation assumptions and/or recovery plan are inappropriate. For example, the Regulator could
require that the Trustee strengthens the actuarial assumptions (which would increase the Plan liabilities and hence impact on
the recovery plan) or impose a schedule of contributions on the Plan (which would effectively amend the terms of the recovery
plan). A copy of the recovery plan in respect of the September 2011 valuation was forwarded to The Pensions Regulator on 2
October 2012, as is required by legislation.
Following a change in legislation in September 2005 there is a potential debt on the employer that could be levied by the
Trustee of the Plan and The Pensions Act 2011 has more recently altered the definition of Series 3 of the Growth Plan SO that
a liability arises to employers from membership of any Series except Series 4. The debt is due in the event of the employer
ceasing to participate in the Plan or the Plan winding up. The debt for the Plan as a whole is calculated by comparing the
liabilities for the Plan (calculated on a buy-out basis i.e. the cost of securing benefits by purchasing annuity policies from an
insurer, plus an allowance for expenses) with the assets of the Plan. If the liabilities exceed assets there is a buy-out debt.
The leaving employer's share of the buy-out debt is the proportion of the Plan's liability attributable to employment with the
leaving employer compared to the total amount of the Plan's liabilities (relating to employment with all the currently
participating employers). The leaving employer's debt therefore includes a share of any 'orphan' liabilities in respect of
previously participating employers. The amount of the debt therefore depends on many factors including total Plan liabilities,
Plan investment performance, the liabilities in respect of current and former employees of the employer, financial conditions at
the time of the cessation event and the insurance buy-out market. The amounts of debt can therefore be volatile over time.
The Growth Plan is a "last man standing" multi-employer scheme. This means that if a withdrawing employer is unable to pay
its debt on withdrawal the liability is shared amongst the remaining employers. The participating employers are therefore,
jointly and severally liable for the deficit in the Growth Plan. As at 30 September 2013 the total deficit calculated on the buy-
out basis was E 219.9m. See note 27 for further details.
35
KING'S SCHOOLS TAUNTON LIMITED
NOTES TO THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2014
27 CONTINGENT LIABILITIES
When an employer withdraws from a multi-employer defined benefit pension scheme which is in deficit, the employer is
required by law to pay its share of the deficit, calculated on a statutory basis (known as the buy-out basis). Due to a change in
the definition of money purchase contained in the Pensions Act 2011 the calculation basis that applies to the Growth Plan will
be amended to include Series 3 liabilities in the calculation of an employer's debt on withdrawal.
The Pensions Act 2011 also proposed regulations which will make "consequential or transitional provisions to avoid adverse
consequences" Should an employer withdraw prior to the regulations coming into force (expected to be at the end of July
2014), they should contact The Pensions Trust to check whether the regulations could affect their debt on withdrawal
calculation.
King's Schools Taunton Limited has been notified by the Pensions Trust of the estimated employer debt on withdrawal from
the Growth Plan, as outlined in note 26, based on the financial position of the Growth Plan as at 30 September 2013. As of
this date the estimated employer debt for King's Schools Taunton Limited was E 1,162,893 including Series 3 liabilities.
28 RELATED PARTIES
The Company is a wholly owned subsidiary of The Woodard Corporation, a registered charity number 1096270, which
is
incorporated in England and Wales. An amount of E 90,034 (2013: E 88,220) was paid in the period to the Corporation by
way of a levy to meet Corporation running costs.
The Company also controls a subsidiary, WST Enterprises Limited, the results of which are detailed in note 3.

TRUSTEES' REPORT
The committee present their report and accounts for the year ended 31 May 2015.
The accounts have been prepared in accordance with the accounting policies set out in note 1 to the accounts
and comply with the charity's governing document, applicable law and the requirements of the Statement of
Recommended Practice, "Accounting and Reporting by Charities" issued in March 2005.
Structure, Governance and Management
Governing Document
The charity is a company limited by guarantee without share capital. The Guarantee of the members, being the
theatre card holders, is limited to a contribution of E1 each in the event of a winding-up. In the event of
dissolution any property whatsoever remaining is to be transferred under Clause 7 of the Memorandum of
Association, to be held on trust for charitable purposes or given to some other institution having similar objects
to
the company.
Recruitment and Appointment of Committee
The committee who are also the directors for the purpose of company law and trustees for the purpose of
charity law, who served during the year were:-
R. Booth, F. Brindle, R. Clark (Resigned 4th March 2015), C. Cliffe, N.W.J. Gay, D. Kettle, S. Kettle, J.A. Lill, M.
Lill, M. Spendlow, N. Warne and J.M. West.
None of the committee has any beneficial interest in the company. All the committee are members of the
company and guarantee to contribute E1 in the event of a winding up.
In accordance with the Articles of Association the following retire at the 2015 Annual General Meeting, but being
eligible, offer themselves for re-election:-
C. Cliffe, M.Spendlow, N. Warne, J. West
Trustee Induction and Training
All trustees are familiar with the practical work of the charity having been trustees for some time, and are kept up
to date by being advised regularly by the company secretary of the relevant content of Charity News and the
Commissions guide, "The Essential Trustee".
Risk Management
The committee have assessed the major risks to which the charity is exposed, and are satisfied that systems are
in place to mitigate exposure thereto.
Organisationa Structure
The charity's organisational structure consists of the main committee, sub committees and other volunteers.
The committee in conjunction with the General Manager have overall control and are the decision makers of the
charity. The sub committees are finance, internal programming, external programming, health and safety,
marketing and customer care. These committees make recommendations to the main committee. The
volunteers are local people who help to maintain the efficient running of the theatre, and make it possible to
produce theatrical performances and other events.
Objectives and Activities
The purposes of the charity are:
- To advance the education of the public in all aspects of dramatic art including the arts of drama, mime, opera
ballet, music, singing, dance and puppetry.
- The development of public appreciation of art by the provision of a theatre and the presentation of public
performances, both by amateurs and professionals; and
-. To further the social and cultural welfare of the local community
Page 2
LOUTH PLAYGOERS SOCIETY LIMITED
TRUSTEES' REPORT
The vision that shapes our activities remains to be the promotion and fostering of knowledge and the
appreciation of the arts by the provision of facilities for the education and recreation of the public in the fields of
art, music and drama. The charity also has the general aim of contributing to the quality of life of the people in
the local community by expanding their horizons through the provision of exciting, challenging and accessible
events.
In shaping our objectives and planning our activities for the year the trustees have considered the Charity
Commission's guidance on public benefit, and fee charging. The organisation relies on grants, box office income,
sale of refreshments and letting of the premises to cover its operating costs. In setting the level of charges and
concessions, the trustees give careful consideration to the accessibility of the theatre to those on low incomes.
The strategies employed to achieve the charity's aims and objectives are to:-
-
Present a broad range of theatre productions and art exhibitions for the enjoyment and education of our local
community;
- Offer opportunities for a broad range of people to get involved in the arts activity exploring their own creative
powers;
- Provide facilities for both amateur and professional artists to develop. Groups in the area are given discounted
rates for hire of space;
- Provide discounted educational workshops for members of the community led by professional artistes;
- Concentrate on involving young people in the arts to help encourage a culture in which different age ranges
play a complimentary part;
- Celebrate the diversity of cultures in society by programming presentations by, and with, artists of different
cultural backgrounds
In putting these strategies into action our major areas of activity are stage performances, educational
programmes, and art exhibitions. Our programme of activities described below focus very much on bringing the
arts to the community. As our strategy makes clear we endeavour to encourage al within our community to take
part in our activities, to attend our theatre, and to view our exhibitions. The drama and art that we provide is
there to be enjoyed by all from those attending local schools or in higher education, through to our programme
with particular appeal to our older residents. Affordability and access to our programme is important to us and is
reflected in our policy set out later in this report.
Achievements and Performance
We seek to combine amateur community events alongside professional events. The total programme achieves
a mix of the arts to suit a range of public tastes with emphasis on presenting popular events which underpin the
viability of the theatre, combined with innovative and exploratory presentations which reach out to the
community. We have presented a good range of Saturday and school holiday matinees for children with suitable
productions for a range of ages from 3 upwards.
Presentation of Dramatical and Musical productions
The main areas of charitable activity and how they were achieved during the year are as follows:
- Our own "in house" production of seven plays running for a minimum of six performances on each occasion;
- A pantomime and musical produced "in house" each running for ten public performances. Further, for the final
dress rehearsal of the pantomime, we agreed to allow the "Louth Lions Club" to invite, and transport, up to 200
members of the community who would otherwise be unable to attend the theatre due to age or disability.
- Performances/presentations by eighteen professional companies or artistes;
- Two visits by the "New London Opera Group", a very good semi-professional company specialising in Gilbert
and Sullivan.
Hire of the theatre to three local schools and two local dance schools for their own productions, other local
groups and individuals, and one emerging company.
Page 3
LOUTH PLAYGOERS SOCIETY LIMITED
TRUSTEES' REPORT
We have experienced a mixed picture in attendances this year. The average attendance for the "in house" plays
decreased from 77% of capacity to 58%. However, the pantomime increased from 95% to 96%; The musical
from 86% to 92% and the professional programme from 67% to 71%.
We involve local schools in a range of expressive arts with professionals in workshops which aim to develop
student's confidence and expression across the range of the arts, including dance, drama, music, and on other
occasions, art with paints, textiles etc, and even creative writing. Where possible, the programme is linked to the
educational syllabus and special events are also provided for persons with learning difficulties to encourage their
freedom of expression, and to enhance their communication skills through the creative arts.
Presentations in this field during the year included:-
- A fourteen day summer school for young people led by professional tutors, resulting in three public
performances;
- Two seven day summer schools for 7 to 12 year olds led by a professiona tutor, culminating in a presentation
of their work for parents, relatives and friends.
- A Saturday drama club run for children of primary school age followed by a drama group for teenagers, each
led by a professional tutor, leading to a public performance;
Other Activities
- Each month local artists are invited to mount an exhibition of their work in the theatre foyer at no cost, which
the public are invited to view free of charge. At such exhibitions, artists are allowed to sell their work on a
commission basis.
- The company has a licensed bar that is open before and during the interval at each performance, and sweets
and ice creams are available for purchase at appropriate times.
- The company seeks to utilise spare capacity in the venue, especially during the daytime, by lettings to local
organisations. During the year we had regular local lets to the local department of Lincolnshire County Council
Disability Learning Group. The venue was also let for training days, lectures and seminars.
Staffing
The company employed 5 part time workers to cover the day to day management of the theatre, the
arrangement of the educational programme, the Box Office openings from 10am to 1pm from Mondays to
Saturdays inclusive, and the regular cleaning of the premises.
We are very involved in the local community and rely heavily upon voluntary help. In addition to those amateur
performers and artists, backstage workers and technicians who display their talents at the theatre, a large
number of volunteers assist with stewarding events and performances, and giving their time freely to assist in the
various departments thus enabling longer opening and lower staff costs than would otherwise be the case.
We wish to thank our volunteers, and also those involved in "The Friends of Louth Playgoers" for their continued
loyal support and help.
Page 4
LOUTH PLAYGOERS SOCIETY LIMITED
TRUSTEES' REPORT
Financial review
Being one of ten visual and performing arts venues in Lincolnshire, working together has enabled us to benefit
from a second successfu grant application to the Paul Hamlyn Foundation and a successful grant application to
the Esmee Fairburn Foundation. This resulted in significant grants being obtained to further the work of the
group with young people.
Our collaboration with four of the ten venues in Lincolnshire continues to be very successful and regular
quarterly meetings ensures that all venues provide a programme of events in line with the Arts Council's aims
and objectives The Arts Council has recently agreed a further three year grant for this collaboration covering the
period 1st April 2015 to 31st March 2018.
Other income, which is by far the greatest majority, is revenue from events within the theatre. This is to a large
extent unknown when preparing annual budgets, but over the past years, we have found that our budgeting is
reasonably accurate, and monthly comparisons with actual results produce early warning signs of any action to
be taken. The company, with the aid of sound financial management, and the support of both its staff and
volunteers, generated a positive outcome with a healthy surplus before depreciation.
The Company does not normally have sums available for investment as apart from retaining a prudent sum in
reserves, most of the funds are spent in the short term. However, during this year, E25,000 was invested with our
bankers on a fixed term to maximise interest rate receivable without prejudicing having sufficient funds available
to settle all invoices promptly.
Our pricing policy
The policy reflects our strategy of seeking to enable all within our community to take part in our activities, to
attend our theatre and to view our exhibitions. The prices for the former ranged from f4 to E15, and admission to
the latter is free.
There are special discounts offered to students under the age of 18 for most performances. Our theatre card
holders receive a discount of up to 12.5% on our productions. We offer one free seat for every twelve in block
bookings for all performances except for companies hiring the theatre who fix their own prices. Where events are
organised within the programme linked to the school curriculum, seats are heavily discounted for student
attendances. On the occasion of educational workshops being conducted by a professional company who are
also presenting a performance, a heavily discounted ticket is available to students attending both events.
Further, we have a policy that wherever possible, a ticket for an under 18 year old at a professional performance
will not exceed f5, and this concession is also applied to the educational programme.
The trustees are very aware of the fact that being based in the eastern part of the East Midlands we are situated
in a relatively low income area, and are satisfied that our seat pricing over the whole programme was such that
any member of our community, whatever their means, was able to join in our activities and attend our theatre.
Reserves Policy
The Management Committee has examined the company's requirements in the light of the main risks to the
organisation, and has established a policy whereby the unrestricted funds, not committed nor invested in
tangible fixed assets held by the company, should be 3 months' expenditure.
The unrestricted fund currently stands at E330,697 of which E292,570 is invested in tangible fixed assets. The
situation arose over 10 years ago when as part of the company's share of funding on the Theatre build, over
E350,000 of our unrestricted funds had to be used. Current Liabilities includes f22,12 of income received in
advance, the average holding over the year being in the region of 210,000. When this figure is added to net
current assets figure of E38, 127 there is sufficient working capital for the next 3 months. The management
committee whilst recognising that the available reserves fall slightly below the expected level believe they will
have no difficulty in continuing the company's activities.

TRUSTEES' REPORT
Plans for future period
The company plans to continue the activities outlined in this report in the coming year at less cost than in the
year ended 31st May 2015. On the other hand the trustees are constantly aware of the fact that the new build
was completed 13 years ago, and that expensive necessary repairs and replacement of equipment will mean
that the trustees must continue the requirement for careful and controlled financial management.
Responsibilities of the Management Committee
The committee are responsible for preparing the financial statements in accordance with applicable law and
United Kingdom Generally Accepted Accounting Practice.
Company law requires the committee to prepare financial statements for each financial year which give a true
and fair view of the state of affairs of the charity, and of its incoming resources and application thereof, including
its income and expenditure for the year.
In preparing these financial statements, the committee are required to:-
- select suitable accounting policies and then apply them consistently;
- make judgements and estimates that are reasonable and prudent; and
- prepare the financial statements on the going concern basis unless it is inappropriate to presume that the
charity will continue in operation.
The committee are responsible for keeping proper accounting records that disclose with reasonable accuracy at
any time the financial position of the charity, and which enable them to ensure that the accounts comply with the
Companies Act 2006. They are also responsible for safeguarding the assets of the charity and hence for taking
reasonable steps for the prevention and detection of fraud and other irregularities.
Members of the Management Committee
Members of the management committee, who are directors for the purpose of the company law and trustees for
the purpose of charity law, who served during the year up to the date of this report are set out previously herein.
In accordance with Company law, as the company's directors, we certify that:-
- So far as we are aware, there is no relevant information of which the company's independent examiners are
unaware; and
- As the Directors of the company, we have taken all the steps that we ought to have taken in order to make
ourselves aware of any relevant information and to establish that the company's independent examiners are
aware of that information.
Asset cover for funds
Notes 16 and 17 to the financial statements set out an analysis attributable to the various funds and a description
of the trusts. These assets are sufficient to meet the charity's obligations on a fund by fund basis.
Small company provisions
This report has been prepared in accordance with the small companies regime under the Companies Act 2006.

Accounting policies
Basis of preparation
The financial statements have been prepared under the historical cost convention and in accordance with
the Statement of Recommended Practice 'Accounting and Reporting by Charities (SORP 2005)' issued in
March 2005, the Financial Reporting Standard for Smaller Entities (effective April 2008 and the
Companies Act 2006.
Fund accounting policy
Unrestricted income funds are general funds that are available for use at the trustees' discretion in
furtherance of the objectives of the charity.
Restricted funds are those donated for use in a particular area or for specific purposes, the use of which is
restricted to that area or purpose.
Further details of each fund are disclosed in note 16.
Incoming resources
Investment income is recognised on a receivable basis.
Assets given for use by the charity are recognised when receivable. These assets have been valued by the
donator at cost value.
Grants receivable are recognised in the period in which they are due. These are allocated to the correct
fund depending on any restrictions that may apply.
Incoming resources are included in the SOFA when the charity is legally entitled to the income and the
amount can be quantified with reasonable accuracy. The resources represents the amount derived from
services provided and goods sold (stated net of VAT)
The turnover is wholly attributable to the activity of dramatics, etc., and is all conducted in the United
Kingdom. Monetary gifts donated to the charity for specific use are recognised as income when they are
distributed to the projects. Any other type of donation gifts are included at valuation and are recognised in
the same way as the above.
No amounts are included in the financial statements for services donated by volunteers.
Resources expended
All expenditure is accounted for on an accruals basis and has been classified under headings that
aggregate all costs related to the category. Where costs cannot be directly attributed to particular headings
they have been allocated to activities on a basis consistent with the use of the resources.
Charitable expenditure comprises those costs incurred by the charity in the delivery of its activities and
services. It includes both costs that can be allocated directly to such activities and those costs of an indirect
nature necessary to support them.
Governance costs
Governance costs include costs of the preparation and examination of the statutory accounts, the costs of
trustee meetings and the cost of any legal advice to trustees on governance or constitutional matters.

Support costs include central functions and have been allocated to activity cost categories on a basis
consistent with the use of resources, for example, allocating property costs by floor areas, or per capita,
staff costs by the time spent and other costs by their usage.

lrrecoverable VAT is charged against the category of resources expended for which it was incurred.

Individual fixed assets costing E500 or more are initially recorded at cost.

Freehold buildings

Stock
Stock is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value, after due regard for obsolete and slow moving

Items donated for resale or distribution are not included in the financial statements until they are sold or

Charitable objects

a School for Boys and Girls or for children of either sex in which they may receive a sound religious,
classical, mathematical, scientific and general education in conformity with the principles and doctrines of
the Church of England."

Report of the Council for the year ended 31 July 2014
The Council present their annual report and the audited consolidated financial statements for the year ended
31 July 2014.
Reference and Administrative Information is set out on pages 3 to 5 of this report. This section also provides
details of Malvern College's governing document, nature of its constitution and its charitable objects. The
financial statements comply with the charity's Royal Charter, applicable Accounting Standards in the United
Kingdom and the Accounting and Reporting by Charities: Statement of Recommended Practice (revised 2005)
and the Charities Act 2011.
Chairman's; statement
The College has had another highly successful year. External examination results have been most
encouraging and in some cases outstanding. In addition to one pupil achieving 45 points for the IB (a feat
only matched by the top 0.25% of candidates worldwide), another three pupils gained 44 points. At "A"
level, 45% of pupils achieved either A* or A grades whilst for GCSE the figure was a highly creditable 60%
achieving those top grades. Nine pupils have been offered places at Oxbridge while many others have
gained places at prestigious North American and other universities throughout the world. However, the
College is ecjually proud of all those pupils who have worked very hard and to the very best of their ability
and managed to gain places in a wide range of universities throughout the UK and beyond
The College has enhanced its academic tracking procedures where pupils' academic progress is carefully
monitored enabling staff to identify those that are doing exceptionally well and those that might need
support. Another important academic development has been a further broadening of the curriculum in
offering Philosophy at IB Higher level as well as Psychology and Critical Thinking at "AS" level.
It was good to see parents and Old Malvernians volunteering their services in a very worthwhile Careers
Evening attended by most of the Sixth Form. A good number of pupils were offered work experience as
well as giver advice about a number of professions during the course of the evening. The College hopes
to repeat this event in the future. Pupil involvement in raising money for charity has been tremendous with
over E14,000 having been raised; wider afield, thirty-three pupils spent three weeks in Ghana where they
taught and spent time involved in building projects.
The school's cultural life was dominated by its production of Oh! What a Lovely War that attracted a large
number of parents as well as other guests The Foundation Year put on a challenging version of Homer's
The Odyssey. Meanwhile on the sporting front the 1st XI continued their success with wins against Harrow,
Repton, Clifton and Bradfield and several of its players were selected for County and regional teams.
Malvern's equestrian credentials also received a boost with one Foundation Year girl representing England
whilst another older girl took part in the Horse of the Year Show and the Home Pony International
competition.
During the year ending 31 July 2014, the College's incoming resources remained strong at E22,764,674
(2013: E20,900,457) including f2,696,727 from donations, mainly towards the Science project. Total
charitable expenditure was E19,989,288 (2013: E18,760,810) and the College's operating surplus for the
year (net incoming resources before transfers) amounted to E2,775,386 (2013: 22,139,647). Earnings
before interest, depreciation and one-off items amounted to E2,732,951 (2013: E2,570,757) which was well
ahead of budget. This strong cash-flow continues to enable the College to meet its scheduled debt
amortisation and invest for the future.
Capital expenditure for the year of f4,917,774 (2013: E2,158,059) included the continued construction of
our new Science facilities 3,173,409 (2013 E1,832,450). The Science project is now nearing completion
and will be ready for occupation by the College in early 2015 We have received generous pledges of
financial support for this project from our Old Malvernian alumni. A very significant anonymous gift of
E2,500,000 was received from the Old Malvernian Society as a substantial contribution to the Science
6
Malvern College
(Incorporated under Royal Charter)
Report of the Council for the year ended 31 July 2014 (continued)
refurbishment project We are most grateful for the support from our donors and from all those who give
generously of their time to the College.
Finally, the College is completing preparations to celebrate its 150th anniversary in 2015; there will be
various events, including a special Ball, receptions, lectures, pupil led activities and other events at venues
here at Malvern, London and in various countries abroad.
The College has continued to expand its provision of public benefit in a wide range of activities more fully
described on pages 16 to 18.
Structure Governance and Management
Recruitment and training of Trustees
When a Trustee vacancy arises, the criteria of skills required, availability and eligibility, as dictated by the
Royal Charter, are identified. On identification of possible new Trustees, they are approached and met by
senior Trustees. The College's elected Trustees are appointed on the agreement of all the existing
Trustees at a Council meeting, on the recommendation of the senior Trustees. Trustees are normally
appointed to serve for a 5 year term.
New Trustees are inducted informally by fellow Council members and the Bursar/Clerk to Council. Training
is undertaken through attendance at Council meetings by interaction with fellow Trustees and genera
involvement in College life.
Committee structure
The College Council continues to meet once per term. A committee of Council, the Management Board,
comprising seven or eight Trustees, the Headmaster, the Bursar, the Senior Deputy Head, the Finance
Bursar and the Headmaster of The Downs Malvern (TDM), meets at least once per month in term time. All
major developments and decisions are presented to the College Council having first been deliberated by
the Management Board. The Senior Management Team (SMT), chaired by the Headmaster meets weekly
and consists of the Bursar, the Senior Deputy Head, the Deputy Head - Logistics, the Deputy Head -
Pastoral, the Deputy Head - Academic, the Headmaster of The Downs Malvern and the Finance Bursar.
This team draws on other expertise throughout the College as is needed. The Headmaster, who has overall
day to day responsibility for the management of the College, consults the SMT, as appropriate and again,
as appropriate, makes recommendations through to the Management Board and ultimately to Council.
Adopting best practice corporate governance guidelines, a College Audit Committee was set up in January
2006 and has met twice yearly since. This committee scrutinises the College's Annual Report and Financial
Statements and its financial procedures and internal controls. It oversees the relationship of the College
with its external auditors. The committee formally reports to the College Council.
Related parties
Malvern College Enterprises Limited (MCEL)
Malvern College Enterprises Limited is the College's wholly-owned trading subsidiary and carries out non-
charitable trading activities for the College. The results of MCEL are consolidated within the overall College
results. Further details of MCEL's activities and performance are given in the Financial Review and Note
4 of the financial statements.
7
Malvern College
(Incorporated under Royal Charter)
Report of the Council for the year ended 31 July 2014 (continued)
The Malvernian Society Limited
The Malvernian Society Limited is a company limited by guarantee that promotes the work and education
at Malvern College, assists in the carrying on of a school or schools and in cases of need assists pupils in
further training. The results of The Malvernian Society Limited are not consolidated with the resu ts of
Malvern College because the society is a separate charity with an independent board of directors.
From time to time, the College receives grants towards the cost of scholarships, exhibitions, bursaries; and
grants for specific projects from The Malvernian Society. See Note 23 of the financial statements.
The Downs Malvern
The Downs Malvern (TDM) is the trading name of The Downs Malvern College Prep School (TDMICP).
The results of TDM are not consolidated with the results of Malvern College because the school is a
separate charity with an independent board of directors. In June 2007, as part of the merger between
Malvern College Prep School and The Downs School (Colwall) Ltd, Malvern College agreed to contribute
f5.5m to the new entity, TDMCP. The funds were applied to a significant development programme
including a new sports hall, all weather pitch, new senior and junior classrooms, new and refurbished
Boarding Houses and new fitted kitchens. The total cost of the project was over f6.Om; the balance being
met by the new Prep School itself. TDM is closely affiliated with the College and the College provides
bursarial support to TDM but retains its independence with its own Governing Body.
Council Members
Certain Council members are considered to be related parties of the College due to transactions between
themselves and the College. See Note 23 of the financial statements.
Risk management
The Council, as Trustees of the Charity, has examined the principal areas of the College's operations and
considered the major risks faced in each of the risk areas by reviewing the risk register prepared ty the
College's SMT. It is the opinion of the Council that the charity has established resources and reviewed
systems which, under normal operating conditions, should allow these risks to be mitigated t:o an
acceptable level in its day-to-day operations. The Council formally reviews the risk register on an nnua
basis. Changes to the College's risk profile are monitored by the College's SMT, Management Board and
Audit Comrnittee.
The major risks are considered to be the occurrence of a critical IT, Health and Safety or management
incident or pupil orientated incident.
Aims, strategies and objectives
Malvern's aim is to foster breadth of education and opportunity based on the academic curriculun and
pastora care at the heart of the school, and to ensure that its pupils, of all abilities, benefit from this.
Within the last academic year, the College had several specific objectives, all of which
complemented the aim stated above -
To promote further excellence at all stages in the school by encouraging high academic standards
and enjoyment of learning.
To seek to evolve and improve its academic, pastoral and co-curricular provision.
To ensure that the extensive capital and ICT investments enhance the experience of the College
for all beneficiaries.
8
Malvern College
(Incorporated under Royal Charter)
Report of the Council for the year ended 31 July 2014 (continued)
To maintain the current level of surpluses through maintenance of pupi numbers prudent cost
control and maximization of all areas to generate funds for the benefit of the pupils.
To continue to recruit high calibre staff and provide extensive and relevant staff training.
To continue to execute the College's marketing and fundraising strategies.
To have due regard for the Public Benefit guidance issued by the Charity Commission.
The strategies that were successfully enacted in the year to achieve these objectives were -
To develop and expand the "Stretch and Challenge" scheme for pupils and apply an increased
emphasis on independent learning.
To build on the Malvern College Leadership programme embracing pastoral, academic and CO-
curricular areas.

Pupil Numbers

(b)
Academic matters, including careers and higher education
University destinations for upper Sixth Leavers
UK universities
93% of the school's UK university applicants have a place on a university course. 78% have a place
on their first choice course and 59% are going to Russell Group universities. 9 applicants will take up
places at Oxbridge, whilst London proved, once again, to be the favourite destination, attracting 18
applicants (amongst them 7 to University College London, 6 to King's College London and 4 to
Imperial)

Overseas universities
Further afield, the College continues to have a significant number of pupils being offered university
places in the United States and Canada (including NYU, Virginia, Syracuse, Boston, Miami, UC
Berkeley, UPenn and McGill) and throughout Europe (including Trinity College, Dublin, The Schiool of
Economics at the University of Bocconi in Italy as well as universities in Madrid, Paris, Istanbul,
Switzerland and the multinational Hult Business School).
The College's International Universities Applications officer has been on visits to London, Madric, New
York, UPenn, Harvard, Georgetown and Florida, and has been working with his counterpart at
Qingdao. The school has also started a weekly in-house SAT preparation society, known as the Stars
and Stripes Club. Pupils have also gained scholarships and places to summer schools at IE Madrid
and Yale.
The school hosted its first International University Fair with universities from Europe, the USA, Canada,
Australia and Asia attending. This is set to become an annual event.
The school's International Universities Applications officer had been trained in the potential application
procedures to be adopted in the event that Scotland seceded from the United Kingdom, thus removing
St. Andrews, Edinburgh, Aberdeen, Glasgow and Dundee from UCAS.
Careers
Hundred (Year 11) and Lower Sixth pupils were profiled using the Morrisby Careers Profiling tests,
with the results analysed and discussed with careers advisors from "Inspiring Futures" (the new name
for ISCO (Independent Schools' Careers Organisation)). The "Expanding Horizons" programme and
an increasing number of Old Malvernians (OMs) provided invaluable work experience for our future
lawyers, medics and engineers.
The Careers Evening in January 2014 proved to be very popular, with 6 parents and OMs giving
seminars about careers in architecture, high finance and law. Several work experience placements
were arranged during the course of the evening.
Public Examination Results 2014
IB
Pupils achieved an average point score of 35.4 in the 2014 examinations.
17 candidates performed outstandingly, scoring 40 or more IB points, with one achieving the dist nction
of the maximum 45 points (only 0.25% of candidates worldwide achieve this) and three scoring 44
points. Overall the results were almost exactly as predicted (up by 0.15).
A Level & AS
The Upper Sixth A Level candidates achieved a record 45% A*-A grades and 72% A*-B grades, our
second best, with a pass-rate of 100% A*-E.
At AS Level, the Lower Sixth candidates achieved 44 % A-B grades. The A-E pass-rate was 91%.
GCSE/IGCSE
This year's GCSE results saw the Hundred perform excellently, achieving 60% A*-A. At the top end
we were particularly pleased by the figure of 32% A*. The A*-C pass rate was 96%. 27 pupils scored
6 A* grades or more.

Oxbridge
This year we had 9 pupils gaining an offer from either Oxford (6) or Cambridge (3). Our interview rate
(90%) was higher this year.
The Education Working Group
The Education Working Group (EWG) of the College Council met on three occasions in the academic
year, interviewing pupils, visiting the Modern Foreign Languages departments and holding discussions
with staff about Enrichment, Tracking pupil progress and the Teaching and Learning Group. The EWG
is currently considering the attachment of individual members of Council to specific teaching
departments which they can then visit separately.
Academic Colours
Academic Ties (for boys) or Badges (for giris) were awarded for the first time in the Summer Term to
pupils who have been placed for four terms on the Academic Honour Roll.
Tracking and Pupil monitoring
In September 2013 new Effort grades with more detailed descriptors were introduced. The College
has continued to develop a new Tracking system and have identified a need for further training of
tutors and Housemasters and Housemistresses in the use of tracking data; INSET on this will take
place at the start of the Autumn term 2014. From September we will introduce YELLIS baseline testing
for the Remove to enhance our tracking of pupil progress through to GCSE.
Pupil academic questionnaires
An online academic questionnaire was completed by our pupils in the third week of the summer term.
The questionnaire returns were very positive with pupils rating very highly the subject knowledge of
their teachers, how well lessons were organised, the support they received from their teachers and the
degree to which they were encouraged to learn independently. A small number of departments
attracted lower scores and an occasional negative comment. In each case the Deputy Head: Academic
discussed these scores and comments with the relevant Head of Department. Appropriate action was
taken and any identified shortcomings were addressed.
Buzz: the Virtual Learning Environment
All staff received 'Buzz' training in September and 'Buzz' training has become a regular strand in our
in-house CPD programme.
Science Schoo Project
The science departments have managed with great stoicism the upheavals occasioned by the
refurbishing of the Science school. Immediately after the November Half-term, Biology and Chemistry
moved back in to the Preston Building and responded with great enthusiasm to their new facilities.
Curriculum developments
In September 2013 we introduced IB Philosophy at Higher Level and, for our AS cohort, the Enrichment
Programme, with the most popular options proving the Extended Project, AS Psychology and AS
Critical Thinking, whilst several pupils chose Italian GCSE or BTEC Sport.
Scholars' Reviews
This academic year, we launched a new system of self-review and review for all of the College's
academic scholars (from FY (Year 9) through to Lower Sixth) in order to help monitor their academic
progress and the opportunities for 'stretch' that we offer.
The Teaching and Learning Group
This year nearly 30 members of Common Room met on several occasions to exchange ideas and
discuss approaches to Assessment for Learning and Independent Learning. The fruits of such cross
fertilisation were shared more widely through our in-house CPD programme and resources were also

Chapel
Links with Great Malvern Priory continue to be strong, with visits from Priory clergy to preach, and whole
school visit:s to celebrate Advent Carols, the annual Priory Science and Faith weekend and our own annual
Commemoration Service. The Chaplain has also preached at the Priory on several occasions.
The usual pattern of weekday Chapel remains: Headmaster's assembly and Chaplain's "thought for the
week" on Mondays; Sixth Form Chape on Tuesdays; Lower School Chapel on Wednesdays; a
presentation on Thursdays from houses, departments or groups with a particular interest. The Chaplain
continues t:o speak each Friday at The Downs Malvern's assembly. Sunday services are at variable times
SO that pupils can participate in the more extensive programme of Co-Curriculum Activities (CCAs): we
have Morning and Evening prayer, College Eucharist and occasional services of Compline.
The Crypt Chapel, which has been set aside for private prayer and meditation, has been out of lise for
most of the year during the works for essential repairs and but was back in use for the Autumn term 2014.
Further works are in preparation for the lighting and sound systems in the main Chapel.
In addition to the typica services, thematic and seasona services have been held. The College eld its
usual services at Remembrance, Advent, Christmas and Commemoration. At Remembrance the address
was given by Major-General Andy Salmon. For Commemoration, in Great Malvern Priory, the preacher
was The Rev'd Dr Ralph Waller, the Principal of Harris Manchester College, Oxford.
During the year there were two baptisms, three weddings and four memorial services held in the Chapel.
In May 2014 the retired former Bishop of Manchester presided at our Confirmation Service. There were
fifteen candidates from the College and two from The Downs, Malvern with an additional three canclidates
prepared for Confirmation in the Roman Catholic Church. The pre-Confirmation retreat took place at
Gloucester Cathedral.

What a Lovely War. A month earlier, the Malvern College Dramatic Society had joined with the Chamber
Choir to present a double bill of Purcell's Dido & Aeneas with Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra

Public benefit
Malvern College has for some time undertaken a wide range of activities, both in terms of engaging with
our local community and making it possible for bright young people who might otherwise not be able to
afford the full fees to benefit from the College's exceptional education in the broadest sense.
The College Council confirms that they have complied with the duty in section 17 of the Charities Act 2011
to have due regard to the public benefit guidance published by the Charity Commission. The significant
activities undertaken to carry out our aims for the Public Benefit and our achievements measured against
those aims are provided on pages 16 & 17 of this report.
Fee Concessions
Bursaries
Where financial circumstances of the parents dictate, the College will award a bursary to enable a child to
attend the school or see a child through to the next natural break point in his/her education. This y'ear,
significant bursary funds were awarded to meet the aims of the College Bursary Policy which are:-
to widen pupi access to the College and ensure that a Malvern education is provided to children
from a broad spectrum of society;
to continue the College's long tradition of providing public benefit;
to meet and if possible exceed the Charity Commission's public benefit requirements applicable
from time to time.
Information about fee assistance through bursaries is provided on the College website and is also
contained within the College scholarship literature.
Bursaries are reviewed annually on the basis of a returned and completed financial circumstances form.
The Bursary committee comprising the Headmaster, Bursar, Registrar and Finance Bursar considers all
bursary applications on a case by case basis.
