The trustees present their Annual Report and financial statements for 2015
Charitable Object
Christchurch Baptist Welwyn Garden City CIO is governed by a constitution
which states:
"The principal purpose of the Church is the advancement of the Christian faith
through evangelism and discipleship. The Church may also advance
education and carry out other charitable purposes in the United Kingdom
and/or other parts of the world."
The church building on Parkway is held by the Baptist Union Corporation Ltd,
on Trusts which are compatible with the above object. The church also
occupied a second building at 41-45 Broadwater Road under license, which
ended in January 2016 and in December 2015 began occupation of a
second permanent building in Peartree site, which is owned directly by the
Church.
Organisational Structure
Members of the church are accepted in accordance with the constitution.
Christchurch is a Charitable Incorporated Organisation (CIO) with Managing
Trustees (Leadership Team) appointed by church members in accordance
with the constitution approved in 2013.
Decision making is also in accordance with the constitution. The Trustees
(Leadership Team) are empowered to make decisions on how the church is
run, however, certain decisions can only be made by the membership of the
church at the church meeting (as detailed in the Constitution) These may be
matters brought to the church by the leadership team for discussion and, as
appropriate, acceptance, or matters raised in a church meeting by members
for further consideration by the leadership team.
Trustees Responsibilities
Charity law requires Trustees to prepare accounts which give a true and fair
view of the state of affairs of the CIO and of its income and expenditure for
the financial year. In doing SO, the Trustees are required to:
a) select suitable accounting policies and apply them consistently;
b) make judgements and estimates which are reasonable and prudent;
c) prepare the accounts on an ongoing concern basis, unless it is
inappropriate to presume that the CIO will continue in operation;
d) follow applicable accounting standards and the Charities SORP,
disclosing and explaining any departures in the financial statements
3
The Trustees are responsible for maintaining proper accounting records which
disclose with reasonable accuracy at any time the financial position of the
Charity and to enable them to ensure that the accounts comply with the
Charities Act 2011 They are also responsible for safeguarding the assets of the
Charity and hence for taking reasonable steps for the prevention and
detection of fraud and other irregularities. The Trustees are also required to be
aware of the Charity Commission's guidance on public benefit and to take it
into account in their decision-making on behalf of the church.
Objectives and Activities
The church's activities seek to meet our principal purpose by sharing the love
of Jesus in practical ways as well as providing ways of explaining our faith to
others - all activities seek to show the love of Jesus and bring people into a
closer relationship with him. The church provides a variety of activities both to
its membership and to the wider community.
The church structures activities under 5 key headings - worship, outreach,
relationships, discipleship and serving. This is reflected in the leadership team
(trustees) with each leader being responsible for one of these areas plus
leaders responsible for administration, property, finance and children &
families.
Public benefit
The leadership team has given consideration to the charity commission's
guidance on public benefit and in particular the specific guidance on
charities for the advancemen of religion. In particular they have ensured the
church provides a variety of activities both to its membership and to the loca
community. The aim is to show the love of Jesus Christ in both word and deed
and to bring people into a closer relationship with him as living Lord through
worship, prayer, teaching, pastoral care, mission and social outreach work.
Significan numbers for 2015
Over 1,800 people served
Over 150 volunteers
Over 15,000 volunteer hours
As part of our desire to ensure that our activities are accessible to all, any
charges are kept to a nominal level and where fees are charged to cover
the costs of events, courses or trips, bursaries are made available for those
who would otherwise be unable to participate.
4
Objectives 2015
Engage a wider range of people in fellowship and serving in the
different ministries of Christchurch, including re-launching The Shape
Course, designed to help people find out where they could serve as
part of the church community, and holding a Ministry Fair
To help people grow deeper in discipleship - especially practical
training and resourcing in personal evangelism
To move into a new church and community centre in Peartree that will
be the Christchurch 'hub' to resource mission across the town - will
require planning consent for change of use and the development of
plans and the completion of remodelling the building.
To develop new partnerships in the Peartree area as we seek to serve
more people
To identify and train leaders within Christchurch
To enjoy and foster our sense of being one church made up of people
of all ages from a diverse range of backgrounds and ethnic groups
To monitor the financial impact of an additional full-time minister and a
building purchase
To send a team to Peru to help develop and encourage the work with
adults with disabilities in Arequipa.
To launch two congregations, Christchurch Parkway & Christchurch
Peartree
How did we do?
The purchase and re-shaping of a new church and community area
took place - with successfU planning permission granted for change of
use, and builders handing over the building in December 2015.
We launched a second Sunday congregation at the original Parkway
site in Sept 2015 - giving US two congregations with a mission focus for
both the Parkway & Peartree areas.
We re-launched the S.H.A.P.E. course and ran it twice through the year
with people discovering or re-evaluating how they are best shaped by
God to serve and minister. The Ministry Fairs gave opportunities for
people to sign up to serve in new ways - much needed with additional
ministries emerging and people required for each base. We ended the
year with some areas requiring additional volunteers to get involved.
We welcomed a former President of the Baptist Union for a Sunday
service with practical training on outreach into neighbourhoods and
the town centre.
5
We developed a reading partnership with Peartree School - a number
of adults from Christchurch go in each week to read with the pupils.
The training of ministry leaders was postponed until 2016
We held an International Celebration - a relaxed, fun informative
evening celebrating the growing rich diversity in the congregation
A Christchurch team went to Arequipa, Peru (Latin Link) to work with a
group of adults and children with special needs and to work alongside
the local church
6
Introduction
let US run with perseverance the race marked out for US, fixing our eyes on
Jesus, the pioneer and perfecter of faith." Hebrews 12:1-2
Over the last few years at Christchurch we have sought to work out our God-
given dream to see lives and communities throughout Welwyn Garden City
transformed by God's love. There has been a sense that this is a marathon
journey not a sprint Perseverance was certainly key as we "ran the race
marked out for US" through 2015.. and SO was the need to keep the source of
our faith journey within focus, fixing our eyes on Christ Jesus throughout the
twists and turns.
Highlights would include the granting of planning permission and subsequent
purchase of Indigo Court, the design process for the re-shaping of the
building into a church and community centre in the Peartree part of town,
the financing of the project and the actual building work. Highlights would
also include the sense of mission and purpose as two different Sunday
morning congregations launched their first services in September.
All these were exciting developments, but also stretching and time-
consuming for many individuals who gave of their time and expertise. 2015
underlined how much Christchurch depends on the ministry and servant-
hearted attitude of SO many in the church. The scope of the ministries and
reach of the church goes way beyond what the staff team can cover - we
really do require everyone with their hands on deck!
We praise God for his faithfulness in guiding US through the different ventures
and for granting US the grace to persevere and pull through the challenges
that inevitably cropped up. We praise God for the many partners, agencies,
grant-making trusts and friends who expressed their support and recognition
of our vision as they supported our planning application for change of use or
promised financial help towards the building purchase and works.
But maybe the highlights above are equalled by the individual stories of lives
that are changing. It has been good seeing people of different ages and
backgrounds taking steps in their discipleship journey. Baptisms are a
particularly special focus for this, and it was a joy to see people new to
church and Christianity coming to know Christ and being baptised This
included youngsters who had grown up in Christchurch, but also those of no
church background who had come through community fun days,
community activities and invitations to church services and events.
7
These glimpses of God at work in people's lives, bringing change and hope,
have certainly helped punctuate the challenging periods of the year and
helped US persevere in Christ.
Read on to see how the many serving activities of Christchurch have helped
many people on a journey of hope and connection with others.
8
Review of significant activities
The centre point of our shared life together is when we gather together on
Sundays for worship and midweek in small groups held in people's homes.
Worship
Worship is central to everything we do at Christchurch by being the
motivation for all our serving activities amongst members and within the
community. We gather for Sunday services aiming to be inclusive and
accessible to all visitors and regular attenders alike by creating an
environment where people can explore what it means to know God
personally and draw closer to Him.
Our sung worship ranges in style to include traditional forms but is mainly
modern with a rotation of live bands. In September, with the spread to two
sites we were pleased to add a number of new musicians to the regular
bands. One band has welcomed two new members at Parkway and the
band has gelled well as they lead a growing congregation. We are very
blessed by the number of those willing to serving in music ministry who
dedicate time to practice and early starts before services. A few times a year
a youth band lead the service and it is great to see this continue as new
young people joining each year while others move on to University.
During the year we provided training for those new to PA and AV and both
sound and vision teams have grown significantly to support our worship at two
sites.
Alongside sung worship is intercessory prayer and individual prayer ministry run
by a team who offer to pray for anyone after every service. Regular prayer is
also an important part of our time at Christchurch with weekly early morning
prayer meetings and gatherings before every service.
Morning services include a variety of media, drama, film clips, songs, quizzes
and games around the theme of the teaching. Once a month, Church
family news allows anyone in the congregation to share a piece of good
news with the church family SO we can celebrate as a community what God
is doing in our lives. This has been especially helpful in allowing the
congregation to get to know each other more as the church grows.
Small groups at Christchurch are run to disciple, grow, challenge and support
those who attend. The majority of people who attend also attend church
regularly and the groups include a range of adults in the church from mums
to seniors. We have 14 small groups across the town and which run at
different times of the day and evening, most running in term time with breaks
9
for holidays. 12 of those groups have been structured broadly geographically,
1
has been run for Mums on a Monday during the day and one has
continued as a group which was initiated specifically for people who have
just finished Alpha but need further continuity before moving into one of the
'geographic' groups.
The small groups have continued to develop over the last year and some
new leaders have come forward to further develop existing groups and to
begin new groups. We have around 35 volunteers leading and hosting
groups. We are always looking for people who would like to host or lead a
group, our vision is to have a small group that would suit everyone in the
church.
Highlights of the year include new people joining groups and stepping into
leadership positions. The church Fun Day was a great time when many of the
groups worked together to provide free fun activities for our local community.
Also many of the groups worked together to help with our big move into our
new building helping to strengthen the sense of community.
Other activities
A large number of activities are run for the benefit of the local community by
volunteers in the church as we seek to share God's love with the local
community.
The ministry to Senior Citizens within Christchurch has continued positively,
with significant growth throughout 2015. We praise God for His grace and
provision in bringing SO many new folk to the activities and for blessing US with
helpers and people to pray for the work and other peripheral support,
commitment and energy when it has been needed at key points during such
a busy year in the life of Christchurch.
Key activities at Parkway are: the monthly Senior Citizens' Lunch; the
fortnightly Harvesters' teatime fellowship; the weekly Reach Out exercise
class; and the Holiday at Home summer seniors' community event. The new
chair-based exercise class, launched at Broadwater Road in September, is
running really well and will transfer to Peartree from 19th January 2016.
Holiday at Home is subsidised with funds from Reach Out. All other regular
ministries are self-financing and continue to be supported with prayer both
around and within the separate events.
It is both a privilege and a testimony to God's leading that we connect
meaningfully with nearly 200 different seniors across the seniors' activities.
Most are sympathetic and receptive to the expression of our faith through
events, speakers, personal testimony, prayer, conversations and home visits
10
and some of our guests attend Sunday services. With the spread to Parkway
for the Sunday morning services and the newly refurbished building at
Peartree, we hope to draw more seniors into the Sunday community and
through the next steps of their persona faith journeys.
The Senior Citizens' Lunch takes place at Parkway on the last Saturday of
each month, where he objective is to serve a hot meal at midday and show
God's love through service, companionship and a short talk during dessert.
Attendance rose throughout 2015 to 65 - 72+ ticket sales per month and it is
anticipated that this will continue to grow, although numbers have to be
capped at 78, due to the limitation of space. The cost of the lunch remains at
E3.50 per head for a two-course meal, including drinks. We now offer
complementary hot beverages from 10.30am and numbers have increased,
bringing a real bUzz to the morning. Surplus funds have been used to
purchase more china, cutlery and cooking equipment to cover the increase
in numbers. We continue to draw helpers from a team of 15-20 volunteers
from within the fellowship. Our younger helpers have increased and are much
appreciated.
The Christmas lunch at just E5.00 for three courses with festive fizz, was an early
sell-out again with 78 tickets sold, representing the largest number of guests to
any single lunch over the year.
Harvesters is our afternoon tea event, held at Parkway twice a month.
Regular guests number 30-35, many of whom are new this year, including
several men. The capacity of the Body and Soul room remains a challenge
with the increasing numbers and walking aids.
A 30-45 minute speaking/entertainment/craft slot forms the basis of the
afternoon, followed by tea and home-made cake. Andrew and Simon, our
pastors, members of the Christchurch fellowship, several local ministers and
representatives from the community have spoken and performed, as have
some of the Harvesters themselves. There is a real sense of excitement and
coming together, which is very encouraging.
A Befriending Ministry was successfully piloted in early 2015 as a planned
programme of home visiting, offering companionship and identifying care
and protection issues for our more vulnerable seniors. This will be reviewed
and possibly expanded in 2016.
We also offered an Alpha course for Seniors and had planned a Songs of
Praise for Senior Citizens to support the Alpha Programme. Although there
was some initial interest, the Alpha course was withdrawn. However, there
are plans to run a Songs of Praise in 2016.
11
Reach Out provides a Strength, Flexibility and Mobility Exercise Class at
Parkway every week all year round. Attendance currently averages 30
people from the local community and there is a waiting list. Following the
class, everyone is invited into the Body & Soul cafe: about 15-20 enjoy
catching up with each other over a cuppa. Some also stay on for the lovely
home-cooked lunches that Body and Soul provides.
A chair-based exercise class was started at Broadwater Road in September.
It runs from 10.15 - 11.15am on Tuesday mornings throughout the year to
overlap with the CA in the hope that it would provide increased exposure of
that service to the Senior Citizens. Numbers rose quickly and most of the 30+
participants have indicated they will be regular attendees at Peartree in
2016.
Both Reach Out classes are self-financing, with surplus funds used to provide
Christmas and Easter gifts for the Seniors and on occasions, to support the
work of other Senior Citizens' ministries, such as Holiday at Home and
Harvesters.
Once again, Holiday at Home was much appreciated during the long
summer break and comprised two consecutive days held at Parkway in mid-
August. The ticket price was E5.00 per day and additional costs were
financed from the Reach Out funds, which enabled US to offer a wide variety
of high quality activities and craft workshops. Each day offered an
opportunity to come together and enjoy all-day refreshments, punctuated by
a variety of activities: acrylic painting workshops, craft tables, embroidery
workshops, colouring tables, jigsaws, quiet rooms, newspapers, music, singing,
floor and table games and a nail bar. We also welcomed the Woodturners'
Association, who guided folk through two different projects, producing top
quality pens and dibbers. In addition, we were blessed to be able to enjoy
the musica talents of a professional London busker, who played and sang
throughout the two days, free of charge, to great acclaim. 60 folk in total
attended the event over the two days, served by a team of 30 helpers from
within the Christchurch fellowship.
During 2015 our Body and Soul cafe continued to open for coffee and
lunches on Wednesdays and Thursdays during term time, between 11.00am
and 2.00pm. We provided meals for about 40 people per day. Thursdays
during 2015 were significantly busier than Wednesdays - with extra people
who had attended the chair based exercise class on the premises staying on
for coffee and/or lunch at Body and Soul. About 90% of the customers came
from the wider community, and the other 10% from within the church. Many
of our regulars are senior citizens and live alone. We have appreciated the
growing links with other parts of the church-work amongst the over 60s. We
12
also welcomed some of the pre-school parents with young children for lunch.
A group from Hornbeams Centre for adults with disabilities were also regulars.
A team of 30 volunteers comprising church members and friends of the
church were involved in menu planning, shopping, vegetable preparation,
cooking, serving, washing up, setting up, tidying up, keeping the accounts
etc. Our very long standing manager eventually left the team when she
moved from the area. Prices charged remained the same during 2015
despite continuing rises in our grocery bill. Occasionally we supplied a meal
for free where this seemed appropriate - or sent a meal out to someone
where we were aware of particular needs. Surplus income of around E4000
was donated to the Tumaini Children's Home near Jinja, Uganda. Body and
Soul also contributed a similar sum to genera church funds in recognition of
fuel used in cooking and heating
Body and Soul has a 5 star (top) rating for Food Hygiene
The Christchurch Hospitality Team, provide self-service tea, coffee, squash
and biscuits at the end of the morning service. We currently provide
refreshments for around 350 adults and children in the mornings and 20-40
adults in the evenings.
Highlights for 2015 include providing refreshments for the various baptismal
and dedication services, as well as the Carols by Candlelight service.
Christchurch continues to offer a warm welcome to those attend our services.
The Welcoming and Stewarding Team comprises 27 volunteers who greet and
seat an ever-growing congregation.
Three welcome evenings were held during 2015 for those who were new to
the church, attended by about 30 people in all.
A British Sign Language (BSL) ministry has begun in recent years We have two
people from the Deaf signing community who come to Sunday morning
services, one lady who attends with her hearing son and one single man.
We have one church member with a level 2 BSL qualification who signs most
morning and some evening services. There are five others who have or are
working towards a level 1 BSL qualification. There is also a group of 12 others
who meet monthly to learn some basic BSL, such as simple greetings requests
for tea, coffee, biscuits etc and look at how best to sign familiar songs used in
church.
The church provides a budget which provides a qualified interpreter for up to
four church services and for the two men's teaching days per year.
13
Children and young people are also well catered for. The church employs a
Children & Families worker, supported by many volunteers and we also have
a part-time youth worker.
On Sunday mornings, we provide a range of age specific groups from a self-
service creche through TotZone, Bubbles and KidZone. Each group has its
own room and a dedicated team of volunteers catering for children from
age 1 up until the end of school year 5 (age 10). The children start off in the
church service for a time of all-age worship before leaving for their own
groups while their parents are able to go back in to the service. The biggest
impact on the Sunday groups this year has been the spread across both sites
on a Sunday morning. From September, we have been running the same
groups at both sites, which has led to an increase in the number of teams and
volunteers needed.
We had 109 children on the books at the end of the year, with about 58
attending most weeks, which is a slight increase in last year. This year we had
very few children who moved up to the youth groups and a large number
move from our Bubbles group to KidZone.
In addition there are a number of other activities run for the benefit of all in
the community.
Kings Club (Parkway) serves between 10 20 children aged 7-10 from 15
different families every Wednesday evening in term time. Some children
come to Christchurch on a Sunday, but the majority come from the local
community and have no other connection with the church. We charge a
small fee of 50p a week which goes towards the costs of the variety of craft
activities each week. Having seen a big drop in numbers last year when we
had a large number of children move up we slowly increased our numbers
during the first two terms however since September numbers have dropped
off and we will spend some time next year looking at ways to advertise. This
group has a lovely core group of children who come and we have enjoyed
the time getting to know them better.
Activities vary week to week and our programme ranges from club nights
when we play a mix of games (Wii, Xbox, PlayStation table tennis and board
games), to cooking, den making and trips out, to walks through the woods in
different seasons, water games - to name just a few! We held an event for
parents to join in: 'Challenge your parent night' where parents came and
experienced a Kings Club night. Parents also joined US for the last session
before the summer for fun and a BBQ. This club is run by a team of six
volunteers.
14
KidZclub (Broadwater) was set up in September 2013 at our Broadwater Road
site, to be a fun group serving children aged 7-10, on Thursday evenings in
term time. Between Jan and July 2015 our numbers grew and we had
around 30 children who regularly came. By September this number had
dropped to around 15 as we had to say good bye to a big group of those
going into year 6. Some families who had been coming had been in
temporary housing and had moved on in the summer and others had started
new groups or changed to our Wednesday group. The majority of the
children come from the local community and have no other connection with
the church. We charge a small fee of 50p a week which goes towards the
costs of the variety of craft activities each week.
Within the group during the earlier part of the year we had a number of
children whose behaviour had been more challenging. Even though this
stretched the team we were able to build relationships with them and their
families. Like Kings Club we enjoyed having the parents come to the
'Challenge your parents night', the children enjoyed a beetle drive night and
we even managed an evening of water games in the summer.
Family Fun events were held at our Broadwater Rd site and provided an
exciting and creative environment encouraging local families to engage in
craft activities with their children. Each session included numerous craft
activities, a story and fun song time -all based on a Bible theme. Aimed at
families with children 0-10 years they run for 1 12 hrs (with morning and
afternoon sessions) with a small charge per family.
We held 3 Family Fun events last year, (Feb half term, Easter and Oct half
term) Our February sessions had 250 adults and children and are theme was
'Noah'. Our Easter Event was only an afternoon session as schools had broken
up that day but we still had a great numbers with 229 adults and children.
October half term we saw 256 adults and children which had a 'Super Hero'
theme.
Some of the families that come are regulars at other activities including
Toddle Inn and First Friday, some are Church members, but the majority come
from the local community through our links with the local Children's Centres
and Schools Partnership Consortium. These events are a great way of building
relationships with local families and introducing them to other activities at
Christchurch. There are 12 volunteers on team who gave 320 hours of their
time to run these events.
First Friday events are similar to Family Fun - but are held every month on the
first Friday of term time after school and are aimed at families with primary
school age children (but younger children are still able to come) Starting with
cakes and drinks, followed by a range of craft based around a Bible story
15
theme and each session ends with a quiz / game / drama based on the Bible
story and a BIG action song. Each session runs for 75 minutes with a small
charge of El per child. These are held at our Parkway site.
We ran 9 events during 2015 - 3 each term. The majority of families come from
the local community and many attend the local school (Applecroft). Most
growth comes from personal recommendations and there is a real buzz
around at every event. Numbers have varied this year from 36 to 65 children
and parents and the families attending change as families with older children
stop coming, parents return to work, and at the other end new families start
to attend. The group is run by a team of 5 volunteers.
In the summer holidays we ran 'Polar Explorer' a Holiday club for children
aged 5-10 (school year 1-5) based on a bible theme with games, songs,
puppets and group time. Children came from the local community, Family
Fun regulars as well as Christchurch families. The club was run for 4 mornings
212 hours each day. A registration fee was payable which covered the cost
of a special Club tee shirt and a small fee was charged for each session. Free
places were made available and taken up by several families.
This was our fourth year of running a summer holiday club. We used the Polar
Explorer Scripture Union material and recreated the main room into our
explorer base with Igloos as each group's base. We had 4 teams that were
split into two age groups; each age group name was an artic animal. 80
children attended over the week with an average of 70 a day as some only
did part of the week. Highlights were using gazebos as Igloos, a wonderful
milk bottle Igloo made by one of the team and their family, seeing many of
our youth take on roles, with plenty of craft, fun games, interesting bible bits,
wonderfu laughter that filled the building and lots of smiling faces. The last
day we invited parents for a picnic which we provided (thanks to a wonderful
member and her team who did the hard work preparing them) and we were
able to show the parents a video clip of the fun we had during the week.
45 volunteers gave about 600 hours between them to run this event together
with our Children & Families worker.
Toddle inn is the toddler group that meets at 10.00-11.30am every Tuesday
during term time at Parkway It is aimed at pre-schoo children and their
parents/carers. We have 35 -45 children at the morning session and have to
run a waiting list for spaces due to the high demand for places. The majority
of the parents/carers come from outside the church, many have no church
link, but some go to other churches and a few from Christchurch.
The session is split into two main parts, firstly a general play in the main hall,
followed by a bible story and songs. Refreshments are then served in the
16
body and soUl room. Most children attend with their parents but we have
some childminders, nannies and grandparents.
As we look forward to 2016, we are looking forward to a new Toddler group
starting at Peartree and Toddle inn will help support this.
Finding Space
This is a drop-in toddler group aimed at young parents or those looking for a
small support group. This group meets at Space in the town centre, the YMCA
Youth and Community centre. Finding Space is a partnership project
between Christchurch, St. Francis and the Free Church. This is a free group
aimed to be easy to access for those parents not attending other parent and
toddler groups. The group is supported by 1 Christchurch volunteer together
with volunteers from the other churches.
Finding Space started at the beginning of June 2008 as soon as YMCA Space
opened. After a challenging few years (with numerous changes of location
and a need for a co-coordinator), and with Space being moved from a town
centre base to be based at the Peartree Road YMCA Hostel site we made
the hard decision to stop this group. We have had a wonderful 6 years both
partnering with the YMCA and other local churches. We still keep in touch
with some of the families we know through this group and see them at our
Family Fun days, the Lounge and other events we run. We had a lovely last
week in July inviting back volunteers who had made this group possible.
Back to school coffee and cake is run as a drop in event in September at the
Parkway site when the children go back to school. For the first 2 mornings of
term, we offered coffee, cake and tissues for parents of both new and
returning children.
Our Children & Families Worker has been a member of Applecroft Children's
Centre Partnership group and also Oak Tree Children Centre Advisory board,
attending their half termly meetings which include health visitors, pre-school
leaders, child minder co-coordinators and other providers of activities for
under-5s in the area. Since the reorganisation in 2015, she has become an
advisory board member for both the Welwyn Garden City and Welwyn and
Knebworth groups. We also have links with the School Partnership.
Our Children and Families worker has been involved with setting up a group
for all those who head-up Children's Work in churches across Welwyn Garden
City. These meet half termly, hosted by each church in turn to pray,
encourage one another and share good practice & ideas.
17
Pathways & Stepping stones: This is just a snapshot of the many activities we
provide at Christchurch to support families & children in our local
communities. One of our aims over the last few years has been to build
pathways and stepping stones for people to experience more of God's love
through different events and activities at Christchurch.
As we review 2015 we get a chance to stop and look back and be reminded
of all the great conversations with families we have had and the positive
feedback we get from families who attend our groups. One parent who
could no longer come to Toddle Inn said 'Thank you for the sessions we
attended. My child had a lot of fun, and I really appreciate the wonderful
work you are doing. I especially enjoyed hearing stories from the Bible and
the songs. We will miss it.
Sunday morning provision for young people is made up of three groups,
which meet during the main service. The groups aim to help the young
people understand and grow in their faith, and give them an opportunity to
discuss this and how it applies to them, and the impact it can have on their
lives.
Distinctive (School year 6) LaunchPad (School year 7 & 8) and LaunchPad+
(School year 9+) meet each Sunday during the morning service. The groups
are open to any young person present on a Sunday morning. The groups aim
to help the young people understand and grow in their faith, and give them
an opportunity to discuss this and how it applies to them, and the impact it
can have on their lives.
In September 2015 the Church spread to two sites, one in Peartree and one
at the Parkway building. Though we were at first unsure of how many young
people would be at the Parkway site, we started a group, which we
retrospectively named Intergr8 for those youth aged (schoo year 6+)
628 runs on a Friday night for those in schools years 6, 7 and 8. It is open to
both church and non-church young people. The evening intends to be a fun
place, where everyone is welcome, and can participate in the various
activates that take place. Some weeks there will be a specific part of the
evening to look at a certain aspect of Christianity, and other weeks this is
undertaken through informal conversation with the young people.
Over the year 30 young people have attended, with an average of 14 each
week. The group is supported by a team of volunteers and our youth worker.
Ignite, After 8's and Youth Alpha
Ignite runs on a Sunday evening following the evening service. It is open to
young people in school year 9+. The group aims to allow a time for socialising,
18
followed by investigating a bible passage, or topic relevant to the young
people present. It is predominantly aimed at those aged (year 11-13).
Following the running of Youth Alpha in the spring of 2015 a second Sunday
night group was created called After 8's. This group allowed those that had
attended Youth Alpha to grow and develop as a group and in their faith, it is
also aimed at those in school years 9+ predominantly (School years 9-11).
Highlights
Running Youth Alpha in spring 2015
Baptism of 3 young people
Forming a new "After 8's group on a Sunday evening
Forming a new "integr8" group at Parkway on a Sunday morning
Overnight camp in September with 25 young people from Christchurch
Christmas Banquet in December with 42 young people from
Christchurch and 628
Furniture Garage has now been running for 18 years providing free furniture,
bedding and household goods donated by church contacts to local families
and individuals in need.
In 2015, we dealt with about 100 requests and offers and helped 24 families.
Other changes include starting a Facebook page where people can donate
and growing links with Recover, a local social enterprise, which have included
the use of their van for collections and deliveries. In 2016 we will be opening
a new dedicated Furniture Garage space on our Peartree site.
Worn Again gives families the chance to fill a bag with good quality 2nd hand
children's clothes for El. People are referred or can attend a coffee morning
arranged through a school partnership or a drop-in group. It also will source
school uniforms where a need is identified by family workers who work for the
school partnership This group serves people in our local communities.
In 2015 Worn Again held 5 events at a local school, and it was accessed
through the Lounge, which takes place weekly at our Peartree site. Worn
Again has also helped with a number of referrals asking for age specific
clothes which included referrals from Christchurch Furniture garage. There is a
small team of 4 who have run this with the support of 2 small groups.
Parish Nursing - our parish nurse started in April 2012 for one day a week
(normally a Tuesday) The project is affiliated to Parish Nursing Ministries UK.
This is a voluntary post which aims to provide holistic health care,
complementing both the work of local health services and that which the
church provides through the ministers, pastoral team and membership
19
The parish nurse sees individuals with health issues who attend, or are
contacts of the church and its activities. She also offers support to those within
the church who are caring for those with health issues in their family or
community. She liaises with other professionals, including GPs and hospitals,
for those with more complex needs.
This year 57 individuals have been supported with physical and/or mental
health issues, ranging from support for parents of newborn babies to assisting
those requiring end of life care. Strong links have been maintained with a
number of local health and community organisations, particularly through the
Welwyn Hatfield Inclusion Forum.
Parish Nursing is an integral part of The Lounge, a drop-in provided alongside
the Citizen's Advice (CA) which commenced in early 2014. This has provided
an accessible route for other agencies to refer individuals who they feel
would benefit from the support Parish Nursing is able to offer.
The aim of The Lounge is to provide a neutral space inside the church building
where members of the local community can meet up socially and come for
support and advice from our Parish Nurse and Children and families worker. It
is also an access and information point for other services both those within the
church such as the Furniture Garage and Worn Again and services known to
US in the wider community such as charities and local authority provision.
The Lounge serves the local community, including people waiting for CA
appointments, and others who have prearranged appointments with
members of the church staff or pastoral team. Our regulars tend to be those
who live nearby some of whom are members of the church and others who
participate in other church run initiatives, for example children's clubs, Finding
space, Body and Soul, Worn again and Furniture Garage.
The Lounge team also invite leaders/ co-ordinators of other local community
services to attend staff lunch, which precedes the lounge session. This enables
US to share information on services and build good referral links, Our lunch
guests have included representatives from CAP and YMCA The New Zion
Food bank, local health visitors and school support workers.
The aim of the Alpha course is to introduce people to Jesus and to answer
questions to those on a spiritual journey. We have church and non-churched
men and ladies from teenagers to senior citizens attending. Christchurch ran
three Alpha courses in 2015, two in the spring and one in the autumn, Monday
evening at Parkway and Wednesday mornings at Broadwater, with a creche
provided. Around 26 guests attended courses this year supported by a team
of 7 leaders and helpers.
20
The Evening Cafe combines a night of performance and entertainment in a
cafe-style setup with delicious puddings, indoor sports and activities, and
fundraising. Admission is free and worthy causes (local and overseas) are
supported through the event, and have an opportunity to inform the
audience about their work. In 2015 over 290 people attended the two
Evening Cafes, held in April and November. Over E3,700 was raised and
shared between:
The Welwyn Hatfield Women's Refuge
Christian Aid Refugee Crisis Appeal
Peru Team 2015
Recover
Band Of Brothers (BOB) is a ministry to men, formed in partnership with
Christian Vision for Men (CVM) aimed at encouraging and developing
support for men including in the discipleship and integration of men in the
church. It aims to engage men through social activities, as well as supporting
their role in family life. It includes the popular 'Men's Breakfast' which meets
monthly.
Social events in 2015 included an evening with former professional footballer
Linvoy Primus and a fabulous midsummer's night walk through the Brocket
estate in June. 'Men Behaving Dadly survival special was held at Harmer
Green woods Scout camp which included afternoon activities and an
overnight camp. This provided a fun environment for dads and children to
spend some quality time together and created opportunities to build
relationships. Just over 60 attended this event with 30 camping overnight. This
included some dads from outside of the church.
Monthly Men's breakfasts and a two teaching days were also held in 2015.
These have a more Christian fOCUS with a variety of guest speakers.
Sister Soul is a ministry to women (and girls 14+) and has run events through
the year including breakfasts and teaching days to encourage Christian
women to grow in their faith.
21
Christchurch also supports overseas mission focussing on a small number of
partnerships where we know and can connect both with the mission and
missionaries - and with what they do. Our current links are with:
Paul and Ruth Turner with Latin Link in Peru. Paul leads the work in Peru
and is also working on strengthening the leadership of the Peruvian
group. Ruth works with short term mission groups from this country who
visit Peru and individuals from Peru itself visiting the UK. They have also
worked with young adults with disabilities helping them make the
transition from school to the community.
Paul and Clare Woodington with Mission Aviation Fellowship in Papua
New Guinea providing flying support to the local communities in the
Highlands
Beni and Irma Xhako in Albania who have a music and worship ministry
in the churches there.
Pastor Nicholas who runs the Tumaini orphanage and a school in
Uganda
Cynthia and lan Chadwell who are working in medical administration
in Nepal with BMS World Mission.
It is important to US as a church to maintain good relational links with those we
support, SO it was good to have a team visit the work in Peru in the
summer and to revisit the church with whom we have been connected and
Arequipa to work with the disabled young adults group there. The
Woodingtons and the Chadwells visited US during the year as well. A group
plan to visit Albania in 2016 to help on a worship conference.
Christchurch is a caring community 'because people matter to God'. The
growing numbers associated with the church continued to bring new
challenges in 2015, presenting a diverse range of pastoral needs.
Pastoral Care is overseen by the lead Minster and a Pastoral Core Team,
which includes our Parish Nurse, and Associate Minister. Most of the caring is
done in and around the growing number of small groups in the church. The
Core group meets every 2 weeks to review and pray over the needs of
individuals in the fellowship, trying to make sure that everyone is linked in.
22
Property
One of our main objectives for this year was to move into a new church and
community centre in Peartree that will be the Christchurch 'hub' to resource
mission across the town. This required planning consent for change of use
and the development of plans and the completion of remodelling the
building.
Having exchanged contracts for the purchase of a former office building in
the Peartree Community in December 2014 we were delighted to be
granted planning permission for change of use of the building to a Church
and Community Centre on 23 April 2015 (for an initial term of five years) - we
then completed the purchase of the building the next day!
Plans to remodel the former workshops and offices into a range of spaces for
community and church use were finalised over the summer and we instructed
builders who started on site in September. An amazing transformation took
place and we took possession of the remodelled building on Friday 18
December 2015.
Over a hundred volunteers spent thousands of hours over the following two
weeks moving US from our temporary home of three years on Broadwater
Road, when most other people were relaxing over the Christmas and New
Year break. It was a mammoth task and amazing evidence of what can be
achieved when people come together as a team bringing their individual
gifts and skills. We had people painting, building kitchens, plumbing, laying
carpets, driving a lorry, dismantling and re-assembling cupboards, making
coffee, making sandwiches as wel as people praying for every aspect of the
project. We couldn't have done this without the support of everyone involved
in SO many different ways.
We were delighted that the first group to use the building was the Citizens
Advice team who have been partnering with US for two years, providing drop
in advice sessions to people from the local community.
We held our first service in the newly named Christchurch Peartree on Sunday
10 January, bringing together all of our Christchurch people, which was a real
celebration of the hard work that had gone into the process over the
previous five years, but especially the work over the Christmas period moving
US in.
The following Sunday Christchurch continued meeting in two locations, with
one congregation meeting in our original building on Parkway in the west side
of the town, where we continue to serve that community.
23
We have invested over El.6million in buying and remodelling this building
creating our second base - the majority of the funding has come from church
members, plus a mortgage of E500,000 (plus grants of E91,500 towards the
kitchen and community cafe.
A formal opening celebration was held at the end of February to which we
welcomed many guests from partnership organisations, as well as local
councillors and the mayor - and we were able to reflect on the journey we
had been on over the previous 5 years, noting God's guidance, blessing and
provision every step of the way.
It was also important to note that this was a milestone - not the end of the
story but the next step of our journey as a church as we seek to serve our
local communities, and we pray that God will continue to go ahead of US as
we continue to build partnerships and identify how best we can use the gifts,
skills and resources that God has given US as we serve the Peartree
community.
Impact
Christchurch has been through a period of rapid change in 2015.
Attendance continued to grow at Sunday morning worship in the Broadwater
Road building in the early part of the year and in September 2015 the church
'spread' into two congregations - one meeting at Broadwater and the other
at our Parkway building. People chose which congregation they wished to
attend, and both quickly settled into fully viable worshipping expressions that
'felt like' Christchurch. The change has had the very positive benefit of
encouraging people to get to know each other better.
The change put some strain on those people serving on Sunday mornings
(preachers, worship bands, children and young people's leaders) but both
congregations continued to attract new people. By the end of the year,
more than 200 adults were present (about 60% at Broadwater and 40% at
Parkway) after children and young people (and their leaders) had separated
to their own groups. Over 300 people in total gather each week.
The two congregations have somewhat different demographics - but both
have a good age range, and diversity. We aim to make our meetings
accessible to people who are exploring 'church' for the first time.
As in 2014 the increase in formal membership of the church (up by 6 to 162)
has not kept pace with the growth of the church generally. 12 new members
were welcomed, one member died and 5 members moved away from the
area. In 2015, we began to transfer our primary membership list to the new
CIO body, and we will complete the change in 2016.
24
11 people confessed their faith in Jesus by being baptised in 2015 4 infants
were dedicated and one church couple was married in the year;
During 2015 the church served over 1,800 people
through its wide range of activities.
As is demonstrated above, many of those attending Christchurch volunteer to
provide a wide range of activities many of which directly benefit the wider
community, who would otherwise have no church links. It is estimated that the
church provided over 15,000 volunteer hours in addition to paying for a
Children & Families Worker and a part time youth worker who initiate and
lead many activities for the benefit of the community, supported by unpaid
volunteers. Many of these activities have grown throughout the year, thereby
enabling more of those in the community to access and benefit from the
activities and resources of the church.
Move to a Charitable Incorporated Organisation (CIO)
In 2013 the trustees and the church took the decision to move the church
from a charity to a Charitable Incorporated Organisation (CIO). The new CIO,
Christchurch Baptist Welwyn Garden City Registration number: 1154616 was
incorporated on 18 November 2013 and work progressed throughout 2014 to
organise the transfer from Christchurch (Baptist), the charity The transfer deed
was signed on 12 April 2015 after the year end, and the transfer of the assets
and liabilities will be completed during 2015/6.
The activities of the church have continued to take place throughout this
time and the details have been reported within the CIO for 2015.

Vision & Future Plans
2015 finished with Christmas services and activities and a final service at Broadwater
Road, all wrapped up with packing boxes, offices and equipment ready for a move.
Over the Christmas and New Year period many volunteers helped tirelessly to
transport this to our new Peartree home and gave hours of their time to prepare
parts of the building for community activities and Sunday services.
So during 2016 we will be continuing our strong links with Citizens Advice and
transferring the Christchurch mid-week groups and activities to the new site. We also
have the opportunity to consider what new ministries might serve the needs of the
Peartree community.
It is important to monitor the effectiveness of the Christchurch "Spread" to two
Sunday morning congregations to see what needs to be done to keep these
communities healthy and focussed on the mission needs of both Parkway and
Peartree sites.
More than ever it is important for US to maintain our five core values of being Christ-
centred (Worship), outward-focussed (Outreach), relationally strong (Relationships),
spiritually growing (Discipleship) and servant-hearted (Serving).
To help US we are focussing on a Bible verse throughout 2016:
But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be
glory both now and for ever! Amen. 2Peter 3:18
This will impact our persona discipleship and the Sunday teaching programme, and
will also challenge US as we seek to extend grace-giving acceptance as we reach
out with God's love in new ways and places.
How we function as one church spread over more than one location will begin to
change and we will invest in building that sense of belonging and healthy
relationships for the onward journey. With new responsibilities we will consider what
the shape of leadership structures should look like, try to get the right people serving
in the right roles and begin the process of listening to God's guidance for the next
steps as a church fellowship
We remind ourselves that our existence and mission is rooted in the nature and
purposes of God, it is His work we are doing, and he equips US for all he calls US to do.
As we seek to make a difference in Jesus' name, person by person, may it be as it
says in our verse for the year - To him be glory both now and for ever! Amen.

Notes to the financial statements for the year ended 31st December 2015
Accounting policies
a. Basis of preparation
The accounts are prepared in accordance with the Accounting Regulations set out under the Charities Act 2011
and with the Charities Statement of Recommended Practice (SORP) Financial Reporting Standard for Smaller
Entities (the FRSSE) 2015.
b. Donations
Donations are accounted for gross when received
c. Legacies
Legacies are accounted for when their receipt is certain and can be properly quantified
d. Investment income
Investment income is included in the accounts in the year in which it is receivable
e. Fundraising and publicity costs
The Church does not make formal appeals for funds and expenditure on these items is therefore not material
f. Grants payable
The Church makes grants to other organisations whose charitable objects complement its work. Grants offered
subject to conditions which have not been met at the year-end date are noted as a commitment but not accrued
as expenditure. Grants are recognised as a liability when the church is under an obligation to make a payment or
the grant is paid over.
g. Governance costs
This represents direct expenditure on the governance of the Church.
h. Fixed assets
The Church premises are included in the balance sheet at cost. In the opinion of the trustees the market value of
the buildings is considerably greater than the carrying value. In the opinion of the trustees it is not practicable to
quantify the difference between these figures.
Fixed assets with a value over E1,000 are written off as expenditure in the Statement of Financial Activities,
unless it is considered appropriate to capitalise the expenditure on the Balance Sheet.
i. Depreciation
Depreciation has not been charged on the Church or Manse premises because in the opinion of the Trustees the
residual value of the asset is not less than the original cost price.
Depreciation on other fixed assets is calculated to write off the cost on a straight line basis over their expected
useful life at the following rates:
Buildings
2.5% pa / 40 years
Computers and equipment
33% pa / 3 years
Fixtures and Fittings / improvement to premises
20% pa / 5 years
Any asset which is considered to have been impaired as a result of damage, obsolescence, or no longer in use
for any other reason is written down at the date on which the impairment is identified.
j- Other expenditure
Expenditure is accounted for on an accruals basis and has been classified under headings that aggregate all cost
related to the category. Where costs cannot be directly attributed to particular headings they have been allocated

k. Fund accounting
Unrestricted funds can be used in accordance with the charitable objectives at the discretion of the trustees.
Funds designated for a particular purpose by the church are also unrestricted.
Restricted funds can only be used for particular restricted purposes within the objects of the charity. Restrictions
arise when specified by the donor or when funds are raised for particular restricted purposes. Further explanation
of the nature and purpose of each fund is included in the notes to the financial statements.
The accounts include all transactions, assets and liabilities for which the church is responsible in law. They do not
include the accounts of church groups that owe their main affiliation to another body nor those that are informal
gatherings of church members.

a result of the merger.
42
18. Pensions
The Church is an employer participating in a pension scheme known as the Baptist Pension Scheme ("the
Scheme"), which was known as the Baptist Ministers' Pension Fund until 31 Dec 2011 ("the Ministers' Fund"). The
Scheme is a separate legal entity which is administered by the Pension Trustee (Baptist Pension Trust Limited).
The Minister is eligible to join the Scheme, which is not contracted out of the State Second Pension.
The main benefits provided by the Ministers' Fund for service prior to 1 January 2012 are a defined benefit
pension of one eightieth of Final Minimum Pensionable Income for each year of Pensionable Service, together
with additional pension in respect of premiums paid on Pensionable Income in excess of Minimum Pensionable
Income. From 1 January 2009 Ministers paid 8% of their Pensionable Income and the employer paid 16%. The
Fund started in 1925 but was closed to future accrual of defined benefits on 31 Dec 2011.
From January 2012, pension provision is being made through the Defined Contribution (DC) Plan within the
Scheme. Members pay 8% of their Pensionable Income and employers pay 6% of members' Pensionable Income
into individual pension accounts which are operated and managed on behalf of the Pension Trustee by Legal and
General Life Assurance Society Limited. In addition, the employer pays a further 4% of Pensionable Income to
cover Death in Service Benefits, the administration of the DC Plan, and an associated insurance policy which
provides income protection for Scheme members in the event that they are unable to work due to long-term
incapacity. This income protection policy has been insured by the Baptist Union of Great Britain with Unum
Limited.
A formal valuation of the Ministers' Fund was performed at 31 December 2013 by a professionally qualified
Actuary using the Projected Unit Method. The market value of the Fund's assets at the valuation date was
E162million.
The valuation of the Ministers' Fund revealed a deficit of assets compared with the value of liabilities of E84million.
As a result of the valuation, in addition to the contributions to the DC Plan set out above, deficiency contributions
from employers to the Ministers' Fund (now the DB Plan within the Scheme) were set at 11% of Pensionable
Income for 2015 and 12% of Pensionable Income for 2016 onwards. The Recovery Plan envisages deficiency
contributions being until 30th June 2035.
As there is a large number of contributing employers participating in the Scheme, the Church is unable to identify
its share of the underlying assets and liabilities of the scheme. Accordingly, due to the nature of the schemes, the
profit and loss charge for the period represents the employer contributions payable. The total pension cost for the
Church was E15,666 (2014 14 212,005)
Consequent upon the departure of the Minister from the church in 2008, the church had a cessation event under
Section 75 of the Pensions Act 1995. This makes the church liable for the proportion of the overal deficit
(assessed by reference to the cost of securing benefits by the purchase of annuities) applicable to its previous
Ministers who were members of the Fund. It is not possible to quantify this debt without an actuarial calculation.
In order, to avoid the cost of such a calculation and because the church may not be able to continue its charitable
activities following payment of the employer debt which arises upon a cessation event, the Pension Fund Trustee
(after consulting the Pensions Regulator) is not currently pursuing the employer debt, but is instead permitting the
church to pay the ongoing deficiency contributions outlined above. However, the Pension Trustee has the right to
quantify and seek payment of the debt at any time at its discretion.
The next triennial actuarial valuation of the DB Plan within the Scheme will be as at 31 Dec 2016 and results are
expected to be published in March 2018.

About the Congregation
The Oxford Jewish Congregation (OJC) was founded in 1842 and has been registered (no.
231853) by the Charity Commission since at least 1969. It is now governed by a Constitution
adopted in 1978, slightly amended in 1993 and 1994 and thoroughly reviewed and then
amended in 2015. Under this, it is managed by a Committee of Trustees (known as the
Council), partially elected annually by its members and partially co-opted. Members pay
annual subscriptions at one of several rates, depending on circumstances, as well as any
additional donations, which they see fit to make. Its objects include the advancement of the
Jewish religion by the maintenance of Religious Services and Hebrew and Religion Classes,
other activities to promote the welfare of the Jews of Oxford and its surroundings, and other
charitable purposes not inconsistent with these objects. Its religious services (including burial
arrangements) and membership are available to all those of the Jewish faith. It nominates
three of the directors of the Oxford Synagogue and Jewish Centre Limited (OSJCL) (see
Section 10 of this Report); the Chairman of the OSJCL Management Committee attends
meetings of its Council by invitation.
Unless otherwise stated, the following individual reports cover the period since the last Annual
Report: approximately December 2017 - November 2018.
3
Annual Report, Oxford Jewish Congregation 2018
1. PRESIDENT'S REPORT
Alison Ryde
My second year as President has been just as interesting and varied as my first. I'm happy
to report that OJC continues to punch above its weight. All legitimate forms of Jewish worship
continue to thrive in our building, and we get good attendances for all services including the
recently established occasiona Sephardi minyanim. It is the duty of the Company to facilitate
such provision where there is a demand for it and where the cohesiveness of the community
is not threatened.
Our new Ark was officially consecrated at a special and splendid service on February 25th
with great joy, and we have enjoyed its solemn beauty and gravitas since then. It's a rea
credit to those who brought this project to successful fulfilment.
I thank the Management Committee for all their steady work in ensuring that the building is
maintained in good working order: there has been new carpet in the Cheder block along with
a new coat of paint in a large part of the building during the Summer months. We are also
blessed with a fantastic caretaking team who are not only efficient but welcoming.
Following last year's Kol Nidre choices of The Bike Project and the SAVE Trust, I was
fortunate to be able to visit the latter in Chennai, South India to see more for myself. It was
a humbling experience. The people whom the project are helping have SO little, and yet strive
to make SO much of what they have. They all belong to the 'dalit' caste, the lowest in Indian
society, condemned to the most menial of jobs. This means that OJC's donation made a
significant difference, enabling the continuation of after-school classes in areas where the
schooling system expects low achievement for its pupils both academically and in life; the
extra help inspires a largely ignored community and achieves improved life outcomes. It also
assured the security of a fantastic programme whereby women acquire computer skills,
enabling them to get better jobs. It was a privilege to see these projects in action. The Bike
Project
has
also
had
a
great
year,
rolling
out
more
cycling
opportunities
to
refugees
in
London, setting up a women's bike group, running a workshop where donated or abandoned
bikes are repaired, and providing training in maintenance. May it go from strength to strength.
Hopefully, this year's appeal for Helen House hospice, right in our local Oxford community,
will be a great success. It is indeed a worthy cause.
A new initiative whereby young people help to clean up the Jewish cemetery in Wolvercote
began last year on Mitzvah Day and is now establishing itself as a useful and educational act
of charity. We hope to include more adults in the scheme in the months ahead.
We are almost entirely dependent on volunteers to run many activities in the community,
including the Kiddush which, since it was set up by Helena Harper, has become a service
which everyone takes for granted. I remind the community that this will only continue only as
long as sufficient members volunteer to prepare it and clear up. The list presently comprises
40 people. We would like to double that number, and are particularly seeking the men in our
community, all of whom are more than capable of cutting fruit, slicing cake, putting crisps in
bowls, and washing up. Any reduction in kiddushim would be a great loss, as it provides a
space in which people socialise together after prayers.
Louise Rahmanou has headed up the Cheder this year, flying solo after being Jill Shatz's
wing-man in preparation. The Cheder is doing well, and the youth groups are also thriving.
Our young people now have direct access to a Council member, Sarah Sheppard, to express
any ideas and requests they have. Lisa Clayden and Jane Appel have, with a group of
parents, been organising children's services more frequently, both on Shabbat and Festivals.
4
Annual Report, Oxford Jewish Congregation
2018
Ester Yadgar has taken over the running of Playshul from Rebecca Blumenfeld. I hope that
the Playshul parents will step up to make her life easier and ensure the smooth continuation
of this vital foundation stone of our children's learning in the OJC context.
We enjoyed celebrating an unusually high number of bar and bat mitzvahs, both of children,
and also adults who had not had the opportunity when younger, in addition to other milestone
events of members, many of whom made use of the OJC and our Simcha services CO-
ordinator, Sally Tarshish.
Sadly, our Chevra Kadisha have also been busy this year. Miriam Kochan passed away at
the start of 2018, and we recently set her stone. She was a great maven of this community
and will be sadly missed.
We are taking our first small steps towards involvement in the Eco Synagogues project, which
is intended as a long-term commitment, in line with our fundamental 'tikkun olam' view of our
place in the world.
This year we did not participate in Open Doors due to a clash with the High Holy Days, but
this will resume next year, and other interfaith and outreach events went ahead as usual.
I have continued to learn a great deal this year, helped by support from my fantastically
supportive Council, my vice-presidents Naomi Clayden and Adam Sterrie, Treasurer Stuart
Kenner, secretary and centre manager Sarah Montagu, as well as the many volunteers in
OJC. I also salute Hila Bram and Orit Braha, both of whom do important work in community,
social, publications and administration.
2. TREASURER's REPORT
Stuart Kenner
for the 12 month period to 31st July 2018
The accounts show 2 columns; (a) "unrestricted" which means we can do anything with the
capital and income and (b) "restricted" which is Henry Posner's legacy; its capital is not to
be spent and its income is restricted to educational purposes.
OJC made a loss of f6,358 (last year profit of 238,614) over the year. Last year's profit was
due entirely to a rise in value of on our investments; this year investment values rose
again by f40,623 (despite us selling f25,000 worth as we needed cash), thus cushioning the
loss; in cash terms, our activities run at a loss. We may anticipate investment values to fall
in the year ahead, SO a bigger loss next year can be expected.
Subscription (membership) income fell 2% to f91,915 (E96,364) and total income fell 1% to
f222,136 (f224,898). Expenditure was f269,117 (2282,484). Of this, E115,200 (f135,000)
was paid to OSJC (Oxford Synagogue and Jewish Centre) which owns and runs the Centre.
Expenditure included f19,484 net for the new ark.
At the year end, OJC had net current assets of 220,708 (230,696) and reserves were
f1,286,16 (f1,292,519). Reserves include retained income from H. Posner's bequest of
f60,756 (E57,076).
It would be wonderful to have more gifts of the type bequeathed by Henry Posner - a lump
sum or income-earning asset with its income earmarked for a particular purpose. As shown
in note 15, Henry's legacy enables us to provide some marvelous educational facilities.
The formal Trustee's report to the Charity Commission is on pages 29-32, followed by
detailed accounts on pages 33-42 of this annual report.
5
Annual Report, Oxford Jewish Congregation
2018
2.1 Investment Committee Report
Peter Da Costa
Peter Da Costa (chair), Simon Fineman, Stuart Kenner and David Silver
The OJC currently has two investment portfolios. Both portfolios are broadly based and
comprise UK and overseas equities, unit trusts and fixed interest stocks. The portfolios are
invested through and managed by a specialist charity stockbroker, J.M. Finn & Co.
The Investment Fund is an expendable endowment fund with capital and income available
for any purpose considered appropriate by the OJC Council. At 31 July 2018 the portfolio
was
valued
at
f538,525
(last
year
2544,934),
producing
an
anticipated
annual
income
of
f17,700 (last year 218,124), a yield of 3.3%. A capital sum of E25,000 (last year 129,790)
was withdrawn from the fund by the OJC Council during the year.
The Henry Posner Fund is a restricted endowment fund whose income may only be used for
educational purposes. The portfolio was valued at E727,493 at 31 July 2018 (E716,889 last
year), producing an anticipated annual income of f27,000 (last year 226,679), a yield of 3.7%.
Stock market prices can both rise and fall. The committee and the fund manager keep a close
eye on the situation. We benefited from a rise this year, as in most previous years.
3. MEMBERSHIP REPORT
Tania Davison and Naomi Clayden
This year sees the OJC membership maintained at just over 300 membership units. Whilst
some members have moved away or left, we are delighted to welcome back some old friends
who have returned after periods elsewhere in the UK or abroad, as well as new members.
We now have 252 female and 195 male members from a number of different countries and
from various locations in and around Oxford.
Our future is in good hands with just over 100 young members under the age of 21. The
majority of our young people attend play-shul, Cheder or youth club, giving Sundays at OJC
a lively and vibrant atmosphere.
Over the past year, we had 51 enquiries about membership which resulted in 22 new people
joining our community. This included 4 families, 12 single members, 3 graduates and 1
friend. We would like to extend them all a warm welcome to the community.
We are still struggling to complete our database by receiving membership forms from a few
members who joined before 1998. We are always available to offer help with the paperwork
if this is needed, SO please contact us if this refers to you.
4. RELIGIOUS AFFAIRS REPORTS
4.1 ORTHODOX SERVICES
Joel Kaye
Committee: Helen May, Isaac Garson, Joel Kaye, Adam Sterrie, Barry Freilich, Mark
Simon, Sarah Montagu.
I mentioned in last year's report that much of the Committee's work involves trying to support
the routines of Orthodox services. As that includes providing leaders for services and parts
of services, I am pleased to report it appears likely we have secured the same people for
Yamim Norayim 5780, as we had this last year. We have also had some new faces on the
6
Annual Report, Oxford Jewish Congregation
2018
bimah, including very competent students and newer members of the resident congregation.
Evidently Orthodox students recognise the OJC as 'home'.
On the subject of service leaders, we must thank Jonathan Webber for once again reading
Megillat Esther; Rabbi Solomon for, amongst many other things, leading Tisha 'Av services
both well attended and Shlomo Mannheim for his reading of Kohelet. Connie Webber's
Purim appeal for Prison Chaplaincy raised over 2500, with Gift Aid. Thanks to members'
generosity, we will shortly have over eighty new green siddurim.
In November 2017 we held our first open meeting for OJC members. A detailed report has
been given elsewhere, but in the context of the Yizkor discussion, I wish to acknowledge that
while individuals are required to send in slips for recital at Yom Kippur, throughout the year
Cyril Levicki not only reminds OJC members of dates for reciting Mourners' Kaddish, but also
provides us with lists for recital of memorial prayers from the bimah.
We deliberately left Duchening (Birkat haCohanim/the Priestly Blessing) out of the open
meeting for wider consultation To some people it is a normal part of Orthodox services. To
others it has 'never' been done at Oxford, and never should be. The OSC cannot be arbiter
on this but is trying to respect OJC members' views by providing a rabbi-led education
session, which we are in the process of arranging and which will then be advertised.
4.2 MASORTI
Caroline Goldstein
This year yielded exciting new connections with Masorti Judaism (MJ) and the student
Egalitarian Minyan (Egal Minyan). In partnership with the Egal Minyan, we hosted a Varsity
Shabbaton service (the same day as Cheder Services Shabbat!) and services on Shemini
Atseret and Simchat Torah. Thanks to Miriam Kunin and BZ Galinsky for their hard work and
all students and Masorti attendees for their contributions.
Caroline represents us at regular Synagogue Chairs' meetings and the new MJ Tefila Forum,
both
national
meetings
for
sharing
communities'
best
practice.
We
had
our
final
visit
from
Rabbi Roni Tabick and our first visit from Jon Pam, the new MJ Community Development
Officer, on Masorti Shabbat. Council support enabled the employment of Rebecca
Blumenfeld by the OJC and MJ to assist with leading Masorti services and teaching the wider
community. She is currently teaching a leyning class and plans to teach service leadership.
We had four bnei mitzvah this year: mazel tov to Eva Clayden, Hannah Brosh, Isaac Salle,
Asher Levinson and their families. We are currently planning three adult bnei mitzvah, which
is a new venture for us.
Rebecca has also encouraged our young post bnei mitzvah to plunge into leyning at services.
We are very proud to see them in action, for example at Isaac's bar mitzvah.
Caroline Goldstein (masorti@ojc-online.org) is our main contact, Adele Moss
(adelemoss@talktalk.net) organises leyning and arranges bnei mitzvah, Rebecca
Blumenfeld (bexblumenfeld@gmail.com) helps with services and teaching, while Penny
Faust (faust@ntlworld.com) represents us on Council.
4.3 PROGRESSIVE SERVICES
Liberal Services Team
We continue to see increasing numbers attend Liberal services and reflecting this growing
interest (and following requests for additional services, particularly festivals, at a Think Tank
7
Annual Report, Oxford Jewish Congregation
2018
in 2017) we added 3 more services to our normal number. This included a Shavuot service
on a Sunday in June, an August service and an extra service in November, making two
services that month instead of just one. We have been using some of the extra time to
explore the draft siddur to be published in 2020. After more time with this version we will
discuss views on it.
In June we also enjoyed hearing Joseph Oakley give us a fine rendering of his Torah portion.
Unusually this year there was no additional rabbinic input beyond having Rabbi Thomas
Salamon and Rabbi Michae Shire leading packed High Holy Day services. Both of these
were greatly enjoyed as were new musical additions by our fine 'choir' of 4, blending their
voices beautifully for us. Another first was having a small group share the Tashlich ceremony
in Wolvercote.
The Liberal services team continued to work well, reporting on and planning the services.
Many members have participated in services but we are always open to more offers to help
with reading and leading services in the year ahead. Bring-a-dish lunches after Shabbat
services continue to be a valuable way to consolidate our supportive community.
4.4 CHILDREN'S SERVICES
Lisa Clayden and Jane Appel
We held a range of services for youngsters over the Chaggim aimed at all ages, from toddlers
to teenagers, whether children of the community or visiting family. On the first day of Rosh
