BROMSGROVE SCHOOL
REPORT OF THE DIRECTORS (Continued)
The Directors, who are the Governors of the School, present their annual report for the year ended 31 August 2018 under
the Companies Act 2006, together with the audited financial statements for the year and confirm that the financial
statements comply with the requirements of the Act, the charity's governing document, applicable law and the Statement
of Recommended Practice: Accounting and Reporting by Charities applicable to charities preparing their accounts in
accordance with the Financial Reporting Standard applicable in the UK and Republic of Ireland (FRS 102) (effective 1
January 2015).
REFERENCE AND ADMINISTRATIVE INFORMATION
The School was founded in 1553 and re-founded on the current site in 1693 by Thomas Cookes. Bromsgrove School was
one of the original fourteen members of the Headmasters' Conference (HMC) when it was founded in 1869. The Pre-
preparatory and Preparatory Schools are twentieth century foundations.
The School was incorporated as a company limited by guarantee on 1 September 2003 under charity number 1098740
and registered company number 4808121.
OBJECTS, AIMS AND ETHOS
Charitable Objects
The objects for which the Charity is established are to advance education and training by the provision and conduct in or
near Worcestershire of any day and boarding school or schools for boys and girls.
The Charity provides education on three sites in Worcestershire to boys and girls from the ages of 2-18. It is the policy of
the School to provide a first class education, which identifies and develops the potential of individual pupils in a variety
of areas, provides them with the best achievable qualifications and prepares them for their future life.
Aims
The Charity constantly aims to provide a first class education to boys and girls from the ages of 2-18.
Within the objects, the School aims to produce happy, creative, moral citizens who live motivated, fulfilled lives while
enriching the lives of others. The School seeks to achieve this through an enlightened, disciplined and broad education
that responds to global change while retaining core values. The core values that the School seeks to foster in its pupils
are:
Humility and Confidence
Compassion and Ambition
Respect and Curiosity
Tolerance and Vision
Ethos
Bromsgrove School is committed to safeguarding and promoting the welfare of all pupils. The School is proud of the
strong pastoral care provided by the House structure in the Senior School and by the form tutors within the Preparatory
and Pre-preparatory Schools. The School has a very caring ethos, which is reflected in all of the School's policies and
procedures The School maintains regular contact with parents through newsletters, social media, informal meetings and
regular reports.
The Govemors are committed to the longstanding principle that charities must exist for the benefit of the public and have
a long tradition of providing public benefit, both through educating pupils at the School and through associated activities
for the benefit of the wider community. The Governors are committed to widening access to the School to ensure that
children who could not otherwise attend the School can benefit from the education it provides.
The School's ethos is to welcome pupils from all backgrounds. Entrance assessments are undertaken to satisfy both the
School and the parents that prospective pupils can cope with the pace of learning and benefit from the breadth of the
education that the School provides. An individual's economic status, gender, ethnicity, sexual orientation, race, religion
or disability do not form part of the assessment process.
3
BROMSGROVE SCHOOL
REPORT OF THE DIRECTORS (Continued)
OBJECTS, AIMS AND ETHOS (continued)
The School is part of a wider community and has a long history of offering a range of educational activities for the benefit
of local children. The School offers activities and access to the School's facilities to provide opportunities for children
other than pupils at the School to benefit from the charity. Speeifically, this year, the Bromsgrove School Swim Academy
provided swimming lessons to 900 children from the local community. The Summer School that runs for eight weeks in
the summer holidays and the Tennis academy are also open to local children. Local primary schools use the swimming
pool for weekly lessons at no charge.
Bursaries and Scholarships
The School is committed to ensuring that there is sufficient opportunity for children whose parents cannot afford the fees,
including those in poverty, to benefit from its educational services and facilities. The Governors and the School
management regularly review the School's Public Benefit Policy as part of the ongoing development of the School's
strategy to widen access.
The Governors are committed to running a means-tested bursary scheme to allow direct access to the educational services
provided. The scheme is designed to assist prospective parents and existing parents on low incomes who for financial
reasons might otherwise be unable to send or continue to send their child to the School. The bursary scheme includes
Admissions bursaries for the parents of new pupils and Hardship bursaries for parents whose financial position worsens
unexpectedly.
Bursaries are entirely means tested and are awarded on an annual basis to parents who satisfy the financial criteria set by
the School in relation to their income and the value of their capital assets.
The School has a Bursary Policy, which is available to both prospective and existing parents. The policy contains an
overview of the bursary scheme and details the procedure for applications and awards of bursaries.
The value of bursaries will be up to 100% of full fees and additional assistance is available to parents to assist with the
associated costs of their child's education. The School allocates a proportion of its total income in each financial year to
fund the bursary scheme. The School's current aim is to allocate not less than 5% of its total income in each financial year
to fund means tested bursaries.
The School's scholarship awards recognise high academic potential or the ability to excel in co-curricular activities.
Scholarships are awarded with a fixed remission of between 2.5% and 5%. Where further assistance is required, a means
tested bursary may supplement scholarship awards.
STRATEGIC REPORT
CURRENT YEAR PLANS
The School's objectives are set to reflect the educational aims and ethos of the School. It is important to the School that
the core values are maintained whilst also aiming to achieve the highest academic standards.
In setting objectives, the Governors and School management give careful consideration to the Charity Commission's
general guidance on public benefit and in particular to its supplementary guidance on advancing education.
The Development Plan for the academic year 2017/18 included the following objectives: -
To promote the Arts within the School. To capitalise on the new superb facilities and introduce a new Arts
programme increasing the number of musical and dramatic performances within the School. To also increase
pupil involvement in the arts as an extra-curricular activity both through performance and through the provision
of technical support.
To improve further the academic offer and performance. In the light of the GCSE reforms, to implement a
new GCSE programme for all subjects commencing in September 2017. All pupils will commence their GCSE
courses at the start of year nine and each course programme will be extended to three years. To also undertake
a review of the sixth form offer to create greater depth and breadth in the programme following the removal of
the AS examinations with an emphasis on engagement.
4
BROMSGROVE SCHOOL
REPORT OF THE DIRECTORS (Continued)
REVIEW OF ACTIVITIES AND ACHIEVEMENTS (continued)
International Foundation Programme. To market the introduction of this new sixth form course and attract
pupils to commence studying this prestigious University of London programme at Bromsgrove from September
2018. To refurbish Webber House to provide a modern, spacious facility for this programme including boarding
accommodation and new teaching facilities. To ensure that all teaching staff selected to teach this programme
are inducted and fully prepared for teaching the specific courses.
To develop initiatives to generate new income streams. To continue to build on the successes of this year and
ensure that such initiatives as the Summer School, the Cricket Festival and the BSSA continue to flourish. To
also consider opportunities to generate additional income streams through the hiring out of the new Performing
Arts facilities.
Public Benefit. To continue to actively market bursaries to widen access in accordance with the School's Public
Benefit Policy To introduce a new marketing campaign in the year, specifically using social media to increase
awareness of bursary opportunities for local children.
REVIEW OF ACTIVITIES AND ACHIEVEMENTS
Principal Activities of the Year
Pupil numbers remain strong at Bromsgrove School. This year, the total roll at Bromsgrove School increased to an
average of 1,965 pupils (2017: 1,939). The Senior School averaged 949 pupils (2017: 950) of whom 437 (2017: 429)
were boarding pupils; the Preparatory School averaged 515 pupils (2017: 495) of whom 72 (2017: 66) were boarding
pupils; Winterfold House averaged 292 (2017: 289) and the Pre-Preparatory School averaged 209 day pupils (2017: 205).
The Governors are particularly pleased about the demand for places in the Preparatory School and continue to be
encouraged by the growth in the number of Prep School boarders.
This year, there has been a continued focus on widening access. The value of means tested bursaries amounted to 4.7% of
income (2017: 5.0%). The charity has also provided fee assistance in the form of scholarships and armed forces
discounts. The value of such additional assistance when added to means tested bursaries represented 7.5% of the charity's
total fee income. Of the 1,965 pupils educated at the school, 492 pupils (25%) received some degree of financial
assistance in the form of bursaries, scholarships, armed forces discounts and staff discounts. The Governors have agreed
an annual bursary budget for the 2018/2019 academic year, which amounts to 5.0% of total fee income.
The development of the Performing Arts at Bromsgrove remains a highly important strategic aim of the Governors. The
new Cobham Theatre and the Routh Concert Hall were both completed at the end of October 2017. The conversion of
Routh Hall also included the building of a new Music School, incorporating music classrooms, green room facilities, a
recording studio and several individual music instrument-teaching rooms. As well as building the new Theatre at
Cobham, the project included a new drama studio, green room facilities and additional Music teaching rooms.
To coincide with the opening of the new facilities, a new Arts programme was introduced which included a significant
increase in the number of concerts, plays and performances across all year groups. The Governors, pupils and staff are all
very pleased as there is a general excitement within the School about the Arts and the opportunities for the future.
As planned, the School introduced a three year programme for all GCSE courses at the start of the academic year. There
has been a smooth transition and initial feedback from staff and pupils is that this change will lead to good academic
outcomes for the pupils.
The University of London International Foundation Programme was developed in the year. Teachers have been trained to
teach the new programme and the Webber boarding house refurbishment has been completed. The programme has been
marketed overseas and the first pupils enrolled in September 2018.
The International Summer School was again very successful this year. Following on from the success in the prior year
and the School's excellent relationships with international agents, 800 weeks of summer courses were sold to
international pupils. In addition, there were approximately 60 local children also attending the summer school activities
programme each day. This initiative continues to be very successful for the school in promoting the school
5
BROMSGROVE SCHOOL
REPORT OF THE DIRECTORS (Continued)
Internationally, attracting and recruiting full-time students, building links with the local community and in securing an
additional income stream.
This year, the School has continued to promote external use of the School's excellent facilities, in particular the boarding
and sporting facilities. The School has continued to develop links with national, regional and local sporting clubs and
associations. The School was very pleased to host both the National Indoor Hockey Finals again this year and a
residential Summer Cricket Festival. The Bromsgrove School Swim and Tennis Academies have continued to flourish
providing swimming and tennis lessons for 900 young children in the local community. The Governors are very pleased
that the new Arts facilities are also being hired out by the local community. The School hosts the prestigious Bromsgrove
International Music Competition each year and there is an increased number of local choirs, orchestras and dance groups
using the facilities.
The Foundation has continued to develop and there have been a number of high profile events providing opportunities for
the School and its alumni to communicate.
Operational Performance of the School
Academie overview
2017/18 produced a strong set of results spanning GCSE, A level, IB and BTEC qualifications, indeed, the GCSE results
are amongst the very highest ever achieved by Bromsgrovians.
42.4% of pupils achieved an A*/9, the highest proportion of the top grade in the School's history. Five pupils gained a
full sweep of straight 9s (A* equivalent) with a further seven students only dropping one grade.
At A level, just under 80% of the year group scored 144 UCAS points, equivalent to 3 As at A level. The School's largest
ever IB cohort achieved an excellent average IB score of 38.4 points (equivalent to 4A* at A level); two pupils scored 44
points and both the Heads of School scored over 40 points.
The breadth of academic offer at Bromsgrove also includes BTECs in Sports Science and Business studies. Of the 48
BTEC entries this year, students achieved 30 Distinction* and 14 Distinctions.
210 pupils in the Upper Sixth cohort achieved 56% A*/A in all exams. Most significantly, 80% secured their first choice
university place, with most leaving to attend the very best universities in the world. Just under 70% of them went to
Russell Group universities.
Given the huge commitment that Bromsgrove's pupils make outside of the classroom, in sport, music, drama, service,
CCF and D of E, their academic achievements are doubly impressive.
Extra curricular
The School prides itself on a broad and varied co-curricular offering across a wide range of sport, cultural and service
activities. Bromsgrove students continue to enjoy an enriching extra-curricular programme.
For the last four years the School has been ranked in the top five of all schools nationally for the strength of its Senior
School Sport over 26 sports as measured by School Sport Magazine. It is very pleasing to see the re-emergence of the
girls' cricket team and there was a memorable performance at New Road for the 1st XV when they again won the
Chesterton Cup. The DT Kitear team, The Chicken, raced their way into the World Championships, finishing as the
second fastest Kitear on the planet and have now moved up from twenty-eighth seed in the world to eighteenth. CCF
continues to flourish, having one of the largest contingents in the country.
The pupils at both the Bromsgrove Preparatory School and Winterfold House School have enjoyed a number of
residential school trips in the year including visits to France, Italy and Switzerland. Both Schools ensure that each year
group from year three to year eight are involved in some form of residential outdoor based activities. These range from
bushcraft weekends in Herefordshire to river studies in Snowdonia.
The opportunities that Senior School pupils have enjoyed this year include trips to Ireland (Rugby and Polities), France
(Languages), Germany (Languages), Spain (Languages), Dubai (Cricket), Prague (CAS) and Madagasear (Biology).

FINANCIAL REVIEW AND RESULTS FOR THE YEAR
Financial Performance
The School achieved net income before investment gains of f4,308,053 which was in line with the School's financial
plan. School expenditure was well controlled in the year to ensure that the surplus required to support the School's
investment programme was secured. The surplus of f4,308,053 is lower than in the prior year (2017: f6,988,165) which
included the acquisition of Winterfold House School in the prior year giving rise to exceptional income of f3,267,910.
Excluding this exceptional item, there is an underlying increase in net income of f587,798. This is mainly due to a growth
in fee income net of additional teaching costs due to higher pupil numbers particularly within the Preparatory School and
a reduction in premises refurbishment expenditure.
In the year, the School generated trading income of f2,931,580 (2017: f2,166,239) from lettings which included the
International Summer School, the Cricket Festival, the hiring out of the sports facilities, the School Shop and the hosting
of several other conferences and events.
The principal source of income to the School is income derived from fees. Fee income accounts for 90% of the total
School's income. Fee income has increased by 6.0% on last year, partially due to the growth in pupil numbers and
partially due to the 4% increase in the fees charged. When setting fees, the Govemnors are mindful of the need to balance
the quality of the educational services provided against the fees charged to parents for those services. Both of these
factors also need to be balanced against the need to provide public benefit. As an educational charity, the School benefits
from tax exemption on the fees charged for the provision of education and on investment income provided that the
income is applied for the School's charitable aims. The financial benefits we receive from these tax exemptions are
applied for educational purposes and indirectly assist us to maintain our public benefit and bursary policies.
Our trading subsidiary continues to operate both the School Shop and the letting of the facilities and provision of catering
services to outside organisations. This trading subsidiary also receives the franchise fee from Bromsgrove International
School Thailand and Mission Hills, Shenzhen. After School management charges, the company contributed 1254,291 to
School funds during the year ended 31 August 2018.
Bromsgrove School Foundation generated net income, including investment gains, of f107,487 during the year ended 31
August 2018 (2017: E109,017). The Foundation is still in the early stages of development, and is expected to grow. The
funds raised will contribute to bursary awards to pupils of Bromsgrove School in the future.
The net cash inflow from operations during the year amounted to 16,313,428 compared to 15,998,524 in the prior year
due to an improvement in working capital. A smaller refurbishment programme in the summer period has also
contributed to this improvement in cash flow.
Investment Policy and Performance
The Directors are permitted to hold a portfolio of investments. The guidance given to the Investment Advisers with regard
to equity investment is to balance growth and income with a medium level of risk. These objectives are to be achieved by
investing prudently in a broad range of fixed interest securities and equities which are quoted on a recognised Investment
Exchange and unit trusts and OEIC'S (open ended investment companies) which are authorised under the Financial
Services and Markets Act 2000.
The Charity's investment performance is benchmarked against the WMA Performance index and managed by Rathbones
on a discretional mandate with the aim of outperforming the benchmark over a rolling three-year period. The actual
performance for the School portfolio in the year was 5.75% compared to the WMA benchmark of 5.59%. The Directors
were satisfied with this performance in the year. The Foundation portfolio performed below the benchmark at 4.91%.
Reserves Policy
At 31 August 2018 the total unrestricted funds of the School amounted to $56,576,349, which forms part of the funding
of the School's expenditure on freehold property. As such, the School does not hold unrestricted reserves, however the
Directors arc satisfied that the School's operating cash flows and external finance facilities are sufficient to meet the
Schools day-to-day working capital requirements. The Directors will use future surpluses in order to continue the policy
of enhancing the educational facilities and services of the School. This policy is reviewed on an annual basis.

Fundraising Policy
The School does not undertake fundraising for the financing of capital investment. All projects within the School are
funding from School resources with external bank financing as and when necessary.
The Foundation's objective is to raise funds ultimately to enable the School to provide places to all deserving pupils on a
needs blind basis. This is a long term ambition which has a focus on friend raising rather than targeted fundraising. It is
intended that gentle appeals are made to all those with a connection to Bromsgrove School ie: alumni and parents through
a fundraising programme of encouraging major gifts, regular giving and legacies. This is supported by a programme of
non- fundraising events designed to encourage interest and involvement with the School. External fundraising companies
are not used and the Foundation does not actively fundraise through targeted appeals or telephone campaigns.
The School has received no complaints related to fundraising in the year.
RISK MANAGEMENT
The Governing Body conducts a formal review each term of the School's Risk Register. The School's Executive
identifies the major risks to which the School and its related organisations are exposed. The School Executive and the Sub
Committee Chairmen review these risks on a rolling basis. Mitigation and control procedures are put in place as
necessary. This procedure and the Risk Register is reviewed by the Risk and Strategy Committee each term and
recommendations are made to the Board regarding confirmation that systems are in place to provide reasonable assurance
that major risks are being adequately managed.
One of the most significant risks for the School continues to be the changes to the A level and GCSE examination
systems. Whilst we were very pleased with the performance of our pupils in the 2018 examinations, we are closely
monitoring performance for programmes which have been subject to curriculum changes.
A further risk is related to the perception of the UK in our international markets. We are very proud of the high number
of intemnational pupils in the school and a reduction in intemational boarding numbers would have a detrimental impact
on the School's income. There is a perceived risk that some international families will be less inclined to send their
children to the UK to be educated at the present time due to concems regarding Brexit.
The Governors continue to be concerned about the risk of a change in government. There is much speculation about a
change in government policy regarding the introduction of VAT on school fees and the removal of charity relief on
business rates. Both of these changes would have a significant impact on the School's financial model.
In the short term, it is also highly likely that the current government will significantly increase the employer contribution
rates on the Teachers' Pension Scheme from September 2019. This risk is being mitigated by undertaking detailed
financial modelling and considering possible cost efficiencies and project delays.

FUTURE PLANS
The Governors together with the School Executive are committed to ensuring that the School continues to provide a first
class education to all of its pupils. All strategic developments are committed to maintaining the School's position in the
competitive market that it operates. The achievement of high standards of academic results and the development of the
School's facilities are imperative to the School's continued success.

new Arts programme increasing the number of musical and dramatic performances within the School. To also
increase pupil involvement in the arts as an extra-curricular activity both through performance and through the
provision of technical support. To also significantly extend the use of the new facilities to the local community,

To improve further the academie offer and performance. To further strengthen the upper end of our
scholastic offer in light of the recent A level reforms. To also successfully implement the new teacher appraisal

International Foundation Programme. To continue to market the introduction of this new sixth form course
and attract pupils to commence studying this prestigious University of London programme at Bromsgrove from
September 2019.
To improve facilities. To continue to ensure that the quality of the boarding facilities at Bromgrove are first
class by completing a major refurbishment of Elmshurst House. To also improve the sports facilities at
Winterfold House by building a new multi-purpose astroturf and new netball/tennis courts.
Public Benefit. To continue to actively market bursaries to widen access in accordance with the School's Public
Benefit Policy. To introduce a new marketing campaign in the year, specifically using social media to increase
awareness of bursary opportunities for local children.

STRUCTURE, GOVERNANCE AND MANAGEMENT
Governing Document
The Charity is governed by its Memorandum and Articles of Association arising from incorporation in 2003, as amended
on 4 October 2015.
Directors and professional advisers
A list of Govemors and professional advisers appears on pages 1 and 2 of this report.
Recruitment and Training of Directors
The Charity's Govemors are appointed at a meeting of the Board of Governors, following a selection process and
recommendation from the Nominations Committee. The Governing body requires breadth and depth of experience to
carry out its duties effectively. When recruiting new Goverors, the Nominations Committee takes into consideration
eligibility, personal competence, specialist skills and local availability.
New Governors are inducted into the workings of the School, including the provision of key information covering Board
policy, School ethos, strategy and financial information. All Govemnors are encouraged to attend training courses and
workshops organised by specialist school organisations.
All Governors give of their time freely and no remuneration was paid in the year. No Govemnor or person connected with
a Govemnor received any benefit from either means tested bursaries or scholarships awarded to our pupils.
Organisational Management
The Board of Directors, as the trustees of the Charity, is responsible for the overall management and control of the School
and meets at least three times a year.
The principal responsibilities of the Board are to:
Ensure the School is run in accordance with its charitable objectives and that all the functions of the School are
authorised by the powers provided by its statutes, regulations and by company and charity law
To appoint the Headmaster
To set, in consultation with the Headmaster and the Executive of the School, the strategy and policies by which
the School will be run
Approve the Development Plan
Ensure that the School meets the objectives that the Board sets from time to time
Control finance by approving budgets and longer-term plans and by approving systems that optimise the chances
that they will be achieved
Understand the extent of duties in relation to risk management and to legal compliance and be satisfied that there
is a rolling programme for meeting them
Ensure that competent professional advice is taken when necessary.
The work in checking the strategy and policies are being correctly carried out is performed by the various committees of
Govemnors as set out below:
Finance and Property Committee - which deals with financial policy and review of budgets and financial
statements prior to approval by the Board
Education Committee - which deals with educational and related operational issues and brings recommendations
and concers with regard to such matters to the Board

Buildings Committee which considers and monitors major build and refurbishment projects within the School
Investment Committee -- which receives termly updates on investment and performance from the Investment
Advisers and reports these matters to the Board together with any proposals regarding changes in the investment
policy set by the Board
Nominations Committee - which considers possible capability gaps with regard to the composition of the Board
and makes recommendations regarding potential new Board members
Health & Safety Committee - this ensures that there are adequate policies and procedures in place to ensure the
health and safety of all pupils and staff and to ensure that the School complies with all legislative changes.
Risk and Strategy Committee -- which assesses the management of all risks encountered by the School and
maintains an oversight of the implementation of the agreed strategic aims on the behalf of the full Board.
Safeguarding Committee - which assesses the management of all safeguarding controls within the School.
Each committee normally meets before the main Board meetings. The membership of the committees is supplemented by
senior staff at the School and by co-opted external appointments.
The day-to-day running of the School is delegated to the School Executive. The School Executive (key management)
comprises of the Headmaster (P Clague), Bursar (L Brookes), Assistant Head (R Scannell), the Headmistress of the
Preparatory and Pre-Preparatory Schools (J Deval-Reed) and the Headmistress of Winterfold House School (D Toms)
The members of the Nominations Committee have responsibility for reviewing the remuneration for the members of the
Executive on an annual basis. The Governors aim to ensure that pay levels are consistent with the market within the
independent school sector and use benchmarking data from professional associations such as AGBIS to guide them.
Group Structure and Relationships
The Charity has a wholly-owned non-charitable subsidiary, Bromsgrove School Enterprises Limited, whose activities and
trading performance are discussed below.
The Charity also holds under trust certain endowed funds under Charity Commission schemes: the Society of Friends
Fund and the David Walters Fund. The terms of the schemes are such that the income is applied for the benefit of pupils
and former pupils of the School.
The School is the sole member of Bromsgrove School Foundation, a charitable company limited by guarantee. The
objects of the company are to promote and advance any charitable purpose connected with Bromsgrove School and to
promote other educational purposes for the benefit of the local community.
The School has established international links under licence agreements with Bromsgrove International School Thailand
and with Bromsgrove School Mission Hills, Shenzhen.
The Headmaster is a member of the Head Masters' and Mistresses' Conference which provides an opportunity to share
expertise and knowledge across the independent school sector. The Conference also permits appropriate representation to
Government and regulators of the views of the sector.
The School also benefits from close links with the Alumni. An Alumni Committee, with representation from Old
Bromsgrovians, the Foundation and the School has responsibility for engaging with Alumni.

STATEMENT OF ACCOUNTING POLICIES
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2018
Basis of preparation
The financial statements have been prepared in accordance with the Financial Reporting Standard applicable in the UK
and Republic of Ireland (FRS102), the Companies Act 2006 and the Statement of Recommended Practice applicable to
charities preparing their accounts in accordance with the Financial Reporting Standard applicable in the UK and Republic
of Ireland (FRS 102).
The charity has taken advantage of the exemption available to a qualifying entity in FRS 102 from the requirement to
present a charity only Cash Flow Statement with the consolidated financial statements.
Having reviewed the funding facilities available to the School together with the expected ongoing demand for places and
the School's future projected cash flows, the Directors have a reasonable expectation that the School has adequate
resources to continue its activities for the foreseeable future and consider that there were no material uncertainties over
the School's financial viability. Accordingly, they also continue to adopt the going concern basis in preparing the
financial statements
The financial statements of the Group include the results and balances of the School consolidated on a line by line basis
with Bromsgrove School Enterprises Limited and Bromsgrove School Foundation. In accordance with Section 408 of the
Companies Act 2006, no separate Statement of Financial Activities is presented for Bromsgrove School.
The School is a Public Benefit Entity registered as a charity in England and Wales and a company limited by guarantee. It
was incorporated on 1 September 2003 (company number: 4808121) and registered as a charity (charity number:
1098740).
Critical accounting judgements and key sources of estimation uncertainty
In the application of the accounting policies, Directors are required to make judgement, estimates, and assumptions about
the carrying value of assets and liabilities that are not readily apparent from other sources. The estimates and underlying
assumptions are based on historical experience and other factors that are considered to be relevant. Actual results may
differ from these estimates.
The estimates and underlying assumptions are reviewed on an ongoing basis. Revisions to accounting estimates are
recognised in the period in which the estimate is revised if the revision affects only that period, or in the period of the
revision and future periods if the revision affected current and future periods.
In the view of the Directors, no assumptions conceming the future or estimation uncertainty affecting assets or liabilities
at the balance sheet date are likely to result in a material adjustment to their carrying amounts in the next financial year.
The following accounting policies have been applied consistently in dealing with items which are considered material in
relation to the School's financial statements.
Fees and similar earned income
Fees receivable and charges for services and use of the premises, less any allowances, scholarships, bursaries granted by
the School against those fees, but including contributions received from restricted funds, are accounted for in the period
in which the service is provided.
Investment income
Investment income from dividends, bank balances and fixed interest securities is accounted for on an accruals basis.
Donations, legacies, grants and other voluntary income
Voluntary income is accounted for as and when entitlement arises, the amount can be reliably quantified and the
economic benefit to the School is considered probable.
Voluntary income for the School's general purposes is accounted for as unrestricted and is credited to the General
Reserve. Where the donor or an appeal has imposed trust law restrictions, voluntary income is credited to the relevant
restricted fund.

STATEMENT OF ACCOUNTING POLICIES
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2018
Acquisition of Winterfold House School
The assets and liabilities transferred from Winterfold House School on I September 2016 have been recognised at the
Directors' best estimate of their fair value on the date of transfer.
Expenditure
Expenditure is accrued as soon as a liability is considered probable, discounted to present value for longer-term liabilities.
Expenditure attributable to more than one cost category in the Statement of Financial Activities is apportioned to them on
the basis of the estimated amount attributable to each activity in the year, either by reference to staff time or the use made
of the underlying assets, as appropriate. Irrecoverable VAT is included with the item of expenditure to which it relates.
Govemance costs comprise the costs of complying with constitutional and statutory requirements. Intra-group sales and
charges between the School and its subsidiaries are excluded from trading income and expenditure.
Tangible fixed assets
Depreciation is provided at rates calculated to write off each asset over its estimated useful life. Equipment is depreciated
at annual rates varying between 10% and 33.3% on cost.
No depreciation is provided on freehold land. Depreciation is provided on freehold buildings at 2% per annum, straight
line, when the buildings are brought into use. The anticipated average life of buildings is estimated by reference to 1
September 1990 (date of commencement of depreciation policy), or date of expenditure since that date.
Investments
Listed investments are recognised at market value as at the balance sheet date. Unrealised gains and losses arising on the
revaluation of investments are credited or charged to the Statement of Financial Activities and are allocated to the
appropriate Fund according to the "ownership" of the underlying assets.
Stock
Stock represents goods for resale and is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
Financial instruments
Basic financial instruments are initially recognised at transaction value and subsequently measured at amortised cost with
the exception of investments which are held at fair value. Financial assets held at amortised cost comprise cash at bank
and in hand, trade and fee debtors, other debtors, accrued income and amounts owed by group undertakings. A specific
provision is made for debts for which recoverability is in doubt. Cash at bank and in hand is defined as all cash held in
instant access bank accounts and used as working capital. Financial liabilities held at amortised cost comprise deposits,
fees in advance, trade creditors, other creditors and amounts owed to group undertakings.
Debtors
Trade and other debtors are recognised at the settlement amount due for the provision of services delivered. Prepayments
are recognised at the amount prepaid or the amount paid in advance.
Cash at bank and in hand
Cash at bank and in hand includes cash and deposits with a short term maturity of six months or less from the date of
opening the deposit account.
Creditors
Creditors are recognised where the School has a present obligation resulting from a past event that will probably result in
the transfer of funds to a third party and the amount due to settle the obligation can be measured reliably. Amounts are
recognised at their settlement amount.

STATEMENT OF ACCOUNTING POLICIES
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2018
Endowment Funds
The Society of Friends Fund:
This represents permanent endowment funds held under a Charity Commission Scheme where the income is to be applied
to further the charitable purposes of Bromsgrove School.
David Walters Fund:
This represents permanent endowment funds held under a Charity Commission Scheme where the income is to be applied
for providing scholarships for pupils at Bromsgrove School or at an approved further education establishment.
Restricted Funds
Restricted funds are funds which are to be used in accordance with specific restrictions imposed by the donor (see Note
13).
Unrestricted Funds
Unrestricted funds comprise the School's general fund, which is available for application in accordance with the School's
objects.
Pension costs
Retirement benefits to employees of the School are provided through two pension schemes. The pension costs charged in
the Statement of Financial Activities are determined as follows:
The Teachers' Pension Scheme - This scheme is a multi-employer pension scheme. It is not possible to identify the
School's share of the underlying assets and liabilities of the Teachers' Pension Scheme on a consistent and reasonable
basis and therefore, as required by FRS102, accounts for the scheme as if it were a defined contribution scheme. The
School's contributions, which are in accordance with the recommendations of the Government Actuary, are charged in the
period in which the salaries to which they relate are payable,
The School also contributes to a defined contribution scheme for non-teaching staff. Contributions are charged to
expenditure when they become payable.
Operating leases
Rentals under operating leases are charged on a straight-line basis over the lease term, even if the payments are not made
on such a basis. Benefits received and receivable as an incentive to sign an operating lease are similarly spread on a
straight-line basis over the lease term.

14 I General Medical Council
IMPROVING WHAT WE DO
Our five strategic aims for 2014-17
To deliver against the ambition of our strategy we are now focusing our work on the following strategic aims.
HELPING TO RAISE STANDARDS IN MEDICAL EDUCATION
01
AND PRACTICE
We will develop our standards, our guidance and the way we support particular
groups of doctors to help them deal with professional challenges. We will make
sure medical education equips doctors to meet these standards.
IMPROVING HOW WE HANDLE CONCERNS
02
ABOUT PATIENT SAFETY
We have seen a significant rise in the number of complaints about doctors in
recent years. To respond to this, we will continue to press for much-needed
reform of the legislative system. We will make sure that concerns about doctors
are first addressed locally wherever possible. We will continue to develop new
ways to reduce the stress for those involved in our fitness to practise procedures.
03
USING INFORMATION IN SMARTER WAYS
We will use and share information in smarter ways to support high standards of
medical practice and to help reduce risks to patients. Putting the information
we hold to best use will help to create a more open system and to safeguard the
interests of patients.
04
WORKING MORE CLOSELY WITH PATIENTS, DOCTORS AND
MEDICAL STUDENTS ON THE FRONTLINE OF CARE
We will have more contact with doctors, medical students and patients so that
we have a better understanding of their lives and work. More of them will be
aware of our guidance and use it to help them maintain standards of patient care.
05
WORKING BETTER TOGETHER
We recognise there are often barriers to better collaboration within and between
organisations - we will work across teams within the GMC to make the best use
of all available knowledge and skills to help us deliver effective regulation.

COUNCIL'S REPORT & FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2015
INTRODUCTION BY THE PRESIDENT OF COUNCIL
Welcome to the Annual Report for 2014-2015. A year ago, I concluded my introduction to the
2013-14 report by noting that the future will be full of opportunity' for College and for
Cheltonians. Not perhaps the most daring of predictions, given that there are always opportunities
for those who take the trouble to seek them out and have the courage to seize them. A year on,
and I'm delighted to be able to tell you that in many spheres College, its staff and most
importantly its pupils, have done exactly that - sought out and successfully seized opportunities.
Significantly for a school that prides itself on the richness and breadth of the education it provides,
our successes in the past 12 months have come in a number of areas - not only in the examination
hall where more than three-quarters of 'A' Level candidates now consistently achieve A* to B
grades, but also on the sports field where the quality of facilities and the regularity of our victories
mean we continue to be the envy of many local, and more distant competitors. Developments in
extra-curricular life, as well as in pastoral care, have also reflected a school that is pushing forward,
refusing to rest on its laurels. The further development of the College's on-site Health Centre
accompanied by the development of a comprehensive pupil wellbeing programme, FLOREAT,
combine to provide an important example of College's relentless drive to seize opportunities
and
drive further improvements.
Of course one of the most significant opportunities of past decades has been the journey from
single-sex boys' school to the fully co-educational Cheltenham College we are now proud to be.
An important step along the way was the decision, a little over three years ago to press ahead with
the building of Westal our latest girls' boarding house. The business plan that lay behind that
decision suggested the new house would pay for itself by the 2022-23 academic year.
Such has been the success of Westal that current predictions mean we'll achieve that important
landmark a full five years ahead of schedule. I'm pleased to be able to report that Westal will have
paid for itself by the end of the 2017-18 and, in the process, will have demonstrated the value of
seeking out and seizing opportunity.
With Westal now full and pressure on girls' places remaining strong we'y gone on to release the
potential of the Victorian cottages to the rear of Thirlestaine House - comprehensively upgrading
them and creating some very special sixth-form accommodation for Chandos girls.
CHANDOS
3
CHELTENHAM COLLEGE
COUNCIL'S REPORT & FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2015
Conscious of not wishing to turn this introduction into a lengthy list of opportunities spotted and
successes achieved I'll stop there, but I do hope that you may have the opportunity to see for
yourself some of the past year's achievements including, of course, our new Science &
Technology Centre at the Prep School.
Of course simply spotting opportunities is never sufficient to ensure progress, and seizing
opportunities almost always requires financial resources. With that in mind I'd like to conclude by
recognising and publicly thanking the many donors whose unstinting generosity has meant that
College has been in a position to deliver the tremendous progress of the past year. It's entirely true
to say that we couldn't have done it without you - thank you.
2016 will mark the 175th anniversary of College and as we prepare for that exciting milestone I
firmly believe we can look to the future with a greater sense of confidence and expectation than
ever before. The work of the past few years has created a wonderful foundation for future success,
and Dr Peterken, the Headmaster; along with his executive colleagues have the full support of the
Council. We very much look forward to working with them throughout the anniversary year ahead.
John Horan

REPORT OF THE COLLEGE COUNCIL
The Council is pleased to present its annual report and the audited financial statements for the year
ended 31 August 2015. The financial statements comply with all statutory requirements and the
requirements of the charity's governing documents.
STATUS & ADMINISTRATION
Cheltenham College was founded in 1841 and is registered with the Charity Commission under
charity number 311720. Details of the membership of the College Council, its executive officers
and professional advisors are provided on the preceding page.
STRUCTURE, GOVERNANCE & MANAGEMENT
Governing Documents
The Charity is incorporated and governed by the Cheltenham College Act 1894 and the Charities
(Cheltenham College) Orders 1976 and 2011.
Council
The governance of College is vested in the President and Council, as laid down in the governing
documents. Membership of Council is as follows: -
The President and Deputy President, elected by Council;
Not fewer than ten and not more than eighteen co-opted members appointed by Council;
Seven members nominated by the Universities of Oxford, Cambridge and such Higher
Education institution as the Council of Cheltenham College may from time to time resolve, the
Cheltonian Association, the Cheltonian Society, the teaching staff of Cheltenham College and
the teaching staff of Cheltenham College Preparatory School.
Its principal sub-committees normally meet between three and six times per year.
Appointment and induction of Council Members
On the occurrence of a vacancy amongst the nominated members of the Council (other than the
member nominated by the Cheltonian Society) the President shall be responsible, on behalf of the
Council, for notifying and entering into negotiations with the nominating authority.
The elections of the members of the Council to be nominated by the teaching staff of either the
College or the Preparatory School are conducted by the Headmaster or by a member or members
of the teaching staff delegated by him, who shall report the methods by which the elections were
conducted and their results to the Council.
Co-opted members of Council are identified and nominated by the Nominations Committee and
elected by Council.
All new members of Council receive a comprehensive briefing pack and induction workshop from
the Bursar and Secretary to Council on trusteeship, the workings of the College, its policies and
objectives Newly appointed, as well as established Council members, are encouraged to attend
training courses, conferences, regulatory updates and other appropriate externally organised events
in order to continually develop the knowledge and expertise of the governing body.
6
CHELTENHAM COLLEGE
COUNCIL'S REPORT & FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2015
Organisational Management
By virtue of The Cheltenham College Act 1894, the Council is responsible for "the entire
management of the concerns and property of the College" and "may receive, invest, lay out and
dispose of all the stocks, effects, funds, money and securities for the benefit of the College" It
meets not less than three times each year. Both the President and Deputy President are ex-officio
members of the principal sub-committees but are not required to chair them.
The Finance, Risk & Development Committee is chaired by Mr Bill Straker-Nesbit and meets not
less than five times a year. This committee sets financial targets for approval by the full Council
and monitors results against such targets. The Committee is also responsible for overseeing risk,
compliance with statutory legislation and facilities development. The College executive team is
responsible for managing the business within the financial parameters and general policy laid
down by Council on the recommendations of the Finance Risk & Development Committee.
The Audit Committee meets at least annually to review the annual accounts and receive the
independent auditor's report.
The Education Committee is a consultative forum in which issues of educational policy, provision
or performance are discussed. Executive authority lies with the Council, which may, however,
through the President, delegate such authority to the Committee. The Education Committee meets
termly and is chaired by Dr Bob Acheson.
Group structure and Relationships
The Charity has three wholly owned trading subsidiaries:
Cheltenham College Services Limited, which provides corporate letting facilities, transport
and retailing services;
Cheltenham College Enterprises Limited, which provides estates development and
management services, printing and equipment services;
Cheltenham College 2nd Hand Clothing Store Limited, which sold uniform on behalf of

Risk Management
The Council has examined the principal areas of the College's operations and has considered the
major risks faced in each of these areas. The Council is responsible for the management of the
risks faced by the College. Detailed considerations of risk are delegated to the Bursar. Risks are
identified, assessed and controls established throughout the year. A formal review of the Charity's
risk management processes is undertaken on an annual basis by Council and monitored termly by
the Finance Risk & Development (FRD) committee.

operations. It is recognised that systems can only provide reasonable, but not absolute, assurance
that major risks have been adequately managed.
OBJECTIVES, ACHIEVEMENTS AND PERFORMANCE
The principal objective of Cheltenham College is to provide an excellent academic and broadly
based education, in a predominantly boarding environment, for boys and girls from the age of
three to eighteen in accordance with Christian principles. Within these Objectives, the Charity also
has to maintain its heritage endowment of Grade I and II listed buildings; various works of art;
artefacts; books and historical documents relating to the College's history, as well as a number of
trust funds held for special purposes in connection with the development of the College's facilities,
the provision of scholarships, bursaries, prizes and for other educational purposes.
This year, particular focus has been given to further improvement of academic performance,
improving the quality of the built environment and continuing to widen access to College for
pupils for whom an independent education would otherwise be unaffordable.
8
CHELTENHAM COLLEGE
COUNCIL'S REPORT & FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2015
The College welcomes pupils from all backgrounds who we believe have the potential to benefit
from the education we provide. An individual's economic status, gender, ethnicity, race, religion
or disability do not form part of the assessment processes. The College is committed to
safeguarding and promoting the welfare of its pupils and expects all staff and volunteers to share
this commitment.
Policy
The Council's fundamental policy is to ensure that: -
the principal objectives of Cheltenham College and Cheltenham College Preparatory School
are met through the proper provision of the necessary staff and other resources to the highest
possible standards; and
a sound financial base is maintained to support these resources and the future development of
College.
Strategies to achieve the year's objectives
Cheltenham College and Cheltenham College Preparatory continued a value-added approach, not
only with the objective of achieving academic excellence but balanced by a strong emphasis on
sport, music and drama. There was also a strong focus on the development of leadership and social
skills together with the provision of a wide variety of activities, including the College's
Humanitarian Aid Projects (CHAPS) in Romania, Kenya and the Shamrock School in Nepal. Both
schools continued to conduct adventurous expeditions and international sports and choral tours.
Links with other schools in both the state and independent sectors have been maintained and the
College has continued to facilitate wide community access to its facilities.
College has a long tradition of strength in the Sciences. In common with other similar schools,
College led the way in the introduction of science to the school curriculum in the nineteenth
century and many Old Cheltonians have gone on to make an impact in their specialist scientific
areas on the world stage. Having completed a E2.5M refit of the College's Science facility in 2014,
a complete refit of the Prep School's Science and Technology building was undertaken in the
Summer of 2015. As it was with the Senior School refit, the building was stripped back to its shell
to facilitate the replacement of the entire mechanical & electrical plant, the roof, windows & doors
and to make the building much more energy efficient. All eight laboratories and classrooms were
fitted out to the same very high standard as the Senior School's facility, creating a teaching and
learning environment to rival the best.
Pupil Numbers
In the year to 31 August 2015 the total number of pupils attending College was 1,058 (2014:
1,036) of whom 432 were senior school boarders, 225 were senior school day pupils and 401
attended the Preparatory School.
Academic
Since his appointment in 2010 the Headmaster has led a determined focus on excellent teaching,
the development of a strong work ethic and the wholesale improvement of study and revision
skills.
Summer 2015 A-level examination results were once again very strong with 75% of all papers sat
being awarded A*to B grades, whilst 45% achieved either an A* or A grade. As a direct result
more than three-quarters of candidates achieved places at Russell Group or other elite universities.
9

COUNCIL'S REPORT & FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2015
At GCSE College celebrated its best ever results. All papers were passed with 65% of grades
at
A* and A, and 88% at grade B and above. 42 Candidates achieved at least 5 A*s.
The focus on delivering academic 'added value' continued through the year and all of these results
are a testament to the hard work of College pupils as well as to the dedication and expertise of
their teachers.
The Prep School too produced excellent academic results, with all Common Entrance pupils being
accepted by their first choice of school and a number being awarded academic scholarships Of the
Year 8 leavers, 89% joined the College and these pupils collectively produced the top performance
in 7 of the 10 subjects on entry to the College. At 11+, four Prep School pupils won scholarship
awards to Cheltenham Ladies' College.
There was no Independent Schools Inspectorate (ISI) inspection this year as an intermediate
boarding inspection in May 2014 had reported that College had been found to be fully compliant
with all appropriate regulatory requirements.
Sport
In 2015 College continued to work to the principle that extra-curricular activity should
complement academic work rather than compete with it. As a result, alongside a very strong set of
academic results, College sport also prospered during the year. Not only were there excellent team
performances but also a significant number of individual pupils achieved national, regional or
county-level honours. In addition, the next stage of the College's Sports' Development Plan saw
excellent upgrades being completed to both of the astroturf pitches and the all-weather tennis
courts.
The College regularly fielded upwards of 12 teams in each of its major sports against all of its
competitors, as well as sustaining a rich and varied programme of competition for the minor sports.
Our Rugby XV got through to the last 16 of the Champions Trophy and notched up impressive
victories over Uppingham, Radley and Rugby; a number of U16's have also been included in the
Gloucester Rugby Academy. The boys' hockey XI spent pre-season in Barcelona before securing
wins over Abingdon and Marlborough. Within the Independent School's Hockey League (ISHL),
the 4th XI secured a title and the U14s progressed to the West of England Finals.
Numbers remained healthy in the Boat Club with upwards of 130 rowers. The lst VIII performed
well, narrowly missing out on qualification for Henley and the Juniors' qualified for the semi-
finals of the National Schools Regatta. After a win at Gloucester, the girls 1st IV produced their
best performance of the season at the National Schools Regatta, narrowly missing out on a place in
the final.
One of College's busiest cricket seasons finished with successes in the Haileybury Festival for the
1st XI, plus victory in the St Peter's, York Festival for the U15's and the U14's reached the ESCA
County Cricket Final. The 1 XI had a virtually unbeaten season with one pupil amassing 974 runs
for the XI.
Girls netball saw the 1st VII have a successful campaign beating King's Worcester, Wycliffe,
Marlborough and Dean Close whilst our U14A team who were unbeaten during the season and
became County Champions. Girls hockey had a memorable tour to Malaysia before the 1st XI
secured wins over CLC, Bradfield and Bloxham, and won a place at the West of England Finals;
the 2XI secured the ISHL title and the U14 and U16 age groups qualified for the West of England
Finals as well with the U16's only losing 1 game all season.
10

COUNCIL'S REPORT & FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2015
In tennis, the girls' 1st VI lost only one match and reached the Regional Finals of the Senior
Students Cup, whilst the 2nd and 5th VI were unbeaten and our girls' cricketers won the U15
Indoor Lady Taverners' Match for Gloucestershire.
Individuals in golf, rackets, badminton, shooting, squash and athletics ensured that Cheltonians
were represented at both regional and national level, therefore highlighting the breadth and quality
of College's sporting provision.
The value of involvement in sport alongside academic endeavour is recognized throughout the
age-range and the Prep School also enjoyed a very strong year with successes, once again, being
recorded by both boys and girls with the top rugby and hockey sides securing victories in the
majority of their fixtures.
In line with the College's objective to widen access to the facilities and education provided by the
College, all of our sports facilities are available for use by external users, including a number of
State Schools, CASCs other sports clubs and most are used on a regular basis. In addition,
individuals were offered the opportunity to enroll in a variety of sports excellence courses hosted
at the College. Local State Schools were also offered the opportunity to participate both in
coaching sessions and a number of sports festivals hosted at both Senior and Junior level by the
College. A number of fixtures were routinely played against State School teams.
Music & Drama
Music, and of course the Chapel, remain at the very heart of College life. The year saw another
diverse and high-quality range of musical performances delivered by the Choir at College,
Gloucester Cathedral and the Cheltenham Music Festival the latter to a sell-out audience. 'Big
Band' demonstrated the diversity of musical talent and interest at College by again delighting a
large and enthusiastic audience at the Cheltenham Jazz Festival. The College's Choral Society
(open to all) gave a crowd pleasing rendition of the Messiah at the start of Advent.
The Prep Schools' Music Day saw nearly 200 pupils from local schools join with the College
pupils and staff for a day of orchestral and choral workshops. This complemented our continuing
provision to musicians, who do not have access to appropriate facilities at their own schools to
take their Royal School of Music examinations at the College, with accompaniment provided by
our own staff, without charge.
Drama, remains a central element of the extra-curricular programme of both schools.
Last year more than 200 College pupils took the stage in five separate productions. The first was
'The Best Days of Our Lives, a farce set in a girls and a boys' boarding school. Shortly
afterwards, and as part of the College's year of commemorations of the start of World War I the
College staged the musical 'Oh What a Lovely War". The production played to "sold out"
appreciative audiences totalling over 1,000 staff, pupils and parents. The year finished with the
Willy Russell classic "Our Day Out", which explored the class system and the impact of poor
education on children.
March 2015 saw the annual charity Variety Show raise several thousand pounds for the College's
Humanitarian Aid Projects at Bradet School in Romania, Gogar Primary School in Kenya and our
new partner school the Shamrock School, Nepal.
The final production saw 25 3rd and 4th form College pupils working together to bring the classic
children's book 'The Railway Children' to life and creating a working railway on stage.
11
CHELTENHAM COLLEGE
COUNCIL'S REPORT & FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2015
At the Prep, it has been another year packed with Drama opportunities and performances. The
Shakespeare Schools Festival saw two casts perform abridged Shakespeare plays at The Roses
Theatre in Tewkesbury, with Year 6 presenting 'Macbeth' and Year 8 'King Lear'. This was the
Prep's seventh year at the festival and it was, as always, an amazing experience for the pupils.
Christmas saw a delightful array of festive entertainment including the traditional Nativity play by
Reception, Kingfishers musical performance of 'Midwife Crisis' and Lower School's pantomime
'Cinders'.
'Private Peaceful', the poignant story of two brothers leaving their peaceful life in the English
countryside to go and fight in the trenches during the First World War, was the main school
production this year. The assembly hall was transformed into a war zone with sandbags, muddy
floor, corrugated metal and barbed wire. Music was performed by the pupils and added to the
intense atmosphere of the show.
The Kingfishers' summer show, 'Pirates versus Mermaids' was spectacular. Lower and Middle
school participated in workshops on both 'Romeo and Juliet' and "The Tempest' and the year
ended with the academic scholars producing a hilarious, farcical, energetic abridged "Twelfth
Night'.
We naturally offer local schools the opportunity to experience the efforts of our pupils by inviting
them to our drama performances. Since drama continues to go from strength to strength, with a
full schedule of shows planned for 2015-16 already, we have decided to introduce LAMDA
lessons and examinations from September 2015.
CCF
The highlight of the year for the CCF Contingent was the opportunity for 28 pupils to represent the
CCF movement at the Cenotaph Remembrance Parade in London in November 2014. In October
the contingent had been joined by over one hundred 3rd Form pupils for a service at the National
Memorial Arboretum. These activities helped to embed a sense of service and sacrifice in the
pupils, with many inspired to continue CCF voluntarily and seek opportunities to develop their
resilience, leadership and communication skills on courses and expeditions.
CCF involvement remains a key element of the rounded education we seek to provide, and equips
pupils with skills that will benefit both them, and the wider community, later in life. In particular,
CCF cadets develop important leadership skills whilst at the same time learning the value of team-
working.

Investments, Funds and Reserves Policies
All investments held by the Charity have been acquired in accordance with the powers available to
the Trustees and are held to produce capital growth and income.
The College finished the year on target for income but market conditions over July and August
2015 resulted in an annual capital growth of only 1% which, in value terms, was E51,000 (2014:
E303,000). The fund managers, wherever possible, have taken a prudent and defensive allocation
stance within equities.
The College made a conscious decision in 2006 to adopt an ethical investment strategy, restricting
investments to exclude any tobacco and armaments providers.
Cheltenham College does not hold any free reserves; all operating surpluses are invested in fixed
assets in order to ensure the continued development of the College. The general reserve,
accumulated over the past 170 years has been retained to cover the fixed assets, provide working
capital and also provide a buffer against fluctuations in income resultant from significant adverse
variations in pupil numbers. In the unlikely event of the need to call upon reserves, the level and
variety of fixed assets held are such that disposal of an appropriate asset could realise sufficient
resources to meet the requirement. The Trustees reviewed the reserves policy as part of their
strategic planning and decided that continued investment in the College's facilities remains
essential to ensure continued recruitment of healthy pupil numbers through the provision of
excellent facilities in both schools.
The Unrestricted Designated Funds are used to hold College Lottery receipts, unused amounts
from bequests and to make provision for future discounts in respect of fees paid in advance.
Cheltenham College holds a prudent proportion of advance fees in liquid investments, and
measures to increase the advance fees reserve have continued. Over time these funds should
naturally deplete.
The Restricted Funds are scholarship income (normally all used in the year of receipt), the

Access Policy
The College does not restrict the education it provides to those who can afford the fees. Our pupils
benefit from learning within a diverse community Our bursary policy and our numerous
community programmes contribute to a widening of access to the education we offer and the
facilities we enjoy.
Bursary Policy and Report
In the spirit of providing public benefit in line with the College's charitable objectives, Cheltenham
College is fully committed to widening access to pupils whose parents would not normally be able
to afford the fees charged. A number of bursaries of up to 100% of the fees are made available to
such families each year, with availability of such support being promoted in the College and
Preparatory School prospectus, on the websites and, if appropriate, in press advertisements.
Bursaries are also used to provide assistance to existing parents whose financial position worsens.
When assessing means, we take a number of factors into consideration including family income,
investments, savings and family circumstances. However, the College does not have a large
endowment and when funding awards we need to ensure we strike the right balance between fee-
paying parents, many of whom make considerable personal sacrifices to fund their child's
education, and those benefiting from the awards. As a consequence not all applications are
successful.
149 (2014: 143) pupils were in receipt of a means tested bursary award ranging from 5% - 100%
of the fees and the combined fee discounts granted to these pupils amounted to E1,766,408 (2014:

least 90% fee remission and 22 of at least 75%. Service bursaries amounting to f243,742 were
awarded to 74 pupils making a total of E2,010,150.

Financial Planning
Timely financial planning is often the key for many parents who are hoping to send their children
to the College and the College offers parents the opportunity to purchase school fees in advance or
through regular monthly contributions. To underline the value we place on continuity for families,
we offer discounts where parents have more than two children at the College.
Scholarship policy Promotion of High Academic Standards.
Scholarships are offered on entry at 11+, 13+ and 16+. The awards are competitive, offered on the
basis of performance in the scholarship assessments and are designed to recognise exceptional
academic potential and/or the ability to excel in our co-curricular activities. Scholarships are
awarded with a fixed fee reduction and where further assistance is necessary, supplemented by a
means-tested bursary. We advertise the availability of scholarship awards widely.
Community Programmes
Members of College teaching staff continued to act as examiners for national public examinations
in their respective fields of expertise and/or added further teaching materials to online and printed
resources libraries. We have assisted local maintained sector schools with teaching resources and
share our university entrance expertise with them through inviting Year 12 pupils to attend
seminars on how to prepare personal statements for UCAS applications. Some members of staff
have been involved in running holiday schools and revision courses, while others either teach in or
organise educational programmes that have encompassed after-school activities at a local primary
school, leading art classes and other adult training programmes. A number of staff members from
both schools continue to serve as Governors of local state-maintained schools. The College has
offered an invitation for partnership to All Saints' Academy and has entered into a community
partnership with St Gregory's Catholic School providing Science Workshops for year 5 and 6
pupils while from September 2015 College 6th Form Students will be undertaking Community
Service at St Gregory's on a weekly basis.
A significant number of members of staff have been involved in partnership schemes with other
schools, clubs and societies ranging from specialist sports coaching to providing Duke of
Edinburgh Award Scheme instruction and to fulfilling the role of pianist for a Cheltenham
community choir Every year local youth groups are invited to the College to use the facilities
such as the climbing wall or participate in community sporting events such as Kwik Cricket.
We have, on many occasions, extended invitations to local maintained schools to send pupils to
College-hosted educational or leadership events as part of our Primary School Outreach Initiative,
whilst our own 5th and Lower 6th pupils undertake regular community service, helping with
literacy tuition in a local primary school, volunteering at a centre for children with disabilities and
visiting the elderly as part of our Local Care Home Outreach Initiative. The College hosts a special

We continued to provide places for children from the maintained sector, and young adults from the
National Star College to gain work experience. The College continues to run apprenticeship

College also provided facilities and staff to support the "Celebration of Craftsmanship" exhibition

NOTES TO THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
1. Principal Accounting Policies
The following accounting policies have been applied consistently in dealing with items which are
considered material in relation to the College and Group's financial statements.
a) Presentation of Accounts
The financial statements have been prepared in accordance with: -
Applicable Accounting Standards in the United Kingdom (United Kingdom Generally Accepted
Accounting Practice).
Accounting regulations issued under the Charities Act 2011.
The Statement of Recommended Practice on Accounting and Reporting by Charities: the
Charities SORP 2005.
b) Basis of Accounting
The financial statements have been prepared in accordance with the historical cost convention as
modified by the revaluation of certain investments and in accordance with the SORP 2005.
c) Basis of Consolidation
The consolidated Statement of Financial Activities and Balance Sheet include the financial statements
of Cheltenham College and its wholly owned trading subsidiaries, Cheltenham College Services
Limited, Cheltenham College 2nd Hand Clothing Store Limited and Cheltenham College Enterprises
Limited. Cheltenham College Charitable Trust, an independently run charity, has been included
to
comply with FRS2.
d) Going Concern
After making enquires, the Trustees have a reasonable expectation that the Charity has adequate
resources to continue its activities for the foreseeable future. Accordingly, they continue to adopt the
going concern basis in preparing the financial statements as outlined in the Statement of Trustees
Responsibilities on page 16.
e) Fees Receivable
Fees receivable consists of charges billed for fees, board and tuition for the School year ended 31st
August, less bursaries and allowances. Fees received for education to be provided in future years are
carried forward as deferred income.
f) Legacies and Bequests
Legacies and bequests are recognised in the financial statements on receipt.
g) Resources Expended
Resources expended are included in the Statement of Financial Activities on an accruals basis.
Overhead and other costs not directly attributable to particular functional activity categories are
apportioned over the relevant categories on the basis of management estimates of the amount
attributable to that activity in the year, either by reference to staff time or space occupied, as appropriate.
The irrecoverable element of VAT is included with the item of expense to which it relates. Costs
of
generating funds includes all staffing and fundraising costs. Charitable activity expenses are allocated
to functional groups on a direct cost basis or apportioned on a staff time basis.

g) Resources Expended (continued)
Governance costs comprise the costs of running the Charity, including strategic planning for its future
development, also internal and external audit, any legal advice for the Council, and all the costs of
complying with constitutional and statutory requirements, such as the costs of Council meetings and of
preparing statutory financial statements and satisfying public accountability.
h) Operating Leases
Operating lease rentals are charged to the Statement of Financial Activities over the lease period.
i)
Pension Scheme Arrangements
The College is involved with a number of pension schemes for its employees.
Cheltenham College contributes to the Teachers' Pension Defined Benefits Scheme at rates set by
the Scheme Actuary and advised to the College by the Scheme Administrator. The Scheme is a
multi-employer pension scheme and it is not possible to identify the assets and liabilities of the
Scheme, which are attributable to the Charity. In accordance with FRS 17 the Scheme is
accounted for as a defined contribution scheme and contributions are accounted for when advised
as due by the Scheme Administrator.
Other staff have the option of joining a defined contribution scheme operated by an insurance
company. The College and members of staff pay fixed percentages of salaries to the insurance
company. The College's contributions are charged in the Statement of Financial Activities.
j) Fund Accounting
Details and the nature and purpose of each fund is set out in notes 22 and 23. Funds held for the
general purpose of the College are held as unrestricted funds. Those held by the College for
specific purposes outwith normal operations such as the College lottery, bequests and the Tinson
hardship fund are held as designated funds and set aside by the Trustees. Those subject to specific
wishes of the donors are included within the relevant restricted or endowed funds.
k) Tangible Fixed Assets
The cost of tangible fixed assets is their purchase cost, together with any incidental costs of
acquisition and is subject to a de-minimus limit of E1,000. Freehold land and buildings include
original cost and subsequent alterations and additions. The cost of land and buildings includes
interest paid on specific related borrowings during the construction period.
D) Depreciation
Depreciation is calculated on a straight-line basis to write off the cost, less estimated residual
value, of fixed assets over their estimated useful lives as follows:
Freehold buildings

Leasehold improvements
Over the remaining term of the lease

Boilers
10% on cost
Computers and electronic equipment
10% 50% on cost
Cars
25% on cost
