Christ's Hospital Association supports the costs of publicity and Alumni relations.
Additional Costs Fund (formerly The Necessitous Children's Fund) provides additional support,
particularly for travel and clothing costs for children from families in exceptiona financial need.
House Fund gives an annual grant to the boarding houses in order to provide additiona resources or
activities.
The Reginald Wood Fund provides additional funds to support musically talented pupils.
The Army Foundation supports children whose parents have served or are currently serving in the
Army.
Restricted Funds
Restricted Funds are accounted for in accordance with the particular terms of the trust arising from the
expressed or implied wishes of donors insofar as these are intended to be binding. Where any such wishes
are not intended to be binding, they are taken into account and recognised in an appropriate Designated or
Unrestricted Fund.
The Sivewright Memorial Fund is restricted to the provision of capital projects that will enhance the
pupils' appreciation of the Arts.
The Daniel Lett Fund supports current and former pupils in developing an interest in and pursuing a
career in law, particularly at the Bar.
Designated Funds
These are Funds created for specific purposes. There is no legal restriction on the way in which the funds may
be applied.
The Premises Fund was established for planned maintenance and other estate works included in the
budget for the year but not yet completed; it also provides for the future development of Bluecoat
Sports.
The Fixed Asset Capital Fund represents the net book value of the fixed assets used for operational
purposes.

CHAIRMAN'S STATEMENT
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2016
In this, my first year as Chairman, I must start by thanking my predecessor, Simon Beloe for his 12 years as
Chairman, during which Marwell Wildlife has seen significant transformation. Building on that extensive
progress, I am delighted to report on the undoubted successes that Marwell has enjoyed in 2016. It has been
a highly productive year, perhaps best exemplified by strong growth in our income and the control of our
underlying costs. This is important as it underpins the importance of economy and efficiency as we seek to
ensure that every penny is wisely spent in furtherance of our charitable objectives. Furthermore that our
conservation work, undertaken by our professional teams both in the UK and overseas is world class in
reputation and complements the dedicated and excellent staff we are fortunate to employ at our Z0O.
Our ambition to increase our charitable output is only limited by our financial resources. As part of our
aforementioned strategy to fund charitable delivery, 2016 saw the start of our largest ZOO development, Energy
for Life, our new Tropica House. This will be a landmark exhibit for the UK and will create an immersive
tropical environment with a rich diversity of animal and plant species, imaginatively configured to give our
guests a unique experience whilst learning more about climate change and nature's solutions for waste and
energy creation. As part of that, Energy for Life will process animal waste and showcase the development of
our energy production as we near our five-year goal of becoming carbon neutral.
The collaboration with Kids Love Nature to open a pre-schoo nursery in 2016 perfectly complements our
existing education offering and builds on our existing curriculum-based work with schools and our higher
education activity, such as our MRes in Wildlife Conservation with the University of Southampton. Marwell can
now truly claim the delivery of lifelong learning, from pre-school, to post-doctoral research.
2016 also saw Marwell achieve an impressive list of records, for example in guest income, and guest numbers
(both in terms of day guests and total guest numbers), our highest ever levels of annual membership, our
highest ever catering and retail income and our largest ever public engagement project, Marwell's Zany
Zebras, with our beautifully painted sculpture trail dominating Southampton and raising awareness not only of
Marwell Zoo, but importantly our work with the iconic and endangered Grevy's zebra species.
Looking to the future, in 2017 we look forward of course to the opening of our new Tropical House and will turn
our attention to development of our next major capital investment, Water and Wetlands, as we start to
redevelop our pygmy hippo and flamingo facilities, and reconfigure the exit from the ZOo, currently a poor last
impression for guests as they walk along the South Road. This work sits within our long term master plan and
demonstrates the ongoing momentum through which Marwell is investing into the ZOO.
I would like to thank my fellow Board members, Marwell's dedicated staff and volunteers, and of course our
guests. The visiting public not only fund our work, but their continued support and enjoyment in visiting us and
learning more of our conservation astivity remains a constant motivation for all that we do.
David Stalker
Chairman of the Board of Trustees
Marwell Wildlife

MARWELL WILDLIFE
(A Company Limited by Guarantee)
TRUSTEES' REPORT
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2016
The Trustees (who are also directors of the charity for the purposes of the Companies Act) present their
annual report together with the audited financial statements of Marwell Wildlife (the company and the group)
for the year ended 31 December 2016. The Trustees confirm that the Annual Report and financial statements
of the company and the group comply with the current statutory requirements, the requirements of the
company and the group's governing document and the provisions of the Statement of Recommended Practice
(SORP) "Accounting and Reporting by Charities" issued in 2015.
Strategic Report
Objectives and Activities
Missions, Objects and Aims
The Charity's mission as reflected in its objects is the advancement of environmental protection and of
education for the public benefit by:
promoting the conservation of biological and other natural resources in particular by restoring and
maintaining species, habitats and functioning ecosystems; scientific management of assurance
populations; and environmental protection;
advancing the understanding and promoting the benefits of nature for society, human health, wellbeing
and quality of life and encouraging participation of individuals, communities and wider society in the
conservation of biological and other natural resources and the environment;
practising and promoting environmental protection and sustainability as an exemplar and through
campaigning and advocacy;
undertaking and sharing the results of research, monitoring and expeditions; and providing opportunities
for scientific education and training; and
maintaining and developing a zoological park as a place of learning and enjoyment and advancing the
husbandry, welfare and conservation of animals.
Strategies to Achieve Aims
In 2012 we examined the cause of footfall decline and also reviewed the spatial configuration of our ZOO and
considered how we can best use and optimise it to further our aims. Our resulting organisational strategy is to
invest over the next ten years significant resources (primarily out of our own cash reserves) into a series of
capital investment projects at the ZOO designed specifically to attract more visitors and, in turn, our income and
profitability and charitable outputs.
Our ten year business plan reflects this strategy and lists three organisational goals which are intended both to
support the strategy and deliver our charitable aims:
Deliver our conservation framework through our zoological park and international work
Grow our business by investing wisely and operating efficiently
Build a vibrant organisation with enthusiastic people focused on shared goals.
4
MARWELL WILDLIFE
(A Company Limited by Guarantee)
TRUSTEES' REPORT
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2016
Significant Activitles that Contribute to Aims:
Restoring species, habitats and functioning ecosystems with particular focus in the UK and Africa.
Managing assurance populations of threatened species in nature and through captive breeding
programmes
Undertaking research and delivering higher education courses.
Delivering education sessions for schools
Advocating sustainable living and improving our environmental performance
Operating a zoological park as a place of learning, to advance animal health and conservation, and to
generate revenue to support activities elsewhere in the world.
Encouraging and facilitating individual and community participation in wildlife conservation.
Public Benefit
The Trustees confirm that they have complied with the duty in the Charities Act 2011 to have due regard to
public benefit guidance issued by the Charity Commission.
The Trustees believe that the pursuit of our aims provides a public benefit in the areas of education, scientific
research and the conservation of endangered species and their habitats. Whilst in order to cover the high
costs of operating Marwell Zoo, admission fees are charged, when setting the level of fees consideration is
given to accessibility to the public. Discounts are available for school visits, students, pensioners and families.
Disabled guests are entitled to free admission for a carer. The charge made for a school classroom session
taught by our in-house education team is well below market rates in order to reach as many pupils as possible.
Annually we hold a daytime event in collaboration with up to two local charities, providing free access and
hospitality to children with long-term illnesses.
Staff Communication and Equality
Marwell Wildlife is committed to the ongoing development of an agile, change-ready and flexible workforce
equipped to take forward new ideas and ways of working, with competent, appropriately cross-skilled
employees and with a greater inclusion of casual workers and volunteers. We ensure that we regularly update
our workforce of the latest strategic developments, financial position and current projects. We do this through
regular, face to face manager and team updates and whole team speed presentations from the CEO.
We continue to support our people with a suite of Health and Wellbeing initiatives throughout the calendar year,
with the aim of providing a safe and healthy working environment that promotes staff well-being and enables
increased commitment and engagement and improved performance and productivity. We foster a climate of
managers taking an interest in the Health and Wellbeing of their people and in doing so the organisation
respects a critical balance, to meet individual needs whilst also delivering on the business plan. In 2017 we
plan to introduce an ongoing programme of Coaching and Mentoring to develop this further.
As a Sunday Times Top 100 Not-For-Profit organisation, our brand and leadership values lie at the heart of
what we do and inform our practice. In 2016 work started on the Marwell Staff Charter, further defining clear
and unambiguous standards, defined goals and an accountability framework which upholds the needs and
preferences of both our employees and our organisation. We understand the value of employee engagement
and facilitate an environment which allows employee voice to be both heard and responded to as we continue
to build upon our open and enabling culture.
5
MARWELL WILDLIFE
(A Company Limited by Guarantee)
TRUSTEES' REPORT
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2016
Our culture can be observed through our daily behaviour and is considered to be our 'tone of voice'. This is
robustly supported by our employment policies and practices, ensuing equality of access to recruitment,
promotion, selection and training regardless of length or service or protected characteristic. We do
not
discriminate and will consider any reasonable adjustments, wherever practical, to enable talented individuals
to apply for and work at Marwell Wildlife.
Achievements and performance against objectives
Biological conservation
In 2016, we planned to:
Review and refresh our Conservation Framework;
Launch a conservation communications strategy to share our successes, raise awareness of the
breadth and depth of our work, promote understanding of the many and varied values and benefits of
nature, and to galvanise support for our conservation initiatives;
Contribute expertise to biodiversity conservation planning across Central Asia and strengthen our
interests in the management of threatened species and ecosystems in the region;
Publish the updated conservation status of antelope species across the world through the IUCN Red
List of Threatened Species as part of our collaboration with the IUCN Species Survival Commission
Antelope Specialist Group;
Collborate on a ground-breaking citizen science survey of endangered Grevy's zebra across northern
Kenya to improve population estimates and inform conservation action;
Review the status of reintroduced addax in Tunisia and produce recommendations for managing these
important populations of this critically endangered species;
Begin a 3 year PhD programme on the ecology and the reintroduction of Britain's rarest reptiles, the
sand lizard and the smooth snake; and
Continue studying the ecology and conservation of large herbivores in the Matopos National Park,
Zimbabwe and their relationship with neighbouring agro-pastoral communities.
In 2016, we:
Reviewed current knowledge to update the status of the world's antelope species to update the IUCN
Red List of Threatened Species as part of our collaboration with the IUCN Species Survival Commission
Antelope Specialist Group;
Collaborated with partner organisations to deliver the 'Great Grevy's Rally' in northern Kenya, drawing
on tourists, landowners and communities to complete a photographic census of Grevy's zebra to
produce the most accurate estimate of population size to date;
Reviewed the status of reintroduced addax in Tunisia and agreed a plan to undertake genetic testing of
this population to enhance understanding of population biology and subsequent management
recommendation;
Formed a collaborative relationship with the Beijing Forestry University to deliver a trans-boundary snow
leopard and ecosystem monitoring and conservation programme across China, Kazakhstan, and
Kyrgyzstan;
Completed two post-graduate studies on the ecology of large herbivores in the Matopos National Park in
Zimbabwe, and collected data on distribution of these species throughout all seasons; and
6
MARWELL WILDLIFE
(A Company Limited by Guarantee)
TRUSTEES' REPORT
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2016
Began a PhD programme on the ecology and reintroduction of sand lizards at Eelmoor Marsh Site of
Special Scientific Interest in Hampshire, UK.
Science and Learning
In 2016, we planned to:
Grow our academic relationships to help reach our research and education goals, and support
conservation delivery;
Agree an extension to the successful MRes in Wildlife Conservation in collaboration with the University
of Southampton;
Align scientific research and education messages to raise awareness of the multiple values of
biodiversity and ecosystems, and steps that can be taken for their conservation and sustainable use;
Collaborate with 'Kids Love Nature' on the opening of a nature nursery for pre-school children at Marwell
Zoo, and with access to our surrounding woodlands and countryside; and
Commence the building of our ambitious new Energy for Life tropical house and design interpretation
about the flow of energy through life, the energy needed to power modern lifestyles and the resulting
challenges for wildlife and the environment.
In 2016, we:
Continued our relationship with the University of Southampton to deliver our joint MRes in Wildlife
Conservation;
Reviewed our education plan to incorporate multiple values of biodiversity, promotion of ecosystem
services and sustainable use of natural resources as an underlying theme of our schools and public
engagement programmes;
Supported the opening of a nature nursery for pre-school children with 'Kids Love Nature', with daily
access to the Zoo and wider countryside;
Began the construction of Energy for Life, a new low carbon energy generation hub and tropical house
exhibit focussing on the flow of energy through life and climate change science; and
Designed and began an outreach programme as part of our wider Marwell's Zany Zebras campaign,
bringing community based wildlife conservation in northern Kenya to life for 100 schools across
Hampshire and 3 other counties, reaching 16,000+ children across all age groups.
Sustainability
In 2016, we planned to:
Begin the first of a five year carbon reduction plan with the aim of becoming a carbon neutral
organisation by 2021;
Design a system for conversion of animal waste to energy that will heat our new tropical house and
other networked buildings in the ZOO; and
Improve infrastructure and install water sub-meters across the Z00 to support water conservation
measures.
7
MARWELL WILDLIFE
(A Company Limited by Guarantee)
TRUSTEES' REPORT
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2016
In 2016 we:
Switched energy supplier and tariff to purchase guaranteed certificate of origin renewable electricity as
an important step towards our goal of becoming carbon neutral;
Devised a plan for generating low carbon for heating for the planned new tropical house and other
networked buildings based on woodchip and animal waste as biomass fuels; and
Identified and repaired leaking water pipes and installed additional stopcocks to improve water
management.
Fundraising Performance
The entire structure of the charity is geared towards fundraising to fulfil our charitable objectives. The
operation of Marwell Zoo is a major part of the charity's activities which makes a significant contribution
towards our aim of educating and inspiring the public to connect with nature. Zoo admission charges together
with the associated donation and gift aid fund the operating costs and allow capital investment in the
development of the Z0O but over and above this contribute funding for our direct conservation work. As
expected of a visitor attraction, Marwell Wildlife undertakes the usual commercia activities such as catering
and a gift shop through a trading subsidiary, Marwell Services Ltd. However, any profit generated by these
operations is donated to the parent charity in order that it be applied to our charitable delivery and hence even
the commercial operations can be deemed part of our fundraising activity.
In 2016, alongside the conventional fundraising activities of legacies, tombola and donations, we delivered
"Marwell's Zany Zebras". This spectacular, family friendly, community based art event attracted 47 business
sponsors, 100 scholls and community groups and hundreds of thousands of visitors to the trails around
Southampton and Marwell Zoo - further raising Marwell's profile and contributing towards the dramatic uplift in
paying visitors enjoyed over the summer. The project culminated in fundraising auctions of both the large and
miniature sculptures. Net funds of E47,114 will be spent on our community based conservation initiatives
around Grevy's zebra in Kenya in 2017.
Investment Performance
During the year, Marwell sold its remaining investment portfolio with Sarasin and Partners and realised a net
gain of E18,714. At the year end, E1,025,355 was held in Virgin Money Charity deposit accounts and the
remainder in NatWest current and special interest bearing accounts. Despite the exceptionally low interest
rates available on deposits, the Trustees took the decision to hold reserves in cash due to the volatility of the
stock market following the EU referendum and the commencement of the Energy for Life building work, a
f7.8m project.
The performance and disposition of the charity's investments and deposits is monitored by the Audit & Risk
Committee at its meetings.
Restrictions to our work
As an organisation we are ambitious in our work. There is much to do and we are limited only by resources
and our imagination. This includes financial resource, for the development of our infrastructure and the funding
of specific charitable related programmes, and also human resource. Marwell is very much a
knowledge-based enterprise and employs a wide variety of talent. As such, limitation on finance to fund such
personnel is also a limiting factor to the delivery of our work to wider beneficiaries, both overseas and in the
UK. Both these factors are acknowledged and reviewed as part of the organisation's risk analysis.
Beneficiaries are selected as communities living alongside threatened wildlife that fits within our broader
conservation strategy and skill set, as well as those who actively choose to engage with us via visiting or
communicating with us.
8
MARWELL WILDLIFE
(A Company Limited by Guarantee)
TRUSTEES' REPORT
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2016
Much of our work overseas is involved with communities where poverty is a contributory factor to managing
conservation outcomes. These initiatives are core to our conservation aims and objectives, and do not
constitute a barrier to our charitable work.
The use of digital media, including better content on our website, zoo-based web cameras and regular
newsletters, both in hard copy and by email, allow for better communication and engagement with those who
wish to be a part of our work but who are unable to visit.
Financial review
In 2016 Marwell welcomed 525,559 guests - an increase of 10% on the previous financial year. Good
summer weather, the births of Amur tiger and Amur leopard cubs and the Marwell's Zany Zebras project all
contributed to the increase in attendance numbers. Work began on the new Energy for Life building and
f1,531,553 of the capital work in progress at the year end relates to this project which is scheduled to open
in 2018.
The surplus for the year was f1,313,161 (2015: E709,860). Restricted expenditure exceeded restricted
income by f39,467 as funds received in previous financial years were spent. The unrestricted surplus was
therefore E1,352,628 (2015: E715,697) and as such can be reinvested in the ZOo or applied towards our
conservation work as we choose. Of our funds of f18,161,672 (2015: E16,848,511) held at the year
end,
f14,204,922 (2015: f12,936,856) were represented by fixed assets - the vast majority of which are the
animal houses and guest services buildings in the ZOO.
The designated funds brought forward from 2015 were used towards the construction of the 'Energy for
Life' building. At their December meeting the Board of Trustees designated a further f1,500,000 of
reserves to be allocated towards the new tropical house and E200,000 to be allocated to larger maintenance
projects at Marwell Zoo.
The trustees have established a reserves policy, the object of which is to ensure the continued operation of
the organisation, including its scientific, conservation and educational programmes. It has been the charity's
policy to hold a base reserve, over and above that held in fixed assets, which is equivalent to at least
four months' operating expenditure. However this policy has been reviewed in light of the significant fixed
asset investment programme commenced in the year and the Trustees consider a base reserve of three
months' operating expenditure to be appropriate. Free reserves at the year-end (excluding the designated
funds referred to above) amounted to E2,167,442, the equivalent of 3 months' operating expenditure.
Plans for future periods
Biological conservation
In 2017, we plan to:
Create a new integrated management plan for the Marwell estate which seeks to enhance biodiversity
as part of sustainable, multi-functional land use and connectivity with the wider landscape;
Advance the reintroduction of North African ostrich in Tunisia and an integrated plan for their
conservation across the region;
With partners including Institut Pasteur, start examining the importance of the spur-thighted tortoise for
Crimean-Congo Haemorrhagic Fever (CCHF) transmission in Tunisia and the consequences for
conservation of the species;
Explore options for capacity building in Ethiopia and the enhancement of conservation efforts for
endangered wildlife, including Grevy's zebra and antelopes;
9
MARWELL WILDLIFE
(A Company Limited by Guarantee)
TRUSTEES' REPORT
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2016
Publish key research papers on the movements and population dynamics of Grevy's zebra in Northern
Kenya;
Maintain our alertness to the effects of drought in Northern Kenya, and the option to provide emergency
feed for Grevy's zebra and local communities' livestock in consultation with Kenya Wildlife Service;
Submit advanced drafts of the ongoing IPBES Asia-Pacific Regional Assessment to regional
governments, develop Key Messages and Statements for Policy Makers;
Assist regional governments in Central Asia with conservation planning for snow leopard through the
Global Snow Leopard and Ecosystem Protection Programme (GSLEP);
Lead workshops on the trans-boundary monitoring of snow leopards and their ecosystem in China and
neighbouring countries; and
Begin the reintroduction of sand lizards at Eelmoor Marsh Site of Special Scientific Interest in
Hampshire, UK.
Science & Learning
In 2017, we plan to:
Publish outcomes of outcomes of recent conservation and research programmes to inform management
of threatened species and their landscapes;
Continue our MRes in Wildlife Conservation and develop further research collaborations with the School
of Biological Sciences at the University of Southampton;
Offer opportunities for research projects, extra-mural studies and final year elective modules for
veterinary degree students from the School of Veterinary Medicine, University of Surrey;
Recruit a Head of Socia Impact & Learning to help broaden and strengthen our education, public
awareness and social impacts in the UK and overseas;
Recruit a Nature Interpreter to develop our collaboration with Kids Love Nature;
Design interpretation for Energy for Life including understanding of the flow of energy through life and
public engagement in climate science; and
Design and deliver interpretation about the evolutionary radiation of lemurs in Madagascar as the initial
stage of Evolution, and part of the new lemur walkthrough experience, Lemur Loop.
Sustainability
In 2017, we plan to:
Review progress and update our Carbon Reduction Plan with the goal of achieving carbon neutrality
within five years;
Complete the design and commission the process for in-house conversion of animal waste to low
carbon energy;
Prepare for adoption of the new 1S014001:2015 standard for certification of our Environmental
Management System; and
Extend access to Marwell by public transport by increasing bus services from hourly to half hourly
during the busy summer period.
10
MARWELL WILDLIFE
(A Company Limited by Guarantee)
TRUSTEES' REPORT
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2016
Structure, governance and management
Constitution
The company is limited by guarantee, and the guarantee of each member is limited to E10. The governing
instrument is the Memorandum and Articles of Association.
Marwell Wildlife owns 100% of the share capital of Marwell Services Limited. Marwell Wildlife owns the land
and all other assets and deals with income and expenditure relating to the operation of the park, including the
upkeep and welfare of the animals and all visitor services, conservation expenditure, and expenditure on
education. Marwell Services Limited deals with all of our trading activities, for example income from our shop,
from our catering operation, and from hiring out the hall for conferences and weddings.
Method of appointment or election of Trustees
The Governing Body of the charity is a Board of not less than five and not more than fourteen Trustees. New
trustees are elected by the Board following a recruitment process which includes interviews by a
subcommittee of the Board and by the Chairman and Chief Executive. Applicants are sought from a
combination of personal referrals, advertised vacancies and executive search organisations. Trustees are
appointed for a three year term but may offer themselves for re-election at the end of each term for a
maximum of 4 terms.
Policies adopted for the induction and training of Trustees
Training of Trustees is reviewed against individual training needs and a full introduction and induction to the
organisation is given to new Trustees upon appointment.
Organisational structure and decision making
The Board normally meets five times a year to review strategy and performance and is helped in its work by
the following Trustee-led committees: Audit & Risk, Capital Expenditure, Conservation (including animal
collection, biodiversity, education and sustainability), Commercial, Ethics, Human Resources & Remuneration,
and
Marketing & Fundraising Committees do not have executive authority but are chaired by a Trustee.
Committees have their own terms of reference and provide linkage back to the main Board and support for
senior management of the charity in their work.
Remuneration Policy
The Trustees consider the Board of Trustees, the Chief Executive Officer and his Executive team, to whom all
day to day management is delegated, to comprise the key management personnel of the charity. The
Executive team comprises the Marketing Director, the HR Director, the Finance Director, the Guest Services
Director and the Director of Conservation. All members of the Board of Trustees give their time voluntarily and
receive no financial benefits from the charity. Any expenses reclaimed from the charity are set out in Note 13
to the accounts.
In examining and awarding executive pay, Marwell uses a variety of sectorial data and benchmarks. This
includes, but is not limited to, the annual ACEVO Pay Survey, publically advertised vacancies for similar
positions within the sector, and market intelligence gleaned through Marwell's own networks regarding direct
comparisons.
11
MARWELL WILDLIFE
(A Company Limited by Guarantee)
TRUSTEES' REPORT
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2016
A Remuneration Committee formed from members of the HR Committee oversees this process, meeting twice
yearly. Although specific adjustments to executive remuneration can be tabled at any time, the committee
normally examines remuneration at its October meeting and currently aims to place executive remuneration in
the median quartile for the sector.
Risk management
Oversight of risk is delegated by the Board to the Audit & Risk Committee who have set aside one committee
meeting a year solely to address this topic and review the Risk Register in detail with a view to a subsequent
full Board report. The Risk Register was completely updated and revised in 2014 to assess the impact of a
range of strategic, regulatory and reputational as well as operational risks and to ensure responsibility for
monitoring and controlling the relevant risk to reduce the likelihood of occurrence or impact is allocated
appropriately.
The most significant risks to Marwell Wildlife are events that impact the delivery of our core products and
services - of which the continued operation of the ZOO which is the major contributor to our charitable outputs is
the most critical. To this end, a thorough review of Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery was undertaken
by al operational departments. As a result, revised business continuity planning has been put in place
focussed on ensuring our critical activities are protected in so far as possible from events outside our control
and the incidence of events without our control is properly mitigated and controlled. In 2017, this planning is
ongoing and will continue to be reviewed, with relevant procedures developed, examined and tested.
In addition to 'business as usual' risk, our major projects (such as Energy for Life) are separately risk assessed
to identify areas of uncertainty and opportunity relating to project work, products and outcomes, as well as the
impact on day to day operations.
Trustees' responsibilities statement
The Trustees (who are also directors of Marwell Wildlife for the purposes of company law) are responsible for
preparing the Trustees' Report and the financial statements in accordance with applicable law and United
Kingdom Accounting Standards (United Kingdom Generally Accepted Accounting Practice).
Company law requires the Trustees to prepare financial statements for each financial year. Under company
law the Trustees must not approve the financial statements unless they are satisfied that they give a true and
fair view of the state of affairs of the charitable company and the group and of the incoming resources and
application of resources, including the income and expenditure, of the charitable group for that period. In
preparing these financial statements, the Trustees are required to:
select suitable accounting policies and then apply them consistently;
observe the methods and principles in the Charities SORP;
make judgments and accounting estimates that are reasonable and prudent;
state whether applicable UK Accounting Standards have been followed, subject to any material
departures disclosed and explained in the financial statements;
prepare the financial statements on the going concern basis unless it is inappropriate to presume that
the charitable group will continue in operation.

Accounting Policies
1.1 Basis of preparation of financial statements
The financial statements have been prepared in accordance with Accounting and Reporting by

accordance with the Financial Reporting Standard applicable in the UK and Republic of Ireland
(FRS 102) (effective 1 January 2015) - (Charities SORP (FRS 102)) the Financial Reporting
Standard applicable in the UK and Republic of lreland (FRS 102) and the Companies Act 2006
Marwell Wildlife meets the definition of a public benefit entity under FRS 102. Assets and liabilities
are initially recognised at historical cost or transaction value unless otherwise stated in the relevant
accounting policy.
The Statement of Financial Activities (SOFA) and Balance Sheet consolidate the financial
statements of the company and its subsidiary undertaking. The results of the subsidiary are
consolidated on a line by line basis.
No separate SOFA has been presented for the company alone as permitted by section 408 of the
Companies Act 2006.
1.2 Company status
Marwell Wildlife is a company limited by guarantee (number 1355272) and registered with the
Charity Commission (number 275433).
The members of the company are the Trustees who are named on the first page of the statutory
accounts. In the event of the charity being wound up, the liability in respect of the guarantee is
limited to f10 per member of the charity.
1.3 Basis of consolidation
The financial statements consolidate the accounts of Marwell Wildlife and all of its subsidiary
undertakings ('subsidiaries').
The company has taken advantage of the exemption contained within 408 of the Companies Act
2006 not to present its own Income and Expenditure Account.

1.4 Fund accounting
General funds are unrestricted funds which are available for use at the discretion of the Trustees in
furtherance of the general objectives of the company and which have not been designated for other
purposes.
Designated funds comprise unrestricted funds that have been set aside by the Trustees for
particular purposes. The aim and use of each designated fund is set out in the notes to the financial
statements.
Restricted funds are funds which are to be used in accordance with specific restrictions imposed by
donors or which have been raised by the company for particular purposes. The costs of raising and
administering such funds are charged against the specific fund. The aim and use of each restricted
fund is set out in the notes to the financial statements.
Investment income, gains and losses are allocated to the appropriate fund.
1.5 Income
All income is recognised once the company has entitlement to the income, it is probable that the
income will be received and the amount of income receivable can be measured reliably.
Gifts in kind donated for distribution are included at valuation and recognised as income when they
are distributed to the projects. Gifts donated for resale are included as income when they are sold.
Donated facilities are included at the value to the company where this can be quantified and a third
party is bearing the cost. No amounts are included in the financial statements for services donated
by volunteers.
Income tax recoverable in relation to donations received under Gift Aid or deeds of covenant is
recognised at the time of the donation.
1.6 Going concern
The financial statements have been prepared on the basis that the charity is a going concern. The
Trustees consider that there are no material uncertainties on the charity's ability to continue its
activities for the foreseeable future. They have approved a detailed income and expenditure budget
for 2016, the charity has a regular stream of income from visitors and its reserves policy means that
it will be able to meet its obligations and have sufficient time to mitigate against any unforeseen
circumstances.
1.7 Trading Income
Turnover comprises revenue recognised by the company in respect of goods and services supplied
during the year, exclusive of Value Added Tax and trade discounts.

1.8 Expenditure
Expenditure is recognised once there is a legal or constructive obligation to make payment to a third
party, it is probable that settlement will be required and the amount of the obligation can be
measured reliably.
All expenditure is accounted for on an accruals basis. All expenses including support costs and
governance costs are allocated to the applicable expenditure headings..
The Costs of Generating Funds are those costs incurred in attracting voluntary income, and those
incurred in trading activities that raise funds.
Charitable Activities include our Conservation and Education programmes, and the operation of the
Zoo in support of those programmes. The costs of our charitable activities include both direct costs
and support costs relating to those activities.
Governance costs include those incurred in the governance of the charity and are primarily
associated with constitutional, statutory and strategic requirements.
Support costs, which include the central office functions such as general management, payroll
administration, budgeting and accounting, information technology and human resources are
allocated across the categories of the Costs of Generating Funds, Charitable Activities and
Governance costs.
Irrecoverable VAT is charged as a cost to the Statement of Financial Activities (within the
appropriate category as noted above).

1.10 Intangible fixed assets and amortisation
Intangible assets costing more than E5,000 are included at cost, including any incidental costs of
acquisition. Subsequent to initial recognition, intangible assets are stated at cost less accumulated
amortisation and accumulated impairment. Intangible assets are amortised on a straight line basis
over their estimated useful economic life. The carrying value of intangible assets is reviewed for
impairment if events or changes in circumstances indicate the carrying value may not be
recoverable.
The useful economic lives of intangible assets are as follows:
Software and IT systems - 10 years
If there are indicators that the residual value or useful life of an intangible asset has changed since
the most recent annual reporting period previous estimates shall be reviewed and, if current
expectations differ the residual value, amortisation method or useful life shall be amended. Changes
in the expected useful life or the expected pattern of consumption of benefit shall be accounted for
as a change in accounting estimate.
Impairment of non-financial assets
The charity assesses at each reporting date whether an asset may be impaired. If any such
indication exists the charity estimates the recoverable amount of the asset. If the recoverable
amount is less than its carrying amount, the carrying amount of the asset is impaired and it is
reduced to its recoverable amount through an impairment in profit and loss unless the asset is
carried at a revalued amount where the impairment loss of a revalued asset is a revaluation
decrease. An impairment loss recognised for all assets is reversed in a subsequent period if and
only if the reasons for the impairment loss have ceased to apply.
1.11 Animals
Marwell Wildlife participates in global cooperative efforts to maintain sustainable populations of
animals which are reliant on the sharing of individuals between zoologica organisations. Veterinary
screening, transport and other costs of receiving animals are expensed during the period of
acquisition. However, with no objective or practical basis for establishing value, animal transactions
are made without monetary consideration. Hence, as is customary among zoological organisations,
the animal collection is recorded at a nominal value.
1.12 Stocks
Stocks are valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value after making due allowance for
obsolete and slow-moving stocks.
1.13 Investments
Investments are stated at market value at the balance sheet date. The Statement of Financial
Activities include the net gains and losses arising on revaluations and disposals throughout the
year.
Investments in subsidiaries are valued at cost less provision for impairment.

Rentals applicable to operating leases are charged to the Statement of Financia Activities over the

Prepayments are valued at the amount repaid net of any trade discounts due.
1.17 Cash at Bank and in hand
Cash at bank and in hand includes cash and short term highly liquid investments with a short

Creditors and provisions are recognised where the company has a present obligation resulting from
a past event that will probably result in the transfer of funds to a third party and the amount due to
settle the obligation can be measured or estimated reliably. Creditors and provisions are normally
recognised at their settlement amount after allowing for any trade discounts due.
1.19 Financial instruments
The group only has financial assets and financial liabilities of a kind that qualify as basic financial
instruments. Basic financial instruments are initially recognised at transaction value and
subsequently measured at their settlement value.

Designated funds
The future capital projects fund has been set up to fund the large investment projects planned as part of
the spatial framework developments. We anticipate that this will be utilised in 2016 and 2017 on the
construction of our Energy for Life.
The fixed assets designated fund was set up to reflect the assets, other than plant and machinery held
by the charity. At the year end assets relating to capital projects that have been derestricted with a net
book value of ENil (2015: ENiI) have been transferred into this reserve relating to land and buildings,
animal houses and capital works in progress which have been transferred from general funds.
Restricted funds
Animal management
Care of the animals, for example animal feed, or clothing for keepers.
British species conservation
Habitat restoration in our ancient woodlands, and the breeding and reintroduction of British species
including, specifically, sand lizards.
Grevy's zebra conservation
Monitoring Grevy's zebra status and movements in East Africa (through collaring and stripe recognition
software techniques), contributing to national conservation strategies and workshops for Grevy's zebra,
equipment for conservation management of local communities, equipment, maintenance and running of
a disease laboratory, training local scientists in surveying and other conservation techniques relating
specifically to Grevy's zebra as well as provision of bursaries for Kenyan students in conservation
related degrees.
Conservation in Kenya
Equipment, biodiversity field work cost and training of local scientists in surveying and other
conservation techniques in Kenya.
Conservation in North Africa
Lobbying at government level to help protect endangered species in North Africa. Post release and
veterinary monitoring of scimitar-horned oryx and addax plus ecological monitoring as well as
monitoring equipment. Rescue rehabilitation and reinforcement of the spur-thigh tortoise as well as
reintroduction and conservation of the red-necked ostrich.

CONTACT : SELSDON CHURCHES NEIGHBOURHOOD CARE
Report of the Directors for the year ended 31 March 2014
The Directors, being the Trustees, present their Report and the Financial Statements for the year
ended 31 March 2014.
Constitution
Contact: Selsdon Churches Neighbourhood Care is a Company No. 6582829, limited by guarantee
and not having a share capital, which is governed by a Memorandum and Articles of Association.
The liability of each member is limited to fl. It is also a Registered Charity No. 1124346
The company was incorporated on 1 May 2008.
The charity was registered with the Charity Commission on 5 J une 2008.
The company commenced operating from 11 October 2008.
Merger of Charities
At a Special General Meeting held on 10 October 2008 the members of Selsdon Churches
Neigbourhood Care, commonly known as 'Contact', (an unincorporated association, Registered
Charity Vo.1012801) voted to transfer the assets and liabilities of Contact to this "new" charity. The
merger was duly registered on the Merger of Charities register maintained by the Charity
Commission.
Directors (the Trustees)
Under the Articles of Association the number of directors is to be not less than three and not more
than eleven, of whom a majority shall be members of the supporting churches. One third of the
directors must retire each year and may stand for re-election at the Annual General Meeting of the
Company. A director must retire from office after reaching the age of 75 or having held office for 9
consecutive years.
The Directors (Trustees) of the Charity are:
Dr Robin T Orchard Chairman
Miss Christine P G Waring Vice chairman

also receive grants from Charitable trusts and donations from other local organisations. The trustees

Risk Policy
The Trustees recognise that in today's litigious society we need to ensure that none of the services
we provide causes a level of dissatisfaction that might prompt a client to take legal action against
Contact. The Trustees have always maintained a 'hands on approach' (and continue so to do) to the
management of Contact thereby ensuring that none of the services and help we provide is beyond
the capability of a good neighbour. The Trustees also ensure that our staff, who provide assistance
with completion of application forms for state benefits for example, have access to and undertake
regular training. The Trustees regularly review the risks we take and take appropriate action to
mitigate them.
Equal Opportunities Policy
Membership of Contact is open to all who wish to support its objects, irrespective of nationality,
ethnic or national origins, sex, marital status, race, colour, political or religious belief, social or
financial standing. Members will be welcome from those with disability who are able to support the
objects of Contact. Contact supports equality of opportunity and will pursue policies to prevent
discrimination. Contact will make available and provide its services to all members of the Selsdon
area regardless of their age, race, colour, nationality, ethnic or national origins, of their sex, marital
status or disability, political or religious belief, social or financial standing.
Vulnerable Adult's Policy
Contact believes that all involved in its activities have the right to be safe and free from harm. To
this end the Management Committee have adopted the policy contained in the London multi-agency
policy and the procedures contained therein to safeguard adults from abuse will be followed. A copy
of the Policy document is kept in the Contact Office or is available to view on line at
http:lwww.croydon.gov.ukhealthsocial/sva/paar
Children's Policy
One of the most important principles of Contact Child protection policy state "that any volunteer who
shall be selected by the designated Child Protection Person (DCPP) to undertake a caring visit in
which a child or children may be involved needs to have attended safeguarding and welfare of
children training"
The volunteers involved in Child care must provide two referees which will be thoroughly checked
and have Disclosure and Barring Service vetting undertaken prior to the commencement of work.
The Contact Child protection policy document is available to view in the Contact office during
norma opening hours.

CONTACT - What We Do
Contact is Selsdon Churches Neighbourhood Care Scheme that provides practical help, advice,
support and information to people living within the Selsdon area and part of Sanderstead, through a
large network of volunteers. Although a churches scheme, Contact welcomes all clients and
volunteers regardless of any religious, political or secular views.
Transport:
Door to door transport to doctors, local clinics, hospitals, etc. for the
less mobile.
Information:
On a wide range of statutory and voluntary services, e.g. specialist
holidays, self help groups, benefits and many more.
Shopping/
Prescription collection:
For the sick, disabled or elderly.
Shopping Bus:
A regular door to door shopping bus to Narlingham Sainsbury's.
Escorts travel with the mini-bus giving help where needed.
Visiting/Befriending:
For housebound or elderly people, needing support or company. We
also provide a hospital visiting service.
Carer Support:
Information, advice and support on services and benefits and how to
apply, completing application forms if required. Providing day and
evening respite for carers.
Practical Help:
Dog walking, 'one off' gardening jobs, wheelchair pushing, basic DIY.
Loan Equipment:
The office has an extensive supply of equipment available for short
term loan including wheelchairs, zimmer frames, indoor and outdoor
walkers, bath aids, TENS machine and many other items. All the
wheelchairs are serviced regularly.
Library Scheme:
A regular door to door service to Selsdon library.
Smoke Alarm Scheme:
Installing smoke alarms and providing battery checks
Young Families:
Supporting families with children or young adults.
Social Events:
For clients, coffee mornings, outings (with assistance), Christmas
party and regular newsletters
Contact Links:
Volunteers throughout our area are each responsible for delivering
Contact information to 25-30 houses once a year and, when
appropriate, offering practical help.
Contact has a paid manager and assistant, both of whom work part time.
In addition, nearly 300 volunteers are involved in Contact, including a team of fifteen office
volunteers and two postmen, to whom the directors and staff extend their heartfelt thanks.

It has been a year of transition at Selsdon Contact. We have said a fond farewell to J anet J ones
who over a period of 24 years started Contact from her kitchen table, with a handful of volunteers
and 40 clients being supported. By the time I took over the management of the Charity on the 31st
March 2014 we had a team of 300 volunteers looking after 300 clients providing all the services
listed on Page 8. It is thanks to the vision dedication and drive of J anet that I have been able to take
over the reins of such a successful local charity.
On the first day in my new ob the key tasks was to produce a report that looks back over the
previous year!! This task would have been impossible without the wonderful support of J asmine and
the rest of fifteen Office volunteers this report is truly a team effort.
On a brighter note we are the selected charity for 'Selsdon Village Club' this year. In February 2014
J anet and J asmine gave a presentation to the club about the work of Contact and at the beginning
of 2015 we will go back to receive the money that they have raised over the year. This type of
activity goes right to the heart of what Contact does, local neighbours and organisations helping one
another and we are all very grateful for the Village Club's support.
Likewise we also get excellent support from our neighbours in the local Sainsbury store. In J une
we were able to hold a collection outside the store and thanks to our team of volunteers who shook
buckets and tins we were able to raise E 648. A most welcome addition to the funds.
Finally on a funding note our thanks should be extended to the local Churches in Selsdon. It has
been a real pleasure to meet with the leaders of the local churches, St. John's, Selsdon Baptist,
Croydon Jubilee and St. Columba's over the last few months to introduce myself. Without the
Churches continued financial support and guidance the work of Selsdon Contact would not be able
to continue.
As ever we are continuing to change our services to meet our clients' needs. One of the innovations
last year was to develop a series of shorter outings to local facilities. Often going out for the whole
day is too much for our clients. With our new minibus we have been able to be more flexible in our
approach to trips. The new shorter outings have included trips to local garden centres and
McDermott's fish and chip shop. The success of these trips has led us to develop a monthly series
of outings this year.
As ever the Christmas party was a huge success with over 70 clients attending. An amazing
transportation operation was put into action to get clients to and from the party, we were again
blessed by the use of St. John's Church Hall and all attending were entertained by the Trinity
School azz Band and Tony/Cary Rapps.
We have been well served by the local schools, J asmine undertook a presentation at Croydon High
School which led to a number of student volunteers joining Contact. We have also been well
supported by pupils from Trinity School.
