BARNABAS FUND
ANNUAL REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2015
TRUSTEES' REPORT
The Trustees of Barnabas Fund ("the Charity"), who are also directors of the Charity for the purposes of the Companies Acts, present
their annual report for the year ended 31 August 2015 under the Companies Act 2006 and the Charities Act 2011, together with the
audited financial statements for that year. The financial statements comply with the requirements of the Companies Act 2006, the Charity's
memorandum and articles of association and the relevant S tatements of Recommended Practice (the Charities SORP).
STATUS AND ADMINISTRATION
The Charity is a registered charity (No. 1092935) and a company (No. 04029536) limited by guarantee that was incorporated on 7 uly
2000. Its registered office is shown on page 2 of this report.
The present Trustees and any past Trustees who served during the year are shown on page 2, together with the names of the senior
management staff and the principal external advisers as at the date of the signing of this report.
CHARITY'S PURPOSE
The Charity's purpose, as set out in the objects clause contained in its articles of association, is:
1.
The advancement of the Christian faith;
2.
The prevention or relief of suffering, poverty and distress;
3. The promotion of Human Rights (as set out in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and subsequent United Nations
Conventions and Declarations) by:
i) educating the public about Human Rights;
ii) raising awareness of Human Rights issues;
iii) providing technical advice to governments and others on Human Rights matters;
iv) eliminating infringement of Human Rights;
4.
The promotion of conflict resolution and reconciliation by all appropriate means;
5. The promotion of religious or racial harmony, equality and diversity;
6. The advancement of citizenship or community development;
7. The relief of those in need by reason of youth, age, ill health, disability, financial hardship or other disadvantage.
CHARITY'S AIM
The Charity's main aim is to help meet the practical and spiritual needs of Christians facing persecution; to encourage, strengthen and
enable local Church and Christian communities so they can maintain their presence and witness; and to tackle persecution by making
known the aspects of faiths and ideologies that result in injustice and oppression of Christians and others. It also aims to facilitate global
intercession for the persecuted Church by providing comprehensive prayer material and to inform and enable Christians in the West to
respond to the growing challenge of Islam in their own countries.
OVERVIEW OF CHARITY'S ACTIVITIES
The Trustees review the purpose, aims and activities of the Charity each year. This review looks at the achievements during the previous
year, beyond just the finances, and explains the number of beneficiaries assisted and the extent of that assistance.
When carrying out the review and planning future activities, the Trustees refer to the guidance contained in the Charity Commission's
general guidance on public benefit and its supplementary guidance on the advancement of religion for public benefit. In particular the
Trustees consider how planned activities will contribute to the aims and objectives they have set.
The Charity has five main activities, namely:
Ministry grants: During the year funds were transferred to Barnabas Aid International who disbursed them to carefully chosen project
partners to enable them to support persecuted Christians in their area.
Education and research: The provision of resources to further the education of the genera public about the needs of the suffering Church
and research into the causes and extent of Christian persecution.
3
BARNABAS FUND
ANNUAL REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2015
Seeking prayer: The provision of a prayer diary and other resources to help supporters pray for the persecuted Church as a whole as well
as individua Christians suffering persecution.
Raising awareness: Providing information, education and generally raising awareness concerning human rights and the Persecuted
Church
Projects assisting the suffering church: Costs associated with assisting the suffering church worldwide that do not fall into the above
categories.
BARNABAS FUND'S PEOPLE
Trustees
Barnabas Fund is grateful to the people who voluntarily give their valuable time to serve on the various committees that are necessary to
ensure Barnabas und's activities are delivered to the highest possible standard. They are very grateful for the wise counsel and support
of the Financial Director, Rosemary Sookhdeo.
Staff
The Trustees wish to record their thanks to the staff of the charity for their sterling service on behalf of the charity, recognis ing that without
their efforts, it would not have been possible to have achieved this excellent result.
Barnabas Fund currently employs 17 staff. All staff joining Barnabas Fund must undertake induction training appropriate to their work
area with the common topics of health and safety and IT. Ongoing professional development training is encouraged and staff are given
the time to attend courses, seminars and conferences as approved by their line manager.
Volunteers
In addition to paid staff Barnabas Fund enjoys the support of a number of individuals and organisations that give time in specific areas of
our operation. The network of voluntary Church and area representatives, known collectively as Partners, make a significant contribution
towards educating local Christians and Churches about the persecuted Church and we are immensely grateful for the time and effort they
dedicate to this work.
Donors
Without our donors none of the valuable work Barnabas Fund does would be possible and the Trustees are grateful for all their support.
STRATEGIC REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2015
REVIEW OF ACHIEVEMENTS AND PERFORMANCE DURING THE YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2015
Policies and Activities
The Objects of the charity include the advancement of the Christian faith, the prevention of suffering, poverty and distress, promotion of
human rights and relief of those in need. The Trustees have determined that the best way to advance these objectives is by strengthening
Christian individuals, churches and communities in places where they are a minority and suffer discrimination, hostility, violence etc. This
is done by providing practical support and alleviating suffering, poverty and distress for Christian members of the public in such situations
in order to enable them to survive and to continue their Christian witness and ministry in order that the Christian faith is maintained,
advanced and promoted in places where it is under pressure or even in danger of extinction.
In accordance with these objects and aims, the charity benefits a certain section of the public, the estimated 200 million Christians living
as minorities in situations of discrimination or persecution on account of their faith or where the Church is under pressure in other ways.
Within this section of the public are a wide range of denominations, nationalities and ethnic groups from a wide diversity of church
backgrounds in over 80 countries. The charity does not restrict its activities geographically and many of those assisted by channelling
4
BARNABAS FUND
ANNUAL REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2015
funds through Barnabas Aid International, are in extreme poverty and distress including those displaced from their homes by natural
disasters, warfare or persecution.
The charity helped to advance the Christian faith by providing, through Barnabas Aid International support for full-time Christian workers,
training for Christian leadership and supplying Christian literature and resources. Other kinds of projects also help to do this by providing
economic assistance which enables Christians and their communities to survive and prosper. F or example, income generation projects
enable Christians who are discriminated against in the jobs market to support themselves and their families. Likewise feeding programmes
are vital for the poorest Christians whether their need arises from natural disaster or from discrimination and persecution. Health needs
are met by medical projects and by water and sanitation projects. The future economic viability and spiritual resilience of the Christian
community are improved by enabling the children of Christian families to get a good education. Without such help it is likely that these
Christians wil continue to live in on-going poverty as despised members of society and being vulnerable to violent attack they may be
forced to flee their homes or even their homeland.
The charity also benefits a wider section of the public in the UK in particular (but also worldwide) by providing information, education and
raising awareness concerning human rights and the persecuted Church, and publishing materials on these issues.
Activities for Achieving Objectives
In accordance with its Articles of Association, Barnabas Fund seeks inter alia to advance the Christian faith and prevent or relieve suffering,
poverty and hardship, including the relief of those in need because of particular disadvantages, and the promotion of human rights.
These objectives are achieved by supporting Christians where they are in a minority and suffer discrimination, oppression or persecution
as a consequence of their faith. Our goal is to strengthen Christian individuals, churches and their communities by providing financial and
other assistance with the aim of relieving poverty, suffering and distress in response to material and spiritual needs identified by local
Christian leaders and para-church agencies.
In furtherance of the above objectives the charity educates the genera public and the Christian public in the UK and elsewhere about the
needs of the suffering Church, provides prayer materials, and speaks on behalf of the suffering Church.
The charity worked by forwarding funds to Barnabas Aid Internationa to be disbursed in grants which will make positive changes to the
wellbeing of Christians suffering discrimination, oppression or persecution for their faith, for example in health, nutrition, housing,
education, access to clean water and economic self-sufficiency. Such grants also aim to improve and expand the resources available to
churches and Christian organisations functioning in such situations, for example by providing buildings, equipment and literature. The
charity also seeks to bring about change in public understanding in the West of the causes of such discrimination and persecution in other
contexts.
Volunteers
The charity is extremely grateful for the support of roughly 380 unpaid volunteers functioning as Church Partners, Area Partners or
Speakers. Some volunteers take on two or more of these roles. These volunteers assist the charity by educating and raising awareness
of the work of the charity and the needs of persecuted Christians. Their roles include speaking at meetings, organising events, distributing
magazines, and displaying and circulating materials. Their educational work increases awareness of the plight of oppressed Christians
and stimulates increased prayer and financial support for the charity. The amount of time given by each Partner varies greatly according
to the time they have available, their skills, health etc. but an approximate average figure would be 30 minutes per month per Partner. In
the last fiscal year there were 156 different speaking engagements in the UK and we now have a dedicated Partnership Coordinator
based in our UK office who is focussed on enabling and equipping the artners and also increasing awareness of the work of Barnabas
Fund.
5
BARNABAS FUND
ANNUAL REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2015
Review of charitable activities
The charitable expenditure for the year has been directed towards the meeting of the key objectives of the charity in the following ways:
Ministry Grants Grant payments were made by forwarding income to Barnabas Aid International which disburses it to the carefully
chosen recipient project partners in the countries where we are assisting.
Education - The bimonthly magazine, "Barnabas Aid", including a special educational pull-out supplement, is sent to 123,812 (2014
120,858) recipients, an increase of 2,954 recipients on the previous year, some of whom receive multiple copies. The great majority of
these are supporters based in the UK but copies of the magazine were mailed to supporters in a further 90 countries.
In 2013 Suffering Church Action Week (SCAW) was introduced to incorporate Suffering Church Sunday and the Barnabas Fund Day of
Prayer held on the lst November each year. This also extends the potential to include coffee mornings, children's events and Bible
studies throughout the week focussing on the Persecuted Church for a whole week rather than just one or two days. SCAW packs have
been provided to individuals and churches for the last few years which include a DVD, prayer resources, children's resources, leaflets
and a sermon outline to provide everything a church might need to hold its own Persecuted Church event.
Raising Awareness The charity continues to issue regular e-mail news updates providing up to date information on relevant situations
around the world. The circulation list for these e-mails has increased by 8% in the year to a year end figure of 28,933 subscribers. There
has been an on-going engagement with our website with the average number of pages viewed being 3.57 during the year. A process of
redesigning the UK website has been completed in order to make it easier to use and more up to date with the latest situations and needs,
with the main objective being that more people will use and engage with our website as a result. On our Facebook account "Likes" have
increased from 6,575 to 7,951 and Twitter "followers" have increased from 4,218 to 5,284.
The charity continues to provide articles for various publications and periodicals and also gives radio interviews. Issues relating to the
persecution of Christians have been the subject of significant recent P arliamentary debate and the charity has provided briefing papers
to Parliamentarians. The charity's network of voluntary Church and Area Partners make a significant contribution towards educating local
Christians and Churches about the ersecuted Church. A series of leaflets highlighting major areas of the charity's work, especially
focussing on the situation in the Middle East, were placed in a variety of publications and generated both one-off and recurring donations
from both new and existing supporters.
Prayer - The bimonthly publication "Barnabas Prayer" giving daily prayer items was circulated to all on the mailing list. In addition, a
monthly "Prayer Focus" report is prepared and circulated both by email and as a paper copy aimed primarily at prayer groups. This
resource is now sent to roughly 29,000 supporters with a further 1,220 hard copies sent out to 744 recipients. rayer items are also
included in e-mail news releases and daily prayer items are also posted on the website and circulated using Twitter and Facebook.
Factors Affecting the Achievement of the Objectives
The Trustees are very grateful to Barnabas Fund supporters for their generous donations throughout the year. The occurrence or
otherwise of natural disasters or man-made conflicts in the areas of the world where Barnabas Fund works can have a considerable
impact on income, as can the general economic climate in the UK and other donor countries.
Many Christian colleagues around the world have given substantia assistance in terms of advice on potential projects and monitoring of
on-going projects. This help enables grants to be given with confidence in a wide variety of contexts.
6
BARNABAS FUND
ANNUAL REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2015
FINANCIAL REVIEW
Against the background of economic uncertainties and cut-backs which affect supporters in both the UK and other Western countries, the
Trustees are very pleased with the financial position of the charity at the end of this financial year. Indeed, the level of income in
the
2014/15 financial year has exceeded expectations and has given us our best financial year so far. The donations income received by
Barnabas Fund for the year was f13,978,578 (2014 f12,281,090) which means that the UK income was not only maintained, but actually
increased by 14% during the year and we are very grateful to all of our supporters for their generous giving.
The number of recurring gifts for which funds were received during the year ended 31 August 2015 was 11,923 (2014 11,025) an increase
of 898 on the previous year. The total amount received via recurring giving in the year ended 31 August 2015 increased by 8% to
f3,032,321 (2014 f2,802,020).
The total number of donations in the form of regular payments received during the year was 125,709 014116,697) an increase of 7.7%
over the number received in the previous year. The Trustees are deeply grateful to supporters willing to pledge their on-going support to
the charity in this very cost-effective form of giving.
In the current economic climate donors are rightly concerned that the charities which they support are making best use of their resources
to meet their charitable objectives. One area of recent concern has been charitable remuneration. During 2014/15 the maximum salary
taken by an employee was f37,000 (f41,300 including pension and national insurance). Barnabas Fund has consistently kept its
overheads to a minimum to enable the charity to ensure that more of each pound donated reaches our persecuted brothers and sisters.
Early in the year the Charity undertook a review of its finance system and moved to SAP Business One. This had been selected
by
Barnabas Aid International as their finance system in August 2014 and The Barnabas Fund Trustees felt it made economic and business
sense to utilise Barnabas Aid International's experience to ensure a smooth transition to a new finance system.
Charitable activity expenditure was 14,246,627 (2014 f17,719,123). The apparent reduction in expenditure is due to the transfer of fund
balances on 1 eptember 2013 to TBF Trust as part of the planned transition of grant making and other international activities from
Barnabas Fund to Barnabas Aid International. Removal of the one-off balance transfer to TBF Trust, consisting of f1,680,204 in restricted
funds and f3,063,305 in general funds, shows that charitable activity expenditure in 2014 was actually f12,975,614. Thus charitable
activity expenditure for 2015 is actually an increase of f1,271,013 or just under 10%
Further details on charitable activity expenditure are shown in the notes to the financial statements and under the relevant charitable
activity headings in the Trustees report.
The charity ensured its income was fully utilised in the year so the result for the year ended 31 August 2015 before the revaluation of
investment assets was fnil (2014 deficit of f4,702,732)
The overall result after the revaluation of investment assets was a surplus of f718 (2014 deficit f4,700,815).
Capita expenditure of f15,755 included expenditure on a new server and telephone system for the Coventry office.
The Trustees believe the Statement of Financia Affairs (SOFA) shows a strong performance by Barnabas Fund.
RESERVES
Restricted Reserves
Restricted unds are funds where the donor has specified to the charity the purpose for which they would like the charity to use their
gift. During the year ended 31 August 2015 Barnabas Fund transferred all balances on restricted funds to Barnabas Aid International.
Barnabas Aid International undertakes to use the funds in accordance with the desires of the donors and in assurance of the Barnabas
Covenant. Further details on how the funds have been spent can be found in the Barnabas Aid International (charity number 1155957)
financial statements.
7
BARNABAS FUND
ANNUAL REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2015
Free Reserves
Free Reserves available for use by the Charity are deemed to be those that are readily realisable, less funds whose use is restricted or
designated for particular purposes. Thus the calculation of Free Reserves excludes fixed assets that continue to be used in the day-to-
day operation of the Charity.
As a matter of policy the Trustees regularly review the value of the reserves required to be held in investments, cash and cash equivalents
not restricted to or designated for any particular purpose. The Trustees have set a target level of reserves of f750,000. This will enable
the charity to meet its operating expenses for a period of between 3 and 6 months should there be a downturn in income for the charity.
At
31 August 2015 the General Reserve was f909,234 (2014 f970,952). Running costs include all staff salaries and other costs
associated with administering the charity and its funds. The Trustees will continue to look to decrease the General Reserve over the next
few years in line with the reserves policy.
The Fixed Asset F und represents the net book value of fixed assets which have been purchased with unrestricted funds. This reserve is
locked into the value of fixed assets and the value can be released only if they are sold.
The IT Fund of f13,500 is held to fund planned major improvements to the information and communication systems of the charity.
The Barnabas Books Fund of f1,911 is a sum set to cover funds due to Isaac Publishing for the distribution of books.
RISK MANAGEMENT
Barnabas Fund's approach to risk management is designed to ensure that it remains alert to those external and internal factors that could
affect its ability to operate effectively, or even at all. The work of establishing the risks facing Barnabas Fund and ensuring suitable
mitigating action is being taken is reviewed regularly by the Management and Trustees. Further information on risk management can be
found in the Trustees' Statement on Governance.
FUTURE PLANS & DEVELOPMENTS
Socio-religio-political factors suggest that the oppression and persecution of Christians in many countries of the world is set to increase.
The major objective for the coming year is to communicate the needs of the Persecuted Church to our supporters with confidence that
they will continue to pray and donate to the work and enable us to increase our support to projects which assist Christians and the Church
in situations of oppression or persecution. The Trustees have been encouraged by a very positive start to the new financial year, with
supporters responding well to appeals to support the work of the Barnabas Family in the Middle East, and more specifically in Iraq and in
Syria.
Planning for the longer term future, the International Trustees have established another charitable organisation in the United States
of
America, the world's largest economy, under the name of Christian Relief International (CRI). This is in anticipation that it may in the
future be helpfu to have a US-based organisation to assist with international functions and grant-making. The Barnabas Covenant is
currently being reviewed and the review is expected to be completed by April 2016.
AND FINALLY
Barnabas Fund gives thanks to God for its continued growth and the Trustees pray that the organisation will be able to continue raising
awareness and providing support and care to the persecuted church for as long as it is needed.
This report, incorporating the Strategic Report, was approved by the Board of Trustees in their capacity as Company directors on 15
February 2016 and signed on their behalf by
Rev McNaughton Chairman
8
BARNABAS FUND
TRUSTEES' STATEMENT ON GOVERNANCE
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2015
Governance
The Charity is governed by its Memorandum and Articles of Association adopted on 7 JJ uly 2000 as amended by Special Resolution
passed on 3 November 2010. The Board of Trustees is responsible for the overall governance of the Charity and meets at least three
times a year.
The Chief Executive (CEO) is responsible for the day-to-day management of the Charity's affairs and for implementing policies agreed by
the Trustees. The CEO is supported by the Chief Operating Officer who has the leadership role in respect of all delegated executive
responsibilities.
The Barnabas Covenant
The Barnabas Covenant a memorandum of understanding agreed in O ctober 2013 between the member organisations of The Barnabas
Family. The Barnabas Family currently comprises Barnabas Fund, TBF Trust, Servants Fellowship International, Barnabas und
(Australia) Ltd, Barnabas Fund (NZ), Barnabas Fund Inc, Isaac Publishing LLC and Barnabas Aid International. The Trustees of the
aforementioned charities and company determined to enter into a collaborative and federated relationship for the purposes of providing
support and aid to the persecuted Church and to Christians who are enduring hardship by virtue of their faith, raising awareness of the
situation, encouraging prayer for them and undertaking advocacy on their behalf. The Barnabas Covenant provides the basis of the
partnership. It is currently being reviewed and the review is expected to be completed by April 2016.
The memorandum and its associated Service Level Agreements are additional to, and in no way substitute for, the Memoranda and
Articles of Association and the trust deed/constitutional documents of the members of the Barnabas family.
Trustee Selection, Induction and Appraisal
Under the Charity's Articles and Memorandum of Association the Trustees may at any time co-opt any person duly qualified to be
appointed as a Trustee to fill a vacancy in their number or as an additional Trustee. In seeking potential appointees the Board look for
individuals who are appropriate to the skills and experience needed by the board and reflect the work of the Charity in pursuit of its
charitable purposes. In practice the Board seeks to appoint Trustees who are passionate about supporting the work of the Persecuted
Church and recruitment of new Trustees focuses on individuals with a long-standing knowledge of the charity who are known personally
to the existing Trustees or who bring particular skills and experience to the work.
At each Annual General Meeting one-third of the Trustees, or the number nearest to one-third, must retire from office. The Trustees to
retire by rotation shall be those who have been longest in office since their last appointment. Any co-opted Trustee holds office only until
the next AGM when they may be re-appointed. The minimum number of Trustees is 3 and there is no limit to the number of Trustees or
to how many times a Trustee may be appointed.
Induction and training of new Trustees includes providing them with copies of the charity's governing documents, "The Essential Trustee:
What you need to know" (Charity Commission publication CC3), and the charity's Statement of Faith. Trustees are normally familiar with
the work of the charity already but any extra information necessary is provided, and they will be shown around the principal office and
introduced to some of the staff.
New Trustees are required to sign a statement that they have read and understood "The Essential Trustee: What you need to know"
(Charity Commission publication CC3), that they are not disqualified from acting as a trustee, that they affirm the charity's Statement of
Faith, and that they will seek to act always in accordance with Biblical principles. Every Trustee mustsigi a Declaration of Willingness to
act as a Charity Trustee of the Charity before they are eligible to vote at any meeting of the Trustees. They are also required to declare
in writing any existing or potential conflicts of interest.
9
BARNABAS FUND
TRUSTEES' STATEMENT ON GOVERNANCE
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 AUGUST 2015
Statement of Trustees' Responsibilities and Corporate Governance
The Trustees are responsible for their annual report and for the preparation of financial statements for each financia year in accordance
with applicable law and United Kingdom Accounting tandards (United Kingdom Generally Accepted Accounting Practice).
Company and Charity law require the Trustees to prepare financial statements for each financial year which give a true and fair view of
the state of affairs of the Charity and which give a true and fair view of the incoming resources and application of those resources of the
Charity for that year, and of the state of affairs as at the end of the financial year.
In preparing these statements, the Trustees are required to select suitable accounting policies, as described in the financial statements,
and then apply them on a consistent basis, making judgements and estimates that are prudent and reasonable and conform to the
methods and principles of the Charities SORP. The Trustees must also prepare the financial statements on a going concern basis unless
it is inappropriate to presume that the Charity will continue.
The Trustees have overall responsibility for ensuring that the Charity has appropriate systems and controls, financia and otherwise. They
are also responsible for ensuring that the Charity keeps proper accounting records which disclose with reasonable accuracy at any time
the financial position of the Charity and enable the financial statements to comply with Companies Act 2006. They are also responsible
for safeguarding the assets of the Charity and for their proper application as required by Charity law, and hence for taking reasonable
steps for the prevention and detection of fraud and other irregularities and to provide assurance that:
The Charity is operating efficiently and effectively;
All assets are safeguarded against unauthorised use or disposition and are properly applied;
P roper records are maintained and financia information used within the Charity, or for publication, is reliable;
The Charity complies with relevant laws and regulations
In so far as the Trustees are aware:
There is no relevant audit information of which the Charity's auditors are unaware; and
The Trustees have taken all steps that they ought to have taken to make them aware of any relevant audit information and to
establish that the auditors are aware of that information.
Internal controls over all forms of commitment and expenditure continue to be refined to improve efficiency. Processes are in place to
ensure that performance is monitored and appropriate management information is prepared and reviewed regularly by both the executive
management and the Trustees. The systems of internal controls are designed to provide reasonable but not absolute assurance against
material mis-statement or loss. They include:
Regular consideration by the Trustees of financial results and non-financial performance indicators;
Delegation of day-to-day management authority and segregation of duties; and
Identification and management of risks.

Any proposal to amend the Memorandum and Articles of Association; Instruments and Rules of Government; Accounting

Expansion of activities beyond core business;
Formation of a subsidiary;
Amendment to pension schemes;
Approval of Annual eport Accounts & financial statements including setting of reserve allocations;
Investment management policies;
Cash management policies (including approved list of counter-parties);

Opening of new banking relationship; and

Risk Management
Serious risks can have a major impact on the ability of a charity to fulfil its charitable aims causing disruption to the business or, at the
most extreme, cause significant financial loss. The Board of Trustees are responsible for the overall running of the charity and need to
be aware of the risks to the business and the processes that are in place to mitigate them. Risk assessment provides a framework for
the Board of Trustees of Barnabas Fund to identify potential risks to which the organisation is exposed and how these can be and are
being mitigated.
The Trustees have a formal risk management process to assess risks and to implement risk management strategies. A risk assessment
is carried out by the Chief Operating Officer on behalf of the Trustees, risks are identified and assessed for impact and probability and an
action plan to control the major risks is prepared.
The risk analysis covers four major areas: compliance, financial, operational and macroeconomic. Failure to comply with any of the
legislation covering the charity would have serious implications; the Trustees have a close working relationship with the charity's legal
and professional advisors to help mitigate this risk.
The Trustees consider that the greatest risk facing the charity is that of a decrease in financial support from the public due to either a
period of recession or financial decline in the UK and the wider Western World and/or reputational damage caused by adverse publicity.
The charity maintains insurance to defend itself against false and malicious claims arising from its publications and other media activities.
Other major risks identified have been mitigated to an acceptable level by ensuring documented procedures are in place and taking other
measures deemed appropriate.
Serious Incident Report
A
serious incident report was filed on 23 May 2014 with the Charity Commission regarding the allegations brought against Patrick
Sookhdeo, the founder, main fundraiser and a significant public face of the Charity. The Charity Commission has been kept updated by
the Trustees and senior staff both before and after Patrick Sookhdeo's trial and subsequent conviction in February 2015. Barnabas und
has been working closely with the Charity Commission in monitoring and mitigating potential reputational damage to the charity.

1. ACCOUNTING POLICIES
The following accounting policies have been applied consistently in dealing with items which are considered material in relation to the
financial statements.
a)
Basis of preparation of financial statements
The financial statements have been prepared under the historical cost convention, with the exception of investments which are
included at market value. The financial statements have been prepared in accordance with the tatement of Recommended
Practice (SORP), 'Accounting and Reporting by Charities' published in March 2005, applicable accounting standards and the
Companies Act 2006.
b) Income
i)
Donations are included in the tatement of Financial Activities at the amounts receivable and received by Barnabas Fund.
Amounts are receivable when the charity has entitlement to funds, certainty of receipt and the amount can be measured
with sufficient reliability.
ii)
Income tax reclaimable in relation to donations received under Gift Aid or deeds of covenant is recognised at the time of
the donation.
iii)
Income receivable in respect of Restricted Funds has been taken directly to the Statement of Financial Activities.
iv) Gifts in Kind (including the donation of shares) are treated as income. The income is the market value for that gift subject
to any adjustment that may be required to recognise the value in use.
V)
The charity also receives the benefit of work carried out by volunteers, the value of which cannot be quantified.
c)
Investment Income
Investment income, including interest, is credited to the Statement of F inancia Activities when receivable and is inclusive of the
taxation recoverable, where applicable.
d)
Allocation of Expenditure
Revenue and capital expenditure is dealt with on an accruals basis inclusive of irrecoverable VAT, where applicable.
Barnabas Fund directly attributes expenditure in so far as is possible and on an accruals basis.
The amount of grants made for charitable projects represents the cash grants paid during the year to Barnabas Aid International.
Barnabas Aid International is responsible for managing the projects supported by the Barnabas amily. A list of grants made
to end recipients can be found in the Barnabas Aid International financial statements.
e)
Governance Costs
Governance costs comprise the costs of running Barnabas Fund, including strategic planning for future development, external
audit, any professional advice for the Trustees and all the costs of complying with constitutiona and statutory requirements,
such as the costs of meetings and preparing statutory financial statements and satisfying public accountability.
f)
Foreign Currencies
Transactions in foreign currencies are recorded using the rate of exchange ruling at the date of the transaction. Balances
denominated in foreign currencies are translated at the rate of exchange prevailing at the year end.
g)
Operating Leases
Rentals payable are charged on a time basis over the term of the lease.

h)
Fixed Assets
The cost of tangible fixed assets includes those costs which are directly attributable to purchasing the assets and bringing them
into working condition. Barnabas Fund does not capitalise interest as part of the cost of tangible fixed assets. Barnabas Fund
capitalises refurbishment costs and any associated capita expenditure where such work provides new facilities. Normal repairs
and maintenance costs are taken to revenue in the year of expenditure
Depreciation is provided at the following rates to write off the cost of Barnabas Fund's fixed assets over their estimated useful
economic lives:
Tenant Improvements
25% reducing balance
Furniture, Fixtures and Equipment, including computer equipment 25% reducing balance
Motor vehicles
25% reducing balance
Barnabas Fund's capitalisation policy is to transfer to the balance sheet only capital assets with a value in excess of f5,000.
i) Fund Accounting
Funds held by the charity are:
Unrestricted funds - consists of the general fund and any designated funds. The general fund represents funds held by
the charity which can be used in accordance with the charitable objects at the discretion of the trustees and which have
not been designated for other purposes.
Restricted funds - these are funds that can only be used for the particular restricted purposes which have been imposed
by the donor or which have been raised by the charity for particular purposes
The charity does not allocate investment income earned between the individual restricted funds as it is considered that the costs
associated with the administrative time taken to carry out such a task across the numerous restricted funds would exceed the
benefit of doing So. Similarly it is the charity's policy to not charge the respective restricted funds for the costs of administering
each individual project Instead such costs are charged to the unrestricted funds. Therefore in essence the charity is adopting a
pragmatic approach in using the investment income to cover the administration costs that relate to individual projects without
allocating the income and expenditure to each fund.
j) Pensions
Barnabas Fund operates a Defined Contribution Pension Scheme for which contributions are charged to the Statement of
Financia Activities as they are incurred.
k)
Reserve Funds
The policy of the Trustees is to maintain in a Designated und such sums as they deem prudent for the future refurbishmen of
the IT and communication systems
In addition, the Trustees maintain a F ree Reserve to provide working capital to create a buffer in case there is a sudden reduction
in donations. The Trustees' policy is to retain a buffer equal to six months of normal charitable operating expenditure
I)
Management of Liquid Resources
The policy for the management of liquid resources is defined by the financial commitments of Barnabas Fund. Barnabas Fund
aims to keep funds on deposit until such time as they are needed to pay for designated projects, as highlighted within the notes
to the financial statements

TRUSTEES REPORT
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31ST AUGUST 2017
The Trustees present their annual report and financial statements of the charity for the year ended 31
August 2017. The financial statements have been prepared in accordance with the accounting policies set out
in Note 1 to the accounts and comply with the charity's constitution document, the Charities Act 2011 and
Accounting and Reporting by Charities: Statement of Recommended Practice applicable to charities
preparing their accounts in accordance with the Financial Reporting Standard applicable in the UK and
Republic of Ireland published on 16 July 2014.
Legal Status
Leigh Lollipops Nursery is a Registered Charity, charity number 1033808
Objectives and Activities for the Public Benefit
The purpose of Leigh Lollipops Pre-Schoo Nursery is to provide a happy and caring learning environment for
children aged from 21/2 to 5 years old, in which every child is supported and encouraged through their learning
journey to develop to their full potential.
The aims of the Pre-schoo as documented in the constitution document are to enhance the development and
education of children primarily under statutory school age by encouraging parents to understand and provide
for the needs of their children through community groups and by:
a) offering appropriate play, education and care facilities, family learning and extended hours groups, together
with the right of parents to take responsibility for and to become involved in the activities of such groups,
ensuring that such groups offer opportunities for all children, whatever their race, culture, religion, means and
ability;
b) encouraging the study of the needs of such children and their families and promoting public interest in and
recognition of such needs in the local areas
c) instigating and adhering to and furthering the aims and objectives of the Pre-school Learning Alliance.
Contribution made by the volunteers
Leigh Lollipops Nursery is run by a volunteer committee, made up mostly of parents/ carers. The overall
management and control of the Nursery will rest with the individual members of the Nursery's management
committee ("the committee"). As well as being responsible for the management of the Nursery the Committee
members are also the charity trustees of the Nursery.
The Committee is elected every year at the AGM; there is a Chairperson, Secretary, Treasurer and a
maximum of eight other elected members.
Achievements and Performance
In the academic year 2016/17 Leigh Lollipops Nursery has exceeded its fundraising target of E3,000. The
money raised will be put into updating and purchasing new equipment for the children to use.
Fundraising monies raised in the previous academic year have been used to purchase a new shed to store
the children's outdoor toys and a new sand & water table which the children have been enjoying during the
Summer Term.
As Lollipops is a charitable nursery they aim to break-even or make a small profit year-on-year. In previous
years this has not been the case and reserves have been weakened due to this. Their current aim is to move
to a break-even/profitable status within the next 3 years. They have made a number of significant changes to
their operation this year in order to reduce costs and maximize income. These changes should bear fruit
in
the coming years.
Page 1
LEIGH LOLLIPOPS NURSERY
TRUSTEES REPORT
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31ST AUGUST 2017
Financial Review
The income of the Nursery comes from government grants, fees from parents and voluntary contributions,
charitable donations and fundraising.
Due to a one-off event the income from government grants and fees from parents this academic year were
lower than usual. The Nursery applied to Surrey County Council for financial assistance and was awarded a
f5,000 conditional grant. Total income for the 2016/2017 year was f66,244 and fundraising income was
f4,672.
The Nursery's expenses are mainly salaries, rent and supplies & utilities. These were similar to prior years
though the total expenditure was slightly higher than the 15/16 academic year due to the one-off purchase of
the storage shed from a charitable donation. Total expenditure for the year was E65,265 and fundraising
expenses were E1,012.
There currently is a cash reserve account which has a balance of E15,365. The aim going forward is that this
account is not used unless there is an extraordinary need and that in future years a proportion of any profits
made will go towards building the reserves up. The Nursery does not earn a material amount of interest on
reserves.
The Nursery depends on children numbers reaching certain levels relative to the average expenditure per
annum. There is a simple formula from the council which enables there to be an estimate of the Nursery's
break-even level for a given expenditure. This is used to manage marketing activity.
The monitoring of Leigh Lollipops' finances is now more regular than previously and the cost of wind-up is
regularly estimated so as to ensure the level of reserves are appropriate.
Structure, Governance and Management
The Nursery operates in adherence to the policies and procedures in its constitution document. The
constitution document is provided by the Pre-school Learning Alliance of which the nursery is a member. The
charity is an unincorporated association currently but will be converted to a CIO in the near future.
The trustees are committee members and consist of 3 officers (Chair, Secretary and Treasurer) and not less
than 2 nor more than 8 other elected members and if the Committee so decides, not more than 3 members
co-opted on to the Committee. At least 60% of the committee members including co-opted members, shall at
the time of election or co-option be parents or guardians of children in the Nursery.
Committee members can serve for a maximum of 10 years. All committee members are volunteers and as
such are not remunerated for their time.

The Treasurer's Report for the AGM
Academic Year Sept 2016 to Aug 2017
8th November 2017
High Level Summary
This accounting year the nursery has a positive net movement in funds of f978. This is a good
result for Leigh Lollipops and represents the first year it has made a positive net movement in
funds since the 2011/2012 year.
Leigh Lollipops previously had significant cash reserves but year on year these were being
reduced due to negative net movements in funds. These cash reserves are now monitored
against the cost of winding up the nursery at a point in time in order to better manage the
business and to adapt to changing circumstances. At the end of the academic year 16/17 the
cash reserves are sufficient to cover the cost of wind-up.
Many operational changes have been made this year and continue to be made in order to
continue the trend of creating a positive net movement in funds year on year and to update the
nursery offering to parents.
This year there was a main route to the nursery closed for close to 9 months. This impacted on
both the level of numbers of new children joining the nursery and the take-up of sessions during
the term by existing children. Both these factors put significant pressure on the income of
Leigh Lollipops during the academic year. This pressure was recognized early and Leigh Lollipops
applied for, and was successful in receiving, a conditional grant from Surrey County Council to
supplement their income during this year.
Expenses were also managed more closely this year and these were at a similar level to those in
2015/2016.
Finally, fundraising was strong during this academic year and provided a boost to the final
income results.
1
1. Large/Unusual Movements in Figures over the Accounting Period
1.1. Income
The largest movements in income were as follows:
Income from Surrey County Council for funded children (over 3 year's old) f26,400
Fee income from parents for non-funded children (under 3's) f18,600
Surrey County Council (other income) f4,000
Voluntary contributions from parents f5,100
Surrey County Council conditional grant f4,700 C a portion of the total grant was rolled over into
the next accounting year)
1.2. Expenditure
The largest movements in expenditure were as follows:
Wages f49,800
Rental f4,300
Nursery supplies f1,900
Training costs f1,400
Accountancy fees* f1,400
Utilities f1,400
Yoga fees f1,250
1.3. Large differences in expense items compared to the 2015/16 accounting figures
Advertising expenses were f80o higher as the nursery invested in marketing in order to have an
occupancy closer to capacity
Training expense were f670 higher than the prior year due to forest school training costs
(another investment for the future)
Activity costs were lower by f880 due to music no longer being offered and less children being in
on Friday's than the prior year for yoga
Sundry expenses were reduced as more categories of expenses were included in the accounts in
order to better manage the business
Accountancy fees* were higher due to Leigh Lollipops changing accountants to Wise & Co. There
was one-off work conducted this year to put previous year's accounts into the correct format and
to peer review some other financial monitoring processes We would expect in subsequent years
for this figure to reduce to E750-f850.
1.4. Other
The shed purchased for the nursery has been accounted for as a tangible fixed asset meaning it can be
depreciated across a fixed time period.

Manager's Report for the Year 2016/2017
Last year's achievements:
Our greatest achievement in 2016/2017 is our sixteen happy, confident and independent
school leavers who left us in July and who are now fully-fledged Reception class pupils. We
have been so enormously proud to see them enjoying their new experiences and settling in so
wel at their respective schools. Each year we are incredibly fortunate and honoured to be
part of the process of preparation for school and it is our aim to ensure the children are as
ready as they can be and to foster in them a desire to learn, develop skills and persevere at
new challenges.
2016/2017 was a particularly challenging time for the Nursery as the closure of Flanchford
Bridge on 16 May 2016, the main access road from Reigate to Leigh Lollipops, had a seriously
detrimental impact on the Nursery by way of a considerable fall in the number of children
attending and the subsequent drop in uptake of available sessions; the Nursery needs a
certain quota of children on roll to ensure that a substantial proportion of the sessions
offered per week are taken up for it to remain sustainable for it to remain open.
Consequently, we implemented a number of new operational initiatives for the Nursery, such
as extending our opening hours and expanding our optional extra-curricular programme of
activities, all of which helped us weather the storm.
Redesigning the Nursery's website: this is even visited by Ofsted!
Developing the Nursery's social media presence and boosting our profile.
Streamlining both our registration procedure and staggered starts for new children.
Increasing Lunch Clubs from two per week to four per week.
Opening for an extra session on Wednesday afternoon in the Summer Term 2017 to give
families more options about attendance.
Forming improved links with the local community. We took a very active role in the inaugural
Leigh Food Festival and Apple Press Day at the beginning of October, Leigh Village Charity
Plant Sale in May and Leigh Flower Show and Country Fayre in July.
The incredibly generous donations we received from parents / carers and staff for our
Harvest Festival celebrations, which were given to St Matthew's Food Bank in Redhill and
passed on to local people in hardship; thank you to everyone who donated.
Endeavouring to make the most of our fantastic outdoor space every day despite the
weather, including use of the wonderful Mud Kitchen made for the Nursery by Charlie Guard.
It is a fabulous addition to the garden for which we are enormously grateful.
Improving the Nursery's storage capacity, including the purchase of our lovely new storage
shed, which was installed in December and immediately put to very good use!
Registered Charity Number 1033808
The charming Christmas Concert, made all the more special by a visit from Father Christmas,
his special elf and a huge sack of gifts for the children
A fabulous Christmas Fayre which raised a really impressive sum of money and got us all in
the festive mood!
The Christmas party on the last day of term always such great fun!
Holly Fuller gaining her Level 2 Certificate in Childcare and Education and joining us
permanently as a Nursey Assistant. Very well done Holly!
Providing exceptional support and assistance to all of our children and their families,
especially those of children with Special Educational Needs going that extra mile whenever
we can!
Developing an improved marketing strategy to raise the Nursey's profile.
Receiving a great response to our Childcare Services' Questionnaire.
Applying for, and being awarded, a grant from Surrey County Council in March 2017, some of
which we used towards training a member of staff as a Level 3 Forest School Leader to
enable us to run Forest School activities to enhance the children's outdoor learning
experiences and help the Nursery to further grow and flourish.
The Ofsted Inspector visited us on Wednesday 15 March 2017, which was a very welcome
surprise! We were extremely pleased to maintain our grading of 'Good'. The inspector gave us
lots of positive feedback about our interactions with the children, the learning environment
and our approach to fostering learning for the group; the Inspection Report can be found on
the Nursery website.
We were utterly thrilled to be awarded a 'Top 10 Recommended Nursery 2017' award, being
rated and recognised as one of the top 10 nurseries in the South East of England! The
www.daynurseries.co.uk awards highlight the most recommended nurseries in each region of
the United Kingdom and celebrate the best provisions in the Early Years'
sector: www.daynurseries.co.ul is the leading UK nursery website with over 4.3 million
visitors per year and 28,795 nursery reviews. To receive this nationally celebrated accolade
is a remarkable accomplishment for Leigh Lollipops Nursery and we feel incredibly honoured
and enormously proud to be recognised as one of the best nurseries by the families and
carers of our wonderful children and we would like to thank our parents / carers for allowing
us the privilege of sharing in their child's learning journey. It's a great achievement to be
recognised for our hard work but particularly from the people who we work hard for!
The many wonderful and successful fundraising events that were held throughout the year. A
huge thank you to the Committee and the fundraising team for all their efforts and hard
work.
Introducing a new online Parent Helper Rota sign-up sheet.
Winning Quiz Night 2017!
Being able to invite our families and friends to so many events throughout the year.
Smooth transition to school, continues to be an important aspect of the Summer Term as we
help prepare the children getting ready for moving on to big school. We are proud to work
very closely with all our local schools and their Reception Class teachers to ensure this
smooth transition.
Registered Charity Number 1033808
Hosting some very successful Open Mornings in which we signed up a number of new families
for 2017/2018.
Making the most of this great learning environment and our wonderful staff, who make the
Nursery a happy, safe and friendly place for both the children and their families.
As always, the Staff excelled themselves with many lovely activities, building relationships with
children and families and just making Leigh Lollipops Nursery everything that it is.
Working with children is enormously rewarding. It is also a challenge as we wish to provide them
with plenty of learning opportunities, make their experiences at Nursery positive and give them a
strong foundation for learning for the rest of their lives!
Thank you to the current committee who have worked so hard to raise funds and support us.
I hope that you have all enjoyed your time on the Committee it can be a very rewarding
experience and certainly means the Nursery can continue to operate with the needs of the
children and families it serves at its core. We really need parents and family members to take up
roles on the Committee and once conversion to the CIO has taken place, as Trustees so that
the Nursery can continue to operate; family involvement is greatly appreciated by both the
children and the Staff.
Our Nursery is a very special place, where young children are nurtured, supported, encouraged
and celebrated through their learning journey to develop to their full potential and as ever, I
would like to say a huge thank you to the children for allowing us to share in their journeys and to
the Staff, the Committee and the parents / carers for all their hard work, commitment and
continued support over the past year.
THANK YOU!

AGM - Chairperson's Report 2016/17
Thank you
As the last academic year 15/16 ended with the closure of Flanchford Bridge, so the beginning
of 16/17 continued to see Lollipops affected by its restricted accessibility for Reigate families
and beyond. This posed immediate problems for the autumn term as numbers and sessions
dropped. It didn't help that the closure over ran wel into 2017. We will hear later from the
Finance and Nursery report and learn of the work which has been undertaken specifically by
Amy Lowry, Alice Gambrill, Adele Turner, and the Committee's fundraising efforts, which have
all helped to stabilise the financial situation.
Adele took on the key role of Treasurer in the autumn term of 2016, and has proved invaluable
in this role, providing transparency and a lot of information, in order for myself and Amy to
continue to make key decisions and help develop and grow the Nursery. It is an ever evolving and
competitive market, and we have to ensure we are providing the service which our busy families
demand.
Charlotte moved into the official role of Supervisor in the autumn term of 2016. It was a
natural transition for Charlotte, who had showed such dedication to Lollipops, was a popular
member of staff, always bringing new and creative ideas, and who had grown in confidence since
she had started. She was supported by a wonderful team, Rebecca (Jones), Julie (Finch), Sara
(Mellows), Sarah (Stewart) and Holly (Fuller). We were delighted when our apprentice Holly
qualified and become a permanent member of staff in January 2017.
It is not said enough, but each of our staff bring such unique qualities to the team. Their
experience of the early year's curriculum and the longevity of our staff are perhaps unrivalled.
The team is further supported by our permanent Volunteers, Mary (Mondays) and our past
Treasurer, Sam W (Tuesdays). We are so grateful for their time and for what they bring to
Lollipops and our children. We are so fortunate to have such a diverse range of staff from Holly
to Mary enriching the experience for our Lollipops children.
Amy and Alice (who you will of ten find based in the kitchen but also buzzing around the floor)
continued to work closely in their roles as Nursery Business Manager and Nursery Administrator
respectively. A specia 'thank you' goes to this formidable team (which must include Adele) who
have worked above and beyond to make many changes to the Nursery, introducing new
initiatives, helping to secure a grant received from SCC, and in changing its charitable status
(which you'll hear more about later and in the Treasurer's report).
Fundraising
Again, I am very proud to announce that 16/17 was the most successful year to date
raising f4,672 (after expenses, giving a net figure of f3,660).
I would like to say a big thank you to the fundraising Committee which included Rebecca
(Jones), Adele (Turner), Sam (Richardson), and Emily (Swanson). They were fully
supported by our family members, Kathy (Cassidy) and Eve (Waddingham). Kathy led the
Christmas event, a wonderful Valentine's Disco, and the Easter activities. Eve did
a
wonderful job representing Lollipops at the Village events especially the Leigh Village
Plant Sale. Teas on the Green was a huge success as always, such an enjoyable event.
Our next event is to organise is our Christmas Fun Fest led by Rebecca (Bex), specifically
aimed at Pre-schoolers. We have already had a good Autumn fundraiser in the way of a
Halloween Party organised by Adele. We will also be holding another Pub Quiz which
proved a success in 16/17 year.
Thank you all for your continued support. We have always tried to keep fundraising fun
and simple, and we are always looking for new ideas and new initiatives. Perhaps you'd like
to organise and lead an event? You will always have a team to help and support and who you
can delegate tasks too. The year 16/17 saw a wonderful presence of staff too, which the
kids love and shows such great team work. Which brings me nicely on to abit about the
role of the Committee and how the Nursery operates.
The Committee
Leigh Lollipops Nursery is a registered charity run by a voluntary committee of parents.
Tonight is very important to us as we will be voting on our new committee for 2017/18.
The way we run ourselves as a committee is governed by our constitution the 2011 Pre-
School Learning Alliance Model Constitution which we have adopted at the last AGM and
we have to abide by certain legal requirements. We must have a committee with a
minimum of five members and a maximum of twelve members. We may co-opt a further
three members at any time after the AGM. We must have the of ficer roles of
Chairperson, Treasurer and a Secretary. Elected Committee Members may stand for ten
consecutive years.
We depend on the support of our parents as without a committee we cannot operate.
The committee is responsible for setting the Nursery's policies; managing and engaging
staff; fundraising and organising social events. The staff is responsible for the day to
day running of the Nursery.
We meet once every month and meetings last between 1 and 2 hours. We also have other
roles which are named so that we can ensure everything runs as smoothly as possible.
In May 2017 we held an EGM (Extrarodinary General Manager) and voted to change the
legal structure of the charity from an unincorporated association to a Charitable
Incorporated Organisation (CIO). Amy did a lot of work on the submission of this
application which we are waiting to hear on. We also have to wait for Ofsted to visit and
re-register us.
Why convert? The CIO was established for one fundamental purpose: to provide a
structure that offers the trustees of charities greater protection against the liabilities
associated with the activities of the charity that they support. This is an advantage that
we felt is vita to the success of our charity, which depends on the contribution made by
these volunteers.
Fundraising will still be an important part of Lollipops. We've discussed this a little and
envisage this being a separate Committee, perhaps being called 'Friends of Lollipops' where
parents can become involved with raising funds without getting involved in the running of
the Nursery.
Members Stepping Down
This year, Sam Richardson and Emily Swanson will be stepping down as well as me as Chair
although I will remain on the Committee.
Sam and Emily had stayed on as Committee members and were invaluable fundraisers even
after their children had left Lollipops. Sam works at M&S and there were endless
donations given to our fundraising events, from Mother's Day flower pots to Easter's hot
cross buns. To say they will be sorely missed is an understatement. Thank you so much,
and I hope a small gesture will go some way in showing our appreciation.
Final Thank You
Finally, I would just like to thank everyone for their support. I have now completed three
full academic years as Chair of the Committee for Lollipops. I took on the Co-Chair role
alongside Amy (Lowry) in September 2014. My son, Daniel, was then new to Lollipops so I
was perhaps not entirely aware of what the role had in store for me. With some
challenges along the way (and not to mention two new-borns), the role has been so very
rewarding. It has been easy to remain committed to Lollipops; it is a unique Nursery which
provides the best early years childcare, and in a beautiful setting. I stand firmly
committed to Lollipops, where my daughter Eloise now goes, and I'm sure I will be part of
the team for many years to come as baby Grace will join in 2019. The Nursery is
continuing to develop and change, and it needs a future Chair to bring in some fresh
guidance and vigour.
So that leaves me to again thank you all.
I will now hand over to Adele Turner for the Treasurer's Report.

Through the tough times
By Darren Simpson, Nurse Specialist and
Kat Tsang Orr, Bloodwise Ambassador
Clinical Nurse Specialist Darren Simpson speaks
to his former patient Kat Tsang Orr about the
importance of nurses who really understand and
listen to the people in their care.
Kat: "You were my favourite Aussie nurse, Darren. You and the other staff who
looked after me during my treatment really did become my second family. I was
in my early 30s and a complete pain Being in hospital was extremely frustrating
I felt trapped, lonely and isolated and often angry, but the nurses kept me going;
popping in to say hello and to ask how I was. I remember a transplant nurse sitting
with me while I had a scary reaction. It sounds like a small thing, but for me it was
huge. I couldn't have got through that time without her."
Darren: "You weren't such a terrible patient Blood cancer has a huge impact on
people's lives It's not only the treatment, which often cures the disease, it's al
aspects of life; work, finance, body image and relationships that are affected Some
patients may lose friends, they want to go home, they want to be the people they
were before It's a lot more complicated than simply being treated for a disease."
Kat: "That's SO true. As patients we need nurses who understand our experiences
and who use knowledge - beyond just that which comes from a text book - to give
advice and reassurance. I knew you had seen lots of patients like me and when you
said it would be okay, I knew it would be. If your family say that, you think they are
just saying it."
Darren: "A large part of being a clinical nurse specialist is listening and talking
to patients as like you Kat, they vent their fears anger and emotions. hear things
no-one else will hear because of the worry it would cause It's an aspect of cancer
care that is as important as clinical care."
Kat: "That's why Bloodwise is so important. Nurses have opportunities to meet
patients like me and learn from us I spoke at a conference about the day I thought
I could go home and found out I couldn't. It was devastating It was all I had to look
forward to and it was taken away at the last minute. The snatching away of a little
bit of hope is huge for patients."
Darren: "Yes, I heard you speak about that. I'm on the Bloodwise Nurses Network
Steering Committee, which means I learn from other nurses and bring that back
to my hospita team. We also help steer the Bloodwise Nurse Education Programme
to support the team to identify unmet needs and work with them to pitch solutions
relevant to nursing practice. There are Bloodwise study days and conferences
where patients shine a light on what wasn't done, what should be done and what
was done right. They really help me keep my knowledge current as blood cancer
is dynamic and changing al the time."
Kat: "It's all paid off for you, Darren You were fantastic. The drugs saved my
physically but you and the other nurses saved me mentally. You were and still are
my second family."

Section D
Achievements and performance
Summary of the main
Launch
achievements of the charity
during the year
Heartstart Malvern was officially launched in January 2017. The aim of
the launch was to promote our training and to launch a public appea for
E75,000 to purchase 50 public access defibrillators. The launch was
extremely successful and was attended by over 100 people. A number of
organisations attending the launch fundraised for Heartstart Malvern
during 2017 and a number of very generous donations have been
received after the end of this reporting period.
Training
Our main achievement for this reporting period has been the delivery of
our training. During this period we delivered 70 training sessions and
have trained over 840 people. This training has been delivered to
individual members of the public who have attended our public training
sessions, to community groups and in schools.
Training Evaluations
Heartstart Malvern invites all adult trainees to complete a formal
evaluation of our training sessions. The main points which we have
identified from our evaluations are:
-
a 100% recommendation from trainees for their friends and family
to attend a Heartstart Malvern training session
-
Most people attending a training session have never been trained
in CPR or to use a defibrillator before attending our training
-
Before attending a training session most of our trainees would not
be confident to perform CPR or to use a defibrillator.
-
After attending a training session a majorly of our trainees
describe themselves as being either confident or very confident to
perform CPR or to use a defibrillator
-
A majority of trainees are from the WR14 (Malvern) or WR13
(surrounding villages) postcodes
Public Access Defibrillators (PADS)
During the reporting period, Heartstart Malvern has installed 6 public
access defibrillators in Malvern. These are defibrillators which are kept in
special cabinets which members of the public can access in an
emergency. The cost of installing a defibrillator and cabinet is
approximately E1,600. Unfortunately, due to current HMRC regulations,
we are required to pay VAT on PADS which is included in the E1,600
installation cost.
Community Engagement
The strapline for Heartstart Malvern is Saving Lives Together. This was
deliberately chosen as it encapsulates the need to engage with the whole
community in order to achieve our objectives. During the year our
volunteers have given numerous talks to different fundraising groups
which has resulted in many generous donations being received.

5
March 2012

Future plans
Heartstart Malvern aims to:
-
Provide free training to at least 1,000 people a year
-
Increase our training in schools SO that every Year 6 pupil is
trained and every secondary school child is trained at least once
during their secondary education.
-
Encourage more local organisations, particularly local businesses
to support our campaign to instal 50 defibrillators around Malvern
-
Work with the ambulance service to increase the number of
Community First Responders in Malvern and the surrounding
villages
