2.22. Service charge sinking funds
Included within the housing units managed by the organisation are 15 leasehold
units. Sinking funds are maintained for the two sites involved to cover medium
term cyclica maintenance. In addition, a maintenance fund is maintained to cover
day-to-day services. Within Community Services there are 56 units which also
have a sinking fund.
2.23. Pension costs
Brunelcare participates in the Social Housing Pension Scheme operated by The
Pensions Trust providing benefits based on final pensionable pay or, for new
entrants on career average salary The assets of the scheme are held separately
from those of Brunelcare. The Pensions Trust is unable to identify Brunelcare's
share of the underlying assets and liabilities of the scheme on a consistent and
reasonable basis and therefore, as required by FRS102, accounts for the scheme
as if it were a defined contribution scheme. As a result, the amount charged to
the profit and loss account represents the contributions payable to the scheme in
respect of the accounting period.
Where the scheme is in deficit and Brunelcare has agreed to a deficit funding
arrangement, a liability is recognised for this obligation The amount recognised
is the net present value of the deficit reduction contributions payable under the
agreement that relates to the deficit. The present value is calculated using the
discount rate detailed in these disclosures. The unwinding of the discount rate is
recognised as a finance cost.
2.24. Supporting People
Charges for support services funded under Supporting People are recognised as
they fall due under the contractual arrangements with Administering Authorities.
2.25. Cyclical repairs and maintenance
Due to the number of properties held and the establishment of regular
programmes of repair and maintenance, Brunelcare does not make provision for
future works but charges actual costs incurred to the income and expenditure
account unless capitalised under component accounting.

Brunelcare is considered to pass the tests set out in Paragraph 1 Schedule 6

taxation in respect of income or capital gains received within categories covered
by Chapter 3 Part 11 Corporation Tax Act 2010 or Section 256 of the Taxation of

21. Pension schemes
21.1 Social Housing Pension Scheme
The company participates in the scheme, a multi-employer scheme which provides
benefits to some 500 non-associated employers. The scheme is a defined benefit
scheme in the UK. It is not possible for the company to obtain sufficient information
to enable it to account for the scheme as a defined benefit scheme. Therefore it
accounts for the scheme as a defined contribution scheme.
The scheme is subject to the funding legislation outlined in the Pensions Act 2004
which came into force on 30 December 2005. This, together with documents issued
by the Pensions Regulator and Technical Actuarial Standards issued by the
Financial Reporting Council, set out the framework for funding defined benefit
occupational pension schemes in the UK.
The scheme is classified as a 'last-man standing arrangement'. Therefore the
company is potentially liable for other participating employers' obligations if those
employers are unable to meet their share of the scheme deficit following withdrawal
from the scheme. Participating employers are legally required to meet their share of
the scheme deficit on an annuity purchase basis on withdrawal from the scheme.
A full actuarial valuation for the scheme was carried out with an effective date of 30
September 2014. This actuarial valuation was certified on 23 November 2015 and
showed assets of 3,123m, liabilities of E4,446m and a deficit of E1,323m. To

agreed that additional contributions will be paid, in combination from all employers

Charitable Objects
Christchurch Baptist Welwyn Garden City CIO is governed by a constitution which states:
"The principal purpose of the Church is the advancement of the Christian faith through
evangelism and discipleship. The Church may also advance education and carry out
other charitable purposes in the United Kingdom and/or other parts of the world."
The church building on Parkway is held by the Baptist Union Corporation Ltd, in trusts which
are compatible with the above objects. The church also has a second building at 20
Tewin Road, which is owned directly by the Church.
Organisationa Structure
Members of the church are accepted in accordance with the constitution. Christchurch is
a Charitable Incorporated Organisation (CIO) with Managing Trustees (Leadership Team)
appointed by church members in accordance with the constitution approved in 2013
Decision making is also in accordance with the constitution. The Trustees (Leadership
Team) are empowered to make decisions on how the church is run, however, certain
decisions can only be made by the membership of the church at the church meeting (as
detailed in the Constitution) These may be matters brought to the church by the
leadership team for discussion and, as appropriate, acceptance, or matters raised in a
church meeting by members for further consideration by the leadership team.
To encourage local ownership and engagement the Trustees have established Local
Teams at each site to be responsible for local mission, organising community events,
building fellowship, identifying potential leaders and identifying and implementing minor
building improvements within a delegated capital budget.
Trustees Responsibilities
Charity law requires Trustees to prepare accounts which give a true and fair view of the
state of affairs of the CIO and of its income and expenditure for the financial year. In
doing SO, the Trustees are required to:
a) select suitable accounting policies and apply them consistently;
b) make judgements and estimates which are reasonable and prudent;
c) prepare the accounts on an ongoing concern basis, unless it is inappropriate to
presume that the CIO will continue in operation;
d) follow applicable accounting standards and the Charities SORP, disclosing and
explaining any departures in the financial statements.
3
The Trustees are responsible for maintaining proper accounting records which disclose with
reasonable accuracy at any time the financial position of the Charity and to enable them
to ensure that the accounts comply with the Charities Act 2011. They are also responsible
for safeguarding the assets of the Charity and hence for taking reasonable steps for the
prevention and detection of fraud and other irregularities. The Trustees are also required to
be aware of the Charity Commission's guidance on public benefit and to take it into
account in their decision-making on behalf of the church.
Objectives and Activities
The church's activities seek to meet our principal purpose by sharing the love of Jesus in
practical ways as well as providing ways of explaining our faith to others - all activities
seek to show the love of Jesus and bring people into a closer relationship with him. The
church provides a variety of activities both to its membership and to the wider community.
The church structures its activities under 5 key headings - worship, outreach, relationships,
discipleship and serving. This is reflected in the leadership team (trustees) with each leader
being responsible for one of these areas plus leaders responsible for administration,
property, finance and children & families.
Public benefit
The leadership team has given consideration to the charity commission's guidance on
public benefit and in particular to the specific guidance on charities for the advancement
of religion. In particular they have ensured the church provides a variety of activities both
to its membership and to the local community. The aim is to show the love of Jesus Christ
in both word and deed and to bring people into a closer relationship with him as living
Lord through worship, prayer, teaching, pastoral care, mission and social outreach work.
Significant numbers for 2017
Over 3,000 people served
Over 200 volunteers
Over 12,000 volunteer hours
As part of our desire to ensure that our activities are accessible to all, any charges are
kept to a nominal level and where fees are charged to cover the costs of events, courses
or trips, bursaries are made available for those who would otherwise be unable to
participate.
4
Objectives 2017
Prayer - to have focussed seasons of prayer during the year, to help US grow in our
prayer life and seek God for his guidance.
Local Teams - to establish Local Teams and appoint a Local Trustee to the
Christchurch Leadership Team (Trustees) to represent each site.
Outreach - to develop the outreach of the church, especially at each location
through the Local Teams.
Leadership Development - through training and a pattern of mentoring.
Sharing the joy of serving Christ - to identify ways of engaging more volunteers at
each site.
Christchurch Spread - to seek God and identify the shape and team for a future
third expression.
Mission - to foster active links with those serving God overseas and in the UK.
Introduce people to Jesus and help people grow as whole-life disciples
How did we do?
Prayer - as part of a 6-week focus in the spring we linked The Prayer Course across
life groups with the Sunday morning teaching and the weekly prayer meeting. In
the late autumn a 24-7 site prayer room was appreciated by all who used it and
the seeds of a permanent space for prayer were sown. One-off prayer evenings
were less well attended.
Local Teams began to meet regularly in 2017 each taking responsibility for
leadership of a local site, organising prayer walks, thinking about how to develop
both people and the buildings for our mission and ministry. The first Local Trustee
was appointed in November 2017 representing the Parkway site.
New mission activities were started in and around the area of each site, including a
new community day at Parkway supported by the whole church, involvement in
Applecroft School fete and supporting the work of the local YMCA hostel with a
barbecue in the summer and gift bags at Christmas. Peartree School visited the
Peartree site for a Christingle service for the very first time. A trial 'Songs of Praise'
took place at the Parkway site welcoming those who know and love hymns from
the different community activities through the week. We also launched and
repeated a new evangelistic course called 'Big Questions' in town coffee shops.
We appointed new leaders to several of the ministries during 2017. To help cultivate
and train leaders we held a second Ministry Leaders Gathering, training and
investing in leaders of groups and activities. We didn't manage to implement a
formal programme for developing emerging leaders, and we continue to
recognise the need for this as the church grows.
We prayed about the potential shape of a future expression and were
approached by one local church who wanted to explore the possibility of
becoming a third expression of Christchurch. This dominated our thinking and
planning until the autumn, when the membership of the other church decided
against exploring this further. We remain open and prayerful about how God will
lead US.
5
As well as visits from missionaries based in Peru, Papua New Guinea and Nepal, a
team went to Albania again to support and teach at the Worship School organised
by Ben & Irma Xhako.
Introduction
12 Be joyful because you have hope. Be patient when trouble comes, and pray at all times.
Romans 12:12 (New Century Version)
Young people matter, little people matter, older people matter, and loca people matter;
we all matter to God. This report expresses the way that the Christchurch community
sought to show in real terms that people matter to God during 2017.
So many people giving their time and energy to serve the community and build the
church, and once again this year we had baptisms at both sites - indicators of spiritual life
as people responded to Jesus and the call of discipleship.
It was also a year where we took another strategic step forward as a church, employing a
full-time Youth Ministry Leader (building on the previously half-time post) to enable the
work with young people to go both "deeper and wider'"'.
Perhaps the most encouraging aspects of the year were the way the Local Teams took
ownership of different elements of mission and fellowship out of a passion for people who
live in the different parts of town and locality. Another highlight was the bronze ECO
Church award, given by A Rocha that encouraged US to reflect on how we care for
God's earth in our shared life as a church.
Our focus on prayer was a powerful reminder that we depend on God's presence and
guidance in order to do all that He is calling US to.
In truth, there is still plenty to do as a church in nurturing our prayer life, developing leaders
and seeing more people engaged in the work of the kingdom. But we should never
underestimate how much we are already doing and the multiplicity of ways we embody
the gospel of Jesus in our generation. Read on and you'll discover some of that for
yourself.
Training of trustees
All new trustees are encouraged to read the Baptist Union documents on becoming a
trustee.
6
Review of significant activities
The centre point of our shared life together is when we gather together on Sundays for
worship and midweek in small groups held in people's homes.
Worship is central to everything we do at Christchurch by being the motivation for all our
serving activities amongst members and within the community. We gather for Sunday
services aiming to be inclusive and accessible to all visitors and regular attenders alike by
creating an environment where people can explore what it means to know God
personally and draw closer to Him.
We embrace a modern style of worship with a rotation of live bands at both sites, with
alternative styles used in some evening services. Young people have taken part in music
and service leading in a number of services across two sites; either as part of another
band, a youth band in their own right or a spoken lead.
Alongside sung worship is intercessory prayer and individual prayer ministry run by a team
who offer to pray for anyone after every service. Regular prayer is also an important part
of our time at Christchurch with weekly early morning prayer meetings and gatherings
before every service.
Morning services include an 'all age slot' (before the children & young people head off to
their age specific groups) using a variety of media, drama, film clips, songs, quizzes and
games around the theme of the teaching. Once a month, Church family news allows
anyone in the congregation to share a piece of good news with the church family SO we
can celebrate as a community what God is doing in our lives. This has been especially
helpful in allowing the congregation to get to know each other more as the church grows.
At Tewin road there is support for deaf and hearing impaired attendees from British Sign
Language (BSL) trained members of Christchurch. This encompasses both the sung
worship and teaching elements of the service.
The Worship team have also supported our women's and men's fellowship and Christmas
services. A new trial of a monthly "Songs of Praise" event at Parkway has also been
started and we have carried this on into 2018.
Life groups at Christchurch are run to disciple, grow, challenge and support those who
attend - helping US as we 'do life together' The majority of people who attend small
groups also attend church regularly and the groups include a range of adults in the
church from late teens to seniors. We have 15 groups across the town and which run at
different times of the day and evening, most running in term time with breaks for holidays.
13 groups have been structured broadly geographically, 1 has been run for Mums on a
Monday during the day and one has continued as a group which was initiated
specifically for people who have just finished the Alpha course but need further continuity
before moving into one of the 'geographic' groups.
7
The small groups have continued to disciple a broad range of people from the church.
We have around 30 volunteers leading and hosting groups of around 6-12 people each.
We are seeking ways to develop new leaders and forms of group as our vision is to have a
small group that would suit everyone in the church.
Highlights of the year included several new people joining groups and others stepping up
into leadership positions. The Peartree Fun Day and Parkway Community Day were great
times when many of the groups worked together to provide free fun activities for our local
community. The life groups have worked through materials linked to our sermon series and
focused on the church's vision for the year. The focus on prayer has helped groups to pray
for each other and beyond groups into the community and wider world.
Other activities
A large number of activities are run for the benefit of the local community by volunteers in
the church as we seek to share God's love with the local community.
There are three core Seniors' ministries: Harvesters, a fortnightly fellowship, two weekly
Reach Out chair-based exercise classes and a monthly lunch. We have served 188
people over the course of the year, many of whom are not actively involved in
Christchurch. Some come from other churches or faiths and some from no faith at all. A
high percentage attend more than one activity, and several attend all activities. Helpers
across all ministries total 26 and there is a back-up team of 10-12 available for cover/short
notice call up.
Harvesters has 72 registered participants and 8 helpers for this fortnightly tea time
fellowship This ministry continued to see strong growth over the year and was moved from
Body and Soul into the Main Hall at Parkway in December in order to accommodate
growing numbers. Increasingly, participants are inviting friends along.
Reach Out provides a Strength, Flexibility and Mobility Exercise Class at both Parkway and
Peartree every week. There are currently 94 registered participants and 7 hosts across the
two sites. The classes at both Parkway and Peartree were running at capacity, with
waiting lists at the year end. Fellowship over coffee and biscuits has become a key focus
for those attending and is an increasingly important source of focus for pastoral care.
Reach Out also held a very successful team building event for the volunteers during the
year.
The Senior Citizens' Lunch continues to be a popular monthly meeting place and always
sells out. There is a maximum capacity of 76 for each event, but over 100 different
individuals have attended through the year. It comprises welcome beverages from 10.30
and a two course lunch with drinks, served at tables at midday by a team of 20 helpers
from Christchurch. There is a short evangelistic reflection during dessert.
Overall the Seniors ministry serves 188 people with about 80 volunteer hours each week
making a total of over 3500 hours per annum.
8
During 2017 Body and Soul cafe continued to open for coffee and lunches on
Wednesdays and Thursdays during term time, between 11.00am and 2.00pm at our
Parkway site. We provided meals for about 40 people per day. Thursdays during 2017
continued to be busier than Wednesdays - with people who had attended "Reach Out"
(chair-based exercise class) on the premises staying on for coffee and/or lunch at Body
and Soul. About 90% of customers came from the wider community, and the other 10%
from within the church.
Many of our regular customers are senior citizens and live alone. We continued to value
the links with other parts of the church-work amongst the over 60s. A number of our
customers have enjoyed the "Songs of Praise" afternoons at Parkway. We continued to
serve the occasional lunch to pre-school parents/carers with young children as wel as a
group on Wednesdays from Hornbeams Centre for adults with disabilities (until
September).
A team of 26 volunteers comprising church members and friends of the church were
involved in menu planning, shopping, soup making, cake baking, vegetable preparation,
cooking, serving, washing up, setting up, tidying up, keeping the accounts etc. -
amounting to at least 75 volunteer hours per week! The team of volunteers is spread
evenly across the two Christchurch congregations. We welcomed a few new staff
members to the team during the year and said goodbye to a long-standing member of
the team at Christmas.
Body & Soul is as much a ministry to the customers as it is to the volunteer team. Being
part of the team has provided a way for some volunteers to find a new place to belong,
to serve and make new friends. Body and Soul were inspected by the council food
hygiene department and maintained a 5-star (top) rating for Food Hygiene.
We kept our prices at the same level in 2017. One of our aims is to provide low cost meals,
SO we worked hard to keep our purchasing matched to the predicted needs - not an
easy task when the numbers of customers varies week by week. Occasionally we supplied
a meal for free where this seemed appropriate - or sent a meal out to people we were
aware of with particular needs. As in previous years, the surplus income of around E6500
was donated to the Tumaini Children's Home near Jinja, Uganda run by Pastor Nicholas.
Body and Soul also contributed E2000 to general church funds in recognition of fuel used
in cooking and heating.
Sadly, we lost a few customers during 2017 through ill-health and death. We have been
pleased to be able to "be Jesus" to our customer and volunteer friends and to support
and pray for them during difficult times. We have welcomed back some regular
customers after a period of illness and also welcomed one or two new 'regulars' providing
a place of friendship as well as a place to get a good meal.
The Deaf ministry continues to grow at Christchurch. Two Deaf adults who use British Sign
Language (BSL) to communicate attend Christchurch Peartree regularly They are
becoming more involved in church life, volunteering and taking part in other activities.
9
There are also two young Deaf adults who attend Christchurch occasionally (these young
Deaf adults also attend Sign Church in Enfield - see below).
Interpreting for Sunday morning services at Peartree is provided most of the time by one
person who is studying for a BSL level 3 qualification. A budget provided some qualified
interpreting for men's teaching events and 6 Sunday mornings covering times when the
volunteer interpreter was away and/or to give the volunteer a break. There is a BSL group
of 6-12 people who meet monthly to learn basic signing, Deaf awareness and to sign
some of the songs commonly sung at Christchurch. One member now regularly leads
some of the songs during the service. Sunday evening services are not signed with the
exception of some Third Sundays and the Carol Service.
The volunteer interpreter and the 2 regular Deaf attendees attended the 'Go! Sign'
conference which is an annual Deaf led Christian worship and teaching day (in BSL) and
started to regularly attend Sign Church in Enfield (hosted at Enfield Baptist Church) which
is held on 2nd Sunday afternoon of the month.
Children and families are also well catered for. The church employs a part time Children &
Families worker, supported by over 60 volunteers:
On Sunday mornings, we provide a range of age specific groups at both of our sites from
a self-service creche, through TotZone, Bubbles and KidZone. Each group has its own room
and a dedicated team of volunteers catering for children from age 1 up until the end of
school year 5 (age 10). The children start off in the church service for a time of all-age
worship before leaving for their own groups while their parents are able to go back in to
the service.
We continue to have around 100 children on our books and average numbers across both
of our sites on a Sunday are 60 plus a number of families with children under 1 regularly
using the creche Generally, Peartree site has more children on a weekly basis.
In addition there are a number of other activities run for the benefit of all in the
community.
There are two mid-week groups for children aged 7-10 that run during term time, Kings
Club (Parkway) on Wednesday and KidZclub (Peartree) on Thursdays Both groups serve
children from a range of different backgrounds - some come to Christchurch on a Sunday
but the majority come from the local community and have no other connection with the
church. Kings Club has around 15 children attending. KidZclub grew to 25, but had a
large number of year 5's who we sadly said good bye at the end of the summer term. We
charge a small fee of 50p a week which goes towards the costs of the variety of craft
activities each week.
Activities vary week to week and our programme ranges from club nights when we play a
mix of games (Xbox Kinect, table football, table tennis and board games to name a few),
to cooking, den making, junk modelling and trips out, to walks through the woods in
10
different seasons, water games - to name just a few! Both groups have enjoyed having
the parents come to a "Challenge your parents" night.
Each week we have a short 'God Slot' where we spend a few minutes doing activities
linked to a story from the Bible and thinking about issues that affect how we live our lives.
We often use short video clips during this time.
All the groups have a rota of helpers who are approved children team volunteers at
Christchurch and have been referenced and DBS checked. All of our children's work
volunteers have mandatory safeguarding training on a regular basis.
Share events are a time to share food together, share faith together, share fun and
worship together, for the whole Church, whatever your age. We run these 4 times a year
on a Sunday afternoon, starting with a 'bring and share' tea, before a time all together as
we share our faith across the generations.
We started Share in the autumn term with looking how we share our story and had fun
making up a story with a few given words, finding out about the people on our table and
learning about the 4points of the cross and how it helps US tells people about Jesus. At the
start of December, we took time to make room for the Manger, as we wrapped people
up with Christmas wrapping paper, took lots of stuff out of a manger SO we could put that
first and learnt a prayer that we could use over the month to remind US of what Christmas
is.
Family Fun events provide an exciting and creative environment encouraging local
families to engage in craft activities with their children - as the parents stay and take part!
Family Fun sessions include numerous craft activities, a story and fun song time -all based
on a Bible theme. Aimed at families with children 0-10 years these are run each half term
holiday for 1 1/2 hrs (with both am and pm sessions) with a small charge per family (E1 per
child 50p per adult) We had up to 350 people at each of these events and the majority
come from the local community. These are generally held at our Peartree site, but we also
held an under-5 'special' at Parkway at Christmas
We held 4 Family Fun events last year, (Feb, May, Oct half term and Easter holiday). Our
February sessions had 334 adults and children and are theme was 'Noah'. At Easter we
had 348 Our May half term Event was around caring for our world with 309 adults and
children. October half term we saw 323 adults and children which had a 'Hero' theme.
Schools broke up very late for Christmas holidays, but many pre-school and non-school
nursery broke earlier, SO we ran a Family Fun for under 5's Christmas special at Parkway,
this was the second time we held a family fun event targeted at the younger families and
engaged 90 adults and children.
Some of the families that come are regulars at other activities including Toddle Inn, First
Friday, a few are Church members but the majority come from the loca community
through our links with the local Children's Centres and Schools Partnership Consortium.
11
These events are a great way of building relationships with local families and introducing
them to other activities at Christchurch.
Family Fun First Friday (First Friday) events are similar to Family Fun, but are held every
month on the first Friday of term time after school and are aimed at families with primary
school age children (but younger children are still able to come) Starting with cakes and
drinks, followed by a range of craft based around a Bible story theme and each session
ends with a quiz / game / drama based on the Bible story and a BIG action song. Each
session runs for 75 minutes with a small charge of El per child. These are held at our
Parkway site.
Families arrive at church from 3.25pm straight after school and are greeted with home-
made cakes, biscuits and drinks. While everyone arrives there are word searches, quizzes
and games while they top up their energy levels with something to eat & drink. After 15
mins we move into the craft room and families are able to go around 8 tables with
different crafts based around the theme for the session. Everyone is encouraged to help
tidy up the tables before going into the main church for an interactive bible story / quiz,
action song and prayer before heading home. We ran 9 events during 2017- 3 each term.
The majority of families come from the local community and many attend the local school
(Applecroft) The growth we have seen comes from word of mouth recommendations
lots of people who come have been told about it from someone who already comes,
there is a real bUZz around at every event - and a lot of mess to clear up afterwards!
Numbers can vary month on month and sometimes we are affected by trips and events
at Applecroft School, we have seen lots of new families towards the end of the year but
as always happen some of our older ones have left.
In the summer holidays, we ran 'Mega Maker' a Holiday club for children aged 5-10
(school year 1-5) we had 102 children attend with an average of 83 a day as some only
did part of the week. Each day was based on a bible theme with games, songs, puppets
and group time. Children came from the local community, Family Fun regulars as well as
Christchurch families. The club was run for 4 mornings - 2 1/2 hours each day. A registration
fee was payable which covered the cost of a special Club tee shirt and a small fee was
charged for each session. Free places were made available and taken up by several
families.
This was our sixth year of running a summer holiday club. We used the Mega Makers
Scripture Union material which had an inventing theme. We had 4 teams that were split
into two age groups; each age group had an inventor as their name and decorated their
bases (labs) around that theme. They spent the 4 mornings discovering things Jesus had
done as well as well as looking at inventions. Highlights were seeing children from across
the town coming together and having such a fun week. As ever our great young helpers
worked very hard and the building was filled with wonderful laughter, smiling faces and
plenty of craft, fun games, and interesting bible bits. The last day we invited parents for a
picnic which we provided (thanks to a wonderful person and her helper) and we were
able to show the parents a video clip of the fun we had during the week.
12
45 volunteers gave about 600 hours between them to run this event together with our
Children & Families worker.
We have two groups aimed at pre-school children and their parents/carers. Toddle Inn
that meets every Tuesday during term time at Parkway and Peartree Tots, a newer group
that started in March 2016 and meets every Thursday during term time at our Peartree site.
Both groups attract 30 or more children and Toddle Inn has a waiting list due to high
demand. The majority of the parents/carers come from outside the church, many have no
church link, but some go to other churches and a few from Christchurch.
Both groups include general play sessions, refreshments, which include healthy snacks and
a bible story and songs. Most children attend with their parents but we have some
childminders, nannies and grandparents. We aim to introduce the children and
parents/carers to basic bible stories and then advertise special church services and events
regularly, such as the 'family fun' events.
Fun4Famlies is a once a month Saturday group aimed for families with their children held
at our Peartree site. We offer a place where families can have some fun, meet other
families and join in some activities. This group meets on the third Saturday of the month.
Families come from mainly outside but some from church. A small fee per family is
charged (E1).
In January we moved the group from the afternoon to the morning, added bacon or
sausage in a roll and partnered with the local children centre as numbers had struggled in
year before. Numbers have risen significantly and we see families arrange to meet up
and start their day with friends here. A member of staff from the local Children's Centre
also attends.
Back to school coffee and cake is provided at our Parkway site for the start of the
academic year in September. This is for parents after dropping their children at school for
the first 2 days of term. We provided tissues for those who were sad or happy that their
children were going back to, or starting, school.
Making links with the Local Community, our Children and Families Worker, has been a
member of the WGC Children Centre advisory board and also Welwyn and Knebworth
Children Centre advisory board. She attends their half termly meetings which include
health visitors, pre-school leaders, child minder co-coordinators and other providers of
activities for under-5s in the area. This has been an opportunity to get to know about and
engage with the other activities locally, as wel as making others aware of the work we do
to support children and families at Christchurch.
We have continued to partner with WGC Children Centre in hosting their 1234 Explore
monthly group which is attended by their outreach workers. As part of this, a Christchurch
volunteer now runs cooking sessions to help encourage families to cook together. They
look at cooking on a budget, providing families with recipe cards and spices to take away
with them. We also keep in touch with the School Partnership which is able to pass any
13
leaflets we have for events on to schools throughout WGC and also let US know about
other events that we are able to sign post parents to.
Links with local churches include a group for all those who head-up Children's Work in
churches across Welwyn Garden City. These meet half termly, hosted by each church in
turn to pray, encourage one another and share good practice & ideas. This is now hosted
by different churches, which has been great to help build bridges between the churches.
The youth ministry at Christchurch serves young people at both sites and in the
community.
Our vision for youth ministry has been to be "Deep and Wide" - to enable young people
to go deep in their faith and establish roots that equip them for the rest of their life; and to
reach out widely to the young people in our town, starting with secondary schools.
Distinctive (School year 6) and Unlimited (School year 7+) meet each Sunday morning at
Peartree. At Parkway, there is a single group Integr8 that includes years 6-11. The groups
are open to any young person present on a Sunday morning. The groups aim to help the
young people understand and grow in their faith, give them an opportunity to discuss this,
to think about how it applies to them and the impact it can have on their lives.
After 8s runs on Sunday evenings with 8-10 young people in year 9 and above. We spend
time chilling out and playing games before having 30 minutes to look at a current issue or
theme with discussion.
628 runs on Friday evenings with most attendees not from Christchurch. It is a great
opportunity to get to know young people outside of the church. There are a variety of
activities including trips out.
Highlights in 2017 include taking 25 young people to Easter Camp at Phasel's wood
activity centre, others attending Soul Survivor and Urban Saints' Purbeck camp, as well as
socia events through the year such as bowling, fireworks and BBQ nights.
There are 20 volunteers working across the different groups in addition to a paid youth
worker. The volunteers have given over 2000 hours in 2017. Our part-time youth worker left
part way through the year and the church has been able to employ a new full-time
worker who started in October.
The Furniture Garage continued providing free furniture, bedding and household goods
donated by church contacts to local families and individuals in need. At the end of the
year, this has been relaunched as House2home and the focUS more on household items
and small pieces of furniture.
Worn Again gives families the chance to fill a bag with good quality 2nd hand children's
clothes for El. People are referred or can attend a coffee morning arranged through a
schoo partnership or a drop-in group. It also will source school uniforms where a need is
identified by family workers who work for the school partnership. This group serves people
in our local communities.
14
Worn Again continues to be able to help families choose good quality clothes, some of
this is through events in two local Peartree schools and other time through direct contact
from a children's centre or schools family worker.
Parish Nursing - our parish nurse works one day a week and also does additional work as
availability allows, averaging 10 hours/ week in total. The project is affiliated to Parish
Nursing Ministries UK. This is a volunteer post which aims to provide holistic health care,
complementing both the work of local health services and that which the church provides
through the ministers, pastoral team and membership
The parish nurse sees individuals with health issues who attend, or are contacts of the
church and its activities. She also offers support to those within the church who are caring
for those with health issues in their family or community. She liaises with other professionals,
including GPs and hospitals, for those with more complex needs.
This year 112 individuals have been supported with physical and/or mental health issues,
ranging from support for parents of newborn babies to assisting those requiring care in
later years. Strong links have been maintained with a number of local health and
community organisations.
Parish Nursing is an integral part of The Lounge, a drop-in service for the local community.
Those who attend are signposted to appropriate statutory and voluntary services. There is
a fruitful partnership with the Christians against Poverty Job Club which operates in the
building during the session. Many of their clients have significant health issues, SO Parish
Nursing can help contribute to a holistic service for this group.
The aim of The Lounge is to provide a neutral space inside the Peartree building where
members of the local community can meet up socially and come for support and advice
from our Parish Nurse and Children and Families worker. It is also an access and
information point for other services both those within the church such as the Furniture
Garage and Worn Again and services known to US in the wider community such as
charities and local authority provision. We work closely with the Food bank at New Zion in
identifying and supporting those in need of Food vouchers.
The Lounge runs alongside the CAP Job Club in the cafe area at Peartee on a Tuesday
afternoon and as such also provides support and company for those who have job club
appointments and others who have prearranged appointments with members of the
church staff or pastoral team. Our regulars tend to be those who live nearby, including
the YMCA hostel, some of whom attend church on a Sunday and others who participate
in other church run initiatives, for example children's clubs, Body and Soul and Worn
again.
The Lounge team meet with the church pastors once a term over a team lunch to review
and share information about the service. We also periodically invite leaders/ co-ordinators
of other local community services to attend this lunch to further consolidate our
partnerships, this includes services such as YMCA and The New Zion food bank.
15
The Lounge is run by 4 volunteers working with our Children and Families worker and Parish
Nurse and is open for 1.5 hours each Tuesday. It continues to run during school holidays.
The Alpha team ran three courses in 2017 to help people take steps in their understanding
of the Christian faith. We experimented with a new course called Big Questions which we
ran in both the spring and summer terms, and then led two Alpha courses in the autumn
(morning and evening courses). These are largely aimed at people outside the church
who want to look into the Christian faith, but some who come are new to faith or want to
know more. There had 25 different people attend all or some of the Big Questions course
in the spring, 7 in the summer, and then 18 at the Alpha courses.
There were a variety of outreach events in 2017 that sought to bless and engage the
community in Welwyn Garden City.
The Peartree Fun Day was run in May at our Peartree base for the second time this year,
with over 500 people attending on the day. The day included a BBQ, inflatables, games,
with attendance from the Fire and Police services. It was al free for those who came.
Over 100 volunteers, some from outside the church contributed in some way on the day.
Drawing on this model, the Parkway community day took place in September with
refreshments, cakes, BBQ, bouncy castle, and various activities, with over 400 in
attendance. Over 50 volunteers made this amazing event possible.
Both community days were absolutely free for everyone attending - as a way of showing
God's love to our local communities.
Together with the other Churches in Welwyn Garden City, we took over a shop in the
Howards Centre on Saturday 10th December and invited shoppers to Get in the Picture
and be part of a pop-up nativity scene, with a printed photo to take away with them.
There were many good conversations during the day, and 20 volunteers worked to make
it possible.
The Evening Cafe combines a night of performance and entertainment in a cafe-style
setup with delicious puddings unsupervised activities for younger children, and
fundraising. Admission is free and worthy causes (local and overseas) have an opportunity
to inform the audience about their work and are supported by donations given on the
evening. In 2017, one Evening Cafe was held on November 12th, was very well attended
and, with the benefit of Gift Aid supplemented donations, over E1,140 was raised for the
loca Christians Against Poverty, one of the country's leading debt counselling charities.
Band of Brothers (BOB) is a ministry to men, formed in partnership with Christian Vision for
Men (CVM) aimed at encouraging and developing support for men including in the
discipleship and integration of men in the church. It aims to engage men through social
activities, as well as supporting their role in family life. It includes the popular 'Men's
Breakfast' which meets monthly.
Social events in 2017 included a fabulous midsummer's night walk through the Brocket
estate and a 'Men Behaving Dadly' survival camp, both in June. The camp was held at a
scout camp in Harmer Green woods with afternoon activities and an overnight camp. This
16
provided a fun environment for dads and children to spend quality time together and
created opportunities to build relationships. Just over 50 attended with 45 camping
overnight including families from our community.
Ten breakfasts held throughout the year some of which have a guest speaker. A men's
teaching morning was held in February and a small group also attended the XCEL men's
conference in Bradford in November.
BOB combined forces with the Sistersoul Extra team to host a comedy night on the 16th
September that included a hog roast. Our guest was Andy Kind who entertained US and
preached the following day at both sites. Over 150 people attended this event.
The ministry for women at Christchurch is made up of 3 elements: Sistersoul, with a focus
on discipleship, fellowship and worship; Sistersoul Extra focuses on building relationships,
and Sister2Sister that focuses on outreach.
The Sistersoul annual teaching day, brought 78 women from 14 years + together for an
afternoon and early evening for worship, teaching & challenge to live out our faith in daily
life. There were also two breakfast meetings, gathering on average 50 women for
teaching, encouragement and breakfast. These aim to encourage women in their daily
walk with Jesus.
Sistersoul Extra brings together women both from the church and outside it together, to
build relationships and have fun. Events this year include a pub breakfast for 20 and a
vintage afternoon tea for 45 people, as well as the joint Comedy night.
Sister2Sister is currently working with the loca YMCA hostel, providing pamper parties for
the women based there. These help to build friendships and give opportunities to support
and encourage the women in their journey.
Christchurch also supports overseas mission focussing on a small number of partnerships
where we know and can connect both with the mission and missionaries - and with what
they do. Our current links are with:
Paul and Ruth Turner with Latin Link in Peru. Paul leads the work in Peru and is also
working on strengthening the leadership of the Peruvian group. Ruth works with
short term mission groups from this country who visit Peru and individuals from Peru
itself visiting the UK. They have also worked with young adults with disabilities
helping them make the transition from school to the community.
Paul and Clare Woodington with Mission Aviation Fellowship in Papua New Guinea
providing flying support to the local communities in the Highlands
Beni and Irma Xhako in Albania who have a music and worship ministry in the
churches there.
Pastor Nicholas who runs the Tumaini orphanage and a school in Uganda
Cynthia and lan Chadwell who are working in medical administration in Nepal with
BMS World Mission.
17
It is important to US as a church to maintain good relational links with those we support, As
well as visits from missionaries based in Peru, Papua New Guinea and Nepal, a team
went to Albania again to support and teach at the Worship School organised by Beni &
Irma Xhako.
Christchurch is a caring community 'because people matter to God'. The growing
numbers associated with the church continued to bring new challenges in 2017,
presenting a diverse range of pastoral needs.
Pastoral Care is overseen by the lead Minster and a Pastoral Core Team, which includes
our Parish Nurse, and Associate Minister. Most of the caring is done in and around the
growing number of small groups in the church. The Core group meets every 2 weeks to
review and pray over the needs of individuals in the fellowship, trying to make sure that
everyone is linked in.
Impact
Christchurch has continued working across 2 sites during 2017. Attendance has averaged
179 adults across the 2 sites with 61% attending Peartree and 39% attending Parkway.
Church membership at the end of 2017 was at 173, 18 new members were welcomed and
7 members left.
Four people confessed their faith in Jesus by being baptised in 2017. Two infants were
dedicated and two church couples were married in the year.
During 2017 the church served over 3,000 people through its wide
range of activities.
As is demonstrated above, many of those attending Christchurch volunteer to provide a
wide range of activities many of which directly benefit the wider community, who would
otherwise have no church links. It is estimated that the church provided over 12,000
volunteer hours in addition to paying for a Children & Families Worker and a Youth Ministry
Leader who initiate and lead many activities for the benefit of the community, supported
by unpaid volunteers. Many of these activities have grown throughout the year, thereby
enabling more of those in the community to access and benefit from the activities and
resources of the church.

Pension liabilities
Along with over a thousand other Baptist churches we are members of the Baptist Union
Pension scheme which is a -employer' Defined Benefit (final salary) scheme whereby
we are all jointly responsible for the overall liabilities. The scheme was closed in 2011 (and
moved to a Defined Contribution scheme), but we continue to remain liable for benefits
accrued for current and previous ministers who are members of the scheme.
Like many defined benefit schemes it has a significant deficit which is being addressed
through additiona deficit contributions from all of the employers
If we were to seek to exit the scheme the estimate of our share of the deficit at 31 December
2017 was E252,400.
While we triggered a 'cessation event' in 2008 when our previous minister left the church our
new (current) minister joined the scheme and we continued making payments and so the
pension trustee has not sought to call in this liability.
We are paying deficit contributions in accordance with the agreed schedule and continue to
engage with the process as we seek to ensure the position is resolved discussions are
underway regarding a number of options to help ameliorate the deficit which we expect will
be agreed and implemented during 2018.

In the autumn of 2018 we'll mark an important milestone: 90 years ago a group of
people in Welwyn Garden City met to seek God about starting a church that would
be a "good news" community - people who wanted to be led by Jesus Christ and
shape their lives by his gospel in such a way that they might lead others to Jesus.
It took faith in God and a confidence in the amazing message we share of life in
Christ. They were people guided by God's Word, God's Spirit and God's
transforming love. As we remember their first steps we want to think again about
how we are a "good news" community in our generation, including the offer of E10O
with the hope of twenty-five projects happening over the course of the year.
We're also aware of the need to trial a new time for the Peartree Sunday morning
gathering to aid the building of community and the integration of people new to
the church.

Outreach - to encourage each group and ministry of Christchurch to
consider how they can 'be good news' and 'share good news' with local
people through 25 mission projects.
Growing leaders - to invest in a group of 10 emerging leaders through
mentoring and teaching.
Administration - To deploy a new church administration system to assist in
regulatory compliance including GDPR.
Christchurch Spread - to actively seek opportunities in new housing
developments across the town & continue to seek God for a third expression.
Staffing - review staffing needs and agree appointments for the next 24
months.
Local Teams - empowering and encouraging Local Teams to continue to
build relationships to increase the impact of local outreach.

Notes to the financial statements
For the year ended 31 December 2017
1. Accounting policies
a. Basis of preparation
The financial statements are prepared in accordance with the Charities Statement of Recommended
Practice (SORP) FRS 102 'The Financial Reporting Standard Applicable in the UK and Republic of Ireland' and
the Charities Act 2011.
The financia statements are presented in Pounds Sterling, generally rounded to the nearest pound.
b. Donations
Donations are accounted for gross when received
c. Legacies
Legacies are accounted for when their receipt is certain and can be properly quantified
d. Investment income
Investment income is included in the accounts in the year in which it is receivable
e. Fundraising and publicity costs
The Church does not make formal appeals for funds and expenditure on these items is therefore not
material
f. Grants payable
The Church makes grants to other organisations whose charitable objects complement its work. Grants
offered subject to conditions which have not been met at the year-end date are noted as a commitment
but not accrued as expenditure.
Grants are recognised as a liability when the church is under an obligation to make a payment or the grant
is paid over.
g. Governance costs
This represents direct expenditure on the governance of the Church.
h. Fixed assets
The Church premises are included in the balance sheet at cost. In the opinion of the trustees the market
value of the buildings is considerably greater than the carrying value. In the opinion of the trustees it is not
practicable to quantify the difference between these figures.
Fixed assets with a value over f1,000 are written off as expenditure in the Statement of Financial Activities,
unless it is considered appropriate to capitalise the expenditure on the Balance Sheet.
i. Depreciation
Depreciation has not been charged on the Church or Manse premises because in the opinion of the
Trustees the residual value of the asset is not less than the original cost price.
Depreciation on other fixed assets is calculated to write off the cost on a straight line basis over their
expected useful life at the following rates:
Buildings
2.5% pa / 40 years
Computers and equipment
33% pa / 3 years
Fixtures and Fittings / improvement to premises
20% pa / 5 years
Any asset which is considered to have been impaired as a result of damage, obsolescence, or no longer in
use for any other reason is written down at the date on which the impairment is identified.
j. Other expenditure
Expenditure is accounted for on an accruals basis and has been classified under headings that aggregate all
cost related to the category. Where costs cannot be directly attributed to particular headings they have
been allocated to activities on a basis consistent with the use of resources.
k. Fund accounting
Unrestricted funds can be used in accordance with the charitable objectives at the discretion of the
trustees. Funds designated for a particular purpose by the church are also unrestricted.
Restricted funds can only be used for particular restricted purposes within the objects of the charity.
Restrictions arise when specified by the donor or when funds are raised for particular restricted purposes.
Further explanation of the nature and purpose of each fund is included in the notes to the financial
statements.
The accounts include all transactions, assets and liabilities for which the church is responsible in law. They
do not include the accounts of church groups that owe their main affiliation to another body nor those that
are informal gatherings of church members.

16. Pensions
The Church is an employer participating in a pension scheme known as the Baptist Pension Scheme ("the Scheme"). The Scheme is a separate legal
entity which is administered by the Pension Trustee (Baptist Pension Trust Limited). The Minister is eligible to join the Scheme, which is not contracted
out of the State Second Pension.
From January 2012, pension provision is being made through the Defined Contribution (DC) Plan within the Scheme. In general, members pay 8% of
their Pensionable Income and employers pay 6% of members' Pensionable Income into individual pension accounts, which are operated and managed
on behalf of the Pension Trustee by Legal and General Life Assurance Society Limited. In addition, the employer pays a further 4% of Pensionable
Income (or 3% if the employer is in the segregated DC section) to cover Death in Service Benefits, administration costs, and an associated insurance
policy which provides income protection for Scheme members in the event that they are unable to work due to long-term incapacity. This income
protection policy has been insured by the Baptist Union of Great Britain with Unum Limited. Members of the Basic Section pay reduced contributions
of 5% of Pensionable Income, and their employers also pay a total of 5%.
Benefits in respect of service prior to 1 January 2012 are provided through the Defined Benefit (DB) Plan within the Scheme. The main benefits for pre-
2012 service were a defined benefit pension of one eightieth of Final Minimum Pensionable Income for each year of Pensionable Service, together with
additional pension in respect of premiums paid on Pensionable Income in excess of Minimum Pensionable Income. The Scheme, previously known as
the Baptist Ministers' Pension Fund, started in 1925, but was closed to future accrual of defined benefits on 31 December 2011.
A formal valuation of the Defined Benefit (DB) Plan was performed at 31 December 2013 by a professionally qualified Actuary using the Projected Unit
Method. The market value of the DB Plan assets at the valuation date was f162 million.
The valuation of the DB Plan revealed a deficit of assets compared with the value of liabilities of f84 million (equivalent to a past service funding leve
of 66%). As a result of the valuation, in addition to the contributions to the DC Plan set out above, it was agreed to increase the standard rate of
deficiency contributions from churches and other employers involved in the DB Plan from 11% of Pensionable Income Minimum Pensionable Income
to be based on a 12% rate from 1 January 2016. The contributions are based on each church's or other employer's position at March 2015. Some
churches and other employers that were only involved in the DB Plan for a short period now pay less than 12%. The Recovery Plan envisages deficiency
contributions continuing until 30 June 2035.
The key financial assumptions underlying the valuation were as follows:

liabilities of the scheme. Accordingly, due to the nature of the Scheme, the profit and loss charge for the period represents the employer contributions
payable. The total pension cost for the Church is f14,437 (2016 f11,903).
Consequent upon the departure of the Minister from the church in 2008, the Church had a cessation event under Section 75 of the Pensions Act 1995.
This makes the Church liable for the proportion of the overall deficit (assessed by reference to the cost of securing benefits by the purchase of
annuities) applicable to its previous Ministers who were members of the Scheme. It is not possible to quantify this debt without an actuarial
calculation. In order to avoid the cost of such a calculation and because the church may not be able to continue its charitable activities following
payment of the employer debt which arises upon a cessation event, the Pension Scheme Trustee (after consulting the Pensions Regulator) is not
currently pursuing the employer debt, but is instead permitting the church to pay the ongoing deficiency contributions outlined above. However, the
Pension Scheme Trustee has the right to quantify and seek payment of the debt at any time at its discretion.]
The next actuarial valuation of the DB Plan within the Scheme, showing the position at 31 December 2016 is currently underway.

Trustees' Report
The trustees present the annual report together with the financial statements of the charity for the period ended
31 May 2017.
Objectives and activities
Public benefit
The trustees confirm that they have complied with the requirements of section 4 of the Charities Act 2011 to
have due regard to the public benefit guidance published by the Charity Commission for England and Wales.
Objects of the charity
To preserve and protect the health of patients, particularly but not exclusively, children, their families and
carers, who have severe physical, mental or life threatening illnesses causing life time disabilities such as
cerebral palsy, down syndrome and fatal illnesses like cancer, by providing and assisting in the provision of
facilities, support services and equipment not normally provided by the statutory authorities.
Activities
The ongoing economic climate continues to make successful and cost effective fund raising very challenging.
Despite this, Angelic Stars works tirelessly to raise sufficient funds to maintain and, when possible, to expand
services to seriously and terminally ill children.
Angelic Stars continues to direct its funds at sick children in the East and West Midlands regions and has
offered much needed support, entertainment and toys to children's hospital wards and hospices.
We continue to be inspired by our supporters who donate, fundraise, put on events and also fancy dress in their
pursuit to helping further our mission in bettering the lives of ill children.
Over the next year Angelic Stars aims to create new and innovative ways of using entertainment to distract
children from the pain and isolation often caused by their illness and treatment.
Without the generosity and thoughtfulness of the general public Angelic Stars could not make these wishes
come true.
Structure, governance and management
Financial instruments
Objectives and policies
The charity's activities expose it to a number of financial risks including credit risk, cash flow risk and liquidity
risk. The use of financial derivatives is governed by the charity's policies approved by the board of trustees,
which provide written principles on the use of financial derivatives to manage these risks. The charity does not
use derivative financial instruments for speculative purposes.
Page 2
Angelic Stars
Trustees' Report
Credit risk
The charity's principal financial assets are bank balances and cash, trade and other receivables, and investments.
The charity's credit risk is primarily attributable to its trade receivables. The amounts presented in the balance
sheet are net of allowances for doubtful receivables. An allowance for impairment is made where there is an
identified loss event which, based on previous experience, is evidence of a reduction in the recoverability of the
cash flows.
The credit risk on liquid funds and derivative financial instruments is limited because the counterparties are
banks with high credit-ratings assigned by international credit-rating agencies.
The charity has no significant concentration of credit risk, with exposure spread over a large number of
counterparties and customers.
Liquidity risk
In order to maintain liquidity to ensure that sufficient funds are available for ongoing operations and future
developments, the charity uses a mixture of long-term and short-term debt finance.
Further details regarding liquidity risk can be found in the Statement of accounting policies in the financial
statements.
The annual report was approved by the trustees of the charity on 9 October 2017 and signed on its behalf by:
Ms Kiran Rai
Trustee

Statement of Trustees' Responsibilities
The trustees are responsible for preparing the trustees' report and the financial statements in accordance with the
United Kingdom Accounting Standards (United Kingdom Generally Accepted Accounting Practice) and
applicable law and regulations.
The law applicable to charities requires the trustees to prepare financial statements for each financial period
which give a true and fair view of the state of affairs of the charity and of the incoming resources and
application of resources of the charity for that period. In preparing these financial statements, the trustees are
required to:
select suitable accounting policies and then apply them consistently;
observe the methods and principles in the Charities SORP;
make judgements and estimates that are reasonable and prudent;
state whether applicable accounting standards have been followed, subject to any material departures
disclosed and explained in the financial statements; and
prepare the financial statements on the going concern basis unless it is inappropriate to presume that the
charity will continue in business.
The trustees are responsible for keeping proper accounting records that disclose with reasonable accuracy at any
time the financial position of the charity and enable them to ensure that the financial statements comply with the
Charities Act 2011, the applicable Charities (Accounts and Reports) Regulations, and the provisions of the
constitution. The trustees are also responsible for safeguarding the assets of the charity and hence for taking
reasonable steps for the prevention and detection of fraud and other irregularities.
Approved by the trustees of the charity on 9 October 2017 and signed on its behalf by:

Independent Examiner's Report to the trustees of Aingelic Stars
I report on the accounts of the charity for the year ended 31 May 2017 which are set out on pages 6 to 13.
Respective responsibilities of trustees and examiner
The trustees are responsible for the preparation of the accounts. The trustees consider that an audit is not
required for this year under section 144(2) of the Charities Act 2011 (the 2011 Act) and that an independent
examination is needed.
It is my responsibility to:
examine the accounts under section 145 of the 2011 Act;
to follow the procedures laid down in the general Directions given by the Charity Commission under section
145(5)(b) of the 2011 Act; and
to state whether particular matters have come to my attention.
Basis of independent examiner's report
My examination was carried out in accordance with the general Directions given by the Charity Commission.
An examination includes a review of the accounting records kept by the charity and a comparison of the
accounts presented with those records. It also includes consideration of any unusual items or disclosures in the
accounts, and seeking explanations from you as trustees concerning any such matters. The procedures
undertaken do not provide all the evidence that would be required in an audit and consequently no opinion is
given as to whether the accounts present a 'true and fair view' and the report is limited to those matters set out
in the next statement.
Independent examiner's statement
In connection with my examination, no matter has come to my attention:
(1) which gives me reasonable cause to believe that in any material respect the requirements:
to keep accounting records in accordance with section 130 of the Charities Act 2011; and
to prepare accounts which accord with the accounting records and comply with the accounting
requirements of the 2011 Act
have not been met; or
(2) to which, in my opinion, attention should be drawn in order to enable a proper understanding of the accounts
to be reached.

Notes to the Financial Statements for the Period from 1 November 2016 to 31 May 2017
1 Accounting policies
Statement of compliance
The financial statements have been prepared in accordance with Accounting and Reporting by Charities:
Statement of Recommended Practice applicable to charities preparing their accounts in accordance with the
Financial Reporting Standard applicable in the UK and Republic of Ireland (FRS 102) (effective 1 January
2015) we (Charities SORP (FRS 102)), the Financial Reporting Standard applicable in the UK and Republic of
Ireland (FRS 102) and the Charities Act 2011.
Basis of preparation
Angelic Stars meets the definition of a public benefit entity under FRS 102. Assets and liabilities are initially
recognised at historical cost or transaction value unless otherwise stated in the relevant accounting policy notes.
Exemption from preparing a cash flow statement
The charity opted to early adopt Bulletin 1 published on 2 February 2016 and have therefore not included a cash
flow statement in these financial statements.
Going concern
The trustees consider that there are no material uncertainties about the charity's ability to continue as a going
concern.
Income and endowments
Voluntary income including donations, gifts, legacies and grants that provide core funding or are of a general
nature is recognised when the charity has entitlement to the income, it is probable that the income will be
received and the amount can be measured with sufficient reliability.
Donations and legacies
Donations and legacies are recognised on a receivable basis when receipt is probable and the amount can be
reliably measured.
Expenditure
All expenditure is recognised once there is a legal or constructive obligation to that expenditure, it is probable
settlement is required and the amount can be measured reliably. All costs are allocated to the applicable
expenditure heading that aggregate similar costs to that category. Where costs cannot be directly attributed to
particular headings they have been allocated on a basis consistent with the use of resources, with central staff
costs allocated on the basis of time spent, and depreciation charges allocated on the portion of the asset's use.
Other support costs are allocated based on the spread of staff costs.
Raising funds
These are costs incurred in attracting voluntary income, the management of investments and those incurred in
trading activities that raise funds.
Page 8
Angelic Stars
Notes to the Financial Statements for the Period from 1 November 2016 to 31 May 2017
Charitable activities
Charitable expenditure comprises those costs incurred by the charity in the delivery of its activities and services
for its beneficiaries. It includes both costs that can be allocated directly to such activities and those costs of an
indirect nature necessary to support them.
Grant provisions
Provisions for grants are made when the intention to make a grant has been communicated to the recipient but
there is uncertainty about either the timing of the grant or the amount of grant payable.
Governance costs
These include the costs attributable to the charity's compliance with constitutional and statutory requirements,
including audit, strategic management and trustees's meetings and reimbursed expenses.
Taxation
The charity is considered to pass the tests set out in Paragraph 1 Schedule 6 of the Finance Act 2010 and
therefore it meets the definition of a charitable company for UK corporation tax purposes. Accordingly, the
charity is potentially exempt from taxation in respect of income or capital gains received within categories
covered by Chapter 3 Part 11 of the Corporation Tax Act 2010 or Section 256 of the Taxation of Chargeable
Gains Act 1992, to the extent that such income or gains are applied exclusively to charitable purposes.
Research and development
Research and development expenditure is written off as incurred.
Trade debtors
are amounts due from customers for merchandise sold or services performed in the ordinary course of business.
are recognised initially at the transaction price. They are subsequently measured at amortised cost using the
effective interest method, less provision for impairment. A provision for the impairment of is established when
there is objective evidence that the will not be able to collect all amounts due according to the original terms of
the receivables.
Cash and cash equivalents
Cash and cash equivalents comprise cash on hand and call deposits, and other short-term highly liquid
investments that are readily convertible to a known amount of cash and are subject to an insignificant risk of
change in value.
Fund structure
Unrestricted income funds are general funds that are available for use at the trustees's discretion in furtherance
of the objectives of the charity.
Page 9
Angelic Stars
Notes to the Financial Statements for the Period from 1 November 2016 to 31 May 2017
Financial instruments
Classification
Financial assets and financial liabilities are recognised when the charity becomes a party to the contractual
provisions of the instrument.
Financial liabilities and equity instruments are classified according to the substance of the contractual
arrangements entered into. An equity instrument is any contract that evidences a residual interest in the assets of
the charity after deducting all of its liabilities.
Recognition and measurement
All financial assets and liabilities are initially measured at transaction price (including transaction costs), except
for those financial assets classified as at fair value through profit or loss, which are initially measured at fair
value (which is normally the transaction price excluding transaction costs), unless the arrangement constitutes
a
financing transaction. If an arrangement constitutes a financing transaction, the financial asset or financial
liability is measured at the present value of the future payments discounted at a market rate of interest for a
similar debt instrument.
Financial assets and liabilities are only offset in the statement of financial position when, and only when there
exists a legally enforceable right to set off the recognised amounts and the charity intends either to settle on a
net basis, or to realise the asset and settle the liability simultaneously.
Financial assets are derecognised when and only when a) the contractua rights to the cash flows from the
financial asset expire or are settled, b) the charity transfers to another party substantially all of the risks and
rewards of ownership of the financial asset, or c) the charity, despite having retained some, but not all,
significant risks and rewards of ownership, has transferred control of the asset to another party.
Financial liabilities are derecognised only when the obligation specified in the contract is discharged, cancelled
or expires.
Fair value measurement
The best evidence of fair value is a quoted price for an identical asset in an active market. When quoted prices
are unavailable, the price of a recent transaction for an identica asset provides evidence of fair value as long as
there has not been a significant change in economic circumstances or a significant lapse of time since the
transaction took place. If the market is not active and recent transactions of an identical asset on their own are
not a good estimate of fair value, the fair value is estimated by using a valuation technique.

PARACHUTE REGIMENTAL ASSOCIATION
REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2016
The trustees present their report with the financial statements of the charity for the year ended 31 December 2016. The
trustees have adopted the provisions of Accounting and Reporting by Charities: Statement of Recommended Practice
applicable to charities preparing their accounts in accordance with the Financial Reporting Standard applicable in the UK
and Republic of lreland (FRS 102) (effective 1 January 2015).
OBJECTIVES AND ACTIVITIES
Objectives and aims
The Objects of the Parachute Regimental Association are:
-
To promote the efficiency of the Parachute Regiment and Airborne Forces by fostering esprit de corps and
maintaining contact between past and present members thereof.
-
To relieve either generally or individually persons who are serving or who have served in the Parachute Regiment
and Airborne Forces or the dependants of such persons who are in conditions of need, hardship or distress.
-
The commemoration and remembrance of those members of the Parachute Regiment and Airborne Forces who
have died while on active service; and the encouragement of public recognition of the sacrifice made by such
persons.
Significant activities
The Association and its branches participate in support and organise a range of activities which provide a public benefit.
These include:
-
Public events to raise awareness about the role of the Regiment, to encourage public support for the Regiment
and to assist in recruitment.
-
Holding events and reunions for past and present members of the Airborne Forces (to assist in promoting esprit de
corps).
-
Acts of commemoration and remembrance (e.g. Regimental Memorial Day at the National Memorial Arboretum,
RBL Field of Remembrance, Armistice Day, Ardennes, Rhine Crossing, Normandy, Arnhem and the Falklands) which
raise public awareness of those who have lost their lives or put themselves at risk in service of the public.
Maintaining a membership network and encouraging social contact in order to identify those former members and
dependants who may be in need from time to time.
-
Providing local Welfare Officers who visit members and dependants who may be sick, recently bereaved, or find
themselves in difficult circumstances.
-
In collaboration with other Regimental Charities, make grants (either individually or to an organisation) to support
past and present members of the Parachute Regiment and Airborne Forces and their dependants who are in need.
Supporting Parachute Regiment recruits whilst undergoing training at the Infantry Training Centre at Catterick.
Page 2

FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2016
ACHIEVEMENT AND PERFORMANCE
Charitable activities
During the year, the charity has undertaken the following activities:
1. Provided financial and organisationa support to the Regional Airborne Forces Days across the Country
2. Attended funerals and memorial services of former serving members of The Parachute Regiment and Airborne Forces.
3. Actively fundraised for other Regimental Charities i.e. The Parachute Regiment Charity and The Airborne Forces Security
Fund.
4. Provided funds and organisational support to the Regimental Memorial Day at Parachute Regiment and Airborne Forces
Memorial at the National Memorial Arboretum.
5. Made donations in support of the maintenance and enhancement of Regimental Memorials.
6. Provided donations in support of the 16 Brigade Pegasus Statue to commemorate the reinstatement of the Pegasus
emblem.
7. Made donations in support of the Regimental Museum (Airborne Assault)
8. Provided grants in support of and organisational support to:
O
72nd Anniversary 'D Day' Commemoration events in Normandy and Arnhem.
O
The 71st Anniversary of the Ardennes Biennial Commemoration service.
O
Recruit Platoon Passing out Parades at ITC Catterick.
O
Support to Airborne 'In-Pensioners' at the Royal Hospital Chelsea.
The Parachute Regiment Executive Committee Biannual meeting.
The Parachute Regimental Association Annual General Meeting and Regimental Memorial Day.
o
Airborne Forces Memorial Parades at Bedworth, Eden Camp, North Yorkshire, Portsmouth, Hardwick Hall,
Chilbolton and Aldershot.
Memorial Parades and Services at St Pauls Cathedral, St Lawrence Jewry Next Guildhall and the Bastion Wall at
the NMA.
O
RBL Field of Remembrance Services at Westminster Cathedral.
The Annual Armistice Parade in Whitehall, London.
