TRUSTEES' ANNUAL REPORT
For the period 1st April, 2017 to 31st March, 2018
Structure, Governance and Management
Uroboros Ensemble Ltd is a Limited Company,
The Charity's Purposes and Administration are regulated by the Company's Memorandum and Articles of
Association, dated 9th November 1982.
The Appointment of New Trustees is by joint decision and mutual agreement between all existing trustees. No
new appointments were made during or since this accounting period.
Risk Management. There have been no incidents to report throughout the period to which this report relates.
Reference and Administrative Details;
The Charity's Name as in the Register of Charities is UROBOROS ENSEMBLE LIMITED.
The Charity's Registration Number is 285952
The Company Registration Number is 1676645
The Address of the Charity and that of the Company Registered Office is:
2 S andfields Farm Cottage, Luddington, Stratford-upon-Avon, Warwickshire CV37 9ASW
Phone 01789 751 325
Email: mail@uroborosensemble.com
The Trustees throughout this accounting period and at the time of the signing of this report are:
Gwyn ritchard (Chairman)
Claudia Klasicka
Attila G aramszegi
Objectives and Activities
The Objectives of the Charity, as set out in its governing document, are "to promote and assist in the
advancement of education of the public at large in the art of music and to extend and increase the
appreciation, knowledge and understanding of the art of music in all its forms"
The Activities of Uroboros Ensemble throughout the period April 1st, 2017 to March 31st, 2018 were
exclusively committed to the organisation of LONDON EAR festival of contemporary music, which took place
March 21-25, 2018.
The aims of London Ear accord precisely with Uroboros Ensemble's declared charitable objectives as defined
above, and also reflect the Trustees' regard to the Charity Commission's guidance on public benefit as defined
on the gov.uk website. Specifically the benefits were achieved by the following means:
Creating new opportunities for emerging and undiscovered composers, both to receive performances
and to compose new works;
resenting, in an accessible context, recent musical developments of which the public is either
unaware, or through lack of exposure finds problematical; breaking down obstructive misconceptions
about such music;
g 11
Giving exposure to musical ideas and developments from different countries, and helping to develop
future international cultural partnerships that will benefit musicians both culturally and financially;
Encouraging young performers to embrace contemporary music, helping them to understand it, and
to engage in its performance, thereby both enriching and widening opportunities for them in the future;
Fulfilling the urgent need for a festiva in centra London, dedicated exclusively to contemporary music,
mostly music of styles that are less frequently heard in the UK;
Building an audience for contemporary music in London, by engaging people from all walks of life, and
of all generations.
The structure of London Ear Festival 2016 was as follows:
TEN CONCERTS were given by world-class performers from Britain and abroad. All performers played music
from their own country, British music, and works from other countries.
RECENT MUSIC (post 1980) featured in all concerts, including works by emerging and undiscovered
composers There were several new commissions and world or UK premieres.
PRE-CONCERT EVENTS, included talks designed to enhance the audience's appreciation of the music, and
allow them to meet composers and performers.
FESTIVAL TICKET PRICES were affordable and included substantial concessionary discounts for children,
students, unemployed, and the disabled. London Ear aims to be as inclusive as possible.
THREE FEATURED YOUNG PERFORMERS gave a recital of centmusic and played alongside established
professionals in a festival ensemble concert. These opportunities greatly enriched the musical experience for
the young musicians at the very start of their professiona careers.
THREE WORKSHOPS, for composers, harpists and flautists, led by internationally respected soloists,
focussed on contemporary techniques.
A COMPOSERS COMPETITION, designed to give much needed exposure to emerging composers (of any
age), attracted a very impressive response, with the finalists' pieces being publicly performed and later
broadcast by the BBC.
FESTIVAL BOOK gave detailed information about the music, the composers and the performers.
A FESTIVAL CLUB enabled audiences to meet and talk with composers and performers in an informal
atmosphere, with scores, CDs etc. on display or to buy, and refreshments available.
Achievements and Performance
The benefits of Uroboros Ensemble's work, uniquely in London Ear festival, fall into two categories: those that
are quantifiable, and those that can only be estimated.
Quantifiable benefits include those to composers, by commission and performance of their work, to young
performers by creating performance opportunity, to students by masterclass and workshop experience, and to
those members of the public who were able to attend events at a concessionary ticket cost, and often free
(children, students, unemployed, disabled).
The estimated public benefit is significant, and concerns the cultural contribution of Uroboros Ensemble's work
to both the musical life of London (and beyond), and to the development of contemporary music in the UK (a
severely under-funded sector). E xtremely enthusiastic audience response, together with full houses at most
events, confirms the contribution that the charity is making with respect to all the six bullet-listed points above
under Objectives and Activities.
P a g e 12
Financial review
Nearly all expenditure and income throughout the period related directly to London Ear Festival, with the
exception of a few very small general administrative costs. The accompanying accounts cover financial activity
related to the festival, up to March 31st, 2018, which principally consisted of raising funds from grants and
donations, and making payments, both prior to and after the festival.
The accounts for the period show income received from Grants within the period amounting to f43,572.57;
these came from the following sources:

TOTAL FESTIVAL INCOME

There were severa recepts and payments related to the festival after March 31, 2018, which will of course
be
included in the next annual report, for 2018-19, but at this stage it can be confirmed that London Ear 2018 was
completed within the projected budget, without a final deficit, and leaving sufficient funds in hand for Uroboros
Ensemble to cover ongoing expenses.
Signed on behalf of the Trustees of Uroboros Ensemble Ltd

ANNUAL REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES OF THE BRENTWOOD SCHOOL CIO
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31ST AUGUST 2017
The Governors of Brentwood School present their annual report for the year ended 31st
August 2017 under the Charities Act 2011, together with the audited accounts for the year.
REFERENCE AND ADMINISTRATIVE INFORMATION
Brentwood School was founded in 1557. It is constituted as a Charitable Incorporated
Organisation and is registered with the Charity Commission under Charity number
1153605.
The School operates two schools, known as Brentwood School and Brentwood Preparatory
School.
There is one Governing Body for both Schools. Details of the members of the Governing
Body, together with the School's executive officers and principal advisers are set out on
pages 2 and 3.
STRUCTURE, GOVERNANCE AND MANAGEMENT
Governing Document
The CIO is governed by its Constitution, last amended on 2nd January 2014.
The Governing Body
The Governing Body is self-appointing. Service on the Board is for a term of five years or
such shorter term as may be agreed by the Governors. Retiring Governors may be re-
elected.
New members of the Governing Body are elected on the basis of nominations from the
Governors and the executive officers based on the specific needs of the Governing Body
and criteria set by the Executive Committee. With regard to these nominations account is
taken of areas such as eligibility, personal competence, expertise and specialist skills as
well as local availability.
The Headmaster, the Head of the Preparatory School, the Senior Deputy Head of the Senior
School and the Bursar attend all meetings of the Executive Committee and the full Governing
Body.
Recruitment and Training of Governors
New Governors are inducted into the workings of the School, including Governing Body
policy and procedures, at induction sessions specifically organised for them by the
Chairman of Governors, the Headmaster and the Clerk to the Governors. The new
Governors also attend specialist external courses on the role and responsibilities of charity
trustees and the Headmaster arranges for Governors to spend time in the School to see how
our teachers deliver the curriculum.
5
Brentwood School
ANNUAL REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES OF THE BRENTWOOD SCHOOL CIO
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31ST AUGUST 2017
Members of the Governing Body attend external trustee training and information courses
designed to keep them informed and updated on current issues in the sector and regulatory
requirements. Invitations to visit the School continue throughout Governors' tenure of office
and they have regular opportunities to meet staff and senior pupils after each Governors'
Meeting.
Organisational Management
The School Governors, as the trustees of the Charity, are legally responsible for the overall
management and control of the Senior School and the Preparatory School. They meet in
formal session as a Board three times a year.
The work of implementing their policies is carried out by ten committees:
The Executive Committee, chaired by Sir Michael Snyder, has oversight of the
School's vision, mission and strategic direction and of measuring objectively the
progress of the School in achieving them. It is responsible for making
recommendations to the full Governing Body concerning the appointment of
Governors to particular roles, the selection of individuals to join the Board and the
appointment of, and terms and conditions of employment of, those members of staff
who are Governors' appointees. The Committee oversees legal and regulatory
matters, the control of assets and governance issues.
The Finance and Audit Committee scrutinises revenue, the budget and capital
expenditure. This Committee also supervises and finalises the audited financial
statements and annual report for approval by the Governing Body and oversees all
strategic risks facing the School. The Committee is chaired by Sir Michael Snyder.
The Education Committee considers all matters pertaining to educational policy.
This Committee is chaired by Ms Rosemary Martin.
The Property Management Committee supervises and monitors capital building
projects and maintenance. The Committee is chaired by Mr Paul Beresford.
The Investment Committee oversees the management of the School's investments in
equities and property. The Committee is chaired by The Lord Flight.
The Scholarships and Awards Committee supervises and monitors the award of
scholarships and bursaries. The Committee is chaired by Mr John May.
The Communications and Development Committee oversees the marketing of the
School, the administration of admissions and the management of alumni relations.
This Committee is chaired by The Lord Black.
The Preparatory School Committee overseas all routine policy matters at the
Preparatory School. It is chaired by Mrs Jenny Jones.
6
Brentwood School
ANNUAL REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES OF THE BRENTWOOD SCHOOL CIO
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31ST AUGUST 2017
The Teachers' Terms and Conditions Sub-Committee was only formed this summer
with the aim of providing advice to Governors on matters affecting the recruitment
and retention of staff. The Committee reports through the Finance Committee to the
Governing Body once a year in the Michaelmas Term. The Committee is chaired by
The Lord Black.
The Brentwood School Enterprises Management Committee oversees the activities
of Brentwood School Enterprises in its support of the School's sporting curriculum
and in its operation as the trading arm of the School. This Committee is chaired by
Mr Bob McLintock.
There is an annual meeting of key Governors and the Senior Leadership Team, offsite
which is the culmination of the strategic development process and sets the School's
strategic direction.
In addition, nominated Governors have special responsibility for oversight of particular
aspects of school life. These are as follows:
Preparatory School Representative Governor: Mrs Jenny Jones
Representative to the Association Of Governing Bodies Of Independent Schools: Mr
Bob McLintock
Governor with Special Responsibility for the oversight of Safeguarding: Professor
Bruce Evans
Governor with Special Responsibility for the oversight of Health and Safety Matters:
Mr Bob McLintock
The day to day running of the Schools is delegated to the Headmaster and the Bursar. They
are supported by their Senior Leadership Teams and together this group, which comprises
the Head of the Preparatory School, the Senior Deputy Head, Deputy Head (Academic) and
Deputy Head (Staffing, Operations and Co-curricular) of the Senior School, the Director of
Finance and the Director of Communications, Admissions and Alumni Relations, are the key
management personnel. The Headmaster, the Head of the Preparatory School, the Senior
Deputy Head and the Bursar attend all meetings of the Executive and full Governors
meetings.
Remuneration is set by the Board, with the policy objective of providing appropriate
incentives to encourage enhanced performance and of rewarding fairly and responsibly
individual contributions to the School's success.
The appropriateness and relevance of the remuneration policy is reviewed annually,
including reference to comparisons with other independent schools to ensure that the
School remains sensitive to the broader issues of pay and employment conditions
elsewhere.
We aim to recruit, subject to experience, at the lower to medium point within our Basic
Salary Scale for teachers, providing scope for rewarding excellence. Delivery of the
7
Brentwood School
ANNUAL REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES OF THE BRENTWOOD SCHOOL CIO
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31ST AUGUST 2017
School's charitable vision and purpose is primarily dependent on our key leadership
personnel and staff costs are the largest single element of our charitable expenditure.
Group Structure and Relationships
The School has now been operating as a Charitable Incorporated Organisation since 1
September 2015 and the processes and output have remained constant since the change
from the Sir Antony Browne School Trust (SABST). The CIO is the sole trustee of the
Permanent Endowment of the SABST which holds the assets of the original endowment,
namely land valued in 1947 at E200,000 under the title deeds EX 788375 and EX 788423.
The Charity has a wholly owned non-charitable subsidiary, Brentwood School Enterprises
Limited. This company is responsible for running the Brentwood School Sports Centre, for
operating the School Shop and for letting School premises and sports fields when they are
not required by the School.
This Brentwood School Foundation has been established within the General Reserves of the
CIO. Its express airs are to build up a fund that can be used to support children who would
not normally be able to afford through the provision of Bursaries and Scholarships. It
concentrates on promoting legacy giving and donations as well as raising money through
high profile events including dinner in the House of Lords.
The Brentwood School Sports Centre provides sports facilities for the School and, outside of
school use, generates additional income for the School by way of membership fees and
letting of facilities to the local community. The excellent facilities provided to the School by
the Sports Centre include an indoor swimming pool, two fitness suites, squash courts and a
sports hall.
Employment Policy
The School is an equal opportunities employer. Full and fair consideration is given to job
applications from disabled persons and due consideration is given to their training and
employment needs. Consultation with employees, or their representatives, has continued
at all levels with the aim of taking the views of employees into account when decisions are
made that are likely to affect their interests.
Volunteers
The School benefits from the close support of the Society of Old Brentwoods and from the
Friends of Brentwood School (Registered Charity Number 1095486), whose generosity we
greatly appreciate. We gladly acknowledge the role played by both these organisations in
the life of the School.
The Governors value and encourage the work of the Society in keeping in touch with alumni
and offering support and advice to Old Brentwoods in the development of their careers. The
latter is manifest in the assistance that members of the Society give in attending our annual
Careers Fair but also in the informal networking that goes on throughout the year and at
alumni events such as 'Drinks in the City'.
8
Brentwood School
ANNUAL REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES OF THE BRENTWOOD SCHOOL CIO
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31ST AUGUST 2017
The Friends of Brentwood School (FoBS) donated a total of E23,438 to the School in the
Academic Year 2016/2017, of which &8,000 is to fund attractive wooden benches that can be
placed around the School to increase the use of the grounds as a social and learning space
for both staff and students.
Investment Policy and Objectives
The School's investment objectives are to balance the current and future needs by:
Maintaining (at least) the value of investments in real terms;
Producing a consistent and sustainable amount to support expenditure and, in
particular, scholarships and bursaries;
Delivering these objectives within acceptable levels of risk.
To meet these objectives, the School's investments as a whole are managed on a total return
basis. The Charity's strategy for investment is set out in a Statement of Investment Policy,
the aim of which is to maximise investment performance by selecting largely equity
investments offering the potential for good returns in the medium term in the commercial
market commensurate with avoiding undue risk of loss. This is to ensure that growth and
income combined, on a long term basis, are equal to the return obtainable on cash and
capital rising in line with the rate of inflation. Some short term cash deposits are held in
notice accounts which are readily accessible and can be used as the School continues to
pursue exciting development projects in lie with its charitable purpose. As much of the
income from the investments as possible is to be re-invested through investing via Fund
'accumulation units'.
Authority is vested in the Investment Committee to monitor performance, set benchmarks
and allocate funds to Fund Managers selected on the basis of the investment opportunities
that they offer and their record of performance. By selecting both the Fund Managers and
the investment funds the Committee has achieved the level of diversification deemed
appropriate to reduce risk and to achieve the investment objective.
The Investment Committee reports regularly to the Executive Committee and the Board of
Governors. The policy of the Governors is that the School's investment portfolio should be
gradually increased in line with the reserves policy.
The investment performance is reported below within the Strategic Report.
OBJECTS, AIMS, OBJECTIVES AND ACTIVITIES
Charitable Object
The School's Object, as set out in the CIO's Constitution, is the advancement of education in
or near Brentwood by providing day or day and boarding schooling. Within this context the
Governors are mindful of the Charities Act 2011 and they have closely monitored the long
standing need to provide public benefit and the Commission's supplemental guidance on
fee charging.
9
Brentwood School
ANNUAL REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES OF THE BRENTWOOD SCHOOL CIO
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31ST AUGUST 2017
Mission Statement
The School's mission is to inspire lifelong learning within a nurturing, culturally creative and
intellectually dynamic community. This is underpinned by our core values of Virtue,
Learning and Manners.
Intended Impact
Within its charitable Objects, the School's intention is to provide a first class education
through strong teaching and learning and by developing broader skills that enable every
pupil to realise his or her potential to the full. This involves emphasis on the co-curriculum
through intellectual, sporting, musical, artistic, team-building and social skills. This policy
develops self-confidence, resilience and life skills in our pupils and inculcates a desire for
lifelong learning. This is supplemented by the development of a community spirit and a
willingness to contribute, in the widest sense to their communities, whilst at the School and
in later life.
In this way, Brentwood School nurtures high achieving, enterprising, articulate individuals
who have the academic and social skills, integrity and commitment to lead responsibly the
next generation.
Aims
The School's aims for the public benefit are to:
Ensure that all pupils achieve the best possible academic results.
Provide a range of opportunities designed to produce well-educated pupils with
good leadership skills who are able to work with a variety of different people and
have a sense of service to others.
Ensure that students emerge as intellectually curious, resilient and enterprising
and independent lifelong learners.
Broaden the School's intake to include children from families who could not
otherwise afford independent education through our bursary programme.
Primary Objectives
The primary objectives of the School to fulfil these aims are to:
Provide a stimulating learning environment in which pupils can develop their
academic potential to the full.
Provide a happy and secure pastoral environment in which pupils can learn to live
together and thus foster a sense of community, co-education, respect for one
another and good citizenship.
Provide pupils with the opportunity to take advantage of a breadth of Co-Curricular
activities in order to develop positively all aspects of their character.
Market the many strengths of Brentwood School and, in particular, to promote the
International Baccalaureate Diploma Programme (IBDP).
10
Brentwood School
ANNUAL REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES OF THE BRENTWOOD SCHOOL CIO
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31ST AUGUST 2017
Maintain a school roll of not less than 1,500 pupils spread between the Senior and
Preparatory Schools.
Continue to offer a substantial sum in financial assistance to deserving families
through bursaries to pupils on entering the School and to award emergency
assistance to parents who suffer a change in their financial circumstances.
Continue to implement and develop the School's building programme.
Strategies to Achieve the Primary Objectives
Whilst the Governors' policy, in line with that of other Independent Schools, is to make some
scholarship awards on the basis of the individual's educational potential, our emphasis has
continued to be on the award of bursaries in order to make the education offered by the
School available to families who would not otherwise be able to afford the School's fees.
Planning for the rebuild and expansion of the Preparatory School has featured in previous
reports and has now reached the final stages of a very long planning process. It is expected
that building work will commence at Easter 2018, subject to planning permission, with
completion anticipated in 2021. This will increase the annual intake by an extra form of 20
every year, culminating in an anticipated School roll of 1,836.
We devised and implemented a number of strategies designed to meet our primary
academic priorities, including the following:
Introducing the concept of 'growth mindset' and developing the teaching of study
skills, especially to examination year groups.
Reviewing and developing intellectual enrichment, challenge in the classroom and
articulating the concept of a 'leamning community'.
Developing a sense of international mindedness across the School, in both
curriculum and Co-Curricular activities.
Continuing to embed and communicate key pastoral safeguarding policies to staff.
Principal Activity
The Charity's principal activity, as specified in the CIO's Constitution, is the advancement
of education in Brentwood to boys and girls from the ages of three to 18 in its two Schools
and, in this, the School has again had a very successful year.
This year, the Senior School averaged 1,127 (2016: 1,127) pupils of whom 63 (2016: were
boarders. The Preparatory School averaged 390 (2016: 388) FTE pupils.
Public Benefit
Brentwood School remains committed to the aim of providing public benefit in accordance
with its founding principles and the terms of its current Constitution. The Governors are
conscious of their responsibility to ensure that public benefit can be measured.
Firstly wider access to our schooling was made available during 2016/2017 through the
Charity's bursaries, grants, awards and other benefactions which, together with fee-
11
Brentwood School
ANNUAL REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES OF THE BRENTWOOD SCHOOL CIO
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31ST AUGUST 2017
concessions, amounted to E2,006,970 (2016: E2,002,129) representing 7.8% (2016: 6:8.1%) of
gross fee income.
The awarding of bursaries is a measurable means of providing public benefit. The
Governors take the view that bursaries awarded to those who would not otherwise be able
to afford the education offered by the School are important, but not to the exclusion of the
much wider benefit that the School provides within the community. Those pupils who attend
the School and who receive financial support contribute to the school community in a variety
of ways, and so the benefit is not purely to these pupils but to the school community and, in
some cases, to the wider community.
We continue to restrict both the overall funding for scholarships and the value of each
scholarship awarded. This has allowed us to allocate the majority of our available funds to
providing places funded by bursaries. Thus, we awarded the equivalent of 13.35 full-fee
places in new bursary grants in Academic Year 2016/2017 (11.25 in 2015/2016). When these
are added to existing bursary awards, the sum in issue to bursary-holders in 2016/2017 was
E1,315,675 (2016: E1,318,487), which is equivalent to 5.1% of gross fee income (2015/2016:
5.3%).
In addition to bursaries, the School has engaged in many other activities to provide benefit
to the public within the School's objectives. Examples include the following:
Activities undertaken by the pupils in support of the local community and to raise funds for
local, national and international charities. We have established a relationship with the new
Grove House School, working directly with the children there who require additional
support, and providing structural and logistical support for their Duke of Edinburgh's Award
Expeditions. We have worked with the Town Council to restore and maintain a local
cemetery and work on conservation projects with the Essex Wildlife Trust.
The Duke of Edinburgh's Award provides a great vehicle for community involvement, and
with high numbers (56 doing Bronze, 121 Silver and 76 Gold) their input into community
activities is enormous.
Wherever possible, the School is pleased to make its facilities available for local people,
organisations, clubs and charities, and we have developed strong links with local dramatic
and musical societies, a variety of sports clubs and the Dioceses of Chelmsford and
Brentwood. In particular, our Sports Centre, Astroturf pitches and playing fields play a
major role in our continuing effort to develop wider community links.
REVIEW OF ACHIEVEMENTS AND PERFORMANCE FOR THE YEAR
Examination Results and University Entrance
International Baccalaureate.
The International Baccalaureate Diploma results were published in July, and, after remarks
our students achieved 37 points on average with one of our students gaining the highest
12
Brentwood School
ANNUAL REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES OF THE BRENTWOOD SCHOOL CIO
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31ST AUGUST 2017
possible score of 45 and getting a place at UCL to read Psychology. Six of the 28 students
achieved over 40 points.
There were 2 top grades (7s) in Higher level Maths, considered difficult, but some
disappointing scores in Physics and Chemistry, alongside some very good scores in the
same subjects. Two students failed to qualify for the Diploma but both have been accepted
by their universities. Once again there were really strong performances from students with
poorer GCSE profiles who have gained places at surprisingly good universities.
A Levels.
The results published on I7th August 2017 were the first year for the reformed A Levels.
These reformed A Levels contain new content to meet the requirements of higher Education,
and less non-examination assessment.
Nationally, A Level results and entries remained stable with small % increases to A* and A*
and A grades. Brentwood achieved 14.9% A* grades, the highest ever achieved by the
School and 44.4% A*-A grades in these examination, that represents a 5.2% increase over
last year.
Seven out of our 8 Oxbridge candidates gained a place and 4 students were awarded places
to study at Medical Schools.
GCSE
Following on from very good International Baccalaureate Diploma and A Level results, as
anticipated, our top GCSE students performed exceptionally well, and after re-marks we
anticipate that our percentage of A* grades are some of the best ever. Eight students, our
highest number ever, achieved a full set of A* grades.
Music and Drama
It has been another wonderful year in Drama and the Performing Arts. Another year of firsts
and yet more opportunities for our massively talented pupils to demonstrate their creative
excellence. October saw the introduction of the Sixth Form Play, which was selected,
produced, directed and performed by members of our Senior cohort.
The highlight of the Lent term drama offering was an exceptional 'Lord of the Flies' with
pupils of the Middle School, and the final result was engaging and terrifying, as the author
had intended. A number of our Senior drama pupils successfully auditioned for the National
Youth Theatre this year.
Our two-year Juniors' cycle came to a thrilling conclusion a few weeks ago with Miss
Passmore's directorial debut and the first Junior Musical in quite some time. 'Peter Pan' was
a massive hit, written by Miss Passmore with music and lyrics by the retiring Mrs Khoo and
choreography by the wonderfully talented Ms Choate.
Other productions this year were "The Complete Works of William Shakespeare

Brentwood School

FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31ST AUGUST 2017
(abridged)', 'Metamorphosis', "The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night Time',
'Crossfire', 'Attempts on her Life', 'Kinder Transport', 'Blue Remembered Hills' and 'Girls
Like That' as well as the numerous original devised pieces created by our GCSE, IB and A
Level pupils and the termly Junior Drama Club performances. In total, there have been
almost fifty plays performed this year.
Sport
We have continued to maximise opportunities for all of our pupils to represent the School
by ensuring that there are as many block fixtures as possible across a wide range of sports.
This ensures that they get the maximum benefit in terms of performance, resilience and team
membership. This year has been a great year for the fencing team with medals being won
in a variety of events culminating in January in the Eastern Region and Madeleine Gale and
Matthew Goodwin being selected to represent Team England in Poland. Our Golfers
reached the regional finals and Matt Luff has won his second SODI World title at the wheel
of his Go-Kart. Football has continued to prosper within the School, the lst XI reached the
final of the Independent School's London Cup and a number of players have signed with
professional clubs.
Collaboration with State Schools and Academies.
The tradition of strong collaboration with state schools and academies has continued,
amongst our many activities the commitment to Westcliff High School for Boys CCF came
to a close and has been replaced by a 3 year arrangement to assist in the establishment of a
CCF at Shenfield High School. The School provides assistance to local state schools to help
their students with Oxbridge entrance, admissions tests for American universities and
application and interview guidance for MDV students from local state schools. We have
provided our Athletics track for the sports days of 2 local state schools and our First XI pitch
is used by Essex FA to host cup final matches and Inter-Counties fixtures.
Developing the School Estate.
The School has gained significant benefit in the improvement of the estate over this decade
and has reaped the rewards of this provision during this academic year. The past year has
been one of consolidation with a number of maintenance projects being undertaken to
ensure that facilities remain in good condition and that Health and Safety measures are taken
where required. The incremental upgrade of laboratories in the Queens Building continued
as well as the installation of a path on The Chase to make it a more pleasant pedestrian
environment. The creation of a social common area for the 2nd Year has transformed the
Lawrence Building, providing it with a bright entrance and a welcoming communal area.
Less glamorously expansion joints have been retrofitted to a number of mid-20th Century
buildings to ensure their stability and longevity. Other estates activity has concentrated on
the prolonged planning process for the rebuild of a significant part of the Prep School and
the Ashton/Reception development.

The School and its Employees.
The performance of the School relies on backbone that is provided by its cohort of loyal and
dedicated employees, both Academic and Support Staff. The School continues to seek to
engage with all employees through a number of fora and provide a 2 way flow of information
to further improve performance.
We continued to provide excellent and engaging INSET programmes using both internal
and external resources as well as providing subsidies to staff to undertake higher degrees
and doctorates.
Fundraising Performance.
The formation of the Brentwood School Foundation was mentioned in the report last year.
Mr David Taylor has been appointed as the Director of the Foundation. Gifts to the
Foundation and to the Bursaries Fund can be used to further the school's charitable objects
including the provision of bursaries and other types of funding to assist students who would
not otherwise benefit from an education at Brentwood. The Friends of Brentwood School
continue to raise funds and make highly targeted and effective donations for the betterment
of the School environment, notably this year the purchase of wooden benches for the
students and staff.
Investment Performance
The School has investments in both property and financial instruments. The cottage in
Wales, donated by an Old Brentwood in 2016 and reported in last year's reports, has been
put up for sale. As at the end of the reporting period it has yet to be sold, although there is
a cash offer on it for E70,000 which we have accepted and it is hoped that this will move to
completion. The property at 81 Corbets Tey Road remains rented to commercial tenants.
The School has also received a bequest of shares and property from a Late Old Brentwood.
Probate was granted on 15 May 2017 and these assets are being disposed of in order to
provide the bursaries requested in the Benefactors will.
FINANCIAL REVIEW
Results for the Year
The consolidated net incoming funds from operations for the year amounted to &4,888,687
(2016: 23,191,498). The net income surplus, including gains on investments and the write
down of an investment property, was &8,105,376 (2016: $5,419,743), as shown in the
Consolidated Statement of Financial Activities. This figure includes Brentwood School
Enterprises' net loss of E3,742 (2016: $15,846), after transfer of the Gift Aid donation of
177,464 to the School.
Trading Subsidiary
The Trading Subsidiary as a whole made a turnover of E1,053,950 (2016: E1,005,754) from
its core operations, of which nearly 68% was generated by the Sports Centre and 32% from
15
Brentwood School
ANNUAL REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES OF THE BRENTWOOD SCHOOL CIO
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31ST AUGUST 2017
the School Shop. Both the operations exceeded their profit targets for the year. This meant
that the Sports Centre made an operating profit of 280,398 and the School Shop made an
operating profit of E93,327.
As a result, the Trading Subsidiary made an operating profit of 2173,722 (2016: E158,473).
This will allow Brentwood School Enterprises (BSE) to make a gift-aided donation to the
School of its taxable profit of E177,464 (2016: E174,319). In addition, strong cash balances
meant that BSE was able to repay E30,000 of the outstanding loan due to the School (reducing
the loan to $94,774). The payment of the donation to the School means that BSE has returned
an overall loss of E3,742.
Reserves Level and Policy and Financial Viability
The School's unrestricted general funds stood at E69.7m (2016: 262.2m) at the year-end, of
which E39.4m (2016: $40.2m) represented funds deployed as part of the School's premises
and equipment, leaving E30.3m (2016: E22.0m) as free reserves, comprising investments
(equities and property) of E24.9m (2016: E21.0m) plus other net assets of E5.4m (2016:
El.lm).
The Trustees have set one year's gross fee income as the target for free reserves. The E30.3m
has now exceeded this target for the first time. This is due to the continued significant
increase in the valuation of the School's investments. The Trustees have set this target for
three reasons: to safeguard the future of the School; to provide income to support the award
of bursaries; and to finance continuing and significant capital expenditure on improvements
to the facilities, infrastructure and buildings on the School campus.
The Governors' policy is not to maintain free reserves in Brentwood School Enterprises.
Note 22 to the Financial Statements sets out an analysis of the assets attributable to the
various funds. We believe that these assets are sufficient to meet the Charity's obligations
on a fund by fund basis.
PRINCIPAL RISKS AND UNCERTAINTIES
The Governors consider the economic turbulence of recent years and the affordability of
fees by parents across the independent sector to be the principal risk faced by the School.
The School achieved a good level of intake for September 2016 but this has been exceeded
for September 2017, however, there is no room for complacency. In setting the fees for
2017/2018, the Governors again reviewed in detail the question of affordability: the School
was faced with more unavoidable increases in operational costs at the same time that we
needed to maintain our funding for future capital development and to support the academic
and Co-Curricular ambitions of the School. In response, we needed to continue to ensure
that our cost-base was as lean as possible but we could not, this year, avoid another above-
inflation fee increase.
Health and Safety is always a significant area of risk management. The level and breadth of
activity at the School is impressive and the risks associated with all the activities are
minimised by thorough planning and risk assessment. Nonetheless, in response to an
16

incident in February 2015, the School has strengthened its practices and procedures for the
assessment and conduct of maintenance work that involves a foreseeable risk (the incident,
and the outcome, was reported to the Charity Commission as a 'Serious Incident').
Detailed considerations of risk are undertaken by the Executive Committee. Each year,
risks are identified and reviewed; they are formally discussed and assessed; and
appropriate controls are established to deal with them. Formal reviews of this process and,
in particular, of the effectiveness of the control measures, are undertaken at regular intervals
throughout the year.
The key control measures used by the Charity include:
Terms of Reference for Trustees and Committees;
Formal agendas for all Board and Committee activity;
Effective Committee structure;
Comprehensive strategic planning, budgeting and management accounting;
Established organisational structure and lines of reporting;
Formal written policies;
Clear authorisation and approval levels;
Annual reviews by the Governors of the School's Health and Safety, Child
Protection and other regulatory written policies in order to ensure effective
application of the correct procedures and to ensure that all vetting procedures
required by law for the protection of the vulnerable are conducted effectively.
The risk management process operated by the School allows the Governors to confirm that
they are satisfied that the major risks have been identified, that their impact has been
assessed and, where necessary, controls have been implemented to mitigate and monitor
those risks that are assessed as high. The Governors regularly review the effectiveness of
current plans and strategies for managing all identified major risks for both the School and
Brentwood School Enterprises. New risks identified during the year included the possible
impact of Brexit, both on affordability (we are in an area heavily dependent on the City) and
on the availability of Visas for overseas students.
FUTURE PLANS
The Board's directives for delivering further progress are contained in two related
documents: the School Improvement Plan for 2016/2017; and the updated 5-year Strategic
Development Plan, covering the period 2015 to 2020, both of which were approved by the
Governors on 6th June 2016 and both will be reviewed on an annual basis. The following
objectives will continue to form the foundation of our future plans:
To continue to ensure that the campus is a safe and attractive environment
for pupils, staff and visitors.
To provide a happy and secure pastoral environment, suitable for both day
and boarding pupils, in which all pupils are offered opportunities for
leadership and service to others.
To provide a stimulating learning environment in which pupils can develop
their academic potential to the full.

1. ACCOUNTING POLICIES
Charity Information
The School is a Public Benefit Entity registered as a Charitable Incorporated
Organisation (CIO) in England and Wales. It was formed on 30th August 2013 and its
charity number is 1153605. On 1st September 2015, the Charity's asset, other than the
property considered to be a Permanent Endowment, were transferred to Brentwood
School CIO from the Sir Antony Browne's School Trust (SABST). The property forming
the Permanent Endowment remains within SABST (charity number 310864).
Brentwood School CIO is the sole corporate Trustee of this Permanent Endowment
and is the registered Title Holder of the property.
The financial statements have been prepared in accordance with the Financial
Reporting Standard applicable in the UK and Republic of Ireland (FRS102) and the
Statement of Recommended Practice applicable to charities preparing their accounts
in accordance with the Financial Reporting Standard applicable in the UK and
Republic of Ireland (FRS 102).
The accounts financial statements have been prepared to give a 'true and fair' view
and have departed from the Charities (Accounts and Reports) Regulations 2008 only
to the extent required to provide a 'true and fair view'. This departure has involved
following Accounting and Reporting by Charities preparing their accounts in
accordance with the Financial Reporting Standard applicable in the UK and Republic
of Ireland (FRS 102) issued on 16 July 2014 rather than the Accounting and Reporting
by Charities: Statement of Recommended Practice effective from 1 April 2005 which
has since been withdrawn.
The functional currency of the School is considered to be GBP because that is the
currency of the primary economic environment in which the School operates.
The accounts are drawn up on the historical cost basis of accounting, as modified by
the revaluation of investment properties and other investments.
Having reviewed the funding facilities available to the School, together with the
expected ongoing demand for places and the School's future projected cash flows,
the Governors have a reasonable expectation that the School has adequate resources
to continue its activities for the foreseeable future and consider that there were no
material uncertainties over the School's financial viability.
The accounts present the consolidated statement of financial activities (SOFA), the
consolidated cash flow statement, and the consolidated and Charity balance sheets
comprising the consolidation of the School with its wholly owned trading subsidiary,
Brentwood School Enterprises. The results of SABST and the Brentwood School
General Charitable Trust (BSGCT) are included within the Charity's figures. No
separate SOFA has been presented for the Charity alone, however the results are
detailed in note 27. The consolidation has been carried out on a line by line basis.
28

The School has taken advantage of the exemptions in FRS 102 from the requirements
to present a charity only Cash Flow Statement, on the basis that it is a qualifying entity
and the Consolidated cash flow included in these financial statements includes the
cash flows of the School.
Critical accounting judgements and key sources of estimation uncertainty
In the application of the accounting policies, Trustees are required to make
judgement, estimates and assumptions about the carrying value of assets and
liabilities that are not readily apparent from other sources. The estimates and
underlying assumptions are based on historical experience and other factors that are
considered to be relevant. Actual results may differ from these estimates.
The estimates and underlying assumptions are reviewed on an ongoing basis.
Revisions to accounting estimates are recognised in the period in which the estimate
is revised if the revision affects only that period, or in the period of the revision and
future periods if the revision affects current and future periods.
In the view of the Trustees, no assumptions concerning the future or estimation
uncertainty affecting assets or liabilities at the balance sheet date are likely to result
in a material adjustment to their carrying amounts in the next financial year.
The following accounting policies have been applied consistently in dealing with
items which are considered material in relation to the School's financial statements.
1.1.
Fees and similar earned income
Fees receivable and charges for services and use of the premises, less any
allowances, scholarships, bursaries and other remissions granted by the School
against those fees, are accounted for in the period in which the service is provided.
Fees received in advance of education to be provided in future years under the
Composite Fee Scheme are held as discount-earning liabilities until either used as
fees or refunded. Investment income eamed on such balances is taken into the
general revenue of the School in the year in which it is earned.
1.2.
Investment income
Investment income from dividends and bank balances is accounted for on an
accruals basis. Income from investment properties is accounted for in the period to
which the rental income relates.
1.3.
Donations, legacies, grants and other voluntary incoming resources
Grants and donations are recognised as income on receipt of funds or when
entitlement of receipt by the School is considered probable.
29
BRENTWOOD SCHOOL
NOTES TO THE FINANCLAL STATEMENTS (CONTINUED)
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 3151 AUGUST 2017
Legacies are recognised as income on receipt of funds or when entitlement of
receipts by the School is considered probable. Entitlement is taken to be the earlier
date of the School being notified of an impending distribution following settlement
of the estate or the legacy being received.
Voluntary income for the School's general purposes is accounted for as unrestricted
and is credited to the General Reserve. Where the donor or an appeal has imposed
trust law restrictions, voluntary income is credited to the relevant restricted fund and
incoming endowments are accounted for as permanent trust capital or expendable
trust capital, according to whether the donor intends retention is to be permanent or
not.
1.4. Expenditure
Expenditure is accrued as soon as a liability is considered probable, discounted to
present value for longer-term liabilities. Expenditure attributable to more than one
cost category in the SOFA is apportioned to them on the basis of the estimated
amount attributable to each activity in the year, either by reference to staff time or
the use made of the underlying assets, as appropriate. The direct costs incurred in
preserving the School's buildings and their contents are shown as a charitable
activity distinct from that of education and grant making.
Irrecoverable VAT is included with the item of expenditure to which it relates.
Governance costs comprise the costs of complying with constitutional and statutory
requirements, such as the costs of Governors' and Executive Committee meetings
and the cost of preparing statutory accounts and satisfying public accountability.
Intra-group transactions between the School and its subsidiary, Brentwood School
Enterprises, are excluded from trading income and expenditure.
1.5.
Tangible fixed assets
The property which was held as at 1st April 1947 is included at its value at that date,
taken as its deemed cost. The historic value of this asset is recognised as a Permanent
Endowment within the consolidated accounts.
Expenditure on the acquisition, construction or enhancement of land and buildings,
vehicles, furniture, machinery, ICT infrastructure and other equipment costing more
than E500 is capitalised and carried in the balance sheet at historical cost. Other
expenditure on equipment incurred in the normal day-to-day running of the School
and its subsidiary is charged to the SOFA as incurred.

1.6. Depreciation
Depreciation is provided to write off the cost of all relevant tangible fixed assets less
estimated residual value based on current market prices, in equal annual instalments
over their expected useful economic lives as follows:

The charity now depreciates assets from the later of the date at which they are
purchased or brought into use.
1.7. Investments
Investment properties are valued as individual investments at their market values as
at the balance sheet date. The commercial property in Upminster was valued by R
Cheke & Co, Chartered Surveyors and Valuers, in June 2015. Rental income is
recognised in the period to which it relates. Purchases and sales of investment
properties are recognised on exchange of contracts.
Listed investments are valued at market value as at the balance sheet date.
Unrealised gains and losses arising on the revaluation of investments are credited or
charged to the SOFA and are allocated to the appropriate fund according to the
"ownership" of the underlying assets.
The Charity's interest in its subsidiary, Brentwood School Enterprises Ltd, is valued
at ENIL (2016: ENIL), as the Company is limited by guarantee, without a share capital.
1.8.
Stock
Stock represents goods for consumption or resale and is valued at the lower of cost
and net realisable value.
1.9.
Deposits from Parents
The Governors have reviewed the contract terms under which pupil fee deposits are
held by the school. Although under normal circumstances these will be repaid over
future years when the pupils complete their education at the School, pupils can leave
at earlier dates. As the School does not have an unconditional right to retain the
individual deposits for at least 12 months after the balance sheet date and, in line with
the requirements in FRS 102, the balance of the deposits held at 31 August 2017 have
been included within current liabilities. The prior year pupil fee deposits balance
has been similarly represented.

1.10. Fund accounting
The charitable trust funds of the School and its subsidiaries are accounted for as
unrestricted or restricted income or as endowment capital in accordance with the
terms of trust imposed by the donors or the Charity Commission.
Unrestricted General Funds are used in accordance with the School's charitable
objects at the discretion of the Governors. Where the Governors decide to set aside
any part of these funds to be used in future for some specific purpose, this is included
accounted for by transfer to the appropriate designated fund held within General
Reserves.
Income generated by the newly established Brentwood School Foundation for the
furtherance of the School's charitable objects, including the provision of bursaries
and the improvement of School facilities and equipment, is recognised as a
designated fund.
Funds were previously set aside by the Governors out of General Funds for the
purpose of repaying Accumulation Orders designated by the Charity Commission.
The Orders expired in November 2015 and the funds were transferred to General
Funds.
Restricted Funds comprise gifts, legacies and grants where there is a trust law
restriction to some specific purpose intended by the donor. Restricted funds are held
within BSGCT and the Bursary Fund.
Endowed Funds are retained for the permanent use of the School. The value of the
property deemed to represent a permanent endowment in accordance with
guidance from the Charity Commission, is retained within the SABST for the
beneficial interest of the Brentwood School CIO.
1.11. Pension Schemes
The Charity contributes to the Teachers' Pension Defined Benefits Scheme at rates
set by the Scheme Actuary and advised to the Governors by the Scheme
Administrator. The Scheme is a multi-employer pension scheme governed by the
Teachers' Pension Scheme Regulations 2014.
The Charity also contributes to individual personal pension schemes for support staff
after three months' service at a rate of 10% of annual basic pay where employees
make a contribution of 5%.
Contributions to both schemes are charged in the SOFA in the period in which the
salaries to which they relate are payable. The School has a stakeholder scheme
available to staff if they wish to participate, but the School does not make employer's
contributions to this scheme.

1.12. Operating leases
Rentals under operating leases are charged on a straight-line basis over the lease
term, even if the payments are not made on such a basis. Benefits received and
receivable as an incentive to sign an operating lease are similarly spread on a
straight-line basis over the lease term.
1.13. Financial instruments
Basic financial instruments are initially recognised at transaction value and
subsequently measured at amortised cost, with the exception of investments which
are held at fair value. Financial assets held at amortised cost comprise cash at bank
and in hand, together with trade and other debtors. A specific provision is made for
debts for which recoverability is in doubt. Cash at bank and in hand is defined as all
cash held in instant access and short notice bank accounts and used as working
capital. Financial liabilities held at amortised cost comprise all creditors except
social security and other taxes, deferred income and provisions.

24. PENSION SCHEMES
Retirement benefits to employees of the School are provided through a defined benefit
scheme and defined contribution schemes, which are funded by the School's and
employees' contributions.
Defined benefit scheme
The School participates in the Teachers' Pension Scheme ("the TPS") for its teaching staff.
The pension charge for the year includes contributions payable to the TPS of E1,307,847
(2016: 21,254,920) and at the year-end 2161,482 (2016 - E163,565) was accrued in
respect of contributions to this scheme.
The TPS is an unfunded multi-employer defined benefits pension scheme governed by
the Teachers' Pension Scheme Regulations 2014. Members contribute on a "pay as you
go" basis with contributions from members and the employer being credited to the
Exchequer. Retirement and other pension benefits are paid by public funds provided
by Parliament.
The employer contribution rate is set following scheme valuations undertaken by the
Government Actuary's Department. The latest actuarial valuation of the TPS was
prepared as at 31 March 2012 and the valuation report, which was published in June
2014, confirmed an employer contribution rate for the TPS of 16.4% from 1 September
2015. Employers are also required to pay a scheme administration levy of 0.08% giving
a total employer contribution rate of 16.48%.
This employer rate will be payable until the outcome of the next actuarial valuation,
which is due to be prepared as at 31 March 2016 and completed in 2018, with any
resulting changes to the employer rate expected to take effect from 1 April 2019. This
valuation will also determine the opening balance of the cost cap fund and provide an
analysis of the cost cap as required by the Public Service Pensions Act 2013.
Defined contribution schemes
The Charity also contributes to individual personal pension schemes for support staff at
a rate of 10% of annual basic pay where employees make a contribution of 5%.
Contributions to these schemes are charged in the SOFA in the period in which the
salaries to which they relate are payable.
25. SUBSIDIARY COMPANY

a company limited by guarantee (Registration number 02019002) which has principal
activities of running sports facilities and a school shop, as all members of that company
are Governors of the School and Trustees of Brentwood School CIO.

Year ended 31 August 2018
Introduction by the President of Council
It has been, as ever, a busy year at College. Our head teacher Alex Peterken departed to take up his
new position at Charterhouse, and Deputy Head Crispin Dawson grasped the mantle as acting head
continuing to take College forward until the arrival of Nicola Huggett, from Blundell's in Devon, as
new head. The recruitment process for a replacement for Prep School head John Whybrow was
successfully undertaken, with Tom O'Sullivan due to arrive in September 2018 from Old Buckenham
Hall; and our new Bursar Phil Attwell arrived in April from University of Exeter, to allow John
Champion to adopt a new role as Secretary to Council. So firstly I may pay a huge debt of gratitude
to Dr Alex Peterken, John Whybrow, Crispin Dawson and John Champion for the contributions that
they have made (and, in the case of the latter two, will continue to make) to College life. And we
look forward to helping Nicky and Tom settle into their leadership roles from September 2018.
This year of change hasn't only been about people. In late 2016 two imposing Regency villas, No.'s
1 and 2 College Lawn, were marketed for sale and after due consideration, Council agreed that
College should seek to purchase them. The business case for our successful offer was predicated
upon the firm belief that, operated as a girls' boarding house, the properties will make a significant
contribution in respect of three key strategic aims - the further enhancement of academic
attainment, reinforcement of our commitment to co-education and the further underpinning of our
financial health.
I'm delighted to report that the initial phase of the new boarding house - 'College Lawn' welcomed
its first intake of girls at the start of September, and that the second phase of the development will
open in September 2018. The Council is convinced that College Lawn will make a substantial and
very positive contribution to Cheltenham College for many years to come.
Unsurprisingly, having more pupils in College places an increased demand upon certain operations
and Council made the decision during the year that it should bring forward plans to refurbish and
increase the capacity of the senior school catering facilities. This project has been a complex and
time-consuming piece of work - one that has required a significant financial investment and which
has presented a variety of difficult engineering and operationa challenges. Nevertheless I'm pleased
to report that the project is complete and our fantastic new dining facilities opened in February
2018, and our catering team, along with pupils and staff, look forward to many happy years of
dining. The refurbishment of the boathouse was also completed during the year, and our pupils
now have a fit for purpose facility in Tewkesbury from which to develop their skills and enjoyment
of this sport.
As part of the on-going commitment to the charitable foundation of Cheltenham College, we have
continued to develop our sector leading partnership work. Through our relationship with All Saints
Academy and St John's Primary School, our pupils and staff have both contributed and benefitted
from involvement with those from other schools. Academic, musical and sporting initiatives have
been at the centre of these partnerships, and we were delighted that our work was recognised by
Page 2
CHELTENHAM COLLEGE
CHELTENHAM

Year ended 31 August 2018
the Independent Schools Council in the report to the Department of Education on partnership
working in the independent schools sector.
The academic attainment of our pupils continues to impress. The attainment levels for our top 100
pupils at A Level would place us in the lofty heights of the leading independent schools, but Council
believes that academic league tables should not be our sole measure of success. Our co-curricular
and extra-curricular programmes are the envy of most schools and we will continue to ensure that
academic progress, alongside the development of the rounded individual, is our approach.
2017 -18 has been a year of change, a year of seized opportunities, and most of all, another year of
positive growth and success. Along with my Council colleagues we remain very proud indeed to be
involved with such a fine school.
William Straker-Nesbit

Annual Report of the Council
The Council is pleased to present its Annual Report for the year ended 31 August 2018 under the
Charities Act 2011.
Status and administrative information
Cheltenham College was founded in 1841 and is registered with the Charity Commission under
charity number 311720.
College operates two schools known as Cheltenham College and Cheltenham College Preparatory
School.
There is one Governing Body for the two Schools called the Council. Details of the membership of
College Council, its executive officers and professional advisors are given on pages 4 and 5.
Structure, governance and management
Governing Documents
The Charity is incorporated and governed by the Cheltenham College Act 1894 and the Charities
(Cheltenham College) Orders 1976 and 2011.
Council
The governance of College is vested in the President and Council, as laid down in the governing
documents. Membership of Council is as follows: -
The President and Deputy President, elected by Council;
Not fewer than ten and not more than eighteen co-opted members appointed by Council;
Seven members nominated, from time to time, by the Universities of Oxford, Cambridge and
such Higher Education institution as the Council of Cheltenham College, the Cheltonian
Association, the Cheltonian Society, the teaching staff of Cheltenham College and the
teaching staff of Cheltenham College Preparatory School.
Appointment and induction of Council Members
On the occurrence of a vacancy amongst the nominated members of the Council (other than the
member nominated by the Cheltonian Society) the President shall be responsible, on behalf of the
Council, for notifying and entering negotiations with the nominating authority.
The elections of the members of the Council to be nominated by the teaching staff of either College
or the Preparatory School are conducted by the Headmaster or by a member or members of the
teaching staff delegated by him, who shall report the methods by which the elections were
conducted and their results to the Council.
Co-opted members of Council are identified and nominated by the Nominations Committee and
elected by Council.
All new members of Council receive a comprehensive briefing pack and induction workshop from
the Bursar and Secretary to Council on trusteeship, the workings of College, its policies and
objectives. Newly appointed, as well as established Council members, are encouraged to attend
Page 6
CHELTENHAM COLLEGE
CHELTENHAM
Council's Report and Financial Statements
COLLEGE
Year ended 31 August 2018
training courses, conferences, regulatory updates and other appropriate externally organised
events in order to continually develop the knowledge and expertise of the governing body.
Organisational Management
By virtue of The Cheltenham College Act 1894, the Council is responsible for "the entire
management of the concerns and property of College" and "may receive, invest, lay out and dispose
of all the stocks, effects, funds, money and securities for the benefit of College". It meets not less
than three times each year. Both the President and Deputy President are ex-officio members of the
principal sub-committees but are not required to chair them.
The Finance, Risk & Development Committee (FRD) is chaired by Mr Tim Smith and meets not less
than five times a year. This committee sets financial targets for approval by the full Council and
monitors results against such targets. The Committee is also responsible for overseeing risk
management, compliance with statutory legislation and facilities development. College executive
team is responsible for managing the business within the financial parameters and general policy
laid down by Council on the recommendations of the FRD.
The Audit Committee is chaired by Mr Chris Cooper and meets at least annually to review the annual
accounts and receive the independent auditor's report.
The Education Committee meets termly and is now chaired by Revd Canon Wilkinson, following the
retirement of Dr Bob Acheson, and is a consultative forum in which issues of educational policy,
provision and performance are discussed. Executive authority lies with the Council, which may,
however, through the President, delegate such authority to the Committee.
The Nominations Committee meets once per term and is chaired by Mr Mike Wynne. Its principal
duties include the review of the composition of the Council in terms of its numbers, skills and
experience as well as succession planning for retiring members.
The Welfare & Safeguarding Committee meets three times a year and is chaired by Mrs Ruth Lewis,
following the retirement of Dr Geraldine Valori. Its principal duties include the review of policies
relating to Child Protection and Safeguarding to ensure compliance with regulatory requirements in
College and Prep, and the monitoring of pupil and staff welfare matters.
Matters relating to strategic planning sit primarily with the Council, which considers proposals for
the development of the School and advises senior management of the strengths and weaknesses of
strategic options. The Council may establish ad hoc committees to undertake more detailed
planning and appraisal of development proposals.
The day-to-day running of the schools is delegated to the respective Heads and Bursar. They are
also supported by Cheltenham Executive Committee (CEC) (the key management for the purposes
of these financial statements) and a number of other senior management teams spanning the
academic, pastora and operational areas of the two schools.
Remuneration
Remuneration of the key management personnel is set by the Council, with the policy objective of
providing appropriate incentives to encourage enhanced performance and of rewarding fairly and
responsibly individual contributions to College's success.
Page 7
CHELTENHAM COLLEGE
CHELTENHAM
Council's Report and Financial Statements
COLLEGE
Year ended 31 August 2018
It is essential for College to engage credible professionals to bring sector expertise, significant
leadership experience and strong capability to drive inspirational teaching and learning excellence,
strong academic results, high quality pastora care, a strong and vibrant community of pupils and
staff, excellent facilities and sound finances. In the light of this strategy, College's pay policy seeks
to:
pay the median to upper quartile range for similar organisations in the UK Independent
Schools sector market but not to compete on salaries with the public or private sectors;
ensure performance is reviewed and reported to the appropriate Committee on an annual
basis;
apply performance related pay elements only where required by the relevant market sector;
and
monitor Independent School sector salary trends through ISBA and through participation in
surveys such as those for Baines Cutler and Haysmacintyre as required.
The appropriateness and relevance of the remuneration policy is reviewed annually, including
reference to comparisons with other independent schools to ensure that College remains sensitive
to the broader issues of pay and employment conditions elsewhere.
College aims to recruit, subject to experience, at the lower to medium point within a band, providing
scope for rewarding excellence. Delivery of College's charitable vision and purpose is primarily
dependent on our key management personnel (with the CEC being the most senior operations
committee) and staff costs are the largest single element of our charitable expenditure.
Employment policy
College is an equal opportunities employer. Full and fair consideration is given to job applications
from disabled persons and due consideration is given to their training and employment needs.
Consultation with employees, or their representatives, has continued at all levels with the aim of
taking the views of employees into account when decisions are made that are likely to affect their
interests. Employees are made aware of the financial and economic performance of College.
Communication with employees continues through normal management channels in a variety of
forms and also through exceptional channels to apprise staff of current issues.
Group structure and relationships

Principal risks and uncertainties
The Council considers the economic turbulence of recent years and the affordability of fees by
parents across the independent sector to be the principal risks faced by College. College is currently
full and expects to expand in the future alongside investments in College Lawn, but the Council
remains acutely aware of the importance of affordability of fees. For September 2018, the Council
has again limited fee changes to a 3.0% increase which we believe to be relatively low compared
with College's peer group. The provision of bursaries remains a key plank in College's strategy to
make fees affordable.
College continues to review the political risks that attach to the independent schools sector. These
include maintenance of charitable status, possible VAT on fees and rates relief on principal buildings.
Health and safety, and pupil safeguarding are always a significant area for risk management and
reflect the immense responsibilities College takes in regard to both pupils and staff. A robust set of
policies is constantly updated and supported by a number of well-established committees which
include the senior officers of College. Recruitment of staff is the first step in inculcating College's
policies in regard to these risks. Further communication of those policies to staff and pupils, and
the monitoring of compliance is a vital part of the ongoing risk management plan.

College is a Public Benefit Entity registered as a charity on 10 June 1965 in England and Wales (number
311722). Its principal office is Bath Road, Cheltenham GL53 7LD.
1. Principal Accounting Policies
The financial statements have been prepared in accordance with the Financial Reporting Standard
applicable in the UK and Republic of Ireland (FRS 102), the Charities Act 2011 and the Statement of
Recommended Practice (the Charities SORP (FRS 102)) ))applicable to charities preparing their accounts
in
accordance with the Financial Reporting Standard applicable in the UK and Republic of Ireland (FRS 102 -
effective 1 January 2017.
The financial statements have been prepared to give a 'true and fair' view and have departed from the
Charities (Accounts and Reports) Regulations 2008 only to the extent required to provide a 'true and fair
view'. This departure has involved following Accounting and Reporting for Charities that prepare their
accounts in accordance with the Financial Reporting Standard applicable in the UK and Republic of Ireland
(FRS 102) issued on 16 July 2015 rather than the Accounting and Reporting by Charities: Statement of
Recommended Practice effective from 1 April 2005 which has since been withdrawn.
(a) Basis of Consolidation
The consolidated Statement of Financial Activities and Balance Sheet include the financial statements of
Cheltenham College and its wholly owned trading subsidiary, Cheltenham College Services Limited.
Cheltenham College Charitable Trust is an independently run charity. The charity is consolidated into
College in order to comply with FRS 102 Section 9. Cheltenham College International Limited was
incorporated during the year; it has yet to commence trading and as such has not been included in the
consolidated financial statements.
College has taken advantage of the exemption available to a qualifying entity in FRS 102 from the
requirement to present a charity only Cash Flow Statement within the consolidated financial
statements.
(b) Going Concern
Having reviewed the funding facilities available to the Group together with the expected ongoing demand
for places and the Group's future projected cash flows, the Council have a reasonable expectation that the
Group has adequate resources to continue its activities for the foreseeable future and consider that there
were no material uncertainties over the Group's financial viability. Accordingly, they also continue to adopt
the going concern basis in preparing the financial statements as outlined in the Statement of Trustees'
Responsibilities on page 18.
(c) Fees Receivable
Fees receivable consists of charges billed for fees, board and tuition for the School year ended 31 August,
less bursaries and allowances. Fees received for education to be provided in future years are carried
forward as deferred income.
(d) Trading Activities
Trading income comprises the trading activities of College and the subsidiaries and is credited to the
Statement of Financial Activities on a receivables basis.

(e) Donations, Grants and Legacies
Donations, grants and legacies are recognised in the financial statements when the Group has entitlement
to the funds, any performance conditions attached to the items of income have been met, it is probable
that the income will be received and the amount can be measured reliably.
(f) Expenditure
Expenditure is included in the Statement of Financial Activities on an accruals basis. Overhead and other
costs not directly attributable to particular functional activity categories are apportioned over the relevant
categories on the basis of management estimates of the amount attributable to that activity in the year,
either by reference to staff time or space occupied, as appropriate. The irrecoverable element of VAT is
included with the item of expense to which it relates. Costs of generating funds includes al staffing and
fundraising costs. Charitable activity expenses are allocated to functional groups on a direct cost basis or
apportioned on a staff time basis.
Governance costs are included in charitable expenditure and comprise the costs of running College
including strategic planning for its future development, also external audit, any legal advice for the Council,
and all the costs of complying with constitutional and statutory requirements, such as the costs of Council
meetings and of preparing statutory financial statements and satisfying public accountability.
(g) Pension Scheme Arrangements
College is involved with a number of pension schemes for its employees.
Cheltenham College contributes to the Teachers' Pension Defined Benefits Scheme at rates set by the
Scheme Actuary and advised to College by the Scheme Administrator. The Scheme is a multi-employer
pension scheme and it is not possible to identify the assets and liabilities of the Scheme, which are
attributable to College. In accordance with FRS 102 Section 28.11 the Scheme is accounted for as a defined
contribution scheme and contributions are accounted for when advised as due by the Scheme
Administrator.
Other staff have the option of joining a defined contribution scheme operated by an insurance company.
College and members of staff pay fixed percentages of salaries to the insurance company. College's
contributions are charged in the Statement of Financial Activities as they fall due.
(h) Fund Accounting
Details and the nature and purpose of each fund is set out in Investment policy and objectives on page 9
of the Annual Report of the Council. Funds held for the general purpose of College are held as unrestricted
funds. Those held by College for specific purposes outside normal operations such as College lottery,
bequests and the Tinson Hardship Fund are held as designated funds and set aside by the Trustees. Those
subject to specific wishes of the donors are included within the relevant restricted or endowed funds.
