(i) Tangible Fixed Assets
The cost of tangible fixed assets is their purchase cost, together with any incidental costs of acquisition
and is subject to a de-minimis limit of f1,000. Freehold land and buildings include original cost and
subsequent alterations and additions. The cost of land and buildings includes interest paid on specific
related borrowings during the construction period.
As detailed in note 12, the value of College's land was revalued in accordance with transition arrangements
permitted under FRS 102, and is now deemed cost of the land.
(j) Depreciation
Depreciation is calculated on a straight-line basis to write off the cost, less estimated residual value, of
fixed assets over their estimated useful lives as follows: -
Freehold buildings
1% - 20% on cost
Furniture & equipment
4% - 33% on cost, based on life expectancy
- Boilers
10% on cost
-
Computers & electronic equipment
10% - 50% on cost
Cars
25% on cost
Other motor vehicles
10% - 50% on cost
Depreciation commences in the year of acquisition or when the asset is brought into use and as a result
assets under construction are not depreciated. College's buildings have to be maintained in good working
order, with many having listed building status. Most of these buildings are therefore considered to have
an expected useful life in excess of one hundred years. In accordance with FRS 102 Section 27.7 the
buildings are tested for impairment annually, because their expected useful life exceeds 50 years. College,
in determining the value of the buildings, has based its consideration on the service potential of the assets
to further their charitable objectives. Depreciation on those buildings not already being depreciated
commenced in September 2000 at a rate of not less than 1% based on their life expectancy. Land is not
depreciated.
(k) Investments
Investment in subsidiaries are stated at cost.
Listed investments are reported at their fair values at the balance sheet date based on their quoted market
prices. Gains and losses arising on investment assets are disclosed separately in the Statement of Financial
Activities which includes realised gains or losses where the investments have been sold and unrealised
where they are still held at the balance sheet date. In both cases the gain or loss is calculated with regard
to the market value at the beginning of the year, or its cost if purchased during the year.

(I) Stock
Stock is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value, after making due allowance for obsolete and
slow moving items. Cost is defined as the average cost of finished goods and raw materials including
transport and handling costs. Net realisable value is based on estimated selling price less further costs
expected to be incurred prior to disposal.
(m) Debtors
Short term debtors are measured at transaction price, less impairment. Details of these financial assets
are set in note 15.
(n) Cash and Cash Equivalents
Cash is represented by cash in hand and deposits with financial institutions.
(o) Creditors
Short term creditors are initially measured at the transaction price. Details of these financial liabilities are
set in notes 16, 17 and 18 below.
(p) Financial Instruments
Basic financial instruments are initially recognised at transaction value and subsequently measured at their
settlement value with the exception of investments and the complex fees in advance scheme, which are
held at fair value.
Financial assets measured at their settlement value comprise cash, trade and fee debtors, group and other
debtors and accrued income. See note 15 for further details.
Financial liabilities measured at their settlement value comprise deposits, trade creditors, bank loans and
overdrafts, group and other creditors, and accruals. See notes 16, 17 and 20 for further details.
College offered an inflation free fees in advance scheme as described in note 19.
The liability recognised in respect of this scheme is considered to be a non-basic financial instrument and
has therefore been classified as a financial liability measured at fair value through profit or loss.
(q) Recognition of Liabilities
Liabilities are recognised once there is a legal or constructive obligation that commits College to the
obligation.
(r) Fees in Advance
Under the current FIA scheme, which was introduced in July 2015, a fee payer may enter into a contract
to pay College in advance for fixed contributions towards the tuition fees for a period agreed with College.
These contributions give rise to a fixed discount on future fees
The discount arising on the contributions is charged to the Statement of Financial Activities on a year by
year basis.
In the event of a parent withdrawing their capital sum from the old FIA scheme, interest arises on the un-
drawn balance at 1% below the bank base rate. Any such interest is disclosed as a potential liability under
the scheme.

(s) Deferred Taxation
Deferred tax is recognised in respect of all timing differences between the treatment of certain items for
taxation and accounting purposes which have arisen but not reversed at the balance sheet date. Full
provision is made without discounting for all deferred tax liabilities. Deferred tax assets are recognised to
the extent that it is more likely than not that they will be recovered against taxable profits.
(t) Redundancy
Redundancy and termination costs only occur where absolutely necessary and are accounted for on an
accruals basis when the commitment to terminate a post of the grounds of redundancy has been made.
(u) Judgements in applying Accounting Policies and Key Sources of Estimation Uncertainty
Estimates and judgments are continually evaluated and are based on historical experience and other
factors, including expectations of future events that are believed to be reasonable under the
circumstances.
The items in the financial statements where these estimates and judgments have been made include the
following:
(i) Useful economic lives of tangible assets
The annual depreciation charge for the tangible assets is sensitive to changes in the estimated useful
economic lives and residual values of the assets. The useful economic lives and residual values are re-
assessed annually. They are amended when necessary to reflect current estimates, based on technological
advancement, future investments, economic utilisation and the physical condition of the assets. See note
12 for the carrying amount of the fixed assets and note 1(j) for the useful lives for each class of assets.
(ii) Impairment of debtors
The group makes an estimate of the recoverable value of trade and other debtors. When assessing
impairment of trade and other debtors, management considers factors including the current credit rating
of the debtor, the ageing profile of debtors and historical experience. See note 15 for the net carrying
amount of the debtors.
(iii) Fees in advance Scheme
As set out in notes 18 and 19 the liabilities of one of the extant Fees in Advance Schemes was closed for
new business in May 2015.

The fair value of the Closed FIA Scheme liability reflects the present value of the future expected fee
income, where the discount rate used represents the financial effect of the expected fee increases forgone
spread over the term of the arrangement. This fair value has been estimated by allocating the estimated
expected future fee increases over the arrangement term on a straight line basis. These estimated
expected future fee increases are reviewed and revised where appropriate on an annual basis. At the year-
end the annualised expected future fee increase over the next five years is calculated on an average
rate

with that which would be generated by a more detailed fair value calculation.

no accrued interest will be payable, calculated on the basis of a discount to prevailing bank base rate, over

22. Pensions
The School participates in the Teachers' Pension Scheme ("the TPS") for its teaching staff. The pension
charge for the year includes contributions payable to the TPS of f1,140,000 (2017: f1,114,000) and at the
year-end fNil (2017 - fNil) was accrued in respect of contributions to this scheme.
The TPS is an unfunded multi-employer defined benefits pension scheme governed by the Teachers'
Pension Scheme Regulations 2014. Members contribute on a "pay as you go" basis with contributions
from members and the employer being credited to the Exchequer. Retirement and other pension benefits
are paid by public funds provided by Parliament.
The employer contribution rate is set following scheme valuations undertaken by the Government
Actuary's Department. The latest actuarial valuation of the TPS was prepared as at 31 March 2012 and
the valuation report, which was published in June 2014, confirmed an employer contribution rate for the
TPS of 16.4% from 1 September 2015. Employers are also required to pay a scheme administration levy of
0.08% giving a total employer contribution rate of 16.48%.

London Transport Museum Annual Report 2017/18
London Transport Museum
We use the story of transport to encourage, enrich and inspire all Londoners and those who
love this city to get the most out of London.
No other city has been defined and shaped by transport the way London has - but the true
impact can be invisible to the people who use our Tube, bus, rail and road services every
day.
The Museum and its collections bring together the past, present and future to show just how
much transport has influenced our modern city, economy and culture. Transport keeps
London moving, working and growing and continues to make life in the Capital better.

MESSAGE FROM THE CHAIR OF TRUSTEES AND MANAGING DIRECTOR
We are delighted to present the Annual Report and Accounts for London Transport Museum
(LTM) for 2017/18, an important year for us as we embark upon an ambitious five-year plan
(the Plan)
It was a busy year across the Museum: we welcomed nearly 400,000 visitors at Covent
Garden and Acton; our Safety and Citizenship team reached 89,000 of London's Year 6
pupils; around 2,900 under-fives participated in our programmes; 3,000 under-15s were
introduced to STEM (science, technology, engineering and maths) careers; our Youth Travel
Ambassadors scheme influenced travel choices at 134 London secondary schools; we
created the new ShapingLDN late debate programme; and we opened a fantastic new
exhibition, Poster Giris, featuring a stunning collection of transport posters by female artists
from 1910 to the present day. Marking the centenary of votes for women, Poster Girls rolled
out the red carpet for a remarkable range of poster work and is bringing many lesser known
female artists into the limelight.
For the Year of Engineering 2018, we launched an exciting programme of events, opened
new exhibitions and completely overhauled our tunnelling gallery which is now known as
'Digging Deeper'. This gallery tells the story of London's deep underground tube network,
from Brunel's Thames Tunnel to Crossrail, which is due to open as the Elizabeth line when
construction work is completed.
An enhanced Collections Online website was launched in May 2017, opening a superb new
digital route to over 60 per cent of our collections and their associated histories. Of the 2,700
additions to the collection this year, the highlight came at the completion of the Leyland
buses appeal with the arrival of a third vehicle, the X2, dating from 1908. The X2 is the
oldest working London double deck bus in the UK and will join the charabanc and the
Chocolate Express to help us tell the story of London's early buses. We waited a long time to
acquire such high-quality vintage Leyland buses and then three came along together!
Hidden London is now well established as a tour programme for disused stations and other
intriguing locations rarely accessed by the public. Some 17,000 tickets were sold during the
year for sites including Down Street, Clapham South Deep Level Shelter and Highgate. We
have exciting plans to expand and grow the programme in the coming years.
To support our work, we achieved financial targets for the first year of the Plan, despite
economic uncertainty and a series of terrible terrorist attacks in central London. It is a
testament to the people of London and the tourists who choose to come to this great city that
our visitor numbers actually increased this year. We will build on this success and pursue
financial resilience by using the charity's key assets - our collections, our people and our
networks to generate income and become more plurally funded. To this end we were very
pleased to secure four-year support worth f1m from Arts Council England as one of their
new National Portfolio Organisations. As ever, our partnership with Transport for London
(TfL) is the bedrock on which our busy and creative museum is built, and we thank all our
friends and colleagues in the TfL group for their support.
We must also thank all the visitors, shoppers, corporate members, sponsors and funders
who gave us their time, their support and their money this year - it is very much appreciated.
The challenge and advice of our Trustee and Enterprise boards, our energetic and talented
staff group and over two hundred volunteers enable LTM to be agile and successful, and on
the Museum's behalf we thank them all for their commitment and inspiration.
Keith Ludeman, Chair of Trustees,
Sam Mullins, Managing Director
London Transport Museum Annual Report 2017/18
Page 4
OUR FIVE-YEAR PLAN 2018-2023
During 2017/18 we began the first year of our new Plan, which sets out how we will remain a
strong, sustainable and engaging charity.
The key objective underpinning the five-year plan is to secure financial sustainability from
2020/21 through investing in our financial resilience, working with our people and partners,
and delivering our charitable purposes. The Plan realises our charitable purpose through
four key strategic areas of activity. It sets out how we will:
1. Be the world's leading museum of urban transport by:
a. Attracting at least 400k visitors each year from audiences reflective of London
b. Undertaking a rolling refurbishment programme of the Covent Garden
galleries
C.
Creating excellent special exhibitions and world class experiences such as
the Hidden London tours
d. Raising customer satisfaction to at least 90 per cent
e. Seeking opportunities to distribute our work across London
2. Share knowledge and provoke conversations about transport and the future of
London through:
a. The ShapingLDN debate series for public audiences
b. The Interchange thought leadership programme for business
C. The provision of research facilities that allow our audiences to explore London
and its transport
3. Stimulate curiosity in our city by:
a.
Promoting science, technology, engineering and maths (STEM) careers
through the Enjoyment to Employment programme
b. Outreach to under-11s through the Safety and Citizenship scheme
C. Delivering the Q stock train and other major restoration programmes
4. Conserve and share our collections by:
a. Increasing visits to the Museum Depot at Acton
b. Caring for 80 vehicles and over 450,000 items in our Designated Collection
C. Increasing online access and usage
To drive the Plan we are investing in our workforce and volunteers, and developing
beneficial relationships with a range of partners. We also have ambitious commercial and
financial targets to build financial sustainability.
A summary of our objectives, taken from the Plan, is given below. To see the full five-year
plan, visit our website: htesillwwiltmuseumcouklaboul.usi16:governance

THE YEAR IN SUMMARY
Each year we set targets for visitor numbers and other key measures that indicate how we
are meeting our charitable objectives.
With nearly 400,000 people visiting the Museum at Covent Garden and our Acton Depot in
west London, 2017/18 was our second-best year ever for visitor numbers. Many central
London cultural attractions reported footfall down this year, so LTM's performance is even
more remarkable as we ended two per cent above last year's result.
The Acton Depot Open Weekend in April 2017 attracted nearly 8,000 visitors, the highest
attendance since the Depot open days began in 1999. The Hidden London programme
provided behind-the-scenes tours for 17,000 people, and our heritage bus fleet, led by the
Battle Bus B2737, operated for 318 hours, being seen by thousands of people at various
events across the country. We were pleased to be able to re-introduce steam train runs this
year, and the Met No. steam locomotive covered 152 miles of operations across the
Underground network. It also operated as a guest vehicle at other heritage railways.
Once again we delivered an exciting programme of activities for our varied audiences,
including Family Fun during school holidays, the innovative ShapingLDN debate series, plus
talks, events and the popular Friday Lates for adult visitors. Poster Girls was the major

POSTER GIRLS: A CENTURY OF ART AND DESIGN
Our exhibition programme is at the heart of our charitable activity, providing access to our
collections, inspiring our learning activities and acting as a catalyst for conservation and new
acquisitions. The headline exhibition for 2017/18, Poster Girls: a century of art and design,
celebrates outstanding poster art created by women designers, illustrators and fine artists for
London's transport over the last hundred years
Early in the twentieth century, poster design became a new form of art. The bright,
innovative medium of pictorial posters, aided by advances in colour printing, quickly became
a primary marketing medium for theatres, shops, tourist destinations and public bodies.
Transport companies saw the potential too, notably the Underground Group. Of the many
posters commissioned for London's transport network, at least 170 are known to have been
by female designers Many more women are likely to have designed transport posters but
their identities are hidden behind initials, or the work has been credited to an advertising
agency. With its deliberately ironic title, the Poster Girls exhibition aims to give these
forgotten design heroines the recognition they deserve. Appropriately in 2018, the centenary
year of votes for women, the exhibition also provided an opportunity to reflect on the
changing social, economic and political conditions that affected women's lives and work over
the last century.
With over 130 posters on display, Poster Girls features well-known designers, such as Mabe
Lucie Attwell, Ruth Hydes, Enid Marx and Zandra Rhodes, alongside lesser known women
such as Freda Lingstrom and Dora Batty. The showcased designers helped change the way
Londoners view the Capita by using a dazzling spectrum of artistic styles and mediums in
their posters: modernist, figurative, flat colour, boldly patterned, abstract, collage and oil.
The exhibition moves from 1910 through to contemporary times, showing how each era
influenced the artists' stylistic approach. Alongside the posters, additional exhibits including
ceramics, textiles, books, film and photographs, help enrich the story. Throughout the
exhibition, the role played by London's transport companies in commissioning female talent
is highlighted.
When Frank Pick took charge of Underground publicity in 1908 there were few poster artists
working in Britain, and almost all were men. In the male-dominated advertising industry,
opportunities for women were mainly limited to book and magazine illustration. From the
start, Pick took a progressive view to commissioning, irrespective of gender, and over the
decade a new group of women poster artists emerged. The Poster Girls exhibition contains
the first known poster by a woman to appear on the transport network - Kew Gardens by
Tram, by Ella Coates in 1910.
During the 1920s and 1930s many more women artists designed posters for the
Underground. Social and politica freedoms were gained after the First World War, and there
was easier access to art education. For women, this meant that becoming a designer was a
viable career option for the first time, although male designers were still paid more and
achieved greater fame than their female colleagues. The Underground played a key role in
championing outstanding design and employed more women artists than rival companies.
The bright and humorous 1925 poster, Summer Sales Quickly Reached by Underground by
Mary Koop, which features in our publicity for the exhibition, perfectly captures the upbeat
mood of the times.
During the Second World War, publicity for leisure was replaced by public information
posters. Far fewer women worked as poster artists in Britain during the 1940s, despite a
London Transport Museum Annual Report 2017/18
Page 9
shortage of wartime designers. After the war, London Transport began to commission
women once more, employing both established female artists like Laura Knight, as well as
emerging talent, including Betty Swanwick and Sheila Robinson. But the number of women
poster designers in the 1950s remained low.
In the 1960s, London Transport publicity followed the contemporary trend for illustrative
posters, rather than the innovative bold designs of earlier periods. Most of the female artists
commissioned at this time were illustrators and teachers who designed posters as one part
of a wider creative output. As competition from television and magazine advertising
increased, the overall number of new commissions declined dramatically from about 100 a
year in the 1930s to less than 20. By the 1970s many of the Underground's posters were
produced anonymously by advertising agencies.
By the 1980s, advertising revenue was in decline, so London Transport began a fine art
poster programme to fill unsold commercial advertising spaces. It represented a revival of
the Underground's earlier tradition for high quality original commissions. Art on the
Underground posters were commissioned directly from artists, with posters printed in large
numbers for extended display across the network. As the economic situation improved in the
1990s, London Transport also produced more traditional, commercial, posters with a direct
'go places - do things' message known as the 'Simply' series. Women designers played a
renewed and prominent role in both campaigns.
Since the formation of Transport for London in 2000, the organisation has continued to
commission posters from individua artists, with women producing some of the most striking
designs. While some of these promote Art on the Underground projects, others carry on the
tradition of enticing passengers to travel off-peak to the countryside or into town for
entertainment and leisure. With their strong graphics and bright colours, these posters are
the direct descendants of those early, innovative, commissions.
Poster Girls runs until January 2019 and is accompanied by a programme of talks and
events. For more details about all aspects of the Museum's programme, including Poster
Girls, see our website: https:l/www.ltmuseum.co.uklwhats-on
To accompany the Poster Girls exhibition, a special publication has been created which
includes additional posters and essays, and is available from the Museum shop or online.

ACCESS AND MUSEUM OPERATIONS
We want our collections, exhibitions and events to be enjoyed by as many people as
possible. Access is provided daily at the Museum in Covent Garden, through tours and open
days at the Museum Depot in Acton, and via the Museum website. Our heritage vehicle
outings, Hidden London tours and a rich programme of special events also help us inspire
audiences with the story of London's journey.
With many central London museums experiencing a reduction in patronage, we were very
pleased to see our visitor numbers grow by nearly two per cent this year. In total, admissions
to Covent Garden and Acton were almost 400,000 making 2017/18 our second most popular
year since the Museum opened in 1980. We also received the highest ever customer
satisfaction index score of 89, and were once again accredited under Visit England's Visitor
Attraction Quality Assurance Scheme (VAQAS). Customer service was a focus throughout
the year with frontline staff attending customer service workshops to raise awareness,
improve skills and maintain our high standards.
After the Designology exhibition closed in April 2017, the Exterion Gallery hosted two more
exhibitions this year. The Prize for Illustration competition entries were as varied and
interesting as ever with some excellent designs inspired by the Sounds of the City theme.
This was followed by Poster Girls: a century of art and design which shone a spotlight on
20th and 21st century female graphic designers. The exhibition which runs until January
2019, features over 130 posters and original artworks, and has been the touchstone for a
public programme that includes Friday Lates and lectures exploring the historical and social
context of the times in which these key designers were producing their work.
Also at Covent Garden this year, we began a five-year plan to update and refresh sections of
our permanent exhibition displays. This involved a comprehensive redevelopment of our
tunnelling gallery. The project benefitted from a Biffa Award grant and was successfully
completed in March 2018 when the new gallery, Digging Deeper, opened to the public. While
the project was underway, the gallery was enclosed by a smart hoarding which included
peep holes SO that visitors could see the work that was going in. This helped us to maintain a
positive message during the closure of the space, and created a sense of anticipation about
the new story that would be unveiled. The new gallery tells the story of tunnelling from
Brunel's Thames Tunnel in 1843 through to the Elizabeth line, combining objects and audio-
visual elements in an immersive and innovative way.
A temporary exhibition, The Secret Life of a Megaproject, also opened this year, uncovering
some lesser-known stories about the Crossrail project, one of the largest civil engineering
undertakings in Europe. The project will culminate in the opening of the Elizabeth line. On a
different note - but no less important for our visitors - we also refurbished the Museum's
customer toilets and updated our Lower Deck cafe, introducing a new menu and a popular
ice cream bar.
At the Museum Depot, we held two major Open Weekends as well as monthly tours. The
April 2017 weekend entitled Secrets of the Underground was our most successful ever, with
nearly 8,000 visitors. As part of the programme of activities, experts were on hand to tell the
stories of hidden underground spaces such as the former Post Office railway Mail Rail and
the Kingsway tram subway. There was also the usual mix of Family Fun, engineering
demonstrations and tours of the collection. In September 2017, the theme was London
Uncovered, celebrating great design with a focus on the special details and distinctive
moquette textiles that make the London transport system unique.
Other public programming in 2017/18 included a huge range of family activities, evening
talks, after-hours adult-orientated craft activities, and the popular Friday Lates. The Late

Debate strand plays an important part in our aim to make the Museum an organisation that
shares knowledge and provokes conversations about transport issues and the future of

EDUCATION AND ENGAGEMENT
We want to inspire everyone to engage with the past, present and future of London's
transport. At the Museum and Depot, and through outreach across London, we offer learning
opportunities, skills development and engaging programming to our visitors, schools, young
people, volunteers and many other communities.
With security fears in the early part of 2017/18 making parents and teachers initially wary of
bringing school groups into central London, bookings for education visits fell to 19,900 this
year. In response, we trialled outreach sessions to schools as part of our flagship Enjoyment
to Employment programme, exploring the science and technology that TfL and its partners
use to keep London moving. These sessions are supported by Engineering Ambassadors -
colleagues from the transport industry who create enthusiasm for the importance of
engineering and offer inspiring role models to students.
In partnership with specialist theatre company Specifiq, we also developed a new activity
based away from central London at Acton Depot which will launch next year. Inspired by
immersive theatre and escape-room games, the interactive adventure 'Mind the Gap' offers
an imaginative way for school children to engage with the LTM collection.
Our community work includes the Battle Bus project which commemorates the contribution
of London buses and bus crew to the First World War. Exhibitions and activities, led by
volunteers and the Battle Bus Apprentice, were held in Camberwell and Tottenham. Using
comic books as an inspiration, school pupils created original artwork and stories, with two
volunteers gaining a Bronze Art Award. We also delivered a ten-week course with
homelessness charity St Mungo's exploring the LTM's moquette collection. The project
culminated in a celebratory event in December at which textile designers Wallace Sewell
unveiled a display of participants' work.
At school holidays and during Acton Open Weekends, visitors can participate in our family
activities programme. This year guests were invited to: build musical instruments using
everyday recycled household materials; make board-games; listen to story-telling; try
picture-making; join in singalongs and craft sessions, and indulge in some festive Christmas
fun. We also worked with nearby communities to raise awareness of LTM among families
with young children, and we were invited to deliver a workshop at the Leslie Palmer Carnival
Pioneers festival at the Westway Trust in Ladbroke Grove. To help bring under-represented
groups into the Museum, we have established a Community Bursary Programme and the
first recipients visited LTM during the summer.
Our education work depends on successful partnerships. The innovative skills-development
and employability programme, Route into Work, is a partnership with TfL and the transport
industry. This year we helped Cleshar recruit six track engineering apprentices and we also
ran a course supported by Dragados, Bombardier, telent and Arriva to help 13 young women
into the construction industry. We also ran a knowledge-sharing event with delegates from
across the cultural sector. In May 2017 we partnered with Central Careers Hub, Milkround
School Leavers and TfL to host a conference which welcomed over 180 careers advisors
and tutors responsible for over 40,000 students. The event provided industry updates,
professional networking opportunities, awareness of opportunities within TfL and information
regarding the education initiatives run by the Museum. An exciting addition to our
employability work was delivered in November 2017 when we held our first Skills Late event.
Over 100 young people aged 16-25, along with parents, teachers, carers and advisors had a
chance to meet up to eight employers at an evening designed to inspire young Londoners
into a career in transport or infrastructure.

respond to a reduction in funding this year. S&C delivers important messages via

In August we used our S&C resources to deliver Be Safe Week at the Museum. We were
joined by other organisations including the Metropolitan Police demonstrating fingerprinting,
and the RNLI delivering water safety messages. In support of a scheme run by the Police
Cycle Safety Team we invited people to sit in an HGV cabin to demonstrate the blind spots
of drivers and how these affect their ability to see cyclists. It was a busy week, with over
6,000 visitors to the Museum during the five days.
We partnered with the police to deliver Project Guardian which also utilises our expertise in
youth engagement activity. This important initiative educates young people to respond to and
report unwanted sexual attention on the transport network. Over 4,000 secondary school
pupils took part in workshops this year, with positive feedback from TfL, schools, participants
and the police.
The Youth Travel Ambassadors (YTA) Programme is aimed at secondary schools across
London, with a focus on peer-led, safe and sustainable travel campaigns Since inception,
the programme has delivered for over a third of London's 800 secondary schools and a new
three-year model of engagement was developed this year to enable the team to reach even
more schools in future. YTA campaigns link directly to the Mayor's Transport Strategy and

was Legacy, Leadership and Life skills, and the Mayor's new Walking and Cycling
Commissioner, Will Norman, was a special guest. Road Safety Week took place in the winter
term during which YTA students delivered assemblies to around 20,000 students in 30
boroughs across London. An independent evaluation report by Canterbury Christchurch
University this year highlighted key strengths of the YTA programme including 'impressive
levels of reach and engagement with schools' and 'outstanding practice in participatory
approaches to youth-led social action'. Over 300 students across more than 30 schools are
enrolled in the new accredited YTA Leadership award.
Our Young People's Skills programme is sector-leading, and we work with young
freelancers, young volunteers and apprentices to deliver learning and community projects
across the Museum. Our Arts Council funded work in this area now includes support and
advice to other organisations, and our Museum appeared as a case study in the Mendoza
Report published in November 2017. This independent review of Museums in England
highlights the way that we have used our apprenticeship programme to diversify and

HERITAGE AND COLLECTIONS
The Museum's collection of nearly half a million objects includes vehicles, posters signs,
uniforms and other items that represent London's unique transport heritage. We ensure
the
collection is properly conserved and cared for SO it can be used as an inspiring and
accessible resource for exhibitions, events and research.
Exploring a fascinating theme within our hugely rich poster and art collection, Poster Girls: a
century of art and design and the accompanying book placed long overdue focus on 20th
and 21st century female graphic designers (see section above). Our Poster Parade mini-
exhibition, At London's Service, also looked at the role of women in London's social history,
using archive posters to highlight the many roles women have undertaken for London
Transport. Other Poster Parade themes this year included The Flow of the River, Myths and
Fairy Tales, and Sounds of the City, the latter accompanying the 2017 Prize for Illustration
poster exhibition of the same name.
Our curatorial team developed the new Digging Deeper gallery which opened in March 2018.
It combines a rich vein of authentic objects with innovative audio-visua elements to create
an immersive experience exploring the construction of London's deep leve Tube system.
Other Year of Engineering exhibitions include The Secret Life of a Megaproject which looks
at the Elizabeth line as it nears operation, and an audio-visua presentation about Crossrail
2, the planned new line that would connect south west and north east London.
It was another busy year for heritage vehicle events. Highlights included Battle Bus helping
to mark the First World War centenary of Biggin Hill aerodrome and paying visits to excited
primary school children in Tottenham and Camberwell. The beautifully restored 1914
Leyland charabanc attended the annual ceremony at the Guildhall for cart-marking by the
Worshipfu Company of Carmen, as well as the 'On the Buses' rally at the Severn Valley
Railway. Several buses from the collection undertook public service runs on numbered bus
routes, including Routemaster RM2 on route 406 between Kingston and Epsom, and 1969-
built single decker MBA582 operating on the 500 and 507 routes out of Victoria. Metropolitan
Railway steam engine Met No. 1 made a welcome return to the Metropolitan line between
Amersham and Harrow-on-the-Hill in September 2017.
This range of events required extensive preparatory work which was undertaken alongside a
full programme of other vehicle restoration projects. This included Waterloo & City car 61,
whose paintwork is vastly improved, and the Q-stock Underground cars which have a
dedicated team of associated volunteers working on a three-year programme to return them
to operational use. Other collections-care work this year included assessing over 14,000
photographs, cleaning and rehousing over 5,000 items in our library's pamphlet collection,
an innovative remote-working volunteer project to support the indexing of library journals,
and the conservation of several stunning original poster artworks. The collection of ticket
machines and passimeters (ticket booths) has also been rearranged to allow a more
visually-appealing display for Acton Open Weekends in 2018.
In total, some 2,700 objects were added to the Museum collection this year, including the
1908 Leyland X2 double-decker bus, and an early enamel sign from Bank Underground
station dating from around 1908. The contemporary collecting programme also generated a
range of objects and digital content including photographs taken around the network on the
tram system, DLR and Emirates Air Line, and oral history interviews with staff working on the
Night-Tube and Woolwich Ferry.
The launch of the Collections Online site in May 2017 was the culmination of many years
activity to update and enhance our object records. This includes library records, which are
available online for the first time. Over 260,000 records are now accessible, including
posters, photographs and audio files. Work has continued since the launch, with 3,300

The Museum's charitable work depends on income generated by commercial activities
fundraising and marketing, and the generous donations of time and money made by
volunteers sponsors, LTM Friends and many other supporters.
London Transport Museum (Trading) Limited
The Museum's trading function operates retail, venue hire and other commercial activities to
provide funds for the Charity. In 2017/18, turnover was slightly lower than last year at f4.3m
(2016/17: f4.4m), but lower operating expenses meant that profit was higher at f1.0m
(2016/17: f0.8m). All profits were distributed to the Museum by way of Gift Aid.
Covent Garden shop
A strong performance saw sales increase by 9 per cent this year, aided by a more strategic
approach to buying and a focus on exclusive toys aimed at the Museum's family visitors. The
redevelopment of the shop over the last year also helped to grow sales by opening out the
retail space, making it brighter and much more flexible. A high-quality exhibition catalogue
was produced to support the Poster Girls exhibition, along with a beautiful collection of
associated gifts that have proved popular with shoppers.
The Museum's Hidden London programme also inspired a range of products. Designs were
created based on the beautiful, historic tiling patterns of disused stations. When applied to
ceramics, tea towels and giftware, these products were in high demand at Christmas and
became bestsellers both in store and online.
Online shop
Despite a small increase in turnover, the online shop did not perform as well as we would
have liked this year. This was partly due to the late launch of the online print-on-demand
poster service, which was affected by the change to a new web shop service provider in
2016/17. We restored full functionality in November 2017 and we now have over 4,000
posters available as high resolution images on the web, with links from the Online Museum
poster collection pages. Posters can be ordered in a wide variety of size and frame options,
and we saw print sales grow by 24 per cent this year, accounting for almost 20 per cent of
total online sales.
Other significant areas of growth for the online shop were books and design-led gifts
including many exclusive products commissioned by our in-house team.
Venue hire
With the Cubic Theatre out of action for some time for refurbishment, turnover was down by
eight per cent. Nevertheless, the Museum still hosted 270 events and welcomed more than
15,000 guests in 2017/18. A festive celebration for 500 US Embassy delegates was our
largest event, and we were also delighted to host Liverpool FC's annual fundraising dinner,
an exclusive event for EDF Energy, and T-Mobile's Breakthrough Awards. Stepping away
from traditional event formats, the Museum also played host to a hackathon and a themed
evening in conjunction with Record Store Day.
In December 2017, comedian and writer David Walliams delighted young visitors to our
Cubic Theatre with an in-character reading of his children's book Ratburger. The event was
booked by Sky, and we are optimistic that we will be able to attract similar business in future,
now that we can offer the upgraded technology installed in the Cubic Theatre.

INTERCHANGE
Our thought leadership programme, Interchange, is an exclusive benefit of the Corporate
Membership scheme. The programme brings together senior transport industry
professionals, leading academics, politicians and policy-makers to share cutting-edge ideas
about transport and urban planning.
The Interchange programme achieved a key milestone this year with the publication of its
first report, Rethinking Urban Mobility, which was produced as a collaboration between LTM,
programme sponsors Gowling WLG and Thales, and research partners Arup. The content of
the report was generated during four Interchange events in 2017 which included input from
60 individuals from over 40 transport-sector organisations. At a series of roundtable
discussions, our guests were asked to consider the challenges facing urban mobility by
addressing three crucial questions:
1) What role should cities play in shaping change?
In the first event of the series, discussion centred around five interlinked topics: cities,
regulation, user data, future wants/needs, and technology. We discussed the 'big trends'
which are disrupting the transport landscape including electrification, new business models
and new market entrants. We discussed how separation between public and private
transport will become less clear in an integrated service economy, and questioned whether
the evolution of mobility systems should be led by the market or by policy and regulation. As
new entrants such as Uber have shown, the relationship between innovation and regulation
is not always an easy one.
2) How will demand responsive transport impact urban systems?
Demand responsive transport (DRT) has the potential to disrupt established transport
systems and help tackle important problems. We asked how transport operators should
engage with ride-sharing and DRT services. Do they continue to manage 'point-to-point'
routes or be responsible for a user's whole journey from door-to-door? It was argued that the
hard constraints of Tube and bus capacity mean DRT may only affect a small percentage of
journeys and will simply improve existing mobility ecosystems, rather than create a new one.
3) Do the economic fundamentals of urban transport systems still add up?
Transformational change in mobility is likely to disrupt the economics of urban transport Can
investment meet the challenge of maintaining a commercially-viable mass transit system in a
future that includes DRT fleets and low-cost autonomous vehicles? Our attendees discussed
the changing competitive dynamic of private companies that can disrupt transport with low
cost assets such as bikes and third-party vehicles They also considered the potential for
technology to open-up new or under-served areas of the city without the need for mass
transit investment, which could in turn unlock private sector capital.
A workshop was also held to bring the threads together and help shape the final report.
Capturing the essence of the discussion sessions, Rethinking Urban Mobility dedicates a
section to each question, examines evidence and related trends, identifies key uncertainties
and importantly, outlines a vision of what 'good' looks like for the future. The report was
launched in February 2018 and was well received by both industry colleagues and the
media. We are grateful to the transport professionals, leaders and decision makers who
gave their time and expertise to the project, and in particular to our panellists at the events:
Richard Bruce (Department for Transport), Lilli Matson (TfL), James Nettleton (InMotion
Ventures), Dr Ron Oren (Transport Systems Catapult), Professor Tony Travers (LSE
London), Mike Waters (Transport for West Midlands), and Helena Zaum (Microsoft).
Download the full report here: ww.ltmuseum.co.uklurbanmobilityreport

Two other topics featured in our Interchange programme this year. At an event in May, Rob
Brighouse (Chair, East West Rail Review) and Dr Peter Hansford (Professor of Construction
and Infrastructure Policy at UCL) led a discussion around the possibility of private sector
finance for an Oxford to Cambridge railway line. This economic corridor is home to over
3,500,000 people and 175,000 businesses, but transport connections are poor and growth is
constrained. The discrete nature of a direct line offers an opportunity for the private sector to
design, build, finance, operate and maintain a railway which could be funded by both revenue
and capture of the increased business and residential land values.
In November 2017, a debate led by Jane Fielding (Head of Employment Law, Gowling WLG)

government to act quickly to confirm its post-Brexit immigration policy, but recognised that
STEM employers also need to be prepared to make their own investment in education and
training through schools, academies, apprenticeships and sponsorship, and through
engaging educators to help them understand the jobs and opportunities that are on offer.

FINANCIAL REVIEW
2017/18 was another year of substantial activity despite reductions in both income and
expenditure. With annual core funding reduced by E0.6r from 2016/17, we embarked on
a five-year plan to rebuild financial sustainability, funded by reserves. The Museum more
than achieved its target this year, making an operating deficit of 1.3m against a planned
E2 2m deficit, and delivered E0.8m of capital improvements against a planned E0.8m,
establishing a base for growth in future years. Largely because of the above, general
reserves grew by a net 3m against a planned draw on these funds of E0.5m.
The Museum ended the year with funds carried forward of E30.0m (2017: E31.2m) after
recording an operating deficit of f1.3m (2017: f0.3m). Some 75 per cent of the Museum's
total funds is made up of the f22.4m Capital Fund (2017: f23.3m) which represents the
book value of the Museum's fixed assets rather than liquid funds readily available for use.
E5.5m has been set aside in a series of designated reserves (see below) and the Museum
has f1.4m of general reserves.
TfL is the Museum's single largest supporter, providing both grant and project funding, and
offering essential services such as finance, payrol and HR at no charge to LTM. The TfL
revenue grant is going through a phased reduction from f6m in 2010/11 to f3m in
2019/20, and this year we received f3.8m (a reduction of E0.6m from 2016/17), plus TfL
Project Grant of f0.2m (2016/17: f0.8m) which was invested in a substantial upgrade of
the Cubic Theatre which will in turn enable greater venue hire income to be generated.

RESERVES
The reserves policy, including target levels, designations and the reasons for holding
reserves, is reviewed regularly, considering the Museum's plans, funding and general
financial position, and having due regard to the guidance issued by the Charities
Commission. The policy is reported to stakeholders via the Annual Report.
The charity has three types of reserves:
(i)
General reserves are unrestricted funds which provide working capital and help
deal with unplanned and unexpected expenditure or loss of funding.
(ii)
Designated reserves are unrestricted funds set aside by the Trustees for a specific
purpose.
(iii)
Restricted reserves are reserves which have been created when donors or funders
restrict the use of funds for a particular purpose.
The Museum has no endowment funds. We are aware of initiatives such as the HLF
Catalyst programme, which encourages organisations to develop endowments through
matched funding, and should such programmes be repeated in the future we would be
keen to explore these kinds of opportunities.
Reserves Policy
During the year, the Reserves Policy and the level of reserves were reviewed in light of
the latest Charity Commission guidance, and taking account of the current and projected
financial position of the Museum. In particular, a risk-based approach with a target range
on general reserves has been adopted as policy.
General reserves
General reserves (i.e., 'free reserves' or 'general unrestricted funds') are funds not
designated or restricted to a particular purpose, nor represented by fixed assets. In
assessing the suitability of the adequacy of the level of free reserves, the Trustees have
had regard to the Museum's diverse income streams, cashflow requirements, the level
of
other designated funds, the organisation's operational risks and the importance of TfL
funding and support in the context of the Museum as a subsidiary company of TfL. An
assessment has been made of the risk associated with each of the Museum's income
streams in the short to medium term, considering the certainty of the income, the targets
for growth and the likely level of fluctuation that could occur. Expenditure has also been
examined to identify the risk of potential increases. From this, a target range of f1.1 1m to
f2.3m was arrived at. The current level of general reserves is f1.4m (2016/17: .1m)
and we are confident that this level is adequate.
Designated reserves
It is the Trustees' policy to designate reserves for three main reasons:
To enable the Museum to plan for major exhibitions and educational programmes,
in advance of securing external sponsorship or other funding, by setting aside
funds to cover the cost of such activities should external income not be
forthcoming.
To contribute towards the cost of asset renewals and other future capital
expenditure associated with the Museum's premises, facilities and fixed assets.

To support the Museum's strategic development plans, in particular the need to
develop the Museum's gallery offer, and to invest in and grow the income

HISTORY OF THE MUSEUM
The Museum can trace its roots back to the 1920s when the London General Omnibus
Company (LGOC) decided to preserve a small collection of buses at Chiswick Works. The
collection has grown and developed considerably since then, and is now at the heart of
the world's leading museum of urban transport.
The earliest objects in the Museum collection include a B type bus and a faithful replica of
George Shillibeer's original 1829 horse-drawn omnibus created in 1929 for the centenary
celebrations of the first bus services in London. The London Passenger Transport Board
(LPTB) inherited these vehicles and the rest of the LGOC collection in the 1930s. They
subsequently added various railway and tramway artefacts, as well as other vehicles
which had reached the end of their operationa lives. The Museum of British Transport was
opened in a disused bus garage in Clapham in 1963 to house the nation's transport
collections, but this closed a decade later when the mainline railway items were set aside
for a new National Railway Museum in York. The remaining artefacts became the 'London
Transport Collection' but were left without a permanent home. Some of the vehicles had to
be mothballed at operational bus garages and the rest were displayed at Syon Park in
Brentford in Middlesex in conditions that were not ideal. The redevelopment of the former
Covent Garden flower market provided a perfect opportunity to create a dedicated central
London venue for the collection, and on 28 March 1980, the London Transport Museum
was opened by HRH Princess Anne.
With just 1,000 items in our possession when the Museum opened, we now care for
nearly half a million objects including trains, buses, trams, signs, photographs, posters,
uniforms and other material. The collection was designated as being of national
importance in 1997 and two years later we opened the Acton Depot in west London, the
first publicly accessible museum store in the UK. Acton Depot is a dedicated site for
housing and conserving items that are not on display at Covent Garden, and there are
regular public tours and popular open weekends.
The Covent Garden building has been significantly refurbished twice since we moved in,
with two further interior floors, a purpose-built lecture theatre, special exhibition galleries
and multiple education spaces added. We now have an ongoing programme of
investment to update the galleries and improve facilities for our visitors.
LTM became a registered charity in 2008, with a Board of Trustees and a clear remit to
deliver public benefit. Our busy schedule now includes a programme of special
exhibitions, late-night events, talks and debates, Acton Depot Open Weekends, bus and
steam train operations, Hidden London tours of disused stations, and education activities
that reach huge numbers of London school children each year.

STRUCTURE, GOVERNANCE AND MANAGEMENT
Legal status and governing documents
London Transport Museum Limited (LTM) is a registered charity incorporated on 6
February 2008 as a company limited by share. It is governed by its Memorandum and
Articles of Association. Under the GLA Act 1999, Transport for London (TfL) has the power
to provide and maintain a museum of transport artefacts, records and other exhibits. While
it is common for charities to incorporate as companies limited by guarantee, the Transport
for London (Specified Activities) Order 2000 requires TfL to carry out museum activities
through a company limited by shares.
Under section 5.1 of the LTM Memorandum of Association, the property and funds of the
Museum must be used only for promoting the objects and no dividend is payable to TfL.
LTM has a wholly owned subsidiary, London Transport Museum (Trading) Limited
(LTMTL) which operates retail, corporate hire and other non-charitable activities to
generate funds to further the Museum's objects. Under a Deed of Covenant, all the profits
of LTMTL are distributed to LTM.
Organisation
The Museum is governed by a Board of Trustees, chaired by Keith Ludeman. The Board
meets at least four times a year for formal business and once a year for a day of strategic
review. Trustees also serve on various Board committees (see below) which meet
regularly throughout the year. In addition, Trustees attend Museum events and activities,
meet informally, and regularly visit other museums and heritage organisations to widen
their knowledge and experience of the cultural sector.
Day-to-day management of the Museum is delegated to the Managing Director, Sam
Mullins, and through him to the Senior Management Team (SMT), employees and
volunteers. The SMT is made up of five Assistant Director (AD) posts, each with distinct
functional responsibilities.
The Trustees and SMT as a group are collectively considered to represent the 'key
management personnel' of the charity - i.e. those persons having authority and
responsibility for planning, directing and controlling the day-to-day activities of the charity.
London Transport Museum (Trading) Limited is governed by a Board of Directors drawn
from the Museum's Trustees and staff, along with a number of independent non-executive
directors.
Trustees
There are up to thirteen Trustees of LTM, three of whom are nominated by TfL and may be
members, officers or employees of TfL or the Greater London Assembly. The Managing
Director of LTM is automatically a Trustee by virtue of his office, and there are up to nine
independent Trustees unconnected with TfL. The Board has established a Nominations
Committee to offer advice and make recommendations regarding the appointment of
independent Trustees. We use personal recommendation and external search to recruit
Trustees with expertise and experience that will support the strategy and operation of the
Museum in areas such as community outreach, education, museum practice, commercial
transportation, finance and governance, retail operations and public relations.
Trustees serve a three-year term following which they may be elected for another three
years. The Articles of Association make allowance for a second extension of up to three
more years in exceptional circumstances. Other than the Managing Director, who is an
employee of LTM, the Trustees receive no remuneration, but TfL offers Trustees (and non-
executive Directors of LTMTL) certain travel concessions. If these are not sufficient,
Trustees may claim travel expenses for attending meetings.

LTM does no harm or detriment through its charitable activities. The health and safety of
staff and visitors are taken very seriously and the Museum operates safety management
systems to reduce and manage risks. We seek to manage our impact on the environment
and we use photovoltaic solar panels on the Museum roof to generate around 2 per cent
of the annual electricity requirement.
(2)
Public aspect: That the Museum delivers benefits to the public in general, and that
these benefits are not unduly restricted and do not give rise to more than incidental
personal benefit.
LTM delivers benefits to visitors at the Museum in Covent Garden and the Depot in Acton,
to users of our website, and to school children and audiences across Greater London who
take part in our educational, community and engagement activities at the Museum and
elsewhere. Our audience development and community outreach work, our skills
development work, and our employability programmes engage with people who would not
normally visit museums and galleries, and help inspire the next generation of engineers
and transport professionals. The Museum at Covent Garden is fully accessible and we
welcome visitors on all but two days of the year. We run special early morning events for
families with children who have special educational needs, and our schools' programmes
run throughout term time.
Our visitors come from across London and the world. We take our heritage vehicles out
onto the roads and rails, make historic disused stations publicly accessible, visit schools
and work with local communities across the Capital. We also loan objects to other
institutions to extend our reach and increase access to our collections. Our
comprehensive, free online resources are available 24 hours a day and include access to
information about exhibits in our gallery as well as thousands of objects not normally on
public display.
Although the Museum charges admission fees, various measures are taken to ensure
that
charges do not unduly restrict access to the collection. These include free entry to the
Museum for anyone aged 17 or under, for carers accompanying disabled visitors, and
reduced admission charges for senior citizens, students and those in receipt of state
benefit assistance. We also offer a community bursary programme. Most Museum
admission tickets are valid for one year to encourage return visits and increase value for
money for visitors. Many of the Museum's outreach programmes are free for participants.
The Safety and Citizenship and Youth Travel Ambassador programmes engage with over
100,000 pupils each year and are delivered at no cost to the schools taking part.
Where the Museum delivers private benefits to individuals or companies, these are
subject to appropriate commercial arrangements undertaken through a subsidiary
company to generate funds for the Museum. No LTM or TfL staff receive private benefit
other than in an incidental way and, with the exception of Sam Mullins who receives
a
salary in respect of his position as the Museum's Managing Director, the Board receive no
payments for their role as Trustees of the Museum.

Safeguarding
London Transport Museum aims to promote opportunities for children and young people
to engage with the richness of our collection, enjoy education and employment
opportunities through the Museum and our wider transport community, and participate in
the debate about the future of London.
At London Transport Museum, we are committed to excellence in the safeguarding of
children, young people and vulnerable adults who engage with all our activities including
our collections, programmes, education and employment initiatives. We believe that the
welfare of children and vulnerable adults is paramount, and that all children and
vulnerable adults, whatever their age, culture, disability, gender, racial origin, religious
beliefs or sexual identity have the right to protection.
We will ensure that all concerns and allegations of abuse will be taken seriously and
responded to swiftly and appropriately; and that our staff, volunteers, associates and
Trustees will be trained and know how to respond to concerns raised.
London Transport Museum will promote a positive ethos of collaboration with children
and/or vulnerable adults. We will take every reasonable step to ensure that all children
and vulnerable adults engaged with our services are safe and protected.
We keep our Safeguarding Policy and procedures under regular review and this year we
invited external experts to scrutinise our Safeguarding processes to ensure we exemplify
best practice A substantial training and communication exercise was also undertaken and
we plan to roll out further safeguarding training, including a programme for Trustees next
year.
During 2017/18 a safeguarding disclosure was made that prompted us to make a
declaration to the Charity Commission. We were made aware of the conviction of one of
our volunteers for an offence unrelated to the Museum but which was nevertheless of a
serious nature. The declaration was managed by our Designated Safeguarding Lead and
Safeguarding Board, following the Museum's Safeguarding Policy and procedures.
Relationship with other charities and organisations
The Museum is an instinctively collaborative organisation that seeks to work with like-
minded partners from the private, public, educationa and not-for-profit sectors to achieve
mutually beneficial goals and enhance the delivery of public benefit. A list of our education
and engagement partnerships can be found in the Strategic Report.
We are fortunate to be supported by the London Transport Museum Friends (LTMF), an
independent charity (no. 285108) established in 1982 which has charitable objectives to
advance public education in the history of transport and in particular by assisting and
encouraging the work and activities of the London Transport Museum'. Museum Director
Sam Mullins is also a Trustee of LTMF, and the Museum provides office space and other
support to the Friends.
Fundraising
London Transport Museum actively pursues funding from the corporate sector, trusts,
foundations, statutory and industry funders and from individuals to fund our charitable
activity and extend our community and audience reach. We seek to establish relationships
with those who have good reason to support the Museum, particularly, those who are
willing and able to work collaboratively with the Museum in the long-term. This includes,
but is not exclusive to, the transport industry and companies who do business with
Transport for London.
London Transport Museum Annual Report 2017/18
Page 48
Before entering into a partnership or relationship, the Museum will assess any potential
harm a partnership could have on London Transport Museum, Transport for London,
Museum audiences and stakeholders.
The decision on whether to develop a partnership or relationship will be based on the
following criteria:
Brand alignment - Is the relationship with a potential sponsor / donor consistent
with our organisational values, mission and plan?
Reputational risk - Could the sponsor / donor relationship bring either London
Transport Museum or TfL into disrepute?
Nature and scale of risk - What are the risks/likelihood of the risks, versus the
potential benefits?
Funding need - Does the relationship deliver on a real need for the organisation?
Value of the partnership - What is the value of the partnership to London Transport
Museum compared with the investment the Museum will need to put in to secure
and manage it? Will the partnership deliver value to the Museum in the long term?
Financial stability - Are we confident that the sponsor/donor will honour the terms
of the relationship, contractual and otherwise?
The above assessments are made by Museum staff. Although the Museum may
occasionally use third party websites such as Virgin Giving to collect donations, we do not
employ the services of professiona fundraisers or commercial participators.
Other than via admission charges for entry to the Museum, only a relatively small amount
of our fundraising activity is aimed at the general public. We do not undertake street
collections, telephone campaigns or employ any fundraising techniques that would
constitute an unreasonable intrusion on a person's privacy, or are unreasonably
persistent, or place undue pressure on a person to give money or other property. We
maintain a database of subscribers to our email newsletter, and where we collect personal
information this is managed in line with Genera Data Protection Regulation. If an
individual has agreed to receive our newsletter, we will send regular updates that will
include information about the Museum's work, as well as our events, special offers and
fundraising activities. Further information about how LTM uses personal information can
be found in our privacy statement:
https:l/www.ltmuseum.co.uk/privacy
The Museum has voluntarily subscribed to the scheme for fundraising regulation in
England, Wales and Northern Ireland by the Fundraising Regulator, although we have
queried the Fundraising Regulator's levy calculation which we believe is too high.
We also pay for membership of the Institute of Fundraising for key members of the
Museum's fundraising team.
We have received one complaint about our corporate fundraising activity from a campaign

The Trustees are content that all donations are in line with the Museum's policies.

The donor specifies that the grant or donation must only be used in future
accounting periods; or
The donor has imposed conditions which must be met before the Museum has
unconditional entitlement.
Income from corporate supporter memberships, commercial trading, sponsorships and
other similar activities where benefits are delivered by the Museum or its subsidiary
trading company, is recognised as the related goods and services are provided.
Investment income is recognised on a receivable basis.
Income from charitable activities includes income received under contract or where
entitlement to grant funding is subject to specific performance conditions which is
recognised as the related goods or services are provided.
b) Expenditure
All expenditure (except capital expenditure) is included in the Statement of Financial
Activities inclusive of any irrecoverable VAT. Expenditure is recognised when a liability
is incurred and is classified under the following principal categories:
Costs of raising funds includes the costs of commercial trading and the
operating costs of the fund-raising department.
Costs of charitable activities include expenditure associated with the operation
of the Museum and its educational and public programmes, and the
management and development of the Museum's collections and exhibitions.
Where costs relate directly to an activity they have been allocated against that activity.
Support costs (including governance costs) that relate to more than one activity have
been allocated to activity cost categories on the basis of staff numbers in each area of
activity (see Note 8).
c) Tangible fixed assets
Individual fixed assets over E10,000 are capitalised at cost.
Tangible fixed assets are depreciated on a straight line basis over their estimated
useful lives as follows:
Plant and equipment
3 - 10 years
Buildings and refurbishments 10 - 35 years
Structural improvements to the fabric of the Museum at Covent Garden are
depreciated over the remaining life of the lease for the building (27 years). Other
building work is capitalised if it is considered that future economic benefits in excess of
the originally assessed standard of performance will flow as a result of that work.

d) Heritage assets
Heritage assets are those assets of historical, artistic or scientific importance that are
held to advance the preservation conservation and educational objects of the
Museum. The Museum collections consist of over 475,000 items which are on loan
from TfL. Assets on loan are not capitalised within these financial statements although
expenditure relating to their use and maintenance is included in the Statement of
Financial Activities.
e) Operating leases
Costs relating to operating leases are charged to the Statement of Financial Activities
on a straight-line basis over the life of the lease.
f) Stock
Stock is valued at the lower of cost or net realisable value. Cost includes only the
purchase price of the items. Provision is made for obsolete and slow-moving items
where appropriate. All stocks relate to the Museum's retail activities.
g) Funds structure
Restricted funds are funds to be used for particular purposes laid down by the donors
or which have been raised for a specific purpose.
Unrestricted funds are funds available for use at the discretion of the Trustees in
furtherance of the Museum's charitable objectives.
Designated funds comprise unrestricted funds that have been set aside by the
Trustees for particular purposes.
The purposes and uses of the funds held in each of these categories are given in Note
16.
h) Pensions
The Museum participates in a pension scheme operated by TfL providing benefits
based on fina pensionable pay. The assets of the scheme are held separately from
those of the Museum. The charity is unable to identify its share of the underlying
assets and liabilities of the scheme on a consistent and reasonable basis and
therefore, as permitted by the multi-employer exemption in FRS 17 'Retirement
Benefits', it is accounted for as if it were a defined contribution scheme. As a result,
the amount charged to the Statement of Financial Activities represents the
contributions payable to the scheme in respect of the accounting period. The
disclosures required under FRS 102 are given in Note 19.
i) Related party transactions
Except in so far as disclosed in Note 20, the Museum has taken advantage of the
exemption set out in section 33 of FRS 102 not to disclose any transactions with other
TfL Group undertakings.

j) Taxation
The Museum is considered to pass the tests set out in Paragraph 1 Schedule 6 of the
Finance Act 2010 and therefore meets the definition of a charitable company for UK
corporation tax purposes. Accordingly, the charity is potentially exempt from taxation in
respect of income or capital gains received within categories covered by Chapter 3
Part 11 of the Corporation Tax Act 2010 or Section 256 of the Taxation of Chargeable
Gains Act 1992, to the extent that such income or gains are applied exclusively to
charitable purposes.
k) Cash flow
The Museum has taken advantage of the exemption, under FRS 102 paragraph
1.12(b), from preparing a statement of cash flows, on the basis that it is a wholly
owned subsidiary undertaking of Transport Trading Limited and its cash flows are
included within the consolidated financial statements of that company which are
publicly available.
I) Financial instruments
Financial assets held by the Museum are classified as "loans and debtors" within the
scope of sections 11 and 12 of FRS 102.
Financial liabilities within the scope of sections 11 and 12 of FRS 102 are classified as
financia liabilities measured at amortised cost.
The Museum determines the classification of its financial instruments at initial
recognition and re-evaluates this designation at each financial year end. When
financial instruments are recognised initially, they are measured at fair value, being
the
transaction price plus any directly attributable transactional costs The subsequent
measurement of financial instruments depends on their classification as follows:
Trade and other debtors
Trade and other debtors are recognised initially at fair value and subsequently at
amortised cost. For trade debtors this is after an allowance for estimated
impairment. The allowance is based on objective evidence that the Museum will
not be able to recover all amounts due, through a review of all accounts and prior
experience of collecting outstanding balances. Changes in the carrying amount of
the allowance are recognised in the Statement of Financial Activities.
The fair value of trade and other debtors is estimated as the present value of
future cash flows, discounted at the market rate of interest at the reporting date.
This fair value is determined for disclosure purposes.
Cash and cash equivalents
Cash at bank and in hand comprises cash balances and bank deposits with
original maturities of less than or equal to three months.
Trade creditors and other payables
Trade creditors and other payables are recognised initially at fair value and
subsequently at amortised cost using the effective interest method.

19. Pensions
Background
The Museum offers retirement plans to its employees. The majority of the
Museum's staff are members of the Public Sector Section of the TfL Pension Fund,
which is a final salary scheme established under trust. Benefits are based on an
employee's length of service and final pensionable pay. The Fund's Trustee is the
TfL Trustee Company Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary of Transport for London.
Under the rules of the Fund, its 18 trustee directors are nominated in equal
numbers by Transport for London and on behalf of the Fund's membership
The TfL Pension Fund's Actuary makes valuations and recommends the level of
contributions to be made by the participating employers to ensure long-term
solvency of the Fund. The latest formal funding valuation of the Fund was carried
out as at 31 March 2015 by the Actuary, a partner of consulting actuaries Towers
Watson, using the projected unit method. A revised Schedule of Contributions was
agreed between the Trustee and the employers following the 2015 valuation of the
TfL Pension Fund.
For the Public Sector Section, employers' contributions for the period from 1 April
2016 until 31 March 2022 will continue to be 31.0 per cent, an additional lump sum
payment was made by TfL during the year ending March 2018. The recovery plan
states that the expectation is that the funding shortfall will be eliminated by March
2022. The Fund deficit on an IAS19 basis (the international accounting standard
under which TfL reports its consolidated accounts) is currently f4,535m.
The underlying assets and defined benefit obligation of the TfL Pension Fund
London Transport Museum Annual Report 2017/18
Page 73
cover a number of Group entities and cannot be readily split between each
undertaking. No contractual agreement is in place to allocate the total net
obligation between the member entities. Thus, in accordance with IAS 19, the TfL
Corporation, as the Scheme sponsor, has recognised the total net defined benefit
obligation in its own individual accounts.
As at the Balance Sheet date, no allocation of the deficit of the fund has been
made between the various TfL Group companies, including London Transport
Museum. Should this position change in future, an allocation may be made and the
Museum may, at that point, become liable for its share of the deficit. There are no
plans for such an allocation to be made.
Further information regarding the TfL Pension Fund can be found in the TfL Annual
Report and Statement of Accounts.
Accounting
The Museum's ultimate parent, Transport for London, and the Museum's fellow
subsidiaries participate in the Public Sector Section of the TfL Pension Fund.
Because the Museum is unable to identify its share of the underlying assets and
liabilities on a consistent and reasonable basis, as permitted by FRS 102, the
Museum treats contributions to the Public Sector Section as if they were
contributions to a defined contribution plan. The Museum's contributions to the

As at 1 February 2017 the primary school
had 139 enrolled students (the school year
started in January 2017) and was
administered by 16 Kenyan staff, including
nine teachers, two administration staff, two
cooks, two cleaners and a security guard.
Students receive not only a primary school
education but a school lunch every school
day. For some of the children, this is their
only meal of the day and for most of the
children it is certainly the most nutritious
meal they receive each day.
In December 2017, 13 students graduated
from Kookaburra Community School.
Kookaburra House
As at 1 February 2017, Kookaburra House
provided accommodation for 21 members
of our school community (mostly children)
who required this emergency
accommodation. As at 31 January 2018,
accommodation was provided for 19
members of our school community.
Kookaburra House is located near the
Kookaburra Community School and has its
own real sense of community.
There are six rooms in Kookaburra House
which are funded by the Kenyan charity's
genera funds or through specific
sponsorship by our supporters.
Kookaburra Graduate Programme
As at 1 February 2017, we had 24 students
being sponsored through high schoo in
Kenya via the Kookaburra Graduate
Programme, in addition to those who had
already graduated from high school in
previous years (20 students in total had
previously graduated from high school
under the Graduate Programme, with an
additional five students leaving the
Graduate Programme before completion of
high school).
The vast majority of these students have
been matched to and supported by
individual sponsors (based in the UK,
Ireland, Canada and Australia). Those
sponsors who are based in the UK pay the
fees through the charity's bank account,
allowing us to benefit from gift aid in the UK
on these payments. Any students who do
not have individual sponsors are supported
by the Kenyan charity's general funds.
Most of the students in high school attend
boarding school SO receive not only an
education, but food and accommodation as
part of their sponsorship.

In addition to events organised by the

The charity continued to be a nominated

the employer of one of the charity's
Trustees. This meant that the charity

two charity film screenings, as well as a
