1.10 Pension Costs
Defined contribution pension plan
The charity operates a defined contribution plan for its employees. A defined
contribution plan is a pension plan under which the charity pays fixed contributions
into a separate entity. Once the contributions have been paid the charity has no
further payment obligations. The contributions are recognised as an expense in the
Consolidated Statement of Financial Activities. The assets of the plan are held
separately from the charity in independently administered funds.
Teachers employed by the charity have membership of the Teachers' Pension
Scheme, administered by the Teachers' Pensions Agency. It provides teachers with
defined benefits upon their retirement. The scheme is a defined benefit final salary
scheme. It is not possible for the charity to identify its share of the underlying
liabilities in the scheme and it is therefore classed as a defined contribution scheme
for the purposes of the accounting requirements of FRS 102 and does not form part
of the pension deficit.
Defined benefit pension plan
The charity operates a defined benefit plan for certain employees. A defined benefit
plan defines the pension benefit that the employee will receive on retirement,
usually dependent upon several factors including but not limited to age, length of
service and remuneration. A defined benefit plan is a pension plan that is not a
defined contribution plan.
The liability recognised in the Balance Sheet in respect of the defined benefit plan is
the present value of the defined benefit obligation at the end of the reporting date
Page 23
Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements
for the year ended 31 March 2018
less the fair value of plan assets at the reporting date (if any) out if which the
obligations are to be settled.
The defined benefit obligation is calculated using the projected unit credit method.
Annually the charity engages independent actuaries to calculate the obligation. The
present value is determined by discounting the estimated future payments using
market yields on high quality corporate bonds that are denominated in sterling and
that have terms approximating to the estimated period of the future payments
('discount rate').
The fair value of the plan assets is measured in accordance with the FRS 102 fair
value hierarchy and in accordance with the charity's policy for similarly held assets.
This includes the use of appropriate valuation techniques.
Actuarial gains and losses arising from experience adjustments and changes in
actuaria assumptions are charged or credited to other recognised gains/(losses)
These amounts together with the return on plan assets, less amounts included in
net interest, are disclosed as actuarial gain/(loss) on defined benefit pension
schemes.
The cost of the defined benefit plan, recognised in profit or loss as employee costs,
except where included in the cost of an asset, comprises:
a) The increase in net pension benefit liability arising from employee service during
the period; and
b) The cost of plan introductions, benefit changes, curtailments and settlements.
The net interest cost is calculated by applying the discount rate to the net balance
of defined benefit obligation and the fair value of plan assets.
The charity operates a defined benefits pension scheme and the pension charge is
based on a full actuarial valuation dated 31 March 2016.
The charity is an admitted body of the Northumberland County Council Pension
Fund ("LGPS") and provides pension arrangements to its employees. The scheme
is classified as a Defined Benefit Scheme based on final pensionable pay and as
such must comply with reporting standard FRS 102. This requires the charity to
disclose certain information concerning assets, liabilities, income and expenditure
related to the scheme for its employees. These disclosures have been prepared by
AON Hewitt the actuary of the Northumberland County Council Pension Fund. The
purpose of the pensions' disclosure is to provide clear information on the impact of
the charity's obligation to fund the retirement benefits of its staff on its financial
position and performance. Even where this obligation is discharged through a
pension fund, the charity is responsible for employer's contributions set at a level to
ensure the liabilities of the fund can be met.
The liabilities of the pension scheme attributable to the charity are included in the
Balance Sheet on an actuarial basis using the projected unit method, that is, an
assessment of the future payments that will be made in relation to retirement

benefits earned to date by employees based on assumptions about mortality rates,
employee turnover rates and projections of earnings for current employees.

for further detail. The net Pension Liability is analysed into the following

Current Service Costs

Defined contribution scheme
The charity operates a defined contribution scheme, which is offered to all new
employees. The assets of the scheme are held separately from those of the charity
in an independently administered fund. An amount of f24,051 (2016-17: E19,559)

Teachers' Pensions Agency in respect of teachers' retirement benefits representing

Defined benefit scheme
On 1 October 2014 when the management of the leisure facilities within
Northumberland moved into Active Northumberland the Loca Government Pension
Scheme (LGPS) relating to these staff transferred into the charitable company.
The LGPS provides defined benefits, based on the member's final pensionable
salary.
Active Northumberland has a commitment from Northumberland County Council via
its Risk Appraisa Panel to subsume Active Northumberland's LGPS pension assets
and liabilities (i.e. any deficit) in the event of Active Northumberland defaulting on

SAFFRON WALDEN UNITED CHARITIES
TRUSTEES' REPORT FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2016
The trustees present their report and the financial statements for the year ended 31 December 2017.
Constitution, objects and policies
The charity's object and principal activity is to provide financial assistance in cases of hardship for
those persons living in the geographic area administered by the former Borough Council of Saffron
Walden.
The Trustees continue to develop and maintain useful links with the statutory agencies including
Social Workers, Health Visitors, District Council Housing Officers, Uttlesford Citizens Advice
Bureau and other local voluntary organisations involved in community welfare.
The management of the charity is by the Chairman of the Trustees acting in consultation with an
emergency sub-committee of Trustees for urgent decisions. Routine daily management and
administration is delegated to the clerk who is subject to report at minuted meetings of the Trustees.
The constitution states that the Trustees should hold at least two ordinary meetings in each year.
The Trustees met as a body on four occasions during the financial year under review.
Development, activities and achievements this year
The Saffron Walden United Charities achieved the objects of the charity by making grants and
donations totalling f45,953 during the financial year ending 31 December 2017.
Financial Review
The statement of financial activities shows net outgoing's for the year of E8,112, the market value of
the COIF investments rose by f105,167 in this year. This was due to the purchase of additional
units plus an increase in value of the investments. The COIF invests in investments which produce
capital growth. They have still received income on a quarterly basis which meets the annual
requirements for distribution. The trustees decide on how much to distribute based on the amount of
income received from the investment.
Future developments
The charity uses the COIF investments that are reviewed annually and the Trustees are committed to
continuing the prudent investment policies that have operated for a number of years and have served
the charity well.
Trustees
All of the Trustees named on Page 1 other than as shown, served throughout the year. The Charity
has the power to appoint additional Trustees as it considers fit to do SO. The constitution regarding
the appointment of trustees changed on 30 November 2004 in accordance with the Order made
under section 26 of the Charities Act dated 16 June 2004.
SAFFRON WALDEN UNITED CHARITIES
TRUSTEES' REPORT FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2016 (Continued)
Statement of trustees' responsibilities
The trustees are responsible for preparing the Trustees' Annual Report and the financial statements
in accordance with applicable law and United Kingdom Accounting Standards (United Kingdom
Generally Accepted Accounting Practice).
The law applicable to charities in England & Wales requires the trustees to prepare financial
statements for each financial year which give a true and fair view of the state of the affairs of the
charity and of the incoming resources and application of resources of the charity for that period. In
preparing these financial statements, the trustees are required to:
Select suitable accounting policies and then apply them consistently;
Observe the methods and principles in the Charities SORP;
Make judgements and estimates that are reasonable and prudent;
State whether applicable accounting standards have been followed, subject to any material
departures disclosed and explained in the financial statements;
Prepare the financial statements on the going concern basis unless it is inappropriate to presume
that the charity will continue in operation.
The trustees are responsible for keeping proper accounting records that disclose with reasonable
accuracy at any time the financial position of the charity and enable them to ensure that the financial
statements comply with the Charities Act 2011, the Charity (Accounts and Reports) Regulations
2008 and the provisions of the trust deed. They are also responsible for safeguarding the assets of
the charity and hence for taking reasonable steps for the prevention of fraud and other irregularities.
Approval
This report was approved by the trustees on 7 June 2018 and signed on their behalf.

Trustees' report
Year ended 31 March 2018
The trustees (who are also directors of the charity for the purposes of the Companies Act) present their annual
report together with the audited financial statements of Mental Health Concern (the company and the group) for
the year ended 31 March 2018.
The trustees confirm that the annual report and financial statements of the company and the group comply with
the current statutory requirements; the requirements of the company and the group's governing document; and
the provisions of the Statement of Recommended Practice (SORP), applicable to charities preparing their
accounts in accordance with the Financial Reporting Standard applicable in the UK and Republic of Ireland (FRS
102) (effective January 2015).
Objectives and Activities
Policies and objectives
Mental Health Concern (known as MHC) sits alongside its subsidiary/primary purpose vehicle Insight Healthcare
as part of "Concern Group".
Our mission is "to improve the mental health and wellbeing of the people we serve".
We are driven by our strong values base, which underpins the way we work with our service users, staff, service
commissioners, and partners. We value:
compassion and hopefulness,
being open and friendly,
inclusivity and fairness,
experience and expertise
hard work, creativity, innovation,
going the extra mile with people to achieve the right outcomes
Strategies for achieving objectives
Our continued success over 31 years of operation is testament to our ability to develop and adapt to the evolving
needs of the people we serve, and of those who commission us. We continually strive to consolidate our
position as a key not-for-profit provider of NHS, Local Authority and European Social Fund services, supporting
people with a wide range of mental health conditions.
The group specialises in:
24 hour nursing services for those with dementia including respite and assessment and a Community
Challenging Behaviour Team.
24 hour nursing services for those with complex mental health problems, supporting their rehabilitation
and recovery.
Supported Housing services.
Community and Wellbeing services, which support meaningful activity and employability.
Through our subsidiary, Insight Healthcare Limited (IH), we provide employee wellbeing services and
primary care mental health services, centred on the delivery of a range of psychological therapies.
Hosting and support for smaller mental health-related projects.
Our management structure is designed to support our frontline services, to provide corporate effectiveness, and
to meet new and ongoing commissioning or service development opportunities.
The Executive Team has recently been reshaped to meet the challenges ahead and a new Director of Finance
and a Director of Corporate Services and Business Transformation have both taken up their posts since the year
end. The revised structure will continue to support our service-driven ethos.
2
Mental Health Concern
Trustees' report (continued)
Year ended 31 March 2018
Activities for achieving objectives
The trustees have continued to review and develop the way we work and how best to lead the group in a
continuingly difficult commissioning environment:
Management reporting structures are under development to provide relevant operational and financial
control.

Older People's Services
We believe passionately in providing good care to people with dementia and their families. We also believe that it
is entirely possible for anybody living with dementia to live a good quality and meaningful life. With the right help,
this is a reasonable expectation for anybody living with dementia.
We have provided specialist dementia services for over 30 years and have learnt that enabling people with
dementia to live well can be demanding, but very rewarding. This is why all of our dementia services and staff
work to a strong set of values that have a clear person-centred focus.
In Gateshead we provide four types of dementia services:
24-hour specialist nursing care
respite
short-term assessment (as an alternative to hospital admission)
community challenging behaviour support

Adult Services
In our Adult Services we support people recovering from mental ill-health, who are often taking their first steps
away from hospital or secure accommodation. Our services are mostly commissioned by the NHS, which means
that we can provide high levels of 24-hour specialist support, and can help those people that many other
organisations cannot.
Our specialist 24 hour nurse-led rehabilitation and recovery services help people with complex mental health
problems to move from secure and hospital-based settings into the community We also provide short-term
relapse prevention packages as an alternative to hospital admission.
We are pleased with what we have helped our service users achieve this year. 17% of people achieved a
meaningful employment / employability outcome, 31% educationa outcomes and 70% to improve independent
living skills. We have supported more than 20% of our service users to move on to more independent
accommodation this year and anticipate the same result next year. This is whilst we are supporting more people
with very significant needs and complex trauma.
Housing with Care and Support
In our Housing and Support Services we help people to secure good quality housing and provide a wide range of
help from quite intensive bespoke packages, right through to low level day-to-day support and advice. Our focus
is on helping people to have independence and to take control over their own lives.
Our Supported Housing service helps people with complex mental health problems to move out of hospital or 24-
hour care and take up a supported tenancy in the community. It is a highly-specialised service with tiers of
support and supervision, which gives people who have often spent many years in institutional environments the
opportunity for independent living and social inclusion.
It consists of four specific services:
Newcastle Supported Housing
Gateshead Supported Housing
Early Intervention in Psychosis (EIP) Supported Housing
Step Ahead Housing Bespoke support packages
We have invested this year in two further properties for the Step Ahead service and we have established a
borrowing facility to acquire further properties as opportunities arise. We have used this capacity to broker two
bespoke intensive support packages for people who have very profound and complex needs, which has enabled
them to live with independence in their own tenancy and communities of choice. We aspire to increase our
provision both in our current operational localities and neighbouring areas
Community and Wellbeing Services
Our Community and Wellbeing Services help over 1,000 people each year to get back into work, education, or
increase meaningful activity. We also help people to rebuild their social support networks and develop
friendships. We support them to navigate through the sometimes complex health and social care system using
our knowledge of what's out there to link people in.

Moving Forward
Our Moving Forward services in Newcastle, Gateshead, and South Tyneside can be accessed by anyone who
has experienced mental health issues. We focus on linking people up with activities, groups and community
resources, with the aim for them to:
rediscover self confidence
learn new skills or rediscover old interests
build a stronger social network and have more people to do things with
get back into education or training
find paid or voluntary work
In this financial year, these services have continued to flourish and grow as we support more people year on
year. To meet this increased demand, we've been working with our staff, clients and commissioners to improve
how we manage new referrals, so we can get to people more quickly.
Together in a Crisis
We were delighted to be commissioned by Newcastle Clinical Commissioning Group to develop a prototype
service called Together in a Crisis. The service is designed to provide support for people who identify as being in
crisis, but who do not meet the threshold for the local NHS mental health crisis service. The service works in
close collaboration with the NHS crisis service, providing practical and emotional support through the specific
issues or problems that are causing distress. We offer:
A listening ear
Short-term support, tailored to the issues the individual is facing
Support to make informed decisions
Links to other support and services
The service has proven to be very effective for people. So far, we have supported over 300 people who are in
crisis to improve their mental health, and other related factors.
Fulfilling Lives
The Fulfilling Lives programme is a Lottery-funded partnership between Mental Health Concern, Changing Lives,
and Oasis Aquila Housing. Together, we help adults who are likely to experience issues relating to three or more
of the following:
mental ill-health
homelessness
drug and alcohol issues
offending
As a core partnership, we have embarked on the second stage of this programme which, for the next four years,
will be mainly focussed on promoting system change for people with multiple and complex needs in Newcastle
and Gateshead.
Mental Health Carer Support
In South Tyneside, we provide support to people who have caring responsibilities for people with mental health
problems. We work in partnership with other professionals to provide emotional and practical help, as well as
helping people to find the support they need in their caring roles.
Ways to Wellness
Ways to Wellness is a social prescribing service for people with long-term health conditions in the west of
Newcastle. The service aims to improve its users' quality of life and reduce their use of mainstream health
services by enabling them to lead healthier lives and better manage their conditions. This is achieved by the
provision of Link Workers, who help patients to identify and work to overcome the current barriers to managing
their long-term health conditions.
During 2017/18 we have taken on more GP surgeries and staff to meet the increased numbers of clients we are
supporting.

Chain Reaction launched in 2015 as a new service commissioned by Newcastle City Council, designed to

Our Insight Healthcare services
Clinical outcomes and patient experience results have remained strong. This year Insight has achieved an
organisational score of 55% on the nationally mandated 'Moving to Recovery' (MtR) clinical outcomes measure;
exceeding both national average performance and contracted standards. This is also a slight increase on our
previous year's performance.
Insight has remained at the forefront of developments to the national primary care mental health agenda. Over
the course of the last year NHS England have launched the 'Integrated IAPT' programme; aiming to increase the
rate of people entering primary care psychological therapies as a proportion of local prevalence from 15% to
25% by 2020. Primarily, this increase is to be delivered by helping people with long term physical health
conditions access psychological therapies, thereby contributing to the NHS Sustainability and Transformation
Plans (STP) and delivering whole system improvements. Over 60,000 referrals were received into Insight
services over the course of the year as a number of Insight localities became early adopter integrated IAPT
services, extending provision into physical health settings throughout the localities we serve. The greatest
increases were in our East Midlands, Medway and East Kent 'Any Qualified Provider' (AQP) localities; where
Insight is amongst a number of providers accredited to deliver locally, but has grown on the strength of
consistently strong delivery. Low waiting times have also meant that GP's continue to refer to Insight as their
provider of choice.

outcomes.

The largest resource we use to provide all of our charitable activities is our workforce. Our continued success is
due to the hard work, dedication and skills of our staff, and the quality of their care is the reason we are well
regarded by our commissioners. Increases in employer pension contributions to 5%, Apprenticeship Levy, and

Our balance sheet remains strong and we have not yet needed to utilise any of the borrowing facility to acquire

existing use valuations. There is not considered to be a need to reduce the value of any of the assets through

Our property and cash assets provide us with the platform for the future development of our services and for

Going concern
After making appropriate enquiries, the Trustees have a reasonable expectation that the company has adequate
resources to continue in operational existence for the foreseeable future. For this reason, they continue to adopt
the going concern basis in preparing the financial statements. Further details regarding the adoption of the going
concern basis can be found in the accounting policies.
Financial risk management objectives and policies
Within the Strategic Risk Register, which is reviewed quarterly by the Trustees, the most significant financial risk
facing Concern Group is the reliance on commissioned public contracts in a continuing period of economic
austerity, and the impact of inflation risk. NHS commissioners are required to look for annual efficiencies in the
costs of their services whilst costs, particularly staffing costs, continue to increase.
Trustees review liquidity through regular reports including income and expenditure accounts, balance sheets and
cash flow forecasts. To date, our liquid assets for the group have been sufficient to mitigate the impact of
quarterly funding from the NHS and the impact of payments in arrears for relevant IAPT services. There are
sufficient physical assets available to the trustees should the need arise to raise funds, through either borrowings
or disposal, to remedy the situation without compromising operations. With increasing growth of contracts which
require specified outcomes before payment is received the pressure on operating cash for the group is growing.
We have approached a number of our larger CCG's with proposals to allow advance payments on account, later
reconciled to outcomes, to mitigate the impact of payment in arrears. We are pleased that all those we have
spoken with SO far have agreed in principle to this arrangement and we will work with them in coming months to
make this happen.
All members of Concern Group are subject to the risk of increases in purchase price of supplies. Where
practical, prices are agreed in advance through the use of supplier quotations and tendering. Our budgeting and
forecasting processes are designed to alert management and Trustees to potential problems. We do not make
charges to the individuals for the services we provide and as such have no exposure to credit risk in relation
to
service users and beneficiaries. Funding from the NHS and local authorities is based on commissioned services
under standard public sector contracts. As this funding is derived from government related public bodies, it is
considered that credit risk is minimal.
Each member of Concern Group has interest bearing assets, in the form of cash deposits, which are subject to
changes in interest rates. The poor levels of interest have been recognised in our investment policy, but the
need for sufficient operating funds to meet liquidity risk requires significant levels of cash to be held.

Principal risks and uncertainties
We have an extensive range of policies and procedures in place, coupled with the requisite training, clinical
supervision, and support to mitigate potential risks. A strategic risk register is maintained, reviewed and updated
by the Executive Team, the Governance Committee and then Board. The controls put in place provide
reasonable, but not absolute, assurance that risks have been adequately mitigated.
The principal risks highlighted by our review and monitoring are:
We work with some very vulnerable individuals and we recognise the risks involved in delivering our
services: to service users themselves, their families, our staff, and to the general public. We have clinical
policies, procedures, supervision and training that are regularly updated and reviewed to ensure our practices
and services minimise potential harm.
Our services are commissioned and we recognise the financial pressures on public funded services as
well as the constantly changing commissioning environment. The Executive Team work closely with all
commissioning groups to ensure that these risks to the Charity are minimised. All new services and re-tenders
are subject to financial and operational review to ensure our standards of delivery are both viable and clinically
sound.
We operate alongside the NHS and other NHS-commissioned services and face competition to recruit
and retain professionally trained, experienced and knowledgeable staff. Our staff understand the financial
position this puts us in and have accepted our attempts to ensure that we have an efficient and sustainable cost
base. We also understand the pressures faced by our workforce and we try to ensure our remuneration
packages are competitive.
Reserves policy
The trustees have considered a risk-based reserves policy, taking into account the issues raised by the strategic
risk register, which has in turn fed the Investment Policy. The trustees have established the need to increase the
level of free reserves from the current E1,165k to E1.8m, to provide additional security against risks that may
arise in future. The three-year business planning cycle necessitates a new strategic plan for 2018 to 2021. We
aim to achieve an annual surplus from operations, through growth of services and increasing operating
efficiencies. We recognise achieving our target will take a number of years, as we manage the pressures of
increasing costs of resources and the availability of income from the ever-tightening commissioning environment.
The trustees believed it was prudent to maintain all its reserves as undesignated for the year ended 31 March
2018. The trustees are satisfied that both the policy on reserves and the current level of reserves are sufficient
to cover risks to the Charity at this time.
Investment policy and performance
The trustees have the power to invest and deal with the monies of the charity not immediately required for the
purpose of its business, in such investments or securities and in such manner as may from time to time be
determined.
The trustees have held investments, other than investments in property for the use of operational services, as
cash on deposit.
Since 2015/16 the trustees have supported the use of available funds to acquire further Step Ahead housing, to
allow service users the opportunity to live in their own home, supported by our professional team. The rental
return from this type of investment is greater than leaving the funds on deposit.

Method of appointment or election of Trustees
The management of the company and the group is the responsibility of the trustees, who are elected and CO-
opted under the terms of the Articles of Association. Terms of office for trusteeship have previously been
established requiring re-appointment every three years, with two members reappointed during the year.
Policies adopted for the induction and training of Trustees
The Articles of Association limit the number of trustees to nine individuals, increased from eight following a
resolution approved on 26 August 2015.
The structure of the trustees' meetings allows them to discuss strategic issues and consider their performance
during the year. It is at these meetings that the trustees consider whether they require additional trustees with
experience and knowledge that is not currently available.
The Articles of Association set out the process for appointment of new members. A Board Member would notify
MHC of the nomination(s) for election to the Board in writing, not less than three days before each annual
general meeting (AGM). At the AGM, the Board would elect the member nominated and also elect a chair and a
vice-chair.
Where it is deemed necessary to elect a new member to the Board at a meeting other than the AGM, the
nominated person would be proposed by a member and seconded by another member of the Board of Directors.
This would follow discussions surrounding the nominee's credibility and suitability for a place on the Board. The
Board of Directors as a body is solely responsible for the election of any new members. All new trustees receive
informal induction from members of the Executive Team.
Pay policy for senior staff
All employees of Concern Group, including all senior staff, are remunerated in accordance with an approved pay
structure, with all roles subject to job evaluation at creation or when changes in responsibilities are required of
the post holder. Employees are appointed to a salary band, which includes a range of salaries to reflect the
experience and skills highlighted in the job evaluation. The range of salaries allows employees to incrementally
increase their earnings towards the top of their salary band subject to performance. Employees undertake
regular performance reviews with their line managers. Any proposed cost of living awards are presented to the
trustees for approval before the start of each financial year.

Organisational structure and decision making
The governing body of the charity is the Board of trustees which has met formally six times this year, with
additional informal meetings when required and a full-day meeting to specifically discuss the business plan.
There are four committees focusing on Quality & Service Delivery, Finance, Human Resources. and
Governance. Information is provided by requisite managers to support Committee Members and the Board in
their role to provide oversight, governance, and advice to the organisation. Every trustee is a member of at least
one committee. The Governance Committee has a membership of the Chair and the Chairs of the three other
committees.
Executive decision making and day-to-day management is vested in a professional team led by the Chief
Executive. The Chief Executive is responsible for advising and informing the Board on the implementation of
agreed organisational strategy, service development and delivery, as well as any requisite changes to the policy,
and practice for the group. He is supported by the Executive Team which is responsible and accountable for the
day-to-day management of clinical services, corporate and financial affairs, HR and business development. The
Chief Executive meets regularly with the Chair of trustees and provides full details of any significant issues as
they may arise between the formal meetings.
Public benefit
The trustees have considered the Charity Commission's guidance on public benefit. The services we offer in the
areas we are commissioned are available free of charge to those who need our support. Our work not only
benefits individuals and their families but also the wider community by reducing the impact and cost of ill-health
to society.
Risk management
The trustees have assessed the major risks to which the company and the group is exposed, in particular those
related to the operations and finances of the company and the group, and are satisfied that systems and
procedures are in place to mitigate our exposure to the major risks.
Information on fundraising practices
The group does not undertake significant fundraising activities. We do have a JustGiving page and we are
registered with the Fundraising Regulator and follow their code of ethics. We have received no complaints during
the year.
Funds held as custodian
The charity works with other organisations in pursuit of its charitable objectives and holds funds as custodian on
behalf of others. During the year, MHC has administered funds on behalf of partner agencies and committees
in order to 'host' and develop projects whose objectives are mental health care-related. These functions are part
of MHC's role as an enabling organisation within the local mental health arena.
Our service users are sometimes unable to take full control of their own financial affairs and we are asked to
receive their welfare benefits on their behalf. We hold residents' money separately from those of the charity and
account to the residents and their carers for our actions. The funds are included within our cash deposits and
the amounts owed to residents are held within creditors.

1.16 Creditors and provisions
Liabilities are recognised when there is an obligation at the balance sheet date as a result of a past

amount of the settlement can be estimated reliably. Liabilities are recognised at the amount that the
company anticipates it will pay to settle the debt or the amount it has received as advanced

the amounts required to settle the obligation. Where the effect of the time value of money is
material, the provision is based on the present value of those amounts, discounted at the pre-tax
discount rate that reflects the risks specific to the liability. The unwinding of the discount is
recognised within interest payable and similar charges.
1.17 Financial instruments
Financial instruments are classified and accounted for as financial assets, financial liabilities or

Financial instruments which are assets are stated at cost less any provision for impairment.

1.18 Deferred taxation
Deferred tax represents the future tax consequences of transactions and events recognised in the
financial statements of current and previous periods. It is recognised in respect of all timing
differences, with certain exceptions. Timing differences are differences between taxable profits and
total comprehensive income as stated in the financial statements that arise from the inclusion of
income and expense in tax assessments in periods different from those in which are they
recognised in the financial statements, Unrelieved tax losses and other deferred tax assets are
recognised only to the extent that it is probable that they wil be recovered against the reversal of
deferred tax liabilities or other future taxable profits.
Deferred tax is measured using the tax rates and laws that have been enacted or substantively
enacted by the balance sheet date that are expected to apply to the reveral of timing differences.
Deferred tax on revalued non-deprecriable tangible fixed assets is measured using the rates and
alloawance that apply to the sale of the asset.
1.19 Pensions
The group operates a defined contribution pension scheme and the pension charge represents the
amounts payable by the group to the fund in respect of the year. The group participated in the NHS
defined contribution pension scheme. The scheme is a mutli-employer scheme where it is not
possible, in the normal case of events, to identify on a consistent and reasonable basis, the share of
underlying assets and liabilities belonging to individual participating employers. Therefore, as
required by FRS102 the group accounts for this scheme as if it was a defined contribution scheme.
The amount charged to the statement of financial activities represents contributions payable to the
scheme in respect of the accounting period.

1.20 Taxation
The company is considered to pass the tests set out in Paragraph 1 Schedule 6 of the Finance Act
2010 and therefore meets the definition of a charitable company for UK corporation tax purposes.
Accordingly, the company is potentially exempt from taxation in respect of income or capital gains
received within categories covered by Chapter 3 Part 11 of the Corporation Tax Act 2010 or Section
256 of the Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992, to the extent that such income or gains are
applied exclusively to charitable purposes.
1.21 Judgements in applying accounting policies and key sources of estimation uncertainty
The group enters into contracts with customers with varying contract periods. Management consider
that the main judgement and source of estimation uncertainty arises from the estimation of progress
within the specified services for amounts held as work in progress, and the assessment of the level
of profitability around key contracts.

Objects and activities of the charity
The purposes of the charity as set out in its governing document
Its objects are to provide or assist in the provision of tacilities tor the recreation or other leisure
time activities for people with disabilities with the object of improving their conditions of life, in
particular, by encouraging recreational and competitive sailing in Devon.
The main activities and achievments undertaken in relation to those purposes
during the year.
During the year DSG had a total of f42) sailing members (those with some disability) and f28)
members and students from Camphil (a registered care home for aduits with leaming disabilities)
and two special schools for children with various disabilities (Bidwell Brook and Oaklands School).
In all DSG provided sailing during the summer giving 517 sails on Tuesdays and Saturdays and, in
addition participated with disabled sailors in Royal Dart Yacht Club's evening races and Dartmouth
Regatta. All the activity took place on or around the River Dart in Devon.
The main activities undertaken during the year to further the charity's purpose for
the public benefit
During the year DSG has provided sailing and related water based activities to a broad cross-
section of the local community, young and old, male and female and for those with a wide range
of
disabilities. The service is provided at modest cost (E25.00 annual membership plus $1.00 per
session). There were provisions to rebate the membership fee in cases of hardship. The trustees

Trustees' Annual Report for the year ended 30 September 2016
The contribution of volunteers during the year.
During the year DSG had 72 registered volunteers, many of whom have their own disabilities, but
who continue to turn up both during the sailing season and throughout the winter to give the time
needed to keep the Charity going It is estimated that volunteers contributed over 5,000 hours of
their time. All volunteers receive at no cost to them, certificated training in Disability Awareness
and many take the various RYA courses covering sailing and power boating as well as specialist
areas such as safety boat, first aid and radio communications.
Fundraising activities during the year.
Funds were raised from a variety of sources during the year ranging from sale of donated items to
donations from 22 individuals and trusts. The largest single donation was E3,500.
The difference the charity's performance during the year has made to the
beneficiaries of the charity.
The Trustees note that over 40 disabled sailors have been supported in their sailing during the
year. Most of these attend regularly as do groups from Camphill, Bidwel Brook and Oaklands
School. For all involved including the carers DSG provided not only access to sailing and the river
but also an opportunity to socialise.

Financial review of the position at the reporting date, 30 September 2016.
The trustees consider the financial performance of DSG during the year to be satisfactory. It has
increased its unrestricted revenue funds by 16,715 during the year. At the year end there was
uncertainly around the proposed redevelopment of Noss on Dart Marina and how this might affect
the operational activities of DSG. There was concern that In the longer term if DSG was to remain
at Noss on Dart, it would have to pay substantially more for the facilities it requires (storage,
pontoon space and car parking). The re -development has not progressed as quickly as
anticipated such that at the date of this report, DSG is continuing to operate on the same basis
as
during the previous year and has now secured a short-term tenancy agreement for its storage
space.

The law requires that the trustees must not approve the accounts unless they are satisfied that

The Trustees are also responsible for maintaining adequate accounting records which disclose

1 Accounting policies
Policies relating to the production of the accounts.
Basis of preparation and accounting convention
The accounts have been prepared on the accruals basis, under the historical cost convention, and in accordance with
the Financial Reporting Standard 102, (effective 1st January 2016) and 'FRS 102 SORP (Statement of Recommended
Practice for Accounting and Reporting by Charities) 2015 (as amended by the Bulletin issued in February 2016)
published by the Charity Commission in England & Wales (CCEW) effective January 2016, (The SORP), and in
accordance with all applicable law in the charity's jurisdiction of registration except that the charity has prepared the
financial statements in accordance with the FRS 102 SORP (Statement of Recommended Practice for Accounting and
Reporting by Charities) 2015 (as amended by the Bulletin issued in February 2016) in preference to the previous
SORP, the SORP 2005, which has been withdrawn, notwithstanding the fact that the extant statutory regulations, the
Charities (Accounts and Reports) Regulations 2008 refer explicitly to the SORP 2005. This has been done to accord
with current best practice
Policies relating to categories of income and income recognition.
Nature of income
Gross income represents the value, net of value added tax and discounts, of goods provided to customers and work
carried out in respect of services provided to customers.
Categories of Income
income is categorised as income from exchange transactions (contract income) and income from non-exchange
transactions (gifts), investment income and other income.
Income from a non-exchange transaction is where the charity receives value from the donor without providing equal
value in exchange, and includes donations of money, goods and services freely given without giving equal value in
exchange.
Income recognition
Income, whether from exchange or non exchange transactions, is recognised in the statement of financial activities
(SOFA) on a receivable basis, when a transaction or other event results in an increase in the charity's assets or a
reduction in its liabilities and only when the charity has legal entitlement, the income is probable and can be measured
reliably.
Income subject to terms and conditions which must be met before the charity is entitled to the resources is not
recognised until the conditions have been met.
All income is accounted for gross, before deducting any related fees or costs.
Donated goods, facilities and services
Donated fixed assets are recognised at the current fair value All such donations are recognised as donation income,
and debited to fixed assets.
Donated goods that are not fixed assets are accounted for at a fair value, unless it is impractical to reliably measure the
value of the donated items.
In the absence of any direct evidence of fair value of donated goods, then a value is derived from the cost of the item to
the donor or, in the case of goods that are expected to be sold, the estimated resale value after deducting any
anticipated costs of sales.
If it is impracticable to measure the fair value of goods donated for resale, or the costs of valuation outweigh the
benefits, the donated goods are recognised as income when sold, with an equivalent amount being recognised as an
expense.

Donated services and facilities (including seconded staff and use of property) are included in the accounts on the
basis of the value of the gift to the charity.
All donated services and facilities are recognised as donation income when received,(provided the value of the gift can
be measured reliably) and recognised as an expense with an equivalent value.
Membership subscriptions
The income and any associated Gift Aid or other tax refund from a membership subscription received by the charity in
the nature of a gift, is accounted for on the same basis as a donation.
The income from a membership subscription received by the charity where the subscription purchases the right to
services or benefits is recognised as income from charitable activities.
Policles relating to expenditure on goods and services provided to the charity.
Recognition of liabilities and expenditure
A liability, and the related expenditure, is recognised when a legal or constructive obligation exists as a result of a past
event, and when it is more likely than not that a transfer of economic benefits will be required in settlement, and when
the amount of the obligation can be measured or reliably estimated..
Liabilities arising from future funding commitments and constructive obligations, including performance related grants,
where the timing or the amount of the future expenditure required to settle the obligation are uncertain, give rise to a
provision in the accounts, which is reviewed at the accounting year end. The provision is increased to reflect any
increases in liabilities, and is decreased by the utilisation of any provision within the period, and reversed if any
provision is no longer required. These movements are charged or credited to the respective funds and activities to
which the provision relates.
Allocating costs to activities
Direct costs that are specifically related to an activity are allocated to that activity. Shared direct costs and support
costs are apportioned between activities.
The basis for apportionment, which is consistently applied, and proportionate to the circumstances, is '-
Staffing on the basis of time spent in connection with any particular activity.
Staffing on a per capita basis, based on the number of of people employed within any partiular activity.
Premises related costs on the proportion of floor area occupied by a particular activity.
Non specific support costs on the basis of the usage of resources, in terms of time taken, capacity used, request
made or other measures
Estimation techniques used in apportioning costs give details
Volunteers
In accordance with the SORP. and in recognition of the difficulties in placing a monetary value on the contribution from
volunteers, the contribution of volunteers is not included within the income of the charity.
However, the trustees value the significant contribution made to the activities of the charity by unpaid volunteers and

Trustees' report
The trustees, who are directors of the company, present their annualrepor and
the charity's financial statements for the year ended 30 April 2018.
Reference and Administrative details of the Charity, its trustees and advisers are
given on page 3
Structure, Governance and Management
Friends of Barnfield Estate Limited is a company limited by guarantee and
registered under the Companies Act 2006 and a registered charity. The liability of
members in the event of the charity being wound up is limited to f1 each.
Trustees who served during the year are as listed on page 3. There is provision
for a minimum number of four trustees on the Board of Directors, each of whom
is subject to annual re-election at the Annua General Meeting.
Trustees are recruited by a variety of methods including recommendations from
existing trustees. The individual who has been recommended is then interviewed
by the Chair and other trustees as appropriate and then elected by the board of
trustees. New trustees are inducted by the Chair and existing board members.
The trustees elect a Chair, a Vice Chair, a Secretary and a Treasurer from their
number.
The trustees are responsible for setting the strategic direction of the charity.
Objectives, activities and achievements
The objects of Friends of Bamfield Estate Limited as set out in its governing
document are to:
(a)
Maintain, improve or provide public amenities to residents of the Barnfield
Estate;
(b)
Protect or conserve the environment;
(c)
Provide recreational and community facilities for the public at large or
those who by reason of their youth, age or infirmity or disablement
financial hardship or social and economic circumstances, have need of
such facilities;
(d)
Promote advancement of education, training or retraining, particularly
among unemployed people, and providing unemployed people with work
experience;
(e)
Promote the relief of unemployment;
(f)
Promote public safety and prevent crime;
(g)
Promote and support healthy lifestyles.
Friends of Barnfield Estate Limited was set up to improve active participation of
tenants and residents in the provision of services on the Bamfield Estate to
support and facilitate an integrated voice and approach to all aspects of Bamfield
regeneration agenda.
Our aim is to help people who are at risk of social and economic exclusion in the
estate: One fundamental indicator of inclusion is participation in the world of
work. Friends of Barnfield Estate Limited is committed to taking people who want
to work and need to work on a journey to improve thelr prospects.
Page 4 of 26
To support our objectives, we have been working with our principal funders - Big
Local Trust, Royal Borough of Greenwich, and other stakeholders to develop the
resources we need to perform our activities.
Revlew of activities
During the year under review the charity has continued with organising
community building/cohesion activities including:
Coffee mornings and Tal Chi exercise on Tuesdays
Adults & Elderly Soclalising on Tuesdays
Youth evenings on Wednesdays and Thursdays
We are providing two Youth Sessions weekly each sessions provide
activities for different age group. This year the youth programme has
improved a lot and holds key events such as - How to tackle gang
and knife crime, various trips and team building activities. Weekly
football is one key activity that the youth engage with more. The
provision youth activities has helped bring young people together
within the Estate and provide opportunity for them to make friends,
interact with old and new friends within the community.
Mothers & Toddlers sessions on Thursday
Our Mothers and Toddlers' session continues to meet the needs of
many mothers who were at home with children. The session ensures
the children are encouraged to stay and play with toys, creative and
practical skills enhanced under the care of registered child minders in
the Barnfield Hub.
Saturday School for Primary and Secondary School Children
Barnfield Educationa Project continues to meet the provision of
quality education for our children. In Barnfield Estate and the wider
community. This project which was meant to be a homework club has
grown into a full supplementary school catering for over 50 children in
attendance every Saturday with some students registered on waiting
list.
The Saturday school enjoys strong partnership with Birkbeck
University of London and the London Museum. The Education Project
successfully organised a family learning event in February 2018 as
part of its intergenerationa learning programme. This event was
facilitated by Birkbeck University of London. Whilst at the Museum of
London, students had an opportunity to consider the effect global
warming to our city and how our city and environment could be
salvage through recycling and the use of eco-friendly power. They
took part in artwork where they were taught the techniques of
designing and making flower pots from recycling materials
The Saturday school conducted successful GCSEIA Level revision
classes during exams time. As a result of effective teaching and
support to our children in 2017/18, we recorded Sso many
achievements and good news through the Education Project. From
brilliant performance in the end of year assessment to fantastic scores
in SATs exams. From good grades in GCSE results to incredible
successes in A- Level exams. We rejolced in their achievement and
Page 5 of 26
celebrated their courage and resilient spirit. In true Barnfield style,
their courage and determination shone through. It's amazing to see
each and every child who attends. the Education Project every
Saturday performing better and better. The Saturday sohool has met
its alms and objectives.
Community social events/partles
Annual Barnfield Oommunity Day
We held our Annual Barnfield Community Day in September 2017 we
had a great turnout and the event was well received as usual. This
event was well attended by many residents in the community and
heartily took part in all the activities to celebrate the day despite the
cold weather.
Annual Trips
Over 300 residents came out with us to our annual trip to the
seaside. This event has greatly increased in number as it attracts
children, adults and the elderly for a day out of the house for fun and
relaxation amongst families and neighbours.
Christmas/End af Year Activities
Every December we have our Christmas Party and this is well
attended by children of all races. Last celebration was filled with
dancing, laughter, food and the presentation of gifts to all children
who attended.
Residents Meetings
We continue our monthly residents' meeting where many residents
attend to discuss issues that concerns us as a community like crimes,
drugs, environmental issues and safety in the community.
Counclllor's Surgery
We have a Councillor meet residents for a surgery on a monthly basis
in the Barnfield Hub to help residents address certain issues of
concerns.
Challenges
There was a deterloration of financial controls since September 2017 which
resulted in the poor financial practices such as retaining cash received for hiring
the premises, not banked in a timely manner, the weaknesses in the financial
controls left Trustees in a vulnerable position open to allegations and claims of
misconduct. The standards of record keeping since that period was also weak
and poor quallfy of reconciliations. There was an urgent need for immediate
action to re-instate proper financial coritrols to ensure that poor financial
practices are corrected.
After resignation of a few Trustees the Charity was without overall management
and direction and up until 6th December 2018, not effectively managed.
These operational constraints in the system were identified, they were openly
discussed with partners and all are being addressed and is being monitored.
The funding strategies were reviewed by the partners and stakeholders during
the year and a there was a greater need to ensure transparency at all times.
Page 6 of 26
Revlew of finances
The statement of financial activities shows that the charity received total income
of f71,529 in the financial year. Having expended a total of E68,034 on its
activities, the 23,495 surplus income arising from the reporting period, prior year
adjustment of f966 plus revenue funds of f108,294 brought forward from the
previous year meant the company ended the financial year with Revenue funds
of f112,755.
Assets
The company's assets held for its own use are stated at a total net book value of
E79,503 (2017: f90,867), made up of 10 Year Leasehold Property with following
net book values: E75,107 Improvement to Property 21,500; Plant & Machinery
2,408 and IT equipment f488. The Charity's main asset the "Barnfield Hub" is a
community resource centre built in March 2014, with funding of over f230,000
drawn down from the Big Local Trust's 10 years funding to the Bamfield
Community. The cost of the Hub was E126,941, this was managed by the
Barnfield Big Local Partnership and was transferred from the Barnfield Big Local
Partnership to Friends of Barnfield Estate Limited under the terms of reference
whereby Friends of Barnfield Estate Limited manages the Hub for the continuous
use of the community. The Hub's facilities include a function room/hall, an office,
a computer room together with a modern fitted kitchen and toilets. We use the
function room week days for the charity's activities; at week-ends the room is
hired by residents of the Estate for socia or other community activities. Modern
communication devises have been fitted; these include a land telephone line and
broadband The computer room is also operational as a training resource with
several high specification personal computers.
Trustees responsiblllties In relation to the financial statement
The trustees are required to prepare financial statements for each financial year,
which give a true and fair view of the state of affairs of the Charity and of its
incoming resources and application of resources, including the net income or
expenditure, for the year. In preparing those financial statements the trustees are
required to:
Select suitable accounting policies and then apply them
consistently;
Make judgements and estimates that are reasonable and prudent;
State whether applicable accounting standards and statements of
recommended practice have been followed subject to any
material departures disclosed and explained in the financial
statements; and
Prepare the financial statements on a going concern basis unless
it
is
inappropriate to presume that the charity will continue in
operation
The trustees are responsible for keeping proper accounting records which
disclose with reasonable accuracy at any time the financlal position of the Charity
and which enables them to ensure that the financial statements comply with the
Companies Act 2006. The trustees are also responsible for safeguarding the
assets of the Charity and hence for taking reasonable steps for the prevention
and detection of fraud and other irregularities.
Appolntment of trustees
At each annual genera meeting, all the members of the board of trustees shall
retire but all are eligible for re-election. Those longest in office shall retire first
Page 7 of 26
The make-up and number of the board of trustees may be varied but not reduced
below four. There are plans for recruiting new trustees to join the board of
trustees in due course.
Reporting Accountants
Impact Accountants have expressed their interest to continue in that capacity.
Approved by the trustees on 25 January 2019 and signed on their behalf by
John lbanga
Secretary

Examine the accounts under section 145 of the 2011 Act;
To follow the procedures laid down in the general Direction given by the
Charity Commission under section 145 (5) (b) of the 2011 Act; and
To state whether particular matters have come to my attention.
Basis of Independent examiner's report
My examination was carried out in accordance with the general Direction given
by the Charity Commission. An examination includes a review of the accounting
recorde kept by the Charity and a comparison of the accounts presented with
those records. It also includes consideration of any unusual items or disclosures
in the accounts, and seeking explanations from you as trustees conceming any
such matters. The procedures undertaken do not provide all the evidence that
would be required-t an audit-an consequently no opinion is given as to whether
the accounts present a "true and fair view and the report is limited to those
matters set out in the statement below.

(FRS102); or

drawn to gainwa proper understanding of the accounts.

Additional governance issues (Optional information)
The Charity Trustees are responsible for the general control and
management of the Charity. The Trustees give their time freely and
receive no remuneration or other financial benefits.
Where appropriate, trustees are granted maternity/paternity leave. A
trustee that has served in a particularly demanding role, e.g. as
Minister or Treasurer, may be granted a period of sabbatical leave.
The Minister, is a Trustee and is paid a reasonable salary with the
benefit of housing being provided thereby providing benefit for his
family.
The Trustees meet together as a body to deal with church business
monthly and formal Managing Trustees meetings take place
quarterly. All meetings are formally minuted. Trustees are
responsible for all decisions taken, and the activities provided by the
Charity.
To assist in the smooth running of the Charity the Trustees have set
up a number of sub-committees that help them oversee certain
aspects of the charity's work. These sub-committees report back
with their recommendations to the full meeting of the Trustees.
A church guide defines the ways of working of the charity - This
was adopted by the members at a meeting on th May 2012.
Upon appointment, all Trustees are made aware of the scope of
their responsibilities under the Charities Act with additional training
given if required. Trustees are given a copy of the Constitution and
a number of Publications from the Charity Commission are also
provided, including the guidance on charities and public benefit and
on the advancement of religion for the public benefit.
The Trustees have assessed the risks the Charity faces and have
conducted a formal risk analysis that identifies the major risks by
area of activity, the nature of those risks, the likelihood of the risks
happening and the measures taken to manage them. The Trustees
review the risks regularly at their meetings. In addition, the individual
sub-committees take responsibility for their area of risk, reviewing
this when they meet and reporting back at the full Trustees meeting.

Additional details of objectives and activities.
The charity carries out a wide range of activities in pursuance of its charitable aims. The Trustees
consider that these activities, summarised below, provide benefit both to those who worship at our
church and the charity carries out a wide range of activities in pursuance of its charitable aims. The
Trustees consider that these activities, summarised below, provide benefit, both to those who
worship at our church and wider communities of Redbourn, Harpenden, Luton and the wider area.
We want to be a Bible believing, gospel living, good news proclaiming, prayerfully dependent
church in order to share the good news of Jesus with the Redbourn community and beyond. We
can say that we have made a start, with God's help, and we are thankful to him for every individua
who has been touched by the Christians at ChristChurch Redbourn. Some have come to know
Jesus and his undeserved kindness for the first time, others have had a fledgling faith revitalized,
restored and strengthened and others have kept going, and served whole-heartedly.
All members of the church are encouraged to be involved, on a voluntary basis, in the church's
activities, sharing their faith and skills with others an 'all-member ministry'. Volunteers are an
important resource within the Church. AIl volunteers working with projects involving children or
other vulnerable groups are DBS checked.
Any grants of above 210000 are reviewed by the managing trustees for adherence to the objects of
the church. If in adherence the church members are asked to vote on the proposal.
Main Achievements and performance of the Charity during the year.
1. Sunday Service
Sunday mornings are the main meeting time and is a time for us to gather as a church family. We
have opportunity to praise God together, to pray together, to encourage one another, to gather
around the word of God together. We work hard to let the text of the Bible speak because what
God has to say is more important than the preacher's wisdom. Prayer is so important, so that God
would keep us humble as we gather, that God would give us ears to hear what the Spirit is saying
to the church through the living, enduring, powerful word of God.
Numbers of regular attenders is between 80-100 on a typical Sunday.
2. Homegroups
Christchurch has expanded the number of groups where the Bible is studied and prayer takes
place from 4 to 6 this year with the addition of another ladies group on Monday mornings and
second Tuesday evening group. Typically, 8-10 attend each of the groups.
This has been a helpful and informal way of studying the bible, through study and questions that
spring from the weekly Sunday sermons
TAR
4
June 2018
3. Munch & Natter
Munch 'N' Natter is our group for over 55s, which meets once a month, on a Friday, for lunch. We
currently have about 20 regular members who attend each month, although our membership list is
roughly 25. We run a 1.5 2 hour session which includes lunch, a quiz and a short talk based on a
passage from the Bible, and we regularly have themed lunches, which might also include other
activities such as a guest speaker, games or, in the summer months, perhaps a trip to a loca
garden centre. Our members are encouraged to bring friends or neighbours along, and at our
specia Christmas lunches, held early in December, we usually cater for around 35 people. Our
team is small, but helpers volunteer to join us on an occasional basis, so that we have time to
spend with our members, provide a welcoming atmosphere, and we can encourage everyone to
get to know each other and, hopefully, form friendships which can extend beyond Munch 'N'
Natter. Our team hopes that all who come will learn a little more about God's love for them, will
have fun, build friendships and be able to enjoy a tasty meal together.
4. Cutting Edge Men's Group
On the third Saturday morning of each month the two Cutting Edge men's Bible study groups
continue
to
meet
for
breakfast,
share
recent
experiences,
help
and
encourage
each
other,
while
studying the Bible and praying together. One of the significant features is the range of ages,
experiences and back grounds of those who attend.
There is a couple of additiona events or visiting speakers 3 times a year.
5. Training (Bible Teaching) evenings
Throughout the year we have sought to develop those involved in teaching the Bible. We have
been running training sessions for smal group Bible study leaders and those teaching the Bible to
children and young people. We have also held training sessions for those on our Pastoral Care
team. Alongside this, a number of 1:1 meetings happen, designed to see people trained and / or
growing in their faith.
6. Children Youth Activities
Sunday morning activities during the service
a. Creche
Creche runs every Sunday morning. We care for children from birth to 3 years old (nursery aged)
whilst their parents attend the morning service. During this time the babies/children have the
opportunity to play with toys, listen to stories and sometimes a craft activity. Occasionally we may
join up with the infant academy in the same room.
b. Infant Academy
A big thank you to all the children who come to our Infant Academy group on Sundays. The grown-
ups would be very lonely without you there each week! About nine of you come each week and you
help us learn stories from the Bible and get to know God better. Some of you like to make arty
crafty things and some of you like playing games. We like to hear what you have been doing in the
week as you chat away and it is good when we talk to Father God asking Him to help us with
something and to say thank you to Him for being our friend. The grown-ups in church like to pray
for us, let's hope they pray that we keep getting to know how special Jesus is and that they pray for
our families and friends too.
c. Junior Academy
Junior Academy is a group for children in school years 3-6. The aim of the group is to try and go
through a book of the Bible and understand what Christians believe based on that particular book.
The sessions are very varied, and include some discussion, some listening, some crafts, some
games (usually linked to the topic) and some reading. Recently we have been trying to follow the
same teaching that the main church is receiving so there's a mixture of Old Testament Narratives,
TAR
5
June 2018
New Testament Letters, and gospels. We try and vary what books we look at so that the children
get a broad understanding of the big picture of the whole bible as they're with us over 3 or so
years.
d. Sunday Access
Our Sunday group for 11-15 year olds has been following the same materia as the wider church.
The aim of the sessions is to teach the bible faithfully in a fun and effective way. The group runs on
alternating Sundays, which gives the opportunity for the teenagers to sit and learn with the adults
every other week to help them learn to get used to listening to longer talks.
7. Children and Youth Midweek groups
a. Starfish
Starfish Baby and Toddlers meets for two sessions on Thursday mornings, the first session is from
9.00-10.15am and the second is from 10.30-11.45am term time only. We have mums, dads,
grandparents and child-minders attending each week. Our sessions include free play, crafts,
singing
and the all-important drink and biscuits. Once a month we tell a Bible story which has been
very well received.
God has blessed Starfish in so many ways since it started 9 years ago, it is such a joy to see so
many people attending the sessions. At the Family Carol service, we see lots of parents,
grandparents, aunts and uncles all coming together to watch their loved ones performing in the
Nativity play. We also hold social events for the mums and carers who attend and this year we
hope to run another parenting course.
b. Daddy & Me
Daddy and me sessions are held twice a year, for Mother's Day and Christmas. The children enjoy
spending time with their Dad's making presents, cards and crafts for their mums. Some of the men
from CCR come along to welcome those dads from Starfish, bacon butties are always on offer
which go down well with everyone there. Praise God for the Dads who commit to come each time.
C. Illuminate
llluminate continues to be a place where children in school years Reception to 6 can come along
for games, crafts and to learn more about the bible and about what Christians believe. Every week
they arrive and have some free play in the church building. We then join together for activities
altogether. These vary from week to week, ranging from games, challenges, crafts and trying out
new things. We then spend some time together listening to a bible talk where they can learn about
Christianity. Often there is time for more activities or more free play afterwards, and at the end of
the session we sometimes wrap up with some singing altogether.
Recently we've been thinking about the book of Isaiah, and before that we spent time looking at the
Reformation and the core statements that came from that about Christian doctrine.
d. Fish Tank
Fish Tank is a youth group that runs every Sunday in term time from 7-8.30pm for school years 7-
13. The session includes games, activities, Bible teaching and snacks/drinks. We aim to be a place
where the teenagers can feel comfortable and cared for, which has been hugely improved since the
addition of 2 extra leaders onto the team. The children are always encouraged to bring friends with
them. At the moment we see about 8-10 children who regularly attend.
e. Ignite CU
Ignite is a Christian Union at Roundwood Park Secondary School run by a teacher there. Mike, the
youth worker at CCR, supports this group by attending each week, joining in with the games and
bringing a short talk on what Christians believe for those who come along. We've spent time
TAR
6
June 2018
looking in the book of Judges recently, as well as tackling some of their questions about
Christianity.
The group sees about 20 teenagers coming each week, and although anyone is welcome, at the
moment all of the attendees are younger boys! Some of the teachers in the school are quite
appreciative that we put something energetic on for them to do, as otherwise all that energy will be
spent, perhaps more mischievously, elsewhere!
Youth work
Our youth worker also regularly meets teenagers who want to discuss things further about
Christianity. These can be 121 or in slightly bigger groups. They are always done in public places
and
with parents' permission, and although time is limited, anyone is welcome to ask. They are an
opportunity for more teaching on the bible and what Christians believe, or for pastoral discussions,
but this is mainly decided by what the teenager wants from the group and what they are
comfortable with.
8. Evangelism
Christmas was a time with many opportunities to engage our community from Carol Services, to
the Redbourn Christmas Market and a few one-off events. We also held a Big Summer Bash, to
which all connected to CCR were invited, along with the Redbourn community.
We held a men's breakfast with ChristChurch Harpenden with a guest speaker sharing his life story
and the part played by faith in Christ. Similarly, we have held a meal-based event at a local
Redbourn pub for men with a speaker.
All of our regular activities involve making the good news about Jesus known to our community.
9. Mission outside Redbourn.
CCR's vision is to develop and encourage folks in the CCR congregation to serve outside the
Redbourn area. The mission team's role is to support, encourage and nurture these activities.
This year a team of 5 people went to Konjic in Bosnia to support a small missionary team there, the
church is now supporting this mission with regular financial support.
Further visits are planned during 2018 to develop the partnership.
Short term plans include encouraging short-term mission: during school / university holidays;
visiting mission activities in other parts of the world such as Malawi; encouraging those returning on
furlough from the mission field as we did year with Jonathan and Rache Morgan who have until
recently been serving in Tanzania.
As part of our mission closer to home the church now supports Luke Larner to work with the town
centre chaplaincy, the Good Shepherd church plant and NOAH charity in Luton.
We have a number of overseas missionaries associated with us that we support on an ad hoc basis
and also individua members have many links.
Plans for the future
Priorities, Training and Growth In the future we are considering how to make better use of our
TAR

June 2018
church building for the good of the local community and to further the aims of the church. This will
be a big focus for 2018.
In addition to our future plans, it is our aim to maintain all our current activities, developing and
expanding these, as and when opportunities arise and there are available resources to undertake
these. We also plan to maintain all our existing activities that are open to or are undertaken in, the
local community.
We are committed to maintaining support for the missionaries and mission organisations that we
are linked to. This support will continue to be in the form of finance and in practical ways such as
teams being sent out to undertake voluntary work with the missionaries.

Treasurer's Report
1st April 2013 to 31st March 2014
The 2013/14 financial year has passed with The Old School House Nursery
achieving a huge amount for our children on the tight budget we have to
work with.
It was a challenging financial year which has seen an overall loss made this
year of f3845.21. This is at a time where SO much has been achieved in
difficult circumstances despite the loss this financia year.
The nursery bank accounts at the end of this financia year are as follows
as at 315 March 2014 bank account f12070.26 and deposit account
f7025.08.
We have been in a similar situation this year to other recent yearswhere
we now see children moving on to primary school much earlier, leaving
nursery numbers low from the end of the summer term. This issue has
been tackled from a number of directions this year as there are obvious
cost implications.
Staff levels were reduced when numbers were very low. With lots of hard
work from staff, nursery was able to remain open for its normal session
times with no closure of sessions. Huge efforts were put in to encourage
interest from new families, to increase our numbers.
It was also decided to increase the hourly fee from f4 to f4.50 in Apri
2014. This should increase fee income for the next financia year. At the
same time costs for staff wages have increased with a rise in the minimum
wage paid to a number of our staff.

As a committee we made the decision that marketing The Old School
House Nursery was important this year to attract new families. We
invested in local media advertising in parish newspapers and magazines, as
wel as a new and improved website, with thanks to Clare Butler. These
have been costly, however vital in trying to attract new families.
Numbers have increased slowly throughout the financial year and it is vital
that this increase in numbers continue as we again loose children to
primary school this summer.
If I can quantify the 'loss' this year, it has been effected by changes to
grant funding. Nursery were warned about changes to funding earlier in
the financial year. Committee members and nursery staff met with Suffolk
County Council staff to discuss the shortfal and sustainability.
This financial year nursery received over f10,000 less in grant funding
compared with the previous financia year and with a general lack of
funding from other sources, such as the sustainability funding that
previous financial years have benefited from, income has been limited.
I feel that the staff and committee have negotiated this difficult time well
and have been able to provide a fantastic nursery experience for our
children day in day out.
It is of note that with grant funding received, nursery provides eligible
parents with childcare for up to 15 hours per week free of charge. The
hourly fee for nursery is now f4.50, nursery receives for each grant funded
hour E3.70 for three and four year old funded places and f4 per hour of 2
year old funded places.
In another area where we have tried to increase income and at the same
time provide a better service to our families, nursery now offers extended
hours at the beginning and end of the nursery day and the newly
